items.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
items.summary: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.

scraped.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
scraped.description: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.
scraped.h1: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
scraped.body_text:
German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU , want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.

It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria 's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.

But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel , the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.

DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.

On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.

If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.

Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.

She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier , a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.

The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats ( SPD ), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.

"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.

A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.

It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.

Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.

The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.

Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.

This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.

items.title: Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough
items.summary: Several Republicans sought to distance themselves from Donald Trump's trade war during the midterms, in some cases asking for specific tariffs to be rolled back. Even so, Republicans lost. Democrats, who were traditionally the party of protectionism, appear to have been pushed into a more pro-free trade stance, and appear ready to try to reach a deal with Republicans.

scraped.title: ANALYSIS | Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough | CBC News
scraped.description: Several Republicans sought to distance themselves from Donald Trump's trade war during the midterms, in some cases asking for specific tariffs to be rolled back. Even so, Republicans lost. Democrats, who were traditionally the party of protectionism, appear to have been pushed into a more pro-free trade stance, and appear ready to try to reach a deal with Republicans.
scraped.h1: Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough
scraped.body_text:
When wildfires were burning across Canada in July, and the smoke was blowing into the United States, Michigan's Mike Rogers was among those demanding punishment.

The now defeated Republican candidate for Senate, echoing U.S. President Donald Trump, said Canada should pay more, on top of the current tariffs, to cover the cost of that pollution.

"Canada must be held accountable for endangering Americans, and I will work with your administration to ensure they are!," he wrote on X , in a reply to Trump.

Rogers had, separately, enthused about the tariffs — telling Fox News they were "really positive" for the U.S. and that it was "absolutely unacceptable" for Canada to be selling cars into his border state.

Fast forward three months and Rogers — struggling in the race for Senate — tried to cast himself as a friend of Canada.

While drinking a Labatt Blue and alluding to hockey, he called for an end to the tariffs in an ad posted four weeks ago.

"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," he said.

A man votes in the primary election at Northwestern High School in Detroit, on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)

It was one of many examples of Republicans trying to distance themselves from Trump's trade war and anti-Canadian rhetoric.

Now, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal, the Democrats are hoping to use Republican discomfort with the cross-border trade war to end tariffs on Canada.

"There is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada," Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, told the WSJ on Wednesday.

Wyden and other Democrats believed they might be able to flip enough Republicans against Trump on the issue to override a veto, the Journal reported. That would likely require persuading about 30 to 35 Republican House members, and 11 to 13 Republican senators, the precise number depending on votes yet to be tallied from Tuesday's elections.

The new House and Senate will be seated on Jan. 3, just two days after punishing 50 per cent tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel are scheduled to take effect.

Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers in Michigan, told the MS Now morning show on Thursday he was keen to work to lift the "stupid tariffs on Canada," and later told CNN that ending Trump's "vanity trade war" was a legislative priority for him in Washington.

"There is no economic reason why we are having a tariff war with our biggest trading partner. This has to end."

That seems to be one of the lessons American politicians will take from the 2026 midterm elections, perhaps with lasting and positive effects for Canada.

From the early days of Trump's second term, Americans have shown very little interest in picking fights with Canada. Although Trump's verbal attacks on Canada were a staple at rallies throughout October, the issue again failed to catch fire within the MAGA coalition.

Exit polls on Tuesday, according to CNN, found that two-thirds of American voters believed tariffs had hurt both the national and their local economies.

What the historic Democrat midterm surge means for Canada

The tariffs were widely seen as having combined with the Iran war to create a double price shock.

Rural America has been hit especially hard by the spike in diesel, which contributed to higher costs for fertilizer. All of the eight main fertilizers used by U.S. farmers cost more than they did a year ago, according to one industry analysis.

Those numbers were key to the massive hemorrhaging of Republican votes in red states such as Kansas.

In two critical Senate races in Maine and Kansas, Republican candidates appealed directly to Trump to cancel or reconsider specific trade actions against Canada in order to avoid harming voters in their states (and therefore their campaigns).

In Maine, Susan Collins first asked him to drop tariffs on road salt, warning that they would dramatically increase costs for small municipalities, which might then have to raise property taxes. Trump complied.

Later, Trump lifted tariffs on about $5.1 billion US worth of goods to help her. (He replaced them with new tariffs on other goods , although for only about half the monetary value.)

Trump's reversals weren't enough to save Collins. Her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson gave his victory speech wearing a button that said "We can't eat road salt!"

Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas speaks at a campaign event for Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Grosse Pointe Woods, Mich., on Oct. 28. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall asked Trump not to proceed with actions against Montreal-based Bombardier, which makes jets in Wichita. Again, Trump complied , but Marshall lost anyway.

Several Republicans mentioned tariffs in post-mortems of the midterm rout.

"Tragically, we alienated rural America," said Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas , who was not up for re-election but saw his junior counterpart lose to Democrat James Talarico. The state's governor also lost to a Democrat.

"Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long."

Cruz blamed the rout, in order, on the high cost of living, corruption, the cost of the war, sub-par candidates and the trade war with Canada.

The tariffs were, meanwhile, a topic of victory speeches in some of the biggest races.

"I will fight to end these chaotic tariffs," said senator-elect Josh Turek after his upset victory in Iowa.

Midterms ‘bluenami’: The exact moment Trump lost control of Congress | About That

Ohio senator-elect Sherrod Brown, famous for opposing NAFTA, said the same.

The success of the affordability message seemed to position Democrats as hard-core free-traders in a way they might not have otherwise been.

"The tariffs are ruining everything," became a kind of slogan for Talarico, who made a video at the Texas State Fair in which he blamed the price of fried Oreos and funnel cake on tariffs.

Tariffs were even an issue down in Mississippi, where underdog Scott Colom accused incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith of going along with them. (That race still hasn't been called.)

Canada is Mississippi's biggest export market , and Colom's region is home to the state's furniture industry, which normally ships about $34 million US worth of kitchen cabinets, bedding and other furniture to Canada annually.

Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party on Tuesday, in Jackson, Miss. (Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today/The Associated Press)

Not only has the cost of framing a sofa or recliner increased because of tariffs on Canadian lumber, but the furniture now also faces a 50 per cent counter-tariff.

And while Mississippi has its own forestry industry, it depends on specialized logging machinery, much of it imported from Canada and also subject to tariffs.

Colom vowed to local media, if elected, that his first job would be to "get the tariff policy back to Congress."

The tariffs "are not working," he repeated in his election-night speech.

Canada's softwood lumber industry might see some irony in the fact that its old nemesis, Wyden, is likely to lead the charge for free trade with Canada. (He's expected to chair the Senate finance committee.)

Wyden is a lumber hardliner who has butted heads with Canada for years, but more recently his positions have reflected a trend seen across the party. The success of the affordability message, linking high costs directly to tariffs and war, has strengthened a previously lukewarm commitment to free trade.

What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

Ohio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028

Elon Musk gets little bang for his buck in U.S. midterms, with possible Democratic investigations to come

Wyden has opposed all of Trump's tariffs on Canada, calling them a "shakedown" and a "reckless abuse."

He says his fellow Democrats plan to "reassert congressional authority" over U.S. trade policy and roll back tariffs Trump instituted under various emergency authorities — good news for Canada.

But perhaps the best news for Canada from the midterms is that politicians in both parties appear to have concluded that tariffs on Canada cost votes, and that opposing them is good politics.

Senior Reporter

Evan Dyer has been a journalist with CBC for 25 years, after an early career as a freelancer in Argentina. He works in the Parliamentary Bureau and can be reached at evan.dyer@cbc.ca.

items.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
items.summary: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations.

scraped.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms | CBC News
scraped.description: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations.
scraped.h1: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
scraped.body_text:
A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations to conduct security sweeps.

No explosives have been found, and the threats have so far proved unfounded. But the spate of hoaxes that affected a number of flights, airports and, as of Friday, news broadcasters has raised concern over the widening impact if the threats continue to spread.

It's not yet clear if the incidents are linked, but the bomb threat hoaxes come on the heels of other European disruptions, including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions .

Here is what we know about the hoaxes targeting airlines and broadcasters in Europe.

What appeared to be a co-ordinated wave of bomb threats targeting European air traffic began on Tuesday.

At least seven flights and a cruise ship received hoax bomb threats , triggering emergency landings, fighter jet escorts and temporary airport closures in countries including Poland, Bulgaria, Italy and Spain.

A second wave was reported on Thursday, with at least 27 flights affected .

Bomb threats force multiple flights in Europe to make emergency landings

On Friday, Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain.

Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov" claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.

The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices and suspended programming, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.

The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.

Reuters was not able to establish the identity of the sender, the origin of the emails or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any or all of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday.

Garda members work outside the offices of Irish National broadcaster RTE on Friday after staff were evacuated from the site following a bomb threat. The broadcaster has claimed the bomb threat is from the same group that has been behind a wave of bomb threats issued to passenger flights around Europe this week. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)

Bomb threats against planes are often communicated to airlines, airports or authorities through anonymous emails or phone calls claiming that an explosive device is on board. Authorities do not always disclose how threats are delivered, because doing so could encourage copycats and compromise investigations.

A Prague airport representative told CNN on Thursday that they had received a threat from an anonymous email addressed to the airport, and Czech police said similar emails went to other European airports.

Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, told Reuters that an airline's security department first runs the report through a checklist. It then alerts the authorities, who may scramble fighter jets or divert the plane to a designated airport for a full sweep.

The vast majority of bomb threats turn out to be false alarms, though all must be treated as real until investigated, which means authorities are forced to scramble to rule out any danger.

No explosive device has been found on the planes affected this week, but every airline must decide whether a threat is credible and act accordingly.

A spokesperson for the British government called this week's incidents "malicious hoax threats" and said it has "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world."

String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe

Bomb threats affect at least 27 flights, leading to emergency landings at several European airports

Airlines are not new to bomb threats, but aviation security experts say the apparent co-ordination and timing of the current incidents is unusual.

All planes, including those threatened on Friday, landed safely.

Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government.

The incidents come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of a campaign of "hybrid" or "grey zone" disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easy to deny and not expected to trigger an armed response.

Countries affected by the disruptions, including Denmark, Poland and ​Romania, have previously accused Moscow. Russia denies any involvement.

An EasyJet aircraft takes off at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan purporting to be from "fighters of the Male State," a far-right anti-feminist movement banned in Russia.

Reuters could not confirm who had sent the email. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up Male State in 2016, said it no longer existed and was not involved in any way.

Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said bomb threats can stem from a wide range of motives, including political grievances, activist campaigns, criminal activity, online groups or state-linked hybrid operations.

European technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen says that since 2022, Europe had faced a range of hybrid operations, including sabotage of critical infrastructure, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference.

“We are under attack all the time,” she told Reuters. “The reason behind these operations is to destabilize our societies and create mistrust among our citizens.”

“It’s not always Russia who is behind different hybrid operations. Quite often, it is Russia.”

Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority.

Even a false alarm can disrupt airlines' operations, with plane diversions and thorough security inspections causing delays for passengers. Carriers typically bear additional costs including fuel, passenger rebooking, crew disruption and aircraft diversions.

Schouten said a sweep means unloading passengers and baggage, searching the aircraft and reloading. That can push crews past duty limits and lead to missed connections and cancellations.

People gather outside the offices of Irish national broadcaster RTE as officials conduct a security sweep after a reported bomb threat on Friday. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)

Air France-KLM chief executive Ben Smith said on Thursday he had never previously seen threats reported in such a co-ordinated fashion.

"We're quite confident that we have in place what we need to ensure that it has minimal or no impact on our operation," Smith told reporters. "So we have no ask today of our governments to change the way they manage these types of situations."

Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice-president of the European Cockpit Association.

Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.

Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."

items.title: Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
items.summary: Thomas Markle, the father of Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, said the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

scraped.title: Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material | CBC News
scraped.description: Thomas Markle, the father of Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, said the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
scraped.h1: Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
scraped.body_text:
WARNING: This article contains details of abuse.

The father of Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by U.S. federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material.

Thomas Wayne Markle, 82, of Lakeland, Fla., is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for Central District of California.

In a statement, it said Markle was arrested on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

It says agents seized approximately 78 items, including two images that depict an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle — with a nude prepubescent girl.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," said FBI Director Kash Patel in a statement, indicating the FBI is still investigating this matter.

Patel also thanked FBI partners in Mexico, Manila and the Marshall Islands law enforcement attachés, who aided the investigation.

This image taken on Sunday shows the entrance to a storage facility where Mexican authorities seized a storage unit with belongings of Thomas Markle during a search for alleged child sexual abuse material, on the outskirts of Tijuana, Mexico. (Guillermo Arias/AFP/Getty Images)

The statement from the U.S. Attorney's Office appears to confirm reports by the Sun, a British tabloid, that Meghan's half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father's home in the Philippines.

"According to an affidavit filed with the complaint, in October 2026, law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding their discovery of suspected [child sexual abuse material] among Markle's possessions in the Philippines," the statement said. "Information from the first individual later led agents to a second unit."

Philippine Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla told reporters on Friday that Thomas Markle Jr. is also being investigated.

"We have a witness saying that underage girls were being brought to his house and we're following it up. We are looking into whether the 60-year-old son, Thomas Markle Jr., was involved in the crime," said Remulla. "To accuse the father is only half the police work."

Thomas Markle Sr. was not at his daughter Meghan's wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

There was no immediate comment from Meghan's representatives on Friday.

Meghan Markle recently said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."

Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama Suits , married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.

Thomas Markle is expected to appear in a Tampa court on Friday.

If convicted, he would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

If you're in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database . ​​

items.summary: An endangered species is returning home months after bushfires destroyed its habitat. An alpine spiny crayfish prepares to be released back into the wild.

scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/erin-somerville/8295700
scraped.h1: Endangered crayfish rescued from Victorian bushfires by conservationists returned home
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: Endangered and Protected Species

An alpine spiny crayfish prepares to be released back into the wild. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

An endangered crayfish species was rescued after bushfires in January tore through Victoria's High Country.

Some are now returning home after months in captivity.

Conservationists expect more species will need rescuing after bushfires amid climate change.

In a rugged corner of Victoria's High Country, two scientists are making their way slowly through fire-scarred bushland that is slowly returning to life.

They are travelling with precious cargo: a group of endangered alpine spiny crayfish that are heading back to their home waterway near Lucyvale.

Tree canopy is recovering at Lucyvale after 2026 bushfires. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

The scientists were here in the immediate aftermath of the January bushfires that tore through the region, and they salvaged 11 endangered crayfish that were at risk of suffocating in the stream from debris and sediment.

The alpine spiny crayfish are restricted in their movement and found in small, isolated pockets that make it tricky for scientists to find, adding to the pressure of rescue efforts as water quality declines after a fire.

"If they aren't rescued they can disappear from these areas," Arthur Rylah Institute senior scientist Will Sowersby said.

Scientists prepare to capture alpine spiny crayfish. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

The alpine spiny crayfish were taken to the Snobs Creek conservation hatchery, which is run by the Victorian Fisheries Authority near Eildon, where they were cared for until water quality improved post-bushfires.

It is the first time the endangered species has been taken into captivity, and it proved a learning curve for staff.

"It's a new process for us," Snobs Creek's senior conservation hatchery officer Dylan White said.

"They are a bit feisty so we have had to separate them, and we have kept them separate this whole time because they will attack each other."

Spiny crayfish being weighed at Snobs Creek hatchery. ( ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf )

As the Victorian High Country starts to spring back to life from the Walwa-River Road bushfire that burnt around 121,000 hectares, scientists are continuing to monitor the alpine spiny crayfish's habitat and ponder their future.

Conservationists hope the endangered crayfish can be included in a future captive breeding program at the Snobs Creek hatchery to help bolster numbers and geographical diversity.

But with another summer on the horizon, Mr Sowersby predicts their work is far from over.

"We know that bushfires are increasing in their frequency and their intensity, so we suspect it's going to be more and more important that we rescue species post-bushfire and that we also establish new populations to (prevent) the risk of an extinction event due to a catastrophic fire," he said.

Topic: Environmental Impacts

Topic: Environmental Impacts

Topic: Crop Harvesting

Topic: Missing Person

Topic: Police

It has been a busy year for Snobs Creek hatchery staff who carry out important conservation work with vulnerable species, especially after natural disasters.

Dylan White is surrounded by rare species at the hatchery. ( ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf )

"Most of these species we have here are so critically endangered they have never been kept in captivity before, so it's really new for everyone," Mr White said.

"The important thing is we are experienced and we are putting that knowledge and skill set towards caring for them and learning more about them."

Some of the species at the facility are found nowhere else in the world.

That includes a special type of galaxias fish that only exists in a sole tributary of the La Trobe River after experiencing a major population collapse in the past decade, and the critically endangered blackfish that were rescued after bushfires tore through the Grampians region.

A blackfish at Snobs Creek hatchery. ( ABC News: Andrew Mangesldorf )

Some species rescued after Victoria's summer bushfires have already been re-released, including more than 100 Macquarie perch and trout cod taken from Seven Creek after the Longwood bushfire.

"It was quite challenging to look after a large number of trout cod at the same time due to their aggressive nature …took up a lot of space," Snobs Creek head of fish production Chris Mullins said.

The species' stay at the facility can be hard work for staff, who have to manage unique diets, water temperature, lighting, and behavioural issues.

Scientists comb an alpine stream for endangered species. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

With Australia predicted to face more natural disaster as climate change progresses, staff value the significance of the hatchery.

"Every year (natural disasters) seems to be getting more and more, so we have got to have a facility here that we can take some of these species as quickly as we can," Mr White said.

"If we weren't doing it no one would be."

items.summary: In a social media post, US President Donald Trump says his chief of staff will leave her post on Monday, less than a week after his Republican Party's disastrous midterm election performance. Donald Trump is expected to make changes after the midterms disaster.

Topic: World Politics

Donald Trump is expected to make changes after the midterms disaster. ( AP: Alex Brandon )

Donald Trump has announced that his chief of staff Susie Wiles will be replaced by her hardline deputy Stephen Miller on Monday.

The US President made the announcement on Friday, local time, in a social media post.

Mr Trump thanked Ms Wiles for doing an "outstanding job" and said she would move to a different role in his "political operation".

In reality, the switch sidelines one of his most senior staff members.

"I want to thank her for her service as chief of staff," Mr Trump's post read. "She has done a great job!"

Analysts have widely speculated Mr Trump will reshuffle his administration after his Republican Party's disastrous performance at this week's midterm elections.

In March, Ms Wiles announced she would be taking time away from her role after being diagnosed with breast cancer.

Topic: World Politics

Topic: World Politics

Topic: US Elections

Topic: US Elections

Analysis by Cam Wilson

Analysts have told the ABC they believe Mr Trump's administration lost its way after Ms Wiles's health battle began.

"Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime," Ms Wiles said in a social media post on Friday, local time.

"I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First."

Mr Miller is best known as the architect of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

The 41-year-old has long helped shape immigration policy in the GOP.

He was Mr Trump's chief immigration advisor during the president's first term.

Before that, Mr Miller worked for Senator Jeff Sessions, who was renowned as one of the chamber's loudest and most uncompromising voices on the subject.

Most recently, Mr Miller has driven the push for mass deportations, pressing ICE leadership to raise arrest numbers and publicly telling officers they would have "federal immunity in the conduct of your duties".

items.title: Convicted rapist Brand facing at least four more investigations
items.summary: From Neil Diamond hits to explosive hallway conversations that prompted a top lawyer to report himself to the bar standards, Russell Brand's trial was a show in itself. British actor and comedian Russell Brand is behind bars this weekend after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

scraped.title: Convicted rapist Brand facing at least four more investigations
scraped.description: From Neil Diamond hits to explosive hallway conversations that prompted a top lawyer to report himself to the bar standards, Russell Brand's trial was a show in itself.
scraped.h1: Convicted rapist Brand facing at least four more investigations after trial
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: Courts

British actor and comedian Russell Brand is behind bars this weekend after being convicted of rape and sexual assault. ( Reuters: Toby Shepheard )

If Russell Brand was at all worried about being found guilty in his four-week rape and sexual assault trial, he was not showing it.

I was standing a few people behind the British actor and comedian in the queue for security checks outside London's Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, when he broke briefly into song.

"Sweet Caroline," he sang to a woman beside him in the line, quoting the famous Neil Diamond hit.

The woman had introduced herself to the star as Caroline, and the pair chatted jovially while waiting to move forward.

Inside court, just minutes later, the jury began its second day of deliberations.

On other mornings, as Brand was greeted at court by a flurry of camera flashes, journalists asked how he was feeling.

"Blessed," was always the reply.

Throughout the trial, the comedian-turned-born-again Christian influencer continued to make social media videos with his wife, Laura, for their millions of followers.

As the court heard harrowing, graphic and often tearful accounts from Brand's six accusers, he did not flinch.

When he gave evidence himself, he did so standing up unnaturally straight.

Russell Brand giving evidence during his trial. ( Reuters: Julia Quenzler )

At crunch time — when the guilty verdicts were read out on Thursday — the comedian stood to attention like a soldier on parade and showed no emotion.

When his lawyer applied for bail ahead of sentencing on Monday, he said his client wanted time to say goodbye to his wife and three children over the weekend.

Outside court and in, this was a defendant who did not seem to think he would go to jail.

British newspapers cover the opening of Russell Brand's sexual assault trial. ( ABC News: Alex Parsons )

Brand has been on trial since mid-October for seven historical sex offences relating to six women spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009.

After eight and a half hours of deliberations, the jury of four women and eight men found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

He was acquitted of a further two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

British actor and comedian Russell Brand arrived at court with his wife Laura on Thursday before he was remanded in custody. ( Reuters: Maja Smiejkowska )

On the steps of Southwark Crown Court afterwards, police praised the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination" of the women, while pulling no punches about Brand.

"Russell Brand used his influence, status, and fame to prey on and exploit women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement," Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from London's Metropolitan Police Service, said.

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his house in 2009. ( Supplied: Metropolitan Police )

During the trial, journalists could only report what was said and done in front of the jury, but with verdicts returned and restrictions lifted, we can now give more detail from one of the most high-profile criminal trials in recent British history.

Brand is no longer a mainstream comedian and actor, and instead styles himself as a Christian influencer, broadcasting online prayer videos and sermons to millions.

His faith was on full public display from day one of the trial. When he was first shown into the dock before jury selection, he went down on one knee and appeared to pray.

British actor and comedian Russell Brand arriving at Southwark Crown Court during the third week of his trial. ( Reuters: Hannah McKay )

During the trial he wore crucifixes of different sizes, he sometimes carried a bible with sticky notes marking pages, and at least one day he was handling what looked like prayer beads.

Unusually for a defendant in a criminal trial, he posted repeatedly on social media — not about the evidence but about his feelings, his faith, and his disdain for the mainstream media.

It can now be reported that Brand's legal team tried to have the case thrown out, before the trial had even begun because of negative press about him.

Russell Brand told the court he did not commit the crimes and believed sexual consent was "fundamental, essential, necessary" and "more important than sex itself".

Barrister Ian Winter KC argued his client could not receive a fair trial because of 2023 media reports with allegations about Brand — allegations that prompted the women who would ultimately be the complainants in this trial to come forward.

Mr Winter's application was denied, but he would go on to say during the trial that the 2023 reporting had "poisoned the well".

The 2023 allegations in the media were not part of the trial.

In an extraordinary moment in the corridor at the end of proceedings, Mr Winter launched a tirade at Sunday Times Chief News Correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who worked on the 2023 investigation.

“I hope you are pleased with yourself,” Mr Winter said.

Ms Urwin responded that she was “pleased justice has been done".

Mr Winter replied, “well, it wasn’t. You f***** it. Congratulations".

On Friday the top silk reported himself to the Bar Standards Board over the exchange.

Photographers greeted British actor and comedian Russell Brand and his wife Laura at court every day of the trial. ( Reuters: Toby Melville )

There were other moments of courtroom drama during the trial.

On day one, lawyers for People Magazine in the US were hauled before Judge Joel Bennathan to explain why the magazine had reported the attempt to have the case thrown out, when a court order had been made to keep that out of the public domain.

Judge Bennathan then put journalists in court and beyond on notice that he would not be lenient if there were further contempt of court risks.

Another day, police arrested a blogger who had identified one of Brand's accusers, all of whom are granted lifelong anonymity by the court.

The man, who had been sitting in the spillover court watching proceedings on a large video screen, was detained for 12 hours, cautioned, and forced to amend his blog posts.

There are more allegations about Brand that we can now report too.

Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mark Rowley said more accusors were likely to come forward. ( Reuters: Chris J. Ratcliffe )

The Metropolitan Police revealed its detectives are currently investigating allegations of rape from two more women in the UK, while there are two civil claims afoot against Brand relating to his time in the US.

The head of Scotland Yard Sir Mark Rowley has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations. He has appealed for them to do so.

Brand, meanwhile, is spending his first weekend behind bars.

Judge Bennathan denied his bail application saying that while he regrets the impact on the 51-year-old's children, their father had the resources to be a flight risk.

The verdict marks a massive fall from grace for the entertainer; once a swaggering exhibitionist performing to huge crowds, now a convicted rapist in a prison cell.

Russell Brand during one of his police interviews. ( Supplied: Metropolitan Police )

For the rape and three sexual assaults he was found guilty of this week, Brand will be sentenced on Monday.

The judge has already flagged the rape conviction alone will mean a "significant custodial sentence".

It’s currently marked down to $255 at various retailers, including Amazon , Guitar Center , and directly from Shure . If you don’t already have a stand, both Amazon and Shure are offering a bundle that includes the mic and a desktop stand for $269, and the white model is also discounted at Amazon .

When our team shared some of our favorite audio gear in late 2024 , we noted that the Mv7 Plus was the mic we send to podcast guests for remote interviews. It’s known for its crisp and clean audio quality, with auto-leveling and denoising, so you can use it without touching an equalizer.

The MV7’s unique shape and sonic profile is inspired by the Shure SM7B ( also discounted ), a microphone that’s often used in professional recording. See All by Justine Calma

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Justine Calma

A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.

With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.

“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge . “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”

The bill sacrifices caution for speed

The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls : rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities .

“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge .

Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.

The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.

The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.

“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”

If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center . Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.

Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”

The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.

The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.

The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.

Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action .

“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”

They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.

“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”

Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release .

“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.

Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.

“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.

Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.

BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.

Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future . Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group . The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.

One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.

The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.

Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.

Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.

The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge . They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within its Muse AI assistant. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows Muse to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the app.

If you connect your space to a relevant app, Muse will update pricing, dates, and other information in the background. Meta says you can create a new space by describing it, and continue to tweak it by asking Muse. You can also interact with your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.

You can add spaces to the sidebar in the Muse app, move them into your main tab, as well as schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.

Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users, along with a “specialized” version of its Muse Wonder AI model. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.

scraped.h1: The folks behind John Wick are back with Karōshi trailer
scraped.body_text:
Stuntman/director Chad Stahelski and 87Eleven bring us an action-packed dystopian, futuristic thriller.

Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. It’s called Karōshi (a Japanese term that means “death overwork”), and Lionsgate released a killer trailer that puts this film at the top of my list of “must see” movies of 2027.

Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden, where some 700 workers die each year from overwork. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide ( karōjisatsu in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise:

Karōshi is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface.

Teo Yoo ( Past Lives ) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries Shōgun , as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.

The trailer opens with Hira’s character lauding the contribution of Ikigai Technologies in helping shape “modern life for millions,” adding praise for employees’ “daily commitment and sacrifice.” Then we see one distraught worker deliberately falling backward to his death from the top of the company’s skyscraper. Enter our protagonist, Hiro, who suspects something more sinister is going on behind the company’s embrace of the samurai path, marked by “integrity” and “honor”—and also violence.

It’s not long before Hiro is battling all kinds of opponents in fine Wickian fashion, including using a paper umbrella to shield himself from the blood spurting from the neck of an opponent he’s just killed—a clever flourish. John Wick would be proud.

Karōshi hits theaters on February 5, 2027.

scraped.title: You know the launch market is tough when satellite companies start building rockets
scraped.description: The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market."
scraped.h1: You know the launch market is tough when satellite companies start building rockets
scraped.body_text:
“The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market.”

There are optimistic plans for spaceflight, and then there are optimistic plans.

AST SpaceMobile is a Texas-based, publicly traded company building very large satellites to provide direct-to-cell communications on Earth. But it has been having trouble finding rides to space. So on Friday, AST announced that it is developing a medium-lift rocket, named Blacklift, which will have the capacity to lift 20 metric tons to low-Earth orbit. Oh, and the company said it would start launching commercially in late 2028.

“The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owner’s economics in the industry,” said Abel Avellan, founder, chairman, and CEO of AST SpaceMobile, in a news release.

To anyone with even a basic understanding of rockets, that timeline is wildly, fantastically, and stupidly optimistic. Still, the announcement is worth examining because it underscores two important trends in today’s launch industry.

First, it’s becoming increasingly apparent that satellite operators planning to deploy large constellations need to secure launch capacity years in advance, as Amazon did nearly half a decade ago. And if they can’t secure that capacity on favorable terms, they are now considering taking the extraordinary step of developing their own rockets.

And secondly, since investors are now recognizing the worsening launch crisis that Ars has been writing about for months, there is apparently capital to be raised for new entrants into the medium-lift launch market. AST is not the only company making fantastical claims of late. A firm called Cowboy Space said in October it was building a large rocket named Big Iron (full credit—that’s an excellent name) to launch orbital data centers. It also claimed its large rocket would make its first flight in 2028.

Sure thing, y’all.

Let’s start with a little history. SpaceX became the first purely commercial launch startup to announce plans to build a new medium-lift rocket about two decades ago, in 2005. The company holds the record for the fastest time to orbit with the Falcon 9 vehicle, with a development time of 4.7 years.

But SpaceX had some significant advantages. By then, the company had been operating for more than three years, had extensive experience with the Merlin engine, and was less than a year away from its first launch of the smaller Falcon 1 rocket. In retrospect, it’s also clear that the company had an insanely talented team of engineers. Finally, the Falcon 9 was quite a bit smaller than the recently announced vehicles, Blacklift and Big Iron. In its initial form, Falcon 9 had a lift capacity of about 10 tons.

What about other companies? Since 2015, a number of other US companies—United Launch Alliance (Vulcan), Rocket Lab (Neutron), Relativity Space (Terran R), Firefly/Northrop Grumman (Eclipse), and Stoke Space (Nova) have announced medium to heavy lift vehicles, ranging in payload capacity from about 7 to 27 metric tons (Blue Origin’s New Glenn is much larger than any of these).

Of these, only Vulcan has reached orbit. It took 8.7 years, with an incredibly experienced launch team behind the vehicle and about $2 billion in aggregate federal support across its suppliers.

Broadly speaking, the track records of these existing launch companies suggest that developing a new medium- or heavy-lift rocket takes five to nine years from public announcement to first orbital launch. Moreover, many of these companies either started with smaller rockets or brought other valuable experience to bear.

AST SpaceMobile’s counterargument is that it won’t be starting from scratch. The company said Friday that it has signed an agreement with Firefly to deliver engines for the first three Blacklift rockets, provide engineering services over a three-year period, and acquire the perpetual license to manufacture the Miranda and vacuum-variant Vira engines from Firefly. Nine Miranda engines will power Blacklift’s first stage.

Yes, engines are typically the hardest part of a rocket’s development. And procuring Miranda engines will shave some time off Blacklift’s development. But it will probably be a year or two, not five. Procuring the Miranda engine—which likely remains at least two years from being tested in flight on the Eclipse rocket—does not eliminate the enormous engineering, manufacturing, testing, and regulatory effort required to develop a medium-lift rocket.

AST SpaceMobile is also paying a pretty penny for this privilege. It has committed $1.3 billion to Firefly for the engine license ($800 million), 27 Miranda engines and nine Vira engines ($250 million), and engineering support ($250 million). If we look just at the engine costs for a single Blacklift rocket, that’s $83 million per vehicle for the first three.

The bottom line is that AST SpaceMobile has made a launch timeline claim that is profoundly disconnected from the historical record of every comparable rocket development program this century. Maybe they’re a bunch of geniuses who will vibe-code the vehicle with Claude or Grok and shock us all.

More likely, though, is that this is a company that desperately needs to launch about 90 more of its massive BlueBird direct-to-cell satellites. Yes, the company has some existing commercial launch contracts with SpaceX, Blue Origin, and other companies. And in its news release, it said, “AST SpaceMobile will continue to use external providers, with agreements now covering in total over 100 BlueBird satellites to be deployed cumulatively between 2027 and 2028.”

But that raises an obvious question: If AST already has agreements covering the deployment of more than 100 BlueBird satellites by the end of 2028, what precisely is Blacklift supposed to accomplish? Do you spend several billion dollars to develop a rocket you don’t actually need?

scraped.title: “Does Meta think we can’t read?” Meta abandons sketchy commercial terms update.
scraped.description: Meta won't force Facebook page owners to allow AI training on linked content.
scraped.h1: “Does Meta think we can’t read?” Meta abandons sketchy commercial terms update.
scraped.body_text:
Meta won’t force Facebook page owners to allow AI training on linked content.

After weeks of backlash —and a failed attempt to quell it —Meta has indefinitely delayed plans to update its commercial terms and require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.

“We’re pausing the ‌changes ⁠as we continue to engage with stakeholders and ​take ​our ⁠time to get this right. ​In the ​meantime, ⁠our existing terms remain in ⁠effect,” a Meta spokesperson told Reuters.

Soon after Meta notified business account holders of the upcoming changes, legal experts warned Nieman Lab that the vague language could allow the company to ignore scraping preferences specified in robots.txt files and exhaustively crawl vast amounts of off-Facebook content for AI training. Since virtually every news publisher has a Facebook page, Nieman Lab sounded the alarm that Meta could potentially avoid millions in licensing fees if the TOS update happened as planned.

Ars broke down the changes after Meta announced them, noting that businesses—including news publishers involved in drawn-out legal battles over unwanted AI scraping—had no way to opt out. To keep a business Facebook page, they had to allow Meta to crawl any linked external sites. The terms even required publishers to create test credentials so Meta’s bots could reliably bypass paywalls.

The changes were initially supposed to take effect on October 30. But Meta pushed that date back to November 20 amid pushback from Facebook users, courts, and regulators around the world. Courts in Brazil and Norway issued preliminary injunctions blocking the terms after organizations in those countries promptly filed lawsuits, Nieman Lab reported .

The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority also opened a formal investigation into whether Meta was exploiting a dominant position to seize valuable AI training data. In a LinkedIn post , Theo Bamber, chief executive of the UK’s News Media Association, pointed to “the continued arrogance of this company to think everyone will just be OK with its actions” as “staggering.”

“Does Meta think we can’t read?” Bamber wrote. He argued that removing the word “train” from the terms of service did little to reassure publishers, since “develop” posed the same threat.

“It’s saying it can use all the content it scrapes to develop ‘any business product’. I mean, come on,” he wrote.

Nieman Lab noted there was bipartisan concern in the US. Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters asking Mark Zuckerberg to withdraw the terms.

On October 28, Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted on X that Meta would do just that, at least for now.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update,” Stone said. “We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders. We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Meta has insisted that it would never use its terms of service to skirt robots.txt. In an update to business page owners, the company offered a “reminder” that “our crawling practices remain unchanged, and content owners can continue to signal their crawling preferences using robots.txt.”

But the company still faced criticism after promising to pull the terms and consult with publishers to get the policy right.

As regulatory and court scrutiny intensified, Nieman Lab noted that Meta took steps to try to assuage publishers’ concerns but “has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service.”

Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post , cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September . Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October , which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”

Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.

The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

items.title: Data center double-down: Hassett says blue wave won't stop AI build-out
items.summary: Data centers are a crucial part of President Donald Trump's push to win the global artificial intelligence race, which he continues despite the midterm results.

scraped.title: Data center double-down: Hassett says blue wave won't stop AI build-out
scraped.description: Data centers are a crucial part of President Donald Trump's push to win the global artificial intelligence race, which he continues despite the midterm results.
scraped.author: Kevin Breuninger
scraped.h1: Data center double-down: Hassett says blue wave won't stop AI build-out
scraped.body_text:
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Friday he expects data center growth to continue as projected, despite the blue-wave election that saw voters overwhelmingly favor limiting the tech infrastructure buildout.

Hassett, on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," acknowledged the dozens of measures on states' midterm ballots seeking to constrain data centers, a crucial part of President Donald Trump 's push to win the global artificial intelligence race.

In at least 46 of the roughly 50 such initiatives on ballots in 2026, majorities voted to restrict development of the facilities, according to Ballotpedia's tally.

"We respect the localities that decide that's what they want to do," Hassett said. "But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren't affected by these ballot initiatives."

"And the stuff after that, you know, there's plenty of room in the U.S. for data center growth to continue, as it was projected ahead of the election," he said.

Hassett said he expects data centers will continue to expand in states with more welcoming governors, and he suggested that even hostile states will eventually come around.

"That's exactly what's going to happen," he said. "That, or what'll happen will be that the benefits of the data centers will be so obvious that people decide to change their minds about the way they regulate them."

Hassett also blamed Thursday's tech-driven market plunge on "uncertainty about what the political change is going to mean for data centers going forward."

"We've now got a ... new majority that maybe is going to go in there and muddle around in there, and I think that markets are anxious about that," he said.

"But I think that the economic strength that we see everywhere else is so strong, and of course, in the end, you could take something that's growing as fast as the data centers and make it grow a little bit slower, and you still have a blockbuster economy."

"And so, I think we're still very, very optimistic about what's going to happen going forward," he said.

The CNBC Voter Poll found 56% of midterm voters identified data centers as either a crucial or major issue — and of those who considered it crucial, 62% favored the generic Democratic candidate.

Trump has strongly embraced AI and data centers and has even tried to reverse their seeming unpopularity by rebranding the tech as "super intelligence," or SI.

In a Truth Social post Friday, Trump made clear that despite the midterm losses, his support for the nascent industry has not faltered.

"As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them," Trump wrote. "They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!"
