scraped.title: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
scraped.description: Trump revealed the shake-up three days after Democrats' landslide victory in the midterm elections, winning majority control of the House and Senate.
scraped.author: Kevin Breuninger
scraped.h1: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles .

Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections , gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump's last two years in office.

Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump's controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government's immigration policies.

Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post , praising his longtime aide as "one of my most trusted advisors."

Wiles, "who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation," the president wrote.

Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP's huge election losses, "let me make this easy on you - I am going to resign," MS NOW reported.

"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime."

"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she wrote.

The official X account for Trump's political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, "It's Miller time."

The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Civil Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump's foes.

Wiles oversaw Trump's winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued "retribution" as president and that he had an " alcoholic's personality ."

Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.

items.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
items.summary: The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October, the highest outside of the pandemic period in a decade.

scraped.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
scraped.description: The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October, the highest outside of the pandemic period in a decade.
scraped.author: Alex Harring
scraped.h1: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
scraped.body_text:
Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.

The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.

About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed " and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.

"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."

It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.

Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.

What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year .

"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.

Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.

"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."

While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.

Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.

Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.

The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.

CNBC reported this week that Disney is planning to axe thousands of jobs , the latest of several waves of layoffs at the media giant this year. American Express said last month that it was slashing head count by 5% as it reorients around artificial intelligence.

"It's difficult to separate what's happening to you or the people around you from the big picture," said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. "When your LinkedIn is filled with layoffs and your social circle features a few folks who have been job seeking for several months, positive narratives about the labor market can seem jarring."

A Holocaust survivor who was injured during a mass shooting at a beach in Sydney during a Hanukkah celebration last year has died.

Eva Geller, who was born in Romania, died on Thursday night in a Sydney hospital, Executive Council of Australian Jewry director Evan Zlatkis said, the Associated Press reported. She was 90 years old.

Geller was one of about 40 people who were injured when two gunmen opened fire on a group gathered at a Hanukkah celebration on Bondi Beach on Dec. 14. Fifteen people were killed.

One of the gunmen, Sajid Akram, was shot dead by police at the scene. His son, Naveed Akram, 25, has been charged with 15 counts of murder, 43 counts of attempted murder and one count of committing a terrorist act.

Rabbi Aron Moss told the Associated Press that Geller had been in relatively good health until she was shot in the leg, but had been admitted to hospital on several occasions in recent weeks with surgical complications.

“She’s a proud mother, grandmother and great-grandmother. A beautiful, positive person who even in these difficult months maintained her positivity,” Moss told the AP on Geller’s family’s behalf, adding that she was told she would never walk again.

“Through sheer determination, she got back up and she did walk again,” he said, noting that walked with a cane after being shot in the leg.

New South Wales State Premier Chris Minns extended his best wishes to her family and loved ones, calling the news of her death “heartbreaking.”

“Almost a year on, we are still living with the pain and aftershock of that evil act. We will never forget Eva or any victim whose life was changed forever,” Minns added.

Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said families across the country still feel the impact of the attack.

“Eva should have been able to celebrate Chanukah in peace and safety and instead, her life was changed forever by an act of terror and antisemitism,” he said in a statement.

New South Wales Police is investigating whether Geller’s death will change the charges brought against Akram and are awaiting advice from the state coroner, Australian authorities told the Associated Press.

The alleged assailant has not yet entered a plea and is scheduled to appear in court on Feb. 24, when prosecutors are expected to finalize the charges. He will face trial in the New South Wales Supreme Court.

Among the victims of the shooting were a 10-year-old girl, two rabbis, a husband and wife who died trying to stop one of the suspects, an 82-year-old grandmother and community volunteer, an 87-year-old Holocaust survivor who died shielding his wife, and a retired police detective.

items.title: Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle arrested by FBI in Florida
items.summary: The Duchess of Sussex said she was 'deeply distressed' by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her estranged father's former home.

scraped.title: Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle arrested by FBI in Florida - National | Globalnews.ca
scraped.description: The Duchess of Sussex said she was 'deeply distressed' by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her estranged father's former home.
scraped.h1: Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle arrested by FBI in Florida
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

Comments closed.

Due to the sensitive and/or legal subject matter of some of the content on globalnews.ca, we reserve the ability to disable comments from time to time.

Please see our Commenting Policy for more.

Meghan Markle’s father was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material .

Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades, according to the FBI .

Markle Sr. is charged with one count of possession of child pornography and expected to make his initial appearance Friday in United States District Court in the Middle District of Florida in Tampa.

“Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

FBI Director Kash Patel said that an investigation revealed that Markle Sr. was “in possession of child sexual abuse material.”

“Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide,” Patel added.

“This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it’s a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children,” said Patrick Grandy, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

FBI special agents searched two storage units registered to Markle Sr., who has rented the units in Los Angeles since 2008, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay, according to the FBI.

Inside the units, agents seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse material.

If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison, according to the FBI.

Markle Sr.’s arrest comes after The Sun , a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half-brother allegedly found images while cleaning out the home of their father in the Philippines.

Meghan’s father denied the allegations against him in a statement to the Daily Mail , saying, “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me.”

“I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of,” he added.

The Duchess of Sussex said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her estranged father’s former home.

“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” Meghan said in a statement to The Associated Press.

She also addressed a letter sent to the Metropolitan Police Service’s Royal and Specialist Protection unit.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” she continued.

Meghan went on to say that she has not had a relationship with her father to protect her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” Meghan said. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” her statement concluded.

Thomas Markle Sr., 82, was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S., The Associated Press reports.

The Sun alleged that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., had recently found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home in the Philippine city of Cebu when he was clearing out the property.

He told the newspaper that he reported the alleged images to police in the Philippines.

Markle Jr., 60, told the outlet that he contacted FBI investigators in the U.S. who are reportedly set to launch their own probe.

“The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law,” an FBI spokesperson told Global News in October.

Last week, British police said they would refer allegations about Meghan’s father to overseas law enforcement agencies, after a review ‌found the claims had not been passed to other authorities when they were first received in 2019.

London’s Metropolitan Police said it had received a letter in January 2019 in ​which the author said they “were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.”

“While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” the Metropolitan police said in a news release .

“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies,” said Metropolitan Police’s Protection Commander Adam Slonecki.

Slonecki said that an internal review had led to the matter being referred to the police watchdog and that the force was now sharing the allegations with overseas authorities.

“In recent days, the Met’s Directorate of Professional Standards has carried out an initial review into our actions following receipt of the letter in 2019,” Slonecki said.

“Following that review, a voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex,” he said.

“In addition, it is our intention to make a number of referrals to relevant overseas law enforcement agencies in relation to the allegations contained within the letter. That process is underway and will be completed in the coming days,” Slonecki added.

—With files from Reuters and The Associated Press

items.title: Investors dive into bonds as global AI tech selloff continues
items.summary: Investors fled to the safety of bonds on Friday as stocks extended their slide in both Europe and Asia after worries around AI wiped trillions of dollars off stock markets.

scraped.description: Investors fled to the safety of bonds on Friday as stocks extended their slide in both Europe and Asia after worries around AI wiped trillions of dollars off stock markets.
scraped.h1: Investors dive into bonds as global AI tech selloff continues
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

Want to discuss? Please read our Commenting Policy first.

Comment

Name

Δ

Investors fled to the safety of bonds on Friday as stocks extended their slide in both Europe and Asia after worries around the AI boom wiped trillions of dollars off the major U.S. indexes.

Europe’s FTSEurofirst and STOXX 600 benchmarks both fell more than one per cent early on as traders continued to fret that the Democrats’ victory in this week’s US midterm elections will lead to tougher rules around AI data centres.

Wall Street saw a modest bounce early Friday, especially for the Nasdaq later after its trillion-dollar plunge on Thursday, although that did not comfort Asia overnight.

Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s KOSPI both slumped about six per cent. For the Nikkei – as for Wall Street – that was the deepest one-day drop since U.S. President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” trade tariff panic of April 2025.

Taiwan plunged more than eight per cent at one point, before cutting losses as authorities scrambled to stem the selling.

“This has been brutal,” James Athey, a fund manager at investment firm Marlborough in London, said, explaining that retail and hedge fund selling were feeding off each other.

“The question is where we go now? We are still looking at indexes that are near record highs and a sector (AI) where capex is still massive. So I think it is going to be a huge test of market sentiment – and the belief in AI – in the coming days.”

The strain on equities meant government bond markets continued to rally, while the U.S. dollar, Japanese yen and Swiss franc all lured safe haven flows in the currency markets.

The yield on the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury note was at 4.84 per cent in Europe, hovering near the lowest level since Sept. 9.

The ten-year Japanese government bond yield dropped as much as nine basis points overnight to 1.795 per cent, the lowest since June 30. Triple A-rated German bunds then saw yields dip to 3.22 per cent, their lowest level since late August.

“Bonds are increasingly behaving like bonds again, with income re-emerging as the primary driver of returns and restoring their traditional diversification benefits,” said Masahiko Loo, chief fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management.

“This looks more like a reassessment of AI policy risk than a reassessment of the AI cycle.”

A near 1.5 per cent rise in Nasdaq futures and a dip in Wall Street’s VIX “fear gauge” pointed to some respite for U.S. markets Friday.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosasaid on Thursday that the state – which already has a large share of U.S. data centres – will introduce new laws around them to protect local residents.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq went on to slump 5.5 per cent on Thursday – or US$2.5 trillion. Some $3 trillion was also wiped off S&P 500 firms, with investors worried the brakes will be applied to the AI boom more broadly.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.”

The jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky ground due to fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns – the meltdown has been spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

Some of Asia’s authorities stepped in overnight to try to soothe nerves.

South Korea temporarily eased rules on retail investors’ leveraged investments and multiple sources told Reuters that Taiwan’s Ministry of Finance called senior executives at state-owned banks, instructing them to support the market.

Taiwan stocks closed down 4.5 per cent, recovering somewhat from their early morning slump. For the week though, the index clocked a 12.2 per cent dive, its biggest since 1991, LSEG data showed.

Korean AI chipmakers also trimmed some of their losses although still closed sharply lower. In Japan, tech investor SoftBank slid 11 per cent, with the cost of insuring its debt against a default jumping to its highest in four years.

“After damage like the sort we’ve been facing, it is difficult to think that we simply can bounce from here,” said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.

“We may be oversold in the short term, but the underlying questions and causes can’t simply be wiped away.”

scraped.title: Joshua Wong sentencing: Hong Kong and int'l reactions
scraped.description: Jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment on Thursday after pleading guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces. HKFP rounds up reactions.
scraped.author: Hong Kong Free Press
scraped.h1: Joshua Wong sentencing: Local gov’t, police, officials hail 10-year jail term amid condemnation from foreign gov’t’s, NGOs
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment on Thursday after pleading guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces, his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law.

See also: Joshua Wong sought leniency to be freed in his 30s, mitigation letter reveals

HKFP rounds up local and international reactions.

Chief Executive John Lee

Wong was “among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability… Wong Chi-fung has repeatedly broken the law, including organising, taking part in, and inciting others to take part in unauthorised assemblies, unlawful assemblies, and contempt of court, demonstrating his utter disregard for the law.”

Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun

“The central government of China firmly supports the Hong Kong SAR in safeguarding national security and punishing in accordance with the law acts that endanger national security.”

Spokesperson for the Hong Kong Legislative Council

“The sentence fully demonstrates the rule of law and justice, reflecting that under the Hong Kong National Security Law, anyone attempting to endanger national security will inevitably be severely punished in accordance with the law… [T]he evidence against Wong Chi-fung was conclusive and he chose to plead guilty…”

Chief Superintendent of Police National Security Department Steve Li

“I sincerely hope that for the rest of his time in prison, apart from reflecting on the wrongdoings he has done to the country and to the Hong Kong SAR, he must seize the opportunity to learn how to respect the law and properly understand his own country.”

Secretary for Security Chris Tang

“Those launching attacks against us are exactly the same external forces that Wong and Law attempted to collude… They must be strongly condemned, and Hong Kong citizens must recognise and acknowledge that clearly.”

European Union External Action Press Team:

“The EU urges Chinese and the Hong Kong authorities to respect international legal commitments under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration and maintain space for political pluralism in line with the ‘one country, two systems’ principle.”

Spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office

“We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

Spokesperson for the US Consulate

“Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong.”

Taiwan Presidential Office Spokesperson Karen Kuo

“Seeking democracy should not be a crime, and young people should not have to sacrifice their freedom for their ideals.”

Asia Director at Human Rights Watch Elaine Pearson

“The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.”

Deputy Regional Director for Amnesty International Sarah Brooks

“Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security… [it] cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction.”

scraped.title: Gov't will facilitate Wang Fuk Court fire anniversary events if 'lawful'
scraped.description: Authorities will assist people wishing to commemorate the victims of the Wang Fuk Court blaze on the tragedy's anniversary later this month, on the condition that such activities are "lawful," Hong Kong security chief Chris Tang has said.
scraped.author: James Lee
scraped.h1: Security chief Chris Tang says gov’t will facilitate Wang Fuk Court fire anniversary events if ‘lawful’
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Authorities will assist people wishing to commemorate the victims of the Wang Fuk Court blaze on the tragedy’s anniversary later this month, on the condition that such activities are “lawful,” Hong Kong security chief Chris Tang has said.

Tang made the remarks when addressing reporters at an event on Thursday, some three weeks ahead of the first anniversary of the deadly fire. The blaze broke out on November 26 last year, engulfing seven buildings in the subsidised housing estate during large-scale renovation works, killing 168 people and displacing over 4,600 residents.

“Many family members and friends want to commemorate this day and we fully understand this. We will do our best to facilitate any actions as long as they are handled lawfully,” Tang said.

In the wake of the blaze last year, Hongkongers set up a makeshift vigil site at the Kwong Fuk Sitting-out Area, a park near the fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court. It was cleared out days after the fire following coordination with the police.

Also in the wake of the tragedy, a government press release blasted “anti-China and destabilising forces” for “making unfounded and slanderous remarks,” and trying to use the fire to “stir up chaos in society.”

Chief Superintendent of the police’s National Security Department Steve Li said after the fire that he had visited the Tai Po site and that he believed “the situation was becoming more and more like that of ‘black-clad violence,'” in reference to clothing worn by 2019 pro-democracy demonstrators.

See also: Tai Po fire: Police oversee overnight removal of flowers, tributes from memorial by volunteers, gov’t staff

He pointed to pamphlets and slogans that were “basically unrelated to the disaster and only aimed to incite hatred.”

The government — and Beijing’s top office on Hong Kong affairs — has continued to reference a narrative accusing certain actors of using the tragedy as a pretence for sowing chaos in the months since the fire.

Tang said on Thursday: “I believe that if they are handled in accordance with the law, we will certainly assist.”

Tang also reiterated part of the government’s reform proposals, saying that the authorities would adopt a multi-pronged approach including introducing legislative amendments and coordinating law enforcement agencies to prevent bid-rigging in the future.

scraped.title: Joshua Wong sought leniency to be freed in his 30s, mitigation letter reveals
scraped.description: Jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has said in a mitigation letter submitted to court before his sentencing on Thursday that his six years in prison reshaped his outlook on life, asking for the utmost leniency so he could walk free in his thirties.
scraped.author: Hong Kong Free Press
scraped.h1: ‘6 years in jail has reshaped my view of life’: Joshua Wong sought leniency to be freed in his 30s, mitigation letter reveals
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has said in a mitigation letter submitted to court before his sentencing on Thursday that his six years in prison reshaped his outlook on life, asking for the utmost leniency so he could walk free in his thirties.

High Court judge William Tam sentenced the activist to 10 years’ imprisonment on Thursday after Wong pleaded guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces, his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law.

The 30-year-old has been behind bars since late 2020, when he was 24. He was due to be released in early 2027 after completing a four-year, eight-month jail term for conspiracy to subvert state power in the landmark “Hong Kong 47” case, but was charged with foreign collusion in June last year.

In a Chinese-language mitigation letter obtained by HKFP, Wong said he had missed his university graduation ceremony and lost more than 2,000 days with his family.

“Unlike my peers born in the 1990s, I was unable to start a family of my own or enter the workforce. Instead, I could only watch the years pass inside a stark cell,” the letter reads.

Wong said that while in prison, he exercised regularly, read books, and learned new skills every day. He added that he was learning the guitar, preparing for the International English Language Testing System (IELTS), and taking multiple legal and business courses organised by local universities.

“I pledge to Your Honour that I will not allow myself to be defined by who I was before the age of 24… When the day comes that I step out of this cell, I pray that I will have washed away the naivety of 24, moving forward with a mature mind, enriched knowledge, and a healthy body,” Wong said in the letter.

The activist also said he hoped to care for his elderly parents and give back to society upon his release.

“My experience of imprisonment under the National Security Law has not made me resistant to gaining a deeper understanding of China. On the contrary, it drove me to read extensively, draw wisdom from the past to reflect on the present… I hope to apply my professional skills to contribute to the socio-economic development of our society in full compliance with the law.”

Wong was accused of conspiring with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and other unnamed individuals after the Beijing-imposed national security law came into effect in June 2020 to request that foreign countries impose sanctions and blockades, or engage in other hostile activities, directed against the governments of Hong Kong and mainland China.

During the 2019 protests and unrest, many protesters campaigned internationally to gather support from Western countries and pressure Hong Kong and Beijing authorities to meet their demands.

Wong said in his mitigation letter that once the national security law came into effect, he realised that calling for foreign sanctions was unlawful and he “promptly ceased all such statements and conduct.”

“However, as the law suddenly came into force, the situation was overwhelming. I attempted to adjust my words and actions amid confusion, yet my legal judgment was not thorough and I was not in a clear mind, leaving me unable to properly determine the legal boundaries for every single act,” Wong said.

“At the time, I believed that reposting publications by others, or urging foreign enterprises on commercial grounds to halt cooperation with police, differed from directly calling for sanctions,” he said, adding: “With respect to all statements I made and posts I published, I admit them in their entirety and accept full responsibility.”

Protests erupted in June 2019 over a since-axed extradition bill . They escalated into sometimes violent displays of dissent against police behaviour, amid calls for democracy and anger over Beijing’s encroachment. Demonstrators demanded an independent probe into police conduct, amnesty for those arrested and a halt to the characterisation of protests as “riots.”

Updated - November 07, 2026 01:11 am IST - Bengaluru

A view of the house in Rajajinagar where Indushekhar allegedly murdered seven members of his wife's family. | Photo Credit: PTI

It was not until the mother of Nalini, one of the seven allegedly killed by cab driver-turned-YouTuber Indushekhar, lodged a missing person complaint that the police found the first clue to the murders. While the murders allegedly took place between October 16 and October 31, the last two bodies were disposed of on November 1 or 2.

Senior police officers said that Sunita, the accused’s wife, and Roopavathi, his mother-in-law, were the first to be murdered. Sunita and Indushekhar had been married for 20 years, and an officer said they had been having regular arguments throughout their marriage. Sunita worked as a typist for an advocate, while Indushekhar was a cab driver. Their respective jobs were often a point of contention between them.

“Indushekhar claimed that he was verbally abused and harassed by his wife and her family, while her brothers also encouraged her to fight with him,” a senior officer said.

Prima facie , the police have found that Indushekhar had been planning the murders for over a year. The growing friction and pent-up anger allegedly came to a head following a recent meeting.

“The accused claimed that Roopavathi had visited his house on October 14, when she and Sunita reportedly verbally abused him. This became a trigger point, and he wanted to eliminate them,” the officer said.

According to the police, Sunita and Roopavathi were murdered first. Subsequently, the accused invited Sunita’s younger brother Shivakumar and his wife Divya to his house on the pretext of hosting a dinner party. The couple were then killed along with their seven-year-old son Puneeth. On October 30, the accused allegedly invited Shankar, another brother of Sunita, and his wife Nalini, and allegedly murdered them.

On November 3, Tungamma, Nalini’s mother, approached the police, stating that her daughter’s phone was switched off and that their house in Srirampura was also locked. Tungamma subsequently went to Indushekar’s house to check on him but found that his house was locked as well.

Sensing that something was amiss, she contacted Divya’s mother Kalavathi, who also said that her daughter and son-in-law were missing. Tungamma then lodged a missing person complaint with the Srirampura police.

Karthik, a shopkeeper near Indushekhar’s house, said a police team visited the house on November 3 and made inquiries about Indushekhar among the neighbourhood residents. “They also came the next day and questioned people because Indushekhar’s house was locked,” he said.

A senior officer told The Hindu that the police grew suspicious and began tracking Indushekhar. Several technical inputs indicated that he was on the move. “Finally, when he was in the city, we tracked him and intercepted his car,” he said.

High drama unfolded near the Rajajinagar police station on Friday as Nalini’s family accused the police of delaying action on their complaint. “We approached the police on November 1 itself, but they did not register our complaint. Only after two days did they take it up,” a family member alleged.

Bengaluru City Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh refuted the allegations and said that action would be taken against the officers if any lapses were found.

While the accused has claimed that he murdered the victims using a grinder stone, the police are yet to ascertain the exact modus operandi . “Only when the bodies are found can we verify the cause of death. We have seized the suspected weapon,” the officer said.

Seemant Kumar Singh, Bengaluru Police Commissioner, said, “As this is a serious case, we will gather all the evidence and present it before a fast-track court. We have deputed senior officers to closely monitor the investigation and ensure that all necessary evidence is collected.”

Published - November 07, 2026 01:10 am IST - WASHINGTON

Newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. File. | Photo Credit: AFP

President Donald Trump said Friday (November 6, 2026) that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.

On his social media site, Mr. Trump praised Ms. Wiles and said she’d continue working for his political organisation. Ms. Wiles also released a social media statement on Friday (November 6, 2026).

"Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Mr. Miller, long a key member of Mr. Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.

Ms. Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Mr. Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post.

Ms. Wiles' departure comes almost immediately after the GOP's midterm thrashing on Tuesday (November 3, 2026). She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Mr. Trump.

The departure also came months after Ms. Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Ms. Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Mr. Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Mr. Miller is one of Mr. Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having jumped on board during his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff, and though he has a wide-ranging portfolio, Mr. Miller is most closely aligned with Mr. Trump’s immigration policy and rhetoric on immigration.

Mr. Miller is a former aide to hardliner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who would go on to serve as Mr. Trump’s first Attorney General.

NEW DELHI

The Supreme Court directed on Friday that individuals with temporary residence in the Agasthyamalai biosphere or those living entirely outside the forest boundaries cannot be classified as traditional forest dwellers merely for cultivating silk cotton within the forest.

“Persons falling in Category II and Category III, as classified in the additional affidavit of September 6 filed by Department of Revenue, State of Tamil Nadu, shall be excluded from consideration as forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers for the purposes of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 or FRA Act,” a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta directed.

According to Tamil Nadu’s own affidavit, 232 persons are cultivating the forest area with temporary residence while 2,767 persons who occupy 2,867.70 hectares land are residing outside the forest boundary and are managing silk cotton cultivation.

The order was passed in furtherance of a May 2026 judgment, which had issued various directions for a structured and time-bound process of eviction, rehabilitation and ecological restoration in the forest areas. The court had ordered the preparation of a division-wise eviction plan, removal of encroachments, and action against identified government servants.

It had imposed a prohibition on approval or commencement of new non-forestry activities or diversion proposals within the Agasthyamalai landscape, and directed continued monitoring of the area by the Central Empowered Committee (CEC).

Justice Mehta, who authored the order, held the State government “primarily responsible” for delaying the receipt of claims under the 2006 Act. Noting that so far only around 40 gram sabhas had become functional to commence the process of inviting claims, the government gave a last opportunity of 30 days to the State government to complete the formation of the remaining gram sabhas. The process of adjudication of the claims would be concluded within a period of five months from the date of constitution of the gram sabhas.

The court further constituted a ‘special committee’ chaired by former Chief Justice of India B.R. Gavai to supervise the expeditious disposal of claims and scrutinise the orders passed by the competent authorities under the 2006 Act.

The Supreme Court directed the CEC to furnish an opinion regarding the government’s view that silk cotton was a ‘minor forest produce’. This is significant for the biosphere. Presently, 3,637.83.2 hectares of the 5,072.64.3 hectares of forest land is under silk cotton cultivation.

Giving a prima facie view against the State’s claim of historical cultivation of silk cotton, the court said “what emerges from the government affidavits is the promotion and sponsored cultivation of silk cotton as a commercial crop”.

“The concept of planned cultivation of commercial crops is totally contrary to the very concept of a naturally occurring minor forest produce. If commercial crops are permitted to be cultivated in the forest areas, the very nature of the forest is bound to change… The fact that large swathes of forest are being destroyed under the garb of cultivation of silk cotton,” the court observed.

Separately, the court directed the CEC to examine the National Highway Authority of India’s proposal relating to NH-744, including the proposed Puliara–Edamon tunnel section, which requires permission for diversion of a limited extent of reserved forest land in the biosphere.

items.title: Putin Places Japan Tobacco Under Russian Control
items.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree placing the Russian operations of Japan Tobacco (JT) under the temporary management of a local company, effectively stripping the Japanese tobacco giant of control over its business in the country and prompting a formal protest from Tokyo demanding that the measure be immediately withdrawn. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Putin Places Japan Tobacco Under Russian Control
scraped.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree placing the Russian operations of Japan Tobacco (JT) under the temporary management of a local company, effectively stripping the Japanese tobacco giant of control over its business in the country and prompting a formal protest from Tokyo demanding that the measure be immediately withdrawn.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Putin Places Japan Tobacco Under Russian Control
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree placing the Russian operations of Japan Tobacco (JT) under the temporary management of a local company, effectively stripping the Japanese tobacco giant of control over its business in the country and prompting a formal protest from Tokyo demanding that the measure be immediately withdrawn.

The decree covers four companies responsible for the Russian operations of JT International, the overseas subsidiary of Japan Tobacco. The move effectively deprives the Japanese company of management rights over its Russian business, although the arrangement has been described as temporary. According to Russia's state-run TASS news agency, JT International has operated in Russia since 1999 and has grown into the country's largest tobacco manufacturer, making the decision a significant development for one of Japan's major overseas corporate operations. The Russian government has been expanding measures to place assets belonging to companies from countries that have imposed sanctions on Moscow under state-directed management. In September, similar action was taken against companies including Swiss food giant Nestle. Japan Tobacco said it was carefully examining the situation and its available options while prioritizing the interests of employees and other stakeholders. "We are closely assessing the situation and possible future courses of action, placing the highest priority on our employees and other stakeholders," the company said. The move comes as relations between Japan and Russia continue to deteriorate. In August, Putin made his first visit to Etorofu, one of the Russian-controlled islands claimed by Japan as part of its Northern Territories. Tensions escalated further in October when Russia's Federal Security Service detained a journalist from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara announced at a morning press conference on November 6 that Japan had lodged a formal protest with the Russian government and demanded the immediate reversal of the decree. Kihara said senior Japanese officials currently visiting Russia, including a senior official from the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and a senior official from the Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Bureau, had joined Japan's ambassador to Russia in delivering the protest directly to Russian authorities. "The senior officials currently visiting Russia, together with our ambassador, have protested to the Russian government and demanded that the measure be withdrawn immediately," Kihara said. He emphasized that the Japanese government would continue monitoring developments closely and take appropriate action in response to the situation. The decision adds to the difficulties facing Japanese companies operating in Russia, where foreign businesses from countries supporting sanctions against Moscow have faced increasing risks of losing control over their local assets.

scraped.title: Typhoon No. 32 Forming, Northern Japan Braces for Blizzards
scraped.description: Central Tokyo recorded its first November summer day in three years on November 6, with temperatures climbing to 25.3 degrees Celsius, while northern Japan faced the threat of violent winds and severe snowstorms from the evening and a tropical depression far south of the country threatened to develop into Typhoon No. 32, potentially the first such storm in 32 years.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Typhoon No. 32 Forming, Northern Japan Braces for Blizzards
scraped.body_text:
HOKKAIDO - Central Tokyo recorded its first November summer day in three years on November 6, with temperatures climbing to 25.3 degrees Celsius, while northern Japan faced the threat of violent winds and severe snowstorms from the evening and a tropical depression far south of the country threatened to develop into Typhoon No. 32, potentially the first such storm in 32 years.

The unusually warm weather came just one day before November 7, which marks Ritto, the traditional beginning of winter in the Japanese calendar, highlighting a sharp contrast between summer-like conditions across parts of the country and the approaching winter weather in the north. Tokyo began November 6 under a blanket of thick fog, which obscured roughly half of Tokyo Skytree. The morning sun could be seen breaking through the mist before skies cleared and temperatures began rising rapidly. By around 2 p.m., central Tokyo had reached 25.3 degrees, a level more typical of September and a dramatic turnaround from the chilly conditions recorded on November 5. It was the first time in three years that the capital had experienced a November day with temperatures reaching at least 25 degrees, the Japan Meteorological Agency's threshold for a "summer day." In Ueno, visitors were seen removing jackets and switching to lighter clothing. One parent said the family had planned to take a child to the zoo wearing a fluffy panda-themed outfit but had to remove it because of the heat. "It was just too hot. We've even turned on a fan," the parent said. Shizuoka City also experienced unseasonably warm conditions, with temperatures exceeding 25 degrees before noon and reaching a daytime high of 25.9 degrees. Residents were seen walking through the streets in short sleeves and shorts. The summer-like temperatures created an unusual atmosphere at Tokyo's Ueno Park, where a Christmas market opened on November 6. Visitors wearing short sleeves and sandals strolled past Santa Claus decorations, while some chose cold drinks rather than traditional hot winter beverages. One visitor explained the choice of apple juice simply by saying, "Because it's hot." At the Togoshi Ginza shopping street in Tokyo, however, the warm weather did little to discourage customers from enjoying oden, a traditional Japanese winter dish of ingredients simmered in hot broth. Diners were seen eating steaming bowls of oden alongside cold beer. "It's warm today, but this is the season for oden," one customer said. While much of central Japan enjoyed unusually high temperatures, weather conditions were deteriorating farther north. Heavy rain struck Niigata City during the afternoon of November 6, while large raindrops battered rooftops in Noboribetsu, Hokkaido, signaling the arrival of increasingly unstable weather. Northern Japan was expected to face potentially dangerous conditions from the evening of November 6, with severe winds and blizzards strong enough to warrant weather warnings. Authorities were concerned that the approaching weather system could bring widespread disruption as rain turned to snow in colder areas. Meanwhile, a tropical depression that had developed over waters far south of Japan was being closely monitored for signs of strengthening. The system, sometimes described as a "typhoon egg," could develop into a tropical storm as early as November 7. If it reaches typhoon strength, it would be designated Typhoon No. 32, marking the first time in 32 years that the western North Pacific has recorded a 32nd named tropical storm within a single year. The potential development would be particularly unusual for November, when Japan is normally transitioning toward winter and tropical cyclone activity affecting the country is generally declining. The dramatic weather contrasts are expected to continue into the following week, when temperatures in Tokyo are forecast to plunge after the brief spell of summer-like warmth. Overnight lows in the capital could fall below 10 degrees Celsius, bringing a sharp return to late-autumn and early-winter conditions after the unusually hot November 6. The rapid temperature changes, combined with the threat of severe winds and heavy snow in northern Japan and the possible formation of another typhoon to the south, underscore the unusually unsettled weather affecting the country as winter approaches.

items.title: Bears May Know When Astringent Persimmons Become Sweet
items.summary: Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas. scraped.title: Bears May Know When Astringent Persimmons Become Sweet
scraped.description: Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Bears May Know When Astringent Persimmons Become Sweet
scraped.body_text:
HYOGO - Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas.

As bear activity increases ahead of hibernation, persimmon trees have been identified as one of the factors attracting the animals into populated areas, raising concerns about encounters with humans. A University of Hyogo study found that bears began eating sweet persimmons as early as late July, while they generally avoided astringent varieties until late November or later. The difference in feeding behavior suggests that bears may be sensitive to changes in the fruit's chemical composition, allowing them to recognize when its bitter taste has diminished. Daisuke Fujiki, an associate professor at the University of Hyogo, said the findings indicate that bears use the concentration of astringent compounds in persimmons to determine whether the fruit is suitable for consumption. "We found that whether the concentration of astringent compounds falls below a certain level appears to be a factor in determining whether bears will eat the fruit," Fujiki said. The findings suggest that bears may be capable of identifying the point at which astringent persimmons become palatable, rather than simply consuming whatever fruit is available. Researchers warn that astringent persimmons could increasingly attract bears as their bitterness naturally declines in the coming weeks, particularly during the period leading up to winter hibernation. However, because sweet persimmons attract bears much earlier in the season, researchers believe that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees in areas vulnerable to bear encounters could be an effective preventive measure. The study highlights the importance of managing fruit trees around residential communities, particularly during autumn when bears are actively searching for food before entering hibernation. scraped.title: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
scraped.description: From rallies in Ohio to a Pennsylvania voting site on Election Day, the tone had noticeably changed among voters in some of the regions that were crucial to electing Donald Trump.
scraped.author: Alec MacGillis
scraped.h1: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

A Closer Look

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican candidates gathered there to help him with.

Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered from a two-year delay in brain development.

Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s unbelievable what’s happening.”

This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises. This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been particularly drawn to Trump all along , working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president during this trying time.

Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling. “The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.

Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other countries to begin with?”

Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter. She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”

It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016, and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of what presidential communication has come to in 2026.

The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”

Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”

When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance: “Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”

There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’” shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s ass! That’s not gay??”

A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the woman who was with him.

A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”

This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew back and forth.

Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed to the spot. Cameras flashed.

A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle East?”

Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked, it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”

On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar, in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,” and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.

Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats! All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”

The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than 100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.

The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through. Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a devastation that had made it highly susceptible to Trump’s message in 2016. But Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen, to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive Intel plant under construction.

The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.

And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,” Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win is if Republicans don’t vote.”

Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25 points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call it a day.

The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016 to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.

But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”

He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,” as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting out of control.”

Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder on the Orient Express.”

For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.

For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation, which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her classroom.

For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of diesel.

For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.

For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our country is OK.”

By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points, as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.

The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win in 2016, through the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol , through Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.

There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me farewell with a parting regret.

“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I do?’”

I have been reporting for ProPublica since 2015, most recently covering the post-pandemic schools crisis.
