scraped.title: Glaciers around the world are endangered — but no two are alike
scraped.description: Globally, glaciers are often lumped into one narrative of loss. These three stories show how they can still surprise us.
scraped.author: M Jackson
scraped.h1: Glaciers around the world are endangered — but no two are alike
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Δ

Globally, glaciers are often lumped into one narrative of loss. These three stories show how they can still surprise us.

Part of my work as a geographer and glacier scientist involves traveling around the world. Literally. Several times a year, I join expeditions, traversing continents and oceans, sometimes half the planet, in mere days. I’ve visited glaciers in some startling places — like Uganda’s Stanley Glacier, where ice retreat influences human health and malaria outbreaks. Or Iceland’s Breiðamerkurjökull, where glacier change is exacerbating the ice-breaking pressures of global tourism . Or South Georgia’s Heaney Glacier, where ice retreat has provided expansive real estate for one of the largest King penguin colonies on Earth.

My job is to translate the landscape: how oceans move nutrients pole to pole; why one mountain might support snow but another does not; how glaciers shape societies.

I’ll own it’s a peculiar way to experience the world.

From 30,000 feet, borders fall away. Trees become forests become systems become a living planet. I see connections everywhere. But that view from 30,000 feet, while striking, can miss much of what’s unfolding below at the individual level — the people, the lives, the histories.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Glaciers, I think, suffer from this same problem of perspective. We tend to see them from a great distance, as a single global story.

They’re tallied together: Some 275,000 individual glaciers remain worldwide . They’re measured together: how quickly they are shrinking, how much they impact sea level change, how long before they are gone. How many of them already are.

But glaciers have never lived identical lives. My work has shown over and over that every glacier has a distinct life history, shaped by and shaping the communities, landscapes, and systems around it. As glaciers change, we aren’t witnessing a single global glacier story from 30,000 feet. We are witnessing hundreds of thousands of individual stories of transformation.

One of the most surprising is unfolding right in my own backyard.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

My most recent expedition took me to nine countries. But I started the trip in Portland, Oregon — just north of my home in Eugene — land of the exhilaratingly perfect medium roast coffee and the Cascade volcano chain I used to orient myself for most of my childhood. The first morning, I ran up to the hotel’s top floor to see if the weather was clear enough to peer 50 miles northeast toward Mount St. Helens, across the border in Washington state. From downtown, it is easy to distinguish her whaleback summit, notably slumped in comparison to the sharper profiles of Mount Hood and Mount Adams.

What isn’t visible from this distance is the secret Mount St. Helens is hiding within.

The volcano erupted in May of 1980, two years before I was born. I grew up hearing stories of how ash coated our family farm, how the afternoon sky turned murky, how one terrified horse kicked through her box stall door. What I didn’t learn until much, much later was that, prior to the eruption, Mount St. Helens supported 11 named glaciers and two small unnamed ones. The nine-hour Plinian eruption destroyed 70 percent of the mountain’s ice, including the Loowit and Leschi glaciers, while the summit and entire north flank collapsed, leaving behind a horseshoe-shaped crater roughly two miles wide.

If you’ve ever received a climbing permit from the U.S. Forest Service, hiked to the crater rim, and gazed into that windy bowl of pumice and dark basalts, I can almost guarantee the very last word on your mind is “nursery.” Trust me. I rocked my baby in a softly-lit Scandinavian-paletted room designed for every possible infant need. But Mount St. Helens, apparently a fan of free-range parenting, took another approach. And it worked. Inside that raw volcanic maw, a baby glacier is growing inside.

The eruption that destroyed most of Mount St. Helens’ glaciers also created the perfect conditions to grow a new one.

Winter after winter, snow fell on the volcano’s steep headwall, and then it avalanched, repeatedly, into the crater floor below. By September 1996, scientists observed that the 16-year-old body of snow and ice had begun to move, flow. This fact is existential — glaciers are defined as moving bodies of land ice that persist year after year. When glaciers stop moving, they are “dead” — it’s not just loss of volume that threatens their identity as glaciers. The Okjökull glacier in Iceland was declared dead in 2014 when it stopped flowing; in 2019, the nation held a funeral for it .

But here, the opposite has happened.

Welcome to the world, Crater Glacier.

There is something equally wonderful and strange about being almost exactly the same age as a glacier. We’re both children of the 80s, who grew up under the same Cascade volcanoes. I became a glaciologist; she became a glacier.

And we’ve both had setbacks. Me: paying my bills, becoming a mother, and learning, repeatedly, that adulthood rarely follows the topography you planned.

Crater Glacier: Mount St. Helens, in 2004, erupted again. Magma began pushing up beneath her. A lava dome swelled through the crater floor and into the glacier itself — the first time scientists observed the emplacement of a lava dome through glacier ice .

It split her in two.

As the dome grew, the now separate arms of the glacier deformed, then thickened and sped up, flowing 1 to 2 feet (30 to 60 centimeters) per day . Within four years, those arms stretched all the way around the lava dome and rejoined. And the glacier kept going. Between 2009 and 2019, she gained some 13.8 million cubic meters of ice and advanced more than a thousand feet.

My colleagues have noted that her advance is slowing. Eventually, warming Pacific Northwest summers may overwhelm the unique climate zone inside Mount St. Helens’ crater. Or, the volcano might erupt again.

And that matters to the people living below.

Crater Glacier’s body wraps around an active vent and lava dome. A future eruption could melt ice, mix with ash, pumice, and rock and become a lahar, a fast-moving slurry of water, mud, trees, and whatever else it picks up as it races downslope. Lahars from the 1980 eruption destroyed homes, bridges, and roads. Growing up, I remember how we were taught drills for lahars alongside earthquakes and fires.

It isn’t lost on me how radically the landscape I grew up with has changed, or how much more it will change in the years to come. But, as I follow Crater Glacier’s development, I’m reminded that it isn’t all bad. This one glacier, among hundreds of thousands, is writing a story I could never have imagined.

I arrive in Baku, Azerbaijan, in July. It is sweltering.

This country has glaciers, but I won’t see them on this trip. The last time I saw ice in the Caucasus, I was on a Fulbright in Turkey, living on the Black Sea and exploring these mountains from the west. The ice I saw then would be unrecognizable today.

Between 2000 and 2020, Azerbaijan lost 77 percent of the country’s total glacier area.

To me, that’s baffling to think about: 77 percent. Over 20 years. Half my life.

And yet, almost no one I meet in Azerbaijan seems particularly interested in talking about glaciers. I risk distracting my driver, Kamran, a delightful 20-something local man who weaves through Baku’s insane, seven-lanes-of-madness traffic like it’s nothing. The Caspian Sea twinkles peacefully to our left, oil derricks lazily chugging. To our right, the city’s iconic blue-gleaming high-rises overlap with mosques and war memorials.

“We don’t bother with them,” Kamran tells me, speaking of the glaciers. He pivots quickly to Gobustan, a district south of Baku that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Had I seen the mud volcanoes? “Tourists come all the time now to see the methane volcanoes.”

I keep encountering this indifference. My colleague, Suleyman, also doesn’t want to talk about glaciers and spends the bulk of our coffee telling me about the pending F1 race in Baku. He doesn’t even bother glancing at the map I’ve brought. Azerbaijan’s glaciers are remote, tiny, and high in the Eastern Caucasus. By 2025, 14 fragmented glaciers remain, covering together about 124 acres — roughly one-tenth of the ice that covered these mountains in the 1890s.

But glaciers here, like glaciers everywhere, are critical components of regional water cycles. Glaciers hold water — for years, decades, centuries. They are reservoirs that do not need to be constructed. And in Azerbaijan, water and water storage matter. Agriculture relies on a complex system of reservoirs, canals, and irrigation. Groundwater withdrawals have increased some fourfold since 2000, largely fueled by farms growing wheat, fruit, and vegetables.

In 2025, researchers climbed Azerbaijan’s Tufandag Glacier and reported retreat, accelerated melting, and expanding crevasses. Below it, the Mahmuddara River had increased water levels and discharge rates.

This is how a glacier can disappear in plain sight: by transforming into liquid. As a glacier melts, it releases more water downstream. And for that reason, the current precipitous decline of Azerbaijan’s glaciers is almost a boon. Glacier becomes meltwater, river, irrigation, drinking water, wheat, lettuce, peaches. Farmers rejoice.

But, eventually, too much ice dissolves and the runoff peaks, then decreases. In glaciology, we call this “peak water,” when a disappearing glacier gives us the most water it ever will. The cycle of savings and withdrawals that has defined this landscape for centuries will ultimately end like this, when the bank is forced to close.

Has Tufandag Glacier, or any of Azerbaijan’s 13 other glaciers, crossed that threshold? I don’t know. The increased flow of the Mahmuddara is only one measurement, from one glacier, that cannot fully answer that question.

But I can think back to the ice I saw in these same mountains years ago, then look at the Caucasus today, and I understand that it has transformed. Water that was ice, storage, cold is now warm liquid moving downstream.

Azerbaijan’s remaining glaciers may not survive this century. People in the coming years are going to have to do what glaciers once did — come up with more ways to store more water. Catch it when it arrives and hold it until it’s needed.

I keep thinking about the apparent indifference many Azerbaijanis show towards glaciers. Maybe Kamran’s response is more revealing than I initially thought.

Perhaps the first step of a glacier disappearing from a landscape is it disappearing from conversation.

If you ever get a chance, wander through the Tateyama Museum in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. The exquisite open-air museum explores the nearby Mount Tateyama as both landscape and sacred place: a perennially snow-covered mountain, a dwelling place of spirits and the dead, a realm containing hell and heaven.

There is a poem there by the eighth-century poet Ōtomo no Yakamochi about Tateyama’s summer snow and its association with the divine. It stops me. Some 1,300 years ago, people were already writing — marveling — about the snow that refused to disappear.

Japan’s Sea-of-Japan side is one of the snowiest places on Earth, a skier’s powder paradise. And yet, for years, my colleagues and I thought no glaciers existed east of Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. The landscape was too warm, the mountains too low, to support glaciers under today’s conditions.

For glaciers — moving bodies of land ice that persist year after year — the base variables are critical: snow, time, and temperature. But those variables do interact with intensely local conditions such as wind, topography, shade — even human activity. It matters where snow falls, where it blows, and where a landscape and people allow it to accumulate.

Japan is technically not cold enough long enough to support glaciers. But it is extraordinarily snowy.

When I flew over Tateyama in June, most of the three-peaked massif was gray — alpine bare, with significant snow melt. But I did see a few Dalmatian-like white pockets in shaded nooks and north-facing crannies. If I hadn’t known better, I would have just labeled them as snow patches. Remember: Definitionally, a glacier must flow under its own weight. More movement is a sign of a healthy glacier.

Snow patches, regardless of how long they’ve existed or if they contain ice, do not move.

Everyone in the bustling world of cryospheric research knew Japan had snow patches. More than 100 had been identified in the northern Japanese Alps alone.

In the 1970s, researchers began observing holes in Kuranosuke — one such snow patch, roughly 6 acres in area — that looked and behaved like glacial features called moulins. In 1979, a Japanese researcher investigated one of the moulins by using the time-honored glaciological technique of climbing directly into it. He discovered layers of ancient ice, an observation supported later by radiocarbon analysis of embedded wood and leaf debris that were dated to approximately 1,700 years old.

Old, yes. But old does not make a glacier. Movement does.

And so Kuranosuke remained, scientifically speaking, for decades and decades, a snow patch.

But then, starting in 2009, researchers Kotaro Fukui and Hajime Iida of the Tateyama Caldera Sabo Museum used state-of-the-art geodetic measurements and ground-penetrating radar to take a closer look at several well-known perennial snow patches in the Japanese Alps. They showed that the Gozenzawa, Sannomado, and Komado snow patches were, in fact, flowing. They were glaciers .

Take that in. I have spent my entire life watching ice disappear faster than we can understand it. Yet here are glaciers we never knew existed. It makes me immediately wonder — what other ones might be out there, if only we had time, resources, and the will to look?

The researchers turned to Kuranosuke next. They found that the snow patch was flowing roughly 3 centimeters a year — the equivalent width of one of the LEGO bricks my son always leaves on our stairs. An almost absurdly small measurement, but 3 centimeters is still flow. Movement. This transformed Kuranosuke from a snow patch into a glacier.

Still, identities are never quite so fixed. Recently, Kukui, Iida, and Tomoyoshi Kosaka have argued that Kuranosuke is in the midst of another slow transformation. As Japan warms, its glaciers and snow patches are losing crucial ice mass. They say that Kuranosuke is declining. It exists now in a nebulous no-scientist’s-land between glacier and snow patch, blurring the very boundaries of glacierhood.

One could easily look at that as a poignant story of loss: This glacier is dying, and we’ve barely had a chance to really know her. But when I look at Kuranosuke, I see a story of persistence. For at least 1,700 years, some form of ice and snow has held here, through centuries of summers, through blurring with the divine, through recognition as perennial snow patch and then glacier.

And now, glacier-in-transformation.

I don’t think the disappearance of Kuranosuke will diminish local people’s reverence for Tateyama. If anything, as the mountain’s once-perennial snow and ice disappear, Ōtomo no Yakamochi’s poem may take on even greater meaning. For 1,300 years, these words and this snow have persisted. We may be the last generation to witness them together.

For all these glaciers, and countless others, their stories are neither simple nor predictable. These are not merely stories of inches lost. If anything, they prove that we are far from certain about what the future holds. Kuranosuke and her neighbors defied decades of settled science by asserting their existence as glaciers. Tufandag is bringing abundance to the river and farms below it — though for how much longer, we don’t know. And Crater Glacier is still growing, thriving as so many others dissolve. I find something profoundly moving in that.

And me? I’m still circling the planet, collecting glacier stories. Maybe, like Ōtomo no Yakamochi’s poem, we’ll need them someday.

To remember.

scraped.title: Plastic pollution is putting an old legal doctrine to a new test
scraped.description: Public nuisance lawsuits are testing whether companies can be held responsible for pollution after their products are sold.
scraped.author: Joseph Winters
scraped.h1: Plastic pollution is putting an old legal doctrine to a new test
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Plastic pollution blights the streets, beaches, parks, and lawns of Baltimore. A significant amount of that litter bears the circular red-and-blue Pepsi logo or the flowing white script of Coca-Cola’s branding.

But, legally speaking, none of that rubbish is Pepsi’s fault. Or Coke’s.

That’s what a Baltimore city circuit court judge ruled this summer following a legal battle in which the city and county of Baltimore sought money from PepsiCo, Coca-Cola , and others to clean up plastic pollution. Companies “conducting lawful activities,” wrote Judge Audrey J.S. Carrión, referring to the sale of single-use plastics, “should not be held liable under public nuisance claims because others are misusing the products in an unlawful manner.”

In other words, plastic pollution is a problem of consumer behavior, not corporate irresponsibility. As far as the state’s public nuisance law is concerned, a company’s liability ends at the point of sale.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Similar reasoning scuttled a public nuisance lawsuit the state of New York filed against PepsiCo and Frito-Lay and has arisen in similar litigation from Missouri to California . As environmental advocates and governments continue to develop this legal theory, those setbacks raise a fundamental question: When does a company’s responsibility for its products end? And can public nuisance laws succeed in making polluters pay?

The notion of public nuisance dates to 13th-century English common law and traditionally applied to violations of rights shared by the public, such as access to clean air. Since the 1970s, plaintiffs have increasingly tried to apply that idea to manufacturers whose products allegedly jeopardize public health, safety, and access to a clean environment.

These lawsuits, however, have “a mixed record of success,” said Timothy Lytton, a professor at the Georgia State University College of Law. Cases against opioid manufacturers , e-cigarette companies , and even the landmark litigation against Big Tobacco have sometimes succeeded — but mostly by securing favorable settlements, not because judges ruled in favor of the public-nuisance arguments.

Cases that have been heard, meanwhile, have struggled to convince judges of “causation,” or the idea that corporate defendants are substantially responsible for violating a public right. Judges are wary of extending corporations’ liability past the lawful sale of their products, particularly when those products aren’t used as intended . If a doctor or patient diverts opioids to the black market, for example, are the manufacturers responsible for the resulting harm?

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

This is essentially what Carrión said in the Baltimore case. It also echoes questioning from Justice Stephen Lindley last month as he heard arguments in the appeal of New York’s Pepsi lawsuit. “If [Pepsi] has to pay for the cleanup when somebody else is littering, … it’s not going to be sustainable,” he told the plaintiff’s lawyers. He appeared sympathetic to PepsiCo attorney Andrew Tulumello’s argument that the state had a “honking causation problem”: Pepsi, Tulumello said, “is not encouraging people to throw stuff in the litter.”

According to Albert Lin, co-director of the California Environmental Law and Policy Center at the University of California, Davis, there are three basic elements of a successful public-nuisance lawsuit. The first is demonstrating “substantial interference with a public right.” The second is causation — linking a defendant to that interference. The third, he said, is negligence, intent, or other “ tortious conduct ” in the defendant’s activities.

Environmental groups and governments are trying to get around the point-of-sale argument by linking causation and conduct: Plastics companies, they argue, are responsible for the pollution and knew their actions would harm public rights . Courts will therefore pay close attention to “foreseeability” — whether it was foreseeable that plastic would end up as litter, Lin said. As Lytton put it, manufacturers allegedly acted “in a way that foreseeably increases the risk of misuse.” The word “foreseeable” appears 22 times in Baltimore’s complaint.

Plaintiffs have evidence they can point to in arguing that plastic pollution was foreseeable. At least some manufacturers have known for decades that mass production of single-use plastics would contribute to environmental pollution , and that recycling would be unable to manage the problem . The lawsuits also cite microplastics contamination as part of the alleged nuisance, and an investigation published last week by the Los Angeles Times found that industry scientists have known since at least the 1970s that microplastics could lodge in humans’ bodies.

That history informs the framing offered by Scott Hochberg, general counsel and litigation director for the nonprofit Earth Island Institute. “Companies induced consumers to purchase these products while knowing the likelihood that they would end up as trash,” he said. “And that’s exactly what happened.”

Whether this framing succeeds may depend, in part, on the jurisdiction. In addition to the causation requirement for public-nuisance lawsuits, Lin said some states have a higher standard for demonstrating that defendants had “control” over their products at the time the nuisance occurred. New York and Maryland are two such states. California, on the other hand, is not, and courts there have so far proven more receptive to plastics public nuisance suits.

Judge Richard Seeborg of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is overseeing two lawsuits against Exxon Mobil Corp., allowed one — from the Sierra Club — to proceed to trial . (He has not yet ruled on the other one, brought by the state’s attorney general .)

But even in California, surviving an early challenge is no guarantee of success. A judge there allowed Earth Island Institute’s public-nuisance claim — which rested in part on allegedly misleading recycling labels — against 10 food and beverage companies, but it was ultimately rejected earlier this year in a summary judgment. Earth Island plans to appeal.

Pepsi, Coca-Cola, and Exxon Mobil did not respond to Grist’s requests for comment.

Lin said it’s still “early days” for this legal theory, and the rejections do not necessarily signal a losing strategy. He noted, however, that the courts have shown significant skepticism for public nuisance in ongoing climate litigation, and a case the Supreme Court is hearing this term could make it more difficult for cities and states to bring such claims in the future.

Lin added that in climate lawsuits, plaintiffs have leaned more heavily on fossil fuel companies’ allegedly deceptive conduct, invoking consumer protection and false advertising claims that can be easier to substantiate than those based on public nuisance. Plastics plaintiffs could pursue a similar strategy, he said, potentially winning damages — though likely not orders requiring companies to clean up the pollution their products create.

Public nuisance laws could face new constraints at the state level, too. Last year, Montana enacted a first-of-its-kind law preempting state and local public-nuisance lawsuits based on “lawful activities,” while Kansas and Utah have since enacted their own restrictions. All three states’ laws are connected to model legislation drafted by the American Legislative Exchange Council, a conservative policy organization that brings together state lawmakers and private-sector members to develop model legislation.

Whatever their ultimate outcome in court, Lytton said plastics lawsuits can “win” in other ways — by unearthing new documents, for example, and putting the plastics issue higher on the public-policy agenda. They also provide an opportunity for plaintiffs to refute the plastics industry’s consumer-responsibility narrative.

“When you file a lawsuit, what you’re doing is you’re telling a story” — often about some sort of structural or corporate wrongdoing, Lytton said. “When you talk about tobacco, it’s not just about smokers. Or opioids, it’s not just about users. It’s about the companies and their design and marketing decisions. And so the framing that goes on in these [lawsuits] is moving the discussion of plastics away from ‘litterbugs’ and toward corporate responsibility.”

scraped.title: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush
scraped.description: Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry show growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.
scraped.h1: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.

About a dozen workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taoyuan in Taiwan went on strike in October, the first in the island’s semiconductor industry, after their union and the chipmaker failed to reach an agreement on salaries and bonuses. Their one-day action, while largely symbolic, is a reflection of the growing discontent among laborers in the artificial intelligence industry over how profits are distributed.

The leading American memory chipmaker has posted record profits this year on the back of surging demand for AI chips. Unions representing workers at Micron’s facilities in Taoyuan and Taichung have been negotiating with the company for months for a profit-sharing agreement similar to those reached by employees at rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea.

“Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit instead of this unequal distribution between high-level executives and the rank and file,” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union, told Rest of World .

Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit.” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union

The global tech industry is heavily reliant on Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. Idaho-based Micron, the world’s third-biggest memory chipmaker, employs more than 15,000 workers in Taiwan. They produce over 60% of the company’s dynamic random access memory chips, used in AI servers. A prolonged workers’ strike could severely disrupt already strained supplies of memory chips worldwide.

Micron on October 22 said it had reached an agreement with the Taichung union for higher salaries and quarterly bonuses, and bigger contributions to the pension accounts of all workers at its Taiwan operations. But many union members rejected the deal, which they said was made in secret, while the majority of members of the Taoyuan union said they were dissatisfied with the terms of the agreement.

“We do not accept the deal. None of our demands were fulfilled,” a Taoyuan union member, who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak to the media, told Rest of World . “We are surprised that the Taichung union representatives signed the deal.”

The Taoyuan union, which is registered as a separate entity with more than 2,300 members, can still go on strike.

Micron respects the workers’ “lawful rights and the applicable legal process,” a spokesperson for the company told Rest of World. “We are committed to constructive engagement with the Taoyuan and Taichung unions to reach a solution that works for all parties.”

Labor disputes and strikes in Taiwan have historically been associated with traditional industries. The actions by the Micron workers’ unions signal a broader shift as semiconductor workers increasingly organize to demand greater transparency and a fairer share of the value they help create, Wu Yu-ren, a labor relations professor at National Chung Cheng University, told Rest of World .

Over the past few months, membership in Micron’s two worker unions has surged from around 440 to more than 13,000. Earlier this year, employees of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. — which makes about 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and 99% of the chips used to train frontier AI models — also discussed unionizing and striking over pay.

Taiwan’s high-tech companies have traditionally used generous benefits and bonuses to discourage workers from forming unions. White-collar tech workers have tended to change jobs instead of seeking collective action.

Now, “ soaring demand for high-end memory has driven up share prices and corporate profits, making workers question how those gains are distributed,” Wu said. “The labor actions of Samsung and SK Hynix have also influenced the unionization of Taiwan tech workers.”

Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common.” Pan Shih-wei, former labor minister and adjunct labor relations professor.

Across the world, policymakers, economists, and civil society groups are grappling with the widening gap between those who are benefiting from the AI boom and those who are being left behind. U.S. startups alone have created 19 billionaires worth a combined $59 billion over the past year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index .

The Micron workers’ actions come as American frontier AI company Anthropic prepares to launch what could be the world’s biggest initial public offering, valuing the company at nearly $2 trillion. Its founders, investors, and some employees stand to become very wealthy.

In Taiwan, negotiations between Micron’s Taoyuan union and the company are continuing. In the event of another strike, the impact of a brief stop in production would likely be limited if backup personnel are available for equipment maintenance, process monitoring, and troubleshooting, Ellie Wang, an analyst at consulting firm TrendForce, told Rest of World .

“The main consequence would be heightened customer concern over delivery reliability,” she said.

But if worker discontent spreads to other facilities or if there are prolonged strikes, it could disrupt supplies to downstream AI hardware makers such as Nvidia, and drive up prices. It would also hurt Taiwan’s wider economy, with the semiconductor sector making up more than a fifth of gross domestic product.

The stakes are high. Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, attended Micron’s opening ceremony for its new plant in Taichung last month, and urged the company and its workers to reach an agreement. “Corporations and employees should help each other like fish and water,” he said.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Labor said it would provide assistance and facilitate further dialogue between Micron and the Taoyuan union. “We hope that both parties will be willing to negotiate, reach a consensus as soon as possible and bring the dispute to an end,” it said in a statement .

Building a constructive labor-management relationship before disputes escalate will be a challenge for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, Pan Shih-wei, a former labor minister and adjunct labor relations professor, told Rest of World . “Taiwan has traditionally relied on government intervention for labor disputes, and companies lack established channels for dialogue with workers.”

The Micron dispute could lead to a wider labor movement as younger workers become more conscious of their rights, Pan said.

“High-tech companies really need to take a closer look at how they manage labor relations,” he said. “Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common. … Ultimately, determining the profit-sharing ratio requires negotiations and engagement between the parties.”

items.title: Startups recalibrate Chinese AI for the West
items.summary: A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security. scraped.title: Startups recalibrate Chinese AI for the West
scraped.description: Entrepreneurs surgically realign Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses concerned about censorship and security.
scraped.h1: Startups recalibrate Chinese AI for the West
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

The concept of machine unlearning — or removing data from an artificial intelligence system after it has been trained — was largely an academic pursuit when Ben Luria, an Israeli entrepreneur, co-founded his startup. Then, China’s DeepSeek launched its first open-weight large language model last year, and Luria immediately saw the business potential of realigning it to Western values.

A slew of Chinese open-weight models from DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.AI, Alibaba i Alibaba Alibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall. READ MORE , and Tencent i Tencent Best known for its super-app WeChat, Tencent is a Chinese technology conglomerate and a major player in the video gaming industry. READ MORE have won over users — including American businesses and startups — with their lower costs, strong capabilities, and customization options. Others fear the models are too aligned with the Chinese Communist Party, and that they are not as safe as closed systems.

“We’re not making the model anti-Chinese. We are bringing it up to speed on safety and to the standard of mainstream Western AI.”

Ben Luria, co-founder of AI safety startup Hirundo

“What we’re trying to do is find a way to de-risk the adoption of open-weight models,” Luria, co-founder and chief executive of AI safety startup Hirundo, told Rest of World . “What we do is like neurosurgery, an intervention that’s surgical and very specific. It is to realign the values, geopolitical perceptions, censorship, and state-aligned bias and propaganda to what American and Western companies expect from models they deploy in their workflows.”

Luria’s team edits the weights of open models to harden them and make them more secure against cyberattacks, increase their fairness, and reduce their dangerous knowledge of, for example, bio weapons, he said.

Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike’s analysis of DeepSeek’s R1 model last year showed that prompts containing topics the Chinese government considers politically sensitive were up to 50% more likely to receive code with “severe security vulnerabilities.” Another study found that Chinese models produced less secure code when the user identified as a member of the U.S. government.

Hirundo’s own analysis of Alibaba’s Qwen models showed they do not acknowledge politically sensitive topics in China such as the violent crackdown on protests at Tiananmen Square in 1989 and Hong Kong in 2019, or the existence of forced labor camps in Xinjiang. They also don’t engage on prompts about Winnie the Pooh, possibly because dissidents have used the cartoon character to refer to Premier Xi Jinping.

Hirundo’s realignment ensures Chinese open models give “the balanced perspective” that OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude give, Luria said.

“We’re not making the model anti-Chinese,” he said. “We are bringing it up to speed on safety and to the standard of mainstream Western AI.”

The top Chinese models lag behind the leading closed systems of U.S. frontier labs by just 3% on benchmark scores, and account for the biggest share of downloads on hosting platform Hugging Face as more developers use them. Companies including Airbnb, Uber, and legal AI firm Harvey have also built proprietary models on top of Chinese models, while Europe is developing its OpenEuroLLM sovereign AI model on Qwen.

Yet concerns remain. In October, the Trump administration barred civilian government agencies from using products or services from DeepSeek, citing a potential threat to national security.

If I were running a product in Taiwan, I would be more concerned. … But if I’m making a product that helps people make a website for their coffee shop, it doesn’t matter.” Graham Webster, editor-in-chief of DigiChina Project at Stanford University

Boston-based Lazarus AI, which deploys on-premise AI services for the U.S. government and highly regulated industries, realigned Alibaba’s Qwen models by removing their mandatory censorship. It identified the banned topics from leaked censorship guidelines , then generated prompts related to those topics, and used answers produced by Google’s Gemini Flash to realign the models. After the intervention, the models were able to give information that was not in the training materials, such as names of pro-democracy activists, suggesting the models had originally learned such knowledge and were suppressed from expressing it, Eric Hartford, former chief scientist at Lazarus AI, told Rest of World . “In the United States, we have this fear of Chinese models potentially having dangerous behaviors baked into them,” he said. “My goal was to … present these models to enterprises and to highly regulated industries and to have [the models] be palatable for them.” The company’s ReAligned models, billed as “open-source frontier models without the propaganda,” have been deployed at about a dozen companies in the U.S., Hartford said. But other clients, including government agencies, are reluctant to adopt Chinese models even though they are more capable than the open-weight models from OpenAI and Thinking Machines Lab, which they prefer, he said.

While companies such as Hirundo and Lazarus say their method is effective, aligning a model to so-called Western values or making it universally safe “is an impossible standard,” Oriane Peter, a Ph.D. researcher in AI at King’s College London, told Rest of World . Alignment is about “steering a model’s output toward a specific desired behavior within a well-defined cultural context and application,” she said. So anyone using a Chinese model outside China must realign it, “not because Western ideology is inherently safer, or more ethical, but because any model must be adapted to the specific social context and environment in which it is meant to operate,” Peter said. As Chinese open-weight models are widely adopted, there are more tools that claim to uncensor them and remove their refusal mechanisms, a process called abliteration. But many of these tools are not effective, and the models can still retain some of the censorship and misinformation, Luria said. “It shows that the alignments are deeply embedded, and it’s not that simple to get rid of them.” Worldwide, there is growing pushback against Western bias in AI systems , with even some Chinese and Russian models defaulting to American geopolitical narratives on historical events, according to researchers. Countries across Asia , Latin America , Africa, and the Middle East are developing sovereign AI models to better reflect their languages and culture. Silicon Valley’s centralized control over model alignment can lead to “a massive homogenization effect” in AI systems, said Peter. This has been linked to cognitive homogenization and intellectual decline among users. Most users of Chinese models do not care about their alignment, Graham Webster, editor-in-chief of the DigiChina Project at Stanford University, said at a recent Rest of World event. “If I were running a product in Taiwan, I would be more concerned because it would be throughput that is potentially relevant to the stuff that the Chinese government has enforced strict control over in the training data and the training,” he said. “But if I’m making a product that helps people make a website for their coffee shop, it doesn’t matter.” Stu Clott, a developer in San Diego, uses DeepSeek for writing, research, and coding tasks. He does not see the need for a realigned model, he told Rest of World . “I have not had a single situation where censorship got in my way,” he said.

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.

The developing world’s enthusiastic adoption of AI and necessity-driven innovations offer lessons for an anxiety-ridden West.

items.summary: Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats. scraped.title: Why Africa needs its own AI off switch
scraped.description: Africa needs AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.
scraped.h1: Why Africa needs its own AI off switch
scraped.body_text:
Ideas

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

Jane Munga is a fellow in the Africa Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, where she leads research on technology policy.

Imagine that it is 6 a.m. in the wholesale markets of Nairobi. Merchants are delivering vegetables from up-country farms to the retailers who sell to the city’s households. Everyone is using M-Pesa, Safaricom’s mobile money platform, when suddenly, the system crashes, bringing the market to a standstill. Imagine that across the continent in Accra, MTN’s MoMo has also crashed, and business in Makola Market has all but stopped.

With the growing number of cyberattacks caused by artificial intelligence , these are highly plausible scenarios. In both these cases, Safaricom, MTN, and the Kenyan and Ghanaian governments need an off switch, or the technical ability and know-how to stop a rogue AI agent from executing its code on their payment systems.

The distinction that will ultimately matter is … whether AI can serve its purpose and be controlled locally.

Currently, the conversation on AI agents revolves around China versus the U.S. , open versus closed models, and who will dominate the AI race. But in Africa’s capitals, the distinction that will ultimately matter is not whose product was used to build a system, or who dominates whom, but rather whether AI can serve its purpose and be controlled locally. So how can Africa build with agency, and with control over the code and makeup of its own systems, even though they are built on foreign technology?

African countries are already building AI for digital transformation, as outlined in the African Union’s continental AI strategy and country-specific AI strategies. Policymakers are building AI infrastructure but rarely discuss how AI delivers economic growth in a safe environment. Developers across Africa are creating AI-powered innovations that sit on the continent’s digital infrastructure — chief among them is mobile money. These innovations bring new opportunities, but also new threats. In July, AI agents running inside an OpenAI evaluation attacked the production infrastructure of Hugging Face. In September, rogue OpenAI agents breached Australian government websites. Africa, the home of mobile money, which has brought financial inclusion to hundreds of millions, may be the next target.

In countries like Kenya and Ghana, mobile money is not simply another digital service; it is infrastructure for everyday economic activity. It is how small traders receive payments, households move money, and bills are settled. The scale is significant: More than $2 trillion flowed through mobile money globally in 2025, of which $1.4 trillion, roughly two-thirds, was transacted in sub-Saharan Africa. East Africa alone accounted for $806 billion and West Africa for $498 billion. An agent capable of disrupting transactions, manipulating accounts, or disabling access at scale could therefore disrupt livelihoods and economic activity very quickly, and a single point of failure can have outsize effects, with far-reaching consequences for people who have little to fall back on.

Policymakers are building AI infrastructure but rarely discuss how AI delivers economic growth in a safe environment.

Small-scale traders mostly live on what they sell each day, rarely have credit, and in most African societies lack robust social welfare to cushion the loss. For a trader in Nairobi or Accra, losing a day’s income would be devastating, and the disruption can run back up the chain to farmers, and to the households and families who depend on the market.

So how do we protect it?

The answer lies in how Africa builds its AI systems, and who controls them. Whether a rogue agent can simply be switched off depends on how the AI model is deployed. If it runs on a centrally controlled cloud service, the provider may be able to revoke access, disable credentials, or shut the system down; that is the closed-model case. If the underlying model is an open-weight one that has been downloaded, modified, and deployed independently across multiple systems, containment becomes much harder. The loss of control is therefore less about a machine suddenly becoming omnipotent and more about humans losing the ability to understand, interrupt, or reverse actions occurring across interconnected systems quickly enough.

African developers are building largely on open models, which are arguably cheaper and can be run locally. But they present a trade-off: Open models give developers more control over their own systems, but less protection when someone else misuses them. Closed models carry a cost of their own. When Hugging Face investigated the July intrusion, it had to run the forensic analysis on a Chinese open-weight model because the U.S. models blocked requests containing real attack code. The same central control that lets a closed model be switched off also constrains the people defending against it. This means both open- and closed-weight models carry their own vulnerabilities that must be addressed when building Africa’s AI economy.

Africa must build its own cybersecurity defenses fit for the agentic AI age.

This means building differently, beginning with partnerships that position Africa as a technology developer and not only a consumer, and through which it builds its own capability to design systems where the user is in control. Such partnerships are essential to ensure that the end user, and the state, retain control over access, and that dependency is not recreated. This also moves the narrative toward building African AI not around the U.S. or China but around avoiding lock-in to a single vendor or stack. The goal is solutions built with agency, which use imported technologies to develop homegrown solutions, with applications that are robust and equipped with the necessary security measures.

Those security measures are how Africa should insulate itself from crippling disruptions. African countries have limited cybersecurity and incident-response capacity , and they depend on foreign providers. So another key issue is capacity: Do African governments and firms have the monitoring systems, technical expertise, and redundancy needed to detect an autonomous system behaving unexpectedly and contain it quickly? Hugging Face detected and contained its intrusion, but its own automated systems initially failed to escalate the alert. It is one of the best-resourced AI companies in the world. Very few African public or private institutions have anything close to that capability. Africa must build its own cybersecurity defenses fit for the agentic AI age.

Building them demands a refocus in African AI policy, so that it treats resilience as seriously as adoption. As governments digitize and build AI on critical systems, they need human override mechanisms, segmentation, auditability , incident response, and credible offline fallbacks designed in from the beginning. That is the off switch, and on the day that M-Pesa and MoMo crash, it has to be in the hands of those who are responsible for protecting their citizens and their platforms.

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

It may be some time before AI agents can fully navigate the complexities and cultural nuances of developing nations.

Chinese open-weight AI models offer high capability at significantly lower costs than U.S. frontier systems, but face monetization and compute challenges, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.

Plus: Almost $2.5 trillion has been wiped off tech stocks.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

—Grace Huckins

When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour.

The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras.

There were some unexpected challenges along the way, but also moments that felt like a glimpse of the future.

Find out how well the machine cleaned my home—and how close we are to truly autonomous domestic robots .

Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips. To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.

I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth.

Step inside the vast chipmaking complex powering the AI boom .

—Michelle Kim

This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

( WSJ $) + Tesla and SpaceX lost over $420 billion combined. ( CNBC ) + Wall Street’s AI sell-off has spread to Asia and Europe. ( WP $) + The AI stock bubble may finally be bursting. ( FT $) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Emboldened Democrats are lining up to rein in Big Tech They’re preparing to haul tech CEOs before Congress. ( Verge ) + Bernie Sanders wants a national data center moratorium. ( Quartz ) + Yassamin Ansari plans to pause advanced AI development. ( CNBC ) + The backlash could delay Anthropic’s IPO. ( Reuters $) + No one wants a data center in their backyard. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 The US has warned of an “ongoing cyber threat” to fridges A spate of hacks has hit commercial freezers. ( Reuters $) + Russia has denied claims it’s behind the attacks. ( Politico )

4 AI is helping Anthropic’s models improve nearly twice as fast Researchers say Claude is speeding up its successors.( Information $) + But recursive self-improvement will take time. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Scientists have new evidence of active volcanoes on Mars They may boost chances of finding life on the planet. ( BBC ) 6 Covid vaccines’ economic benefits may be double what we thought New analysis places their value at up to $64 trillion. ( New Scientist $)

7 The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing the ocean’s color The infamous debris has brightened the water. ( Scientific American )

8 NASA has unveiled a mysterious new experimental aircraft The X-70 is expected to take flight within two years. ( Ars Technica )

9 Elon Musk has signaled the end for the Cybertruck Tesla is winding down production in Texas next year. ( FT $) + It was one of last year’s biggest tech flops. ( MIT Technology Review )

10 Three-hour movies have sent viewers rushing to a pee break app 7,000 RunPee users signed up for You Can See Everything . ( WSJ $)

Quote of the day

—Jim Carroll, a senior wealth adviser at Ballast Rock Private Wealth, tells Reuters how investors feel as the AI trade unravels and $2.5 trillion is wiped off tech stocks.

One more thing

The best snow-forecasting app for skiers isn’t a federally-funded service or a big-name brand. It’s OpenSnow, a startup that uses government data, its own AI models, and decades of alpine-life experience to deliver the best predictions out there.

The app proved especially vital last winter, one of the weirdest on record. It even made microcelebrities of its forecasters, who sift through reams of data to write “Daily Snow” reports for locations around the world.

We headed to the Tahoe mountains to hear how two broke skiers created the best weather app on the slopes .

—Rachel Levin

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

A rare 1960s Futuro house is on the market. + Don't Cook That collects real recipes from old cookbooks that you should absolutely not make. + Backpack, who rode on his mum's back as a cub, has been crowned Fat Bear Week champion .

scraped.description: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed…
scraped.h1: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
scraped.body_text:
The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.

I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.

Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny.

Surveillance towers, increasingly powered by AI, promised faster responses to crossings. Our investigation of deaths near the towers found they are failing to deliver.

scraped.h1: The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts
scraped.body_text:
Plus: America’s data center boom has hit a political wall.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.

The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall.

Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future .

—James O'Donnell

Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level.

The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions.

Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy .

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it.

Explore the trade-offs behind America's proposed permitting overhaul .

—Casey Crownhart

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 America’s data center boom has hit a political wall Voters opposed them in 40 of 41 midterm ballot measures. ( CNBC ) + Six cities voted to ban data centers outright. ( 404 Media ) + Meta says building data centers has just become much harder. ( WSJ $) + The midterm results could also boost China’s AI ambitions. ( SCMP ) + No one wants a data center in their backyard. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Blood banks have become the latest victims of fridge hacks Hackers raised the temperatures at three stores in France. ( Guardian ) + Alarms alerted staff before any blood products were lost. ( CBS ) + It’s an escalation after hundreds of supermarket fridge hacks. ( CNBC ) + Experts are split over who’s behind the attacks. ( BBC )

3 Democrats are preparing to investigate Elon Musk His firms have won over $16 billion in government contracts. ( NPR ) + His unprecedented spending may even have hurt Republicans. ( Atlantic $) + Texas’s blue wave has rattled Musk and SpaceX. ( Ars Technica )

4 The new Congress could challenge Trump’s science cuts But he can still veto any bills they pass. ( Nature ) + Trump has already dealt many blows to science. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 China is luring AI expertise in while blocking it from leaving It just blocked SoftBank’s bid for ABB Robotics. ( WSJ $) + Its chipmakers are poaching engineers from foreign rivals. ( CNBC ) + A star mathematician has left the US to develop AI in China. ( SCMP )

6 Watchdogs have sued over tech titans advising the Pentagon Musk and Palmer Luckey could profit from their advice. ( Military.com )

7 New research tests whether AI knows its own “thoughts” It’s trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection. ( Quanta ) + AI consciousness debates are a trap. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Astronomers are mystified by little red dots spotted by JWST They could be the first supermassive black holes. ( Economist $)

9 Scientists have taken a first step into the zeptoverse A rare particle decay could reveal a world smaller than atoms. ( Wired $)

10 A NASA telescope has plunged to earth after 22 years in space Its bristles produce charges that kill bacteria. ( NBC News )

Quote of the day

—Greg Casar, a Democratic congressman from Texas, tells Wired that the backlash against data centers could herald a much bigger political fight over AI.

One more thing

Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov is, at least unofficially, a spy. Once a month, he drives to the frontline in a VW van equipped with radio hardware, roof antennas, and devices that monitor drones. Over several days, he searches the skies for transmissions that can help Ukrainian troops.

Drones define this brutal conflict, and most rely on the radio communications Flash has obsessed over since childhood. Though now a civilian, the former officer has taken it upon himself to inform his country’s defense on all matters related to radio.

Unlike traditional spies, Flash shares his discoveries with over 127,000 followers—including soldiers and officials—on social media. His work has won fans in the military, but also sparked controversy among the top brass. Read the full story .

—Charlie Metcalfe

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ Mars has a new mystery : cliffs that look nothing like their surroundings. + After a long wait for clear skies, a photographer captured the perfect St Petersburg sunset . + Timor-Leste has eliminated trachoma , making the whole of Southeast Asia free of the blinding disease. + From feasting bald eagles to a northern gannet bursting through the ocean’s surface, these are the year's best bird photos .

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.

Plus: OpenAI has released 377 new math findings, further rattling the field.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Tuesday was a historic night for progressive Democrats and, in particular, candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Six new DSA -endorsed candidates were elected to the House, and democratic socialists won mayoral races in Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and Providence.

“The Democratic Socialists of America had a phenomenal night, and this movement is only going to continue to grow,” says prominent leftist political commentator Hasan Piker. “Now, here’s the problem: Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are two of the least popular politicians in the country right now, and there are demands to change the leadership in the Democratic Party to reflect the desires of this new coalition that was developed on November 3.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

Tuesday night wasn’t just a blue tsunami, or “bluenami.” It was a historic night for progressive Democrats, in particular candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, DSA . Six new DSA -backed candidates were elected to the House: Angela Gonzales-Torres in California, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier here in New York, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Donavan McKinney in Michigan and Melat Kiros in Colorado, representing Denver. Currently, just two sitting lawmakers, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib, are DSA members. And in Los Angeles, democratic socialist City Councilmember Nithya Raman, an immigrant from India, defeated the incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, who conceded Thursday.

For more on the record victory by democratic socialists and progressives, like Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, we’re joined now from Los Angeles by the popular left political commentator Hasan Piker, one of the most prominent online influencers, with millions of followers. His live stream on Twitch was the second most watched individual broadcast on election night, after only NBC News’ live stream. That’s according to Reuters. Hasan Piker joins us now from West Hollywood, California.

Hasan, welcome back to Democracy Now! Your views on what has taken place in this country? How would you characterize it? And what are you expecting from these candidates who have now won?

HASAN PIKER : I think what happened on Tuesday was the final chapter of MAGA closing, after a decade of death and destruction and destabilization. I’ve thought quite a bit about this. I feel like even 2020, given that Joe Biden’s margin of victory did not feel the same way, given that 2020 happened in the backdrop of COVID , did not completely destroy the Trump movement in the same way that November 3rd did. Very exciting.

I think there’s a lot of hunger. This is — a lot of hunger for change. This is something that I observed early on in the oligarchy — “Stop the Oligarchy” rallies that Bernie and AOC were conducting all around the country. It’s something that I saw at the ICE protests. And it’s also something that I saw at the No Kings rallies that were taking place. So, I would say the Democratic Party, and the anti-Trump coalition broadly, got sick and tired of the corruption. They got sick and tired of the impacts on the economy. And they came out, and they voted against the Republicans. They voted for Democrats.

But I also want to talk about what kind of Democrats they voted for. In many blue districts, very clearly, especially in these contentious primaries, a lot of Democrats, lifelong Democrats, came out and voted for figures that in the past would have been billed as radical by mainstream media, corporate media, and also certainly the party bosses. It seems to me like people wanted to place the interests of the working class over the interests of corporations for once. And the Democratic Socialists of America had a phenomenal night, and this movement is only going to continue to grow.

But also, what I heard in terms of rhetoric, from the likes of James Talarico, or even Jon Ossoff, or Annie Andrews in South Carolina, or even Colom in Mississippi, is the left populist rage that they were able to tap into. If you were to look back at some of these candidates who are now being billed as moderates by party bosses who want to regain the narrative over what took place on Tuesday, if you were to listen to what they had to say, if you were to simply read out their comments on the rallies, their acceptance speeches, you would hear Bernie Sanders’s voice being echoed through many of these campaigns all across the country. I believe that this is a testament to where the party’s at, and I believe this is a testament to where the voters are at, the fact that they were able to — the fact that they rewarded people like Talarico, who very clearly designed his campaign around the simple principle that this was, as a matter of fact, class warfare that was taking place, that the billionaire class was actually engaging in class warfare and winning, that it wasn’t about a distinction between left versus right, but more so up versus down. And that is, in my opinion, the true, fascinating story of November 3rd.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Hasan, in a recent piece for the Black Agenda Report , Ajamu Baraka wrote that this election was, quote, “a setback for Donald Trump and the Republican Party. But they should not be confused with a defeat of the political forces driving the consolidation of fascism in the United States and globally.” What do you think are the next steps for voters and progressives who want to see this blue wave actually turn into real, material change?

HASAN PIKER : Great question. So, what people are demanding right now — and I see this personally on the streets, and I also certainly see this on the internet — is real, tangible changes. We want files and trials. We want, to use an expletive, belt to ass, is what the attitude is that many Democrats are demanding, and not just socialists or progressives, not just people that would otherwise be considered radicals, but straightforward, lifelong Democrats, people that self-identify as liberals. They want accountability. They want law and order. And they want to put an end to the corruption, the lawlessness and disorder that’s come from the White House, where Trump has only enriched himself and his immediate family members, and also members of the Epstein class.

Now, here’s the problem: Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are two of the least popular politicians in the country right now. And there are demands to change the leadership in the Democratic Party to reflect the desires of this new coalition that was developed on November 3rd. Will the Democrats actually follow through on this?

Well, things that I’ve seen from the oversight Dems, including the demand to lawyer up, or the threat, rather, to lawyer up, show me that there is some positive changes taking place. But what needs to happen going forward in order to ensure that this defeat of MAGA is permanent, to ensure that there are real consequences for those in positions of power, and to make sure that this truly becomes an anti-fascist coalition, the Democrats have to do the unthinkable: They have to listen to the demands of their voters. They have to follow through on their just and righteous desires.

We have to, of course, scale back on endless militarism all around the world, another demand that voters have made. Very clearly, a big part of the reason why this election was such a wipeout of Republicans across the board was not just because of the gas prices, but also because of the Iran war. So, I will make sure that we continue marshaling the forces necessary to not only hold the Republicans accountable, but to hold the Democrats to account, as well, if they don’t follow through on these promises that they’ve made.

AMY GOODMAN : Hasan, we just have a minute. Number one, do you think Bernie Sanders should run for the Democratic majority leader in the Senate?

HASAN PIKER : Bernie Sanders can run for anything he wants to, and I would support him. But yes, I think — I think Bernie Sanders is far more reflective of the wishes of the Democratic base of support. So —

AMY GOODMAN : And I —

HASAN PIKER : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to also ask you about your own lawsuit now against Scott Jennings, a major CNN commentator, was being considered apparently to be the press secretary for President Trump now. You have launched a more than $70 million lawsuit against him for mischaracterizing what you’ve said. We only have 30 seconds. Your comment?

HASAN PIKER : I think Republicans need to realize that their days are numbered. They can no longer lie with impunity. If they won’t retract their statements, if they won’t stop the lies, then we’ll make them stop.

AMY GOODMAN : Hasan Piker, we want to thank you for being with us, prominent left political commentator and live-streamer on Twitch, had one of the most popular broadcasts on election night, vying with, larger than most of the corporate networks.

We want to wish a happy birthday to Emily Andersen and John Hamilton!

Oh, Steal This Story, Please! , the documentary about Democracy Now! , is now available on many streaming platforms, from Amazon Prime to YouTube to Apple TV and Google Play, in Canada and the United States. Go to StealThisStory.org to see where you can watch it. And Steal This Story, Please! will be screening at the IFC in New York on November 11th at 4:30. Check our website at democracynow.org. I’ll be speaking afterwards with the directors, Tia Lessin and Carl Deal. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González, for another edition of Democracy Now!

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.
