scraped.h1: You turn to us for voices you won't hear anywhere else.
scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago voted for Democrats in large numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate. Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in an historic victory, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Democratic Latino governors.

“Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state,” says Democracy Now! co-host Juan Gonzalez. “Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latino voters towards Democrats in state after state. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago swung to Democrats in huge numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate.

Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in historic victories, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Latinx Democratic governors. On Tuesday night, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa defeated the incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott with a margin of over 700,000 votes. This is a clip from her speech.

GOV .- ELECT GINA HINOJOSA : I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas.

AMY GOODMAN : That was Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaking in Austin, Texas, right after she was declared the winner.

And this is California Governor-elect Xavier Becerra addressing supporters Tuesday night in Sacramento after he easily defeated Republican challenger Steve Hilton.

GOV .- ELECT XAVIER BECERRA : Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era. Tonight, I have a message for all those who have been made to feel afraid. There’s a new sheriff in town, and he’s got a law degree and a union card. If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight.

AMY GOODMAN : For more on the significance of these victories, we turn to Juan González, yes, co-host of Democracy Now! , author of, among other books, Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America .

Juan, can you talk about this massive Latino victory across the country? What was expected? What wasn’t expected?

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, well, Amy, it’s been quite a week in U.S. politics, and I’ve been poring over the voting returns and the exit polls the past two days to glean a clearer sense of the trends and outcomes that maybe the major media may have missed, and not just about Latinos.

Let’s begin with the turnout, which I believe is always key. It tells you how motivated and mobilized people were. Well, nationally, the turnout was 63% of registered voters. Now, that’s high by historic standards for a midterm, because, remember, it’s always less voting in the midterms. But it’s still a lower rate than either the Biden midterm election of 2022 or the first Trump midterm elections of 2018. So, while some areas of the country may have had a historic turnout, across the country this was not the highest turnout of any midterm in recent years.

And the most notable shift occurred among white voters. They made up 73% of all ballots cast. That’s the same percentage that they made in 2022. But while they voted 58% for Republicans four years ago — and I’m comparing it midterm to midterm, not midterm to the presidential election — this time they split almost evenly between Republicans and Democrats. So you’re talking a huge shift among white voters away from the Republican Party and to the Democratic Party.

What about people of color, who represented 23% of the electorate? The turnout rate for Blacks and Latinos nationwide stayed about even, or even possibly dropped a little bit, compared to 2022. And both groups, though, shifted much more to Democrats than previously. Black voters nationwide went from about 86% to 90% this year, and Latinos moved from 60% Democratic to — it depends on who you look at. The national exit poll said it went to 64%. The New York Times voter trend says it went to 69%. But both groups shifted nationwide significantly toward Democrats.

But here’s the biggest surprise that no one has paid any attention to, is that what happened among Asian Americans. They not only doubled their share of the electorate — they went from 2% in 2022 to 4% in this year — but 71% of Asian Americans voted for Democrats. That’s a 13-point shift from what Asian Americans did in 2022. And I have to think that the wars in Gaza and Iran, the Trump administration’s banning of travel from many Asian and Middle Eastern countries, its constant belittling of that region’s countries and cultures, the deportation even of refugees from Afghanistan, all have dramatically transformed how Asian Americans view the two major political parties.

Now, there’s been a lot of attention to the Latino vote, and which I’ve been studying for decades, obviously, as you mentioned Harvest of Empire . But we have to begin with what I’ve always called the Brown Belt. That’s a vast area of six Western and Southwestern states where Latinos make up as much as 30% or more of the total population — talking about Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and California. And, of course, as you mentioned, in Texas and California, the first elected Latino governors in both of those states. But the most startling trends came at the congressional level.

Take northern Nevada, for example. Democrat and former social worker Teresa Benitez-Thompson defeated a Republican incumbent to become the first Democrat ever to win that state’s 2nd Congressional seat, a district that Trump won by 14 points in 2024. With her victory, all four of Nevada’s congressional districts are held — will be held by Democrats.

In southern Arizona, JoAnna Mendoza, a 20-year Navy and Marine Corps veteran, flipped another Republican seat. And meanwhile, an emergency room doctor, Dr. Amish Shah, a former state legislator, won the 1st Congressional District in another Republican seat with a large — a district with a large Latino population.

In Colorado, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a Latino attorney and former state legislator, defeated a Republican incumbent in a district in Denver’s northern suburbs with the highest percentage of Latino voters in the state.

Of course, Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics. Remember those five [seats] that Trump ordered redrawn to elect more Republicans? Well, the voters didn’t cooperate. Democrats held on to four of those five seats. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen, two moderate congressmen, prevailed in their reelections. Democrat Leticia Gutierrez rode a wave of anti-mass deportation and anti- ICE sentiment to defeat her Republican opponent in the redrawn 9th District outside of Houston. That’s the seat that Al Green, the longtime congressman, used to hold. And in the San Antonio area, former Deputy Sheriff Johnny Garcia won in the newly created 35th District. And at the same time, Republicans lost two other seats in Texas to Latino Democrats. In West Texas, former educator Katy Padilla Stout won a congressional district that had been in Republican hands for the past six elections. That’s followed the resignation of Representative Tony Gonzales in the wake of sexual misconduct and the ethics scandal. And in the lone Rio Grande Valley seat held by Republicans, the famed Grammy-winning Tejano singer Bobby Pulido, who describes himself as a conservative Democrat but favors immigration reform, he defeated Republican Monica De La Cruz, who was thought to be a rising Republican star.

Now, here’s another surprise that no one’s paid attention to, maybe the biggest Texas bright spot that has escaped notice. I’m talking about the remarkable performance by Greg Casar, the chairman of the House Progressive Caucus. He’s also a democratic socialist and someone we have interviewed on Democracy Now! numerous times. He ran for reelection, but to a seat formerly held by Congressman Lloyd Doggett, after Republicans moved Casar’s hometown of Austin out of his district and into this reconfigured district, and Doggett agreed to retire. Well, Casar won that race as expected, but he did so in a super landslide. He amassed over 254,000 votes. That’s 70,000 more votes than any other congressional candidate got in Texas this year — for a socialist in Texas. By my calculations, Casar received the fifth-highest vote in the U.S. out of all of the candidates for the 435 House seats.

The bottom line is that Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state. Republicans not only lost the governor’s seat, a U.S. Senate seat, other statewide races, several state House and Senate seats, but instead of winning five new congressional seats, they ended up with a net loss of one. If Democrats are able to consolidate some of those Texas gains in the coming years, national politics will never be the same. That’s why progressive organizers and fundraisers should be looking at Texas, like the civil rights movement of the 1950s regarded Mississippi and Georgia, as the place to send resources and train new leaders for the upcoming 2028 election.

Meanwhile, over in California, all five Republican districts that Democrats redrew ended up flipping to Democrats. Two of those five went to Latinos. Randy Villegas, a progressive community college professor, won a seat in the Central Valley in the 6th District, and Linda Sánchez prevailed in Orange County’s redrawn district.

And it’s not just the Brown Belt where Latinos had an impact. In Pennsylvania, where Democrats flipped four Republican seats, 73% of the state’s Latinos voted for Democrats, according to The New York Times . That’s a 26-point shift from the 2024 election. And it almost certainly fueled Democratic victories in two of those districts, where Latinos make up 15 to 25% of the population. That’s the 8th District, around Scranton, where the city’s Democratic Mayor Paige Cognetti won, and the 7th District, around Allentown, Bethlehem, where retired firefighter Bob Brooks ousted the Republican incumbent.

So, Democrats controlling Congress, however, does not offer any certainty that a new era of progressive government is dawning in Washington. We shouldn’t forget, for example, that South Texas Democrats have historically been more conservative than those in other parts of the country. So it remains to be seen how those Texas victories will ultimately affect legislation in the new Congress.

In addition, the country’s billionaire class will doubtless ramp up its torrent of cash donations directed at the new Democratic majority, hoping to buy off enough of them or foment sufficient infighting among them to kill or stall any substantive efforts at truly progressive legislation.

So much damage has already been perpetrated on American society by the lawlessness and corruption of the Trump era that it will take who knows how long to repair. To do so, progressives will need to contend not only with their — with the billionaire class and the corporate Democrats, who never tire of conspiring to control things, with Trump for the next two years and his MAGA faithful; they must also contend with their own ultra-left activists, who will increasingly demand no compromise by the new Democratic majority, as if this week’s election was some kind of revolutionary sea change, and not just a much welcome shift in the seesaw world of late-stage neoliberal capitalism, which is what I think it is.

AMY GOODMAN : Juan González, thanks so much for that analysis. Juan, of course, co-host on Democracy Now! and author of a number of books, including Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America .

Coming up, we’ll be joined by Hasan Piker, the popular political left commentator and live-streamer, who had one of the biggest streaming broadcasts on election night, number two just after NBC , beating out the networks. He campaigned heavily in the last months with many progressives and DSA candidates. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Copper Kettle” by Stephanie Coleman and Nora Brown, performing at the Brooklyn Folk Festival. This year’s festival is this weekend, and Democracy Now! will be there.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Mississippi’s race for the U.S. Senate remains too close to call: Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,000 votes with 96% of votes counted as of Friday morning. Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 points in 2024. If elected, Colom would be the first Democrat to win the state in 40 years and the first African American since 1875, during the Reconstruction era. Colom, the former district attorney for northeast Mississippi, made the issue of affordability central to his campaign. He has sharply criticized national Democrats for writing off Mississippi and failing to invest in his campaign early on.

“The entire country shifted left. But when you look at it regionally, the biggest shifts took place in the South — Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Louisiana,” says Cliff Albright, executive director of Black Voters Matter. That “wave of energy” was “largely led by Black voters who were most under attack with the mid-decade racial gerrymandering that was taking place. It clearly backfired, and all it did was to wake up a sleeping giant.”

“Without the extreme gerrymandering, without the extreme voter restrictions that have been seen throughout the South, [the] wave would have been even bigger,” adds Chris Kromm, executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies. “There’s a real opportunity for engaging more voters and really pushing the region in a more progressive direction.”

AMY GOODMAN : We begin today’s show in the Deep South, where Mississippi’s Senate race remains too close to call. Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by more than 1,800 votes as election officials process provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots. Just two years ago, Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 points. If elected, Scott Colom would be the first Democrat to win the state in 40 years and the first African American since 1875, during Reconstruction.

Colom made the issue of affordability central to his campaign, and in an ad that went viral, he blasted Senator Hyde-Smith for saying Mississippians should, quote, “pick another protein,” unquote, if they’re upset over high beef prices. The ad features Mississippians saying they’d rather pick another senator.

HUGH KEETON : The price of beef continuing to go up.

SEN . CINDY HYDE - SMITH : You know, you have so many proteins to choose from.

MISSISSIPPI VOTER 1: Pick another protein? [bleep], I’d rather pick another senator instead.

MISSISSIPPI VOTER 2: Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.

MISSISSIPPI VOTER 3: Pick another protein? What the [bleep]?

SCOTT COLOM : Pick another senator instead.

AMY GOODMAN : Scott Colom is a former district attorney for northeast Mississippi. In 2022, President Biden nominated him to the federal bench, a nomination blocked by Colom’s opponent in this race, incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Colom has sharply criticized national Democrats for writing off Mississippi and failing to invest in his campaign. Early on, he told reporters, quote, “Mississippi was never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause.” This is Colom speaking to NBC News.

SCOTT COLOM : The reality is our country does not do well when it ignores places like Mississippi. … You can’t lead with doubt. You have to believe. You have to lead with belief, and that’s where the power is. When you believe things, you can actually achieve it. And there’s some people in the party that they are just treading water. Right? “What’s the path to least resistance to get to 51? Oh my gosh, we did it.” That’s not the right way to think. In this particular moment, you have to think about how can we win everywhere, because we need to represent working people in a way where we actually deliver.

AMY GOODMAN : The potential electoral upset in Mississippi is part of a much broader political shift across the South, where Democrats have scored major victories in states long considered Republican strongholds.

For the latest on Mississippi and more on the sea change in the South, we’re joined by two guests. In Durham, North Carolina, we’re joined by Chris Kromm, the executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies, publisher of its online magazine Facing South . And we’re joined by Cliff Albright, co-founder of Black Voters Matter. He’s been in Jackson, Mississippi, for much of this week, including election night, but is now back in Atlanta, Georgia, where we’ve spoken to him many times before.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! Cliff Albright, let’s begin with you. To say the least, Colom feels betrayed by the Democratic Party for not backing him sooner, and yet he has shocked the nation in being ahead in this — very narrowly, in this race, where he may be, though it’s not finalized yet, unseating the incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. Tell us what happened in Mississippi.

CLIFF ALBRIGHT : Yeah. Good morning, Amy. and good morning to my good friend Chris.

Yeah, you know, you all may not be able to claim it, but we’re claiming it. He’s claiming it. He’s ahead. He’s been ahead since election night. His lead continues to grow as they continue to count absentee ballots. We’re continuing, many organizations — it’s an incredible coalition of organizations down there in Mississippi that are fighting right now to make sure that every vote gets counted, people that were forced to do affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, in some states it’s known as, trying to get organized to make sure that all of those ballots get counted, that people that didn’t have ID get their ballots fixed, get the ballots cured, to get all those votes counted. So we believe that he’s winning and, at the end of the day, that he’s going to be the winner.

But what happened is, in spite of the rest of the country really ignoring Mississippi — and I got to say that in addition to Mississippi, the points that he made about that state, the same could be said about Louisiana, which got even less support than his race got, and still came within a razor-thin margin. The same can be said about Florida — right? — Alabama. All of these states have been ignored, have been underresourced, underinvested. There are amazing groups doing work on a shoestring budget. But because of the tide of Black voter enthusiasm, largely fed by the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, which gutted the Voting Rights Act, ever since that decision, we’ve seen a wave of organizing, a wave of momentum. Of all the shifts that took place in the country — and to be clear, the entire country shifted left — but when you look at it regionally, the biggest shifts took place in the South — Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Louisiana. All those points had shifts between 20 and 24 points. And so, the wave of energy, largely led by Black voters who were most under attack with the mid-decade racial gerrymandering that was taking place — it clearly backfired, and all it did was to wake up a sleeping giant.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Chris Kromm, I wanted to ask you your reaction to the results in Mississippi. And if you could talk a little bit about the history of the two candidates?

CHRIS KROMM : No, absolutely. In an incredible year for Democrats in the South, the story of Scott Colom in Mississippi is one of the most remarkable. I mean, here you have a longtime leader in the Black community in Mississippi up against a longtime Republican. And the history that you brought out was incredibly important to the backdrop to this race, where he was put forward as a federal district nominee from the Biden administration in the fall of 2022, and almost every politician in Mississippi backed him, including the Republican Senator Roger Wicker, but the one person who blocked his nomination is the current senator from Mississippi, [Cindy] Hyde-Smith. And what you see there is — so, there’s a personal history there. And she really seemed determined. You know, she thought she had this race. She was kind of phoning it in. And, you know, to their credit, the Democrats, I think, late in the game kind of realized that this is a race that could be won.

And what you’re seeing now, I think, is really interesting, where armies of lawyers have come to Mississippi. The Republican lawyers are saying that they want to segregate those ballots, pull them aside, that came in, the affidavit ballots, or called provisional ballots elsewhere in the country, and pull those aside. Democratic lawyers and civil rights lawyers are saying that that’s not something you can do in Mississippi. And so this is really turning out to be an important legal battle. But as Cliff said, the trend lines are all going in the direction of Colom. And given that personal history, but also the long political history in Mississippi, it would be truly historic if he can come out on top.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Chris, in other states, the victories by Democrats at the top of the ticket have had an impact on the — on other races, less high-profile races. What’s happened there in Mississippi?

CHRIS KROMM : Yeah, well, I think that’s something really important to understand, is that these Senate races — so, if Scott Colom wins, which I think is very likely, that’ll be six Democrats who have won statewide U.S. Senate races. And those races really drove a lot of turnout that benefited, played a role in U.S. congressional races and statewide races. And so, you see that playing down the ballot, where this overall shift — as Cliff noted, that there was a 20-point shift overall in the South, when you look at the '24 presidential vote to what happened in the Senate races, a 20-point shift in the Democratic vote margin from ’24 to ’26. And that played out all down the ballot and even in races where — as Cliff notes, the places where Democrats came up short. What it really showed was the possibility of what's possible in Southern states. And I think that’s going to change forever people’s ideas about what the political map looks like nationally and the importance of the South in driving the national political agenda.

AMY GOODMAN : Cliff Albright, I know you have to leave in a second. You’re back in Atlanta, Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms is now the first African American woman governor in the country. And you’ve just been in Mississippi. One of the most remarkable shifts in this country is the massive voter turnout. In many countries, many more people vote, percentage-wise, than in the United States, but it is growing here. If you can talk about also what this lack of Democratic establishment support has meant for Colom, but also Angie Nixon, who came so close to defeating the incumbent in Florida without that support? As Colom has pointed out, if only she had had that from the beginning. Your final comments on what you’re taking away from this election, as you say in Mississippi they’ve accepted that Colom has won, even if the rest of the country doesn’t, and if you think it could be stopped? I mean, here you have Cindy Hyde-Smith, who prevented Colom — she might be sorry now — from being appointed to the federal bench. She blocked Biden’s nomination.

CLIFF ALBRIGHT : Yeah, you know, I think that — so, a couple of things. On the Georgia thing, in addition to Keisha becoming governor, all the way down the ballot — to the point that Chris was just making, all the way down the ballot, it’s almost every state office in the state of Georgia is now going to be led by a Black woman — labor commissioner, agriculture, education — all the way down, except for lieutenant governor, where Josh won that one. But so, it’s absolutely remarkable, and it’s a sign of what could happen all across the South with the proper investment. What’s been happening in Georgia, you know, in 2020, in 2022, with Warnock winning again, this year, this has been from years of investment, the kind of investment that Mississippi, Louisiana, Florida has not seen.

Florida is insane, the way that people have turned their backs on the state of Florida and declared that it was hopeless, even after Andrew Gillum came close in 2018, and then just people just wrote it off. And for Angie to do what she did — and shoutout to her — on almost little, very little investment, really says what the potential is in the South. We’re hoping that the narrative or the question, the debate around what strategy makes sense in the South — do you invest in Black and Brown voters and mobilize that base? Right? Or do you continue to look for these unicorn Trump voters that swing back and forth? This year should really put that debate to an end, but I have a feeling it’s going to continue.

The last thing I’m going to say, Amy, is — and this is very important — with all these victories, there’s a risk that people lose sight of the structural barriers that still exist, the voter suppression that is still taking place. I know the Mississippi coalition is very insistent that people hear that story about things that still went wrong in this election. And this goes for across the South. And a lot of times what happens is, when we win, against all odds, that people say, “Oh, the voter suppression wasn’t that bad.” They said this about Warnock in '22. They said, “Oh, I guess that voter suppression bill wasn't that bad.” No, we were able to overcome the suppression, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not a structural barrier. The racial gerrymandering that took place has still given Republicans a structural edge, that’s been covered in a wave year, but it’s still something that’s got to be corrected. The Supreme Court’s decision has still got to be fixed. We still need voting rights legislation. And that, with investment, means there’s nothing that we can’t achieve all across the South.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Chris Kromm, I wanted to ask you if you could talk a little bit about what’s happened in North Carolina in this election.

CHRIS KROMM : Remarkable. Not only did you have at the top of the ticket, it looks like Roy Cooper is going to win by 19 to 20 points when all is said and done in terms of counting the ballots, but again, you go down the list. Four of the biggest upsets in U.S. congressional races were in North Carolina. It looks like at this point that we’re going to go from a delegation that, despite extreme gerrymandering, was a 10-4 in favor — delegation in favor of Republicans, will flip to a delegation that’s 10-4 in favor of Democrats.

Incredible stories like the longtime speaker of the House, Tim Moore, who created his own district through redistricting so he could win, was upset by a Black woman in District 14. In the mountains of North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene had devastated the region, you had a farmer, Ager, who’s going to — who’s won that race in District 11.

Just down the ballot, upset after upset, and it really showed that it was a combination of the political environment, how at the top of the ballot, the excitement and the investment that happened, but also some solid grassroots organizing, historic Black and Latino voter turnout. It really was the perfect storm, and it showed what’s possible. And again, I think this is a story — a lot of other Southern states could look like a North Carolina with the right investment, with the right attention. And so, the story of North Carolina, I think, is one that people should be paying attention to across the country, and also about what’s possible in the South.

AMY GOODMAN : And, Chris Kromm, we recently spoke to Justin Pearson, Justin Pearson who ran for Congress from Memphis. He really took on the data center there, as did his brother. He did lose, but he lost by just 2,000 votes in his gerrymandered district. So, even in that case, can you talk about the significance of this in Tennessee?

CHRIS KROMM : Well, this is what’s so important to understand, is that for all of the wins, and there were — you know, Democrats held on to 40 congressional seats, House seats. They are going to flip about 10 to 14 seats. I think that number is growing every day as new results come in, but it’s going to be about another 14 seats. If you think about how much bigger that wave would have been without the extreme gerrymandering, without the extreme voter restrictions that have been seen throughout the South, that wave would have been even bigger. And it really points to the importance of voting rights.

And Pearson is a great example of this. There’s over 30 data centers in the Memphis area. He is an out — a leader in that fight and talking about what the implications are for the community. And so, he didn’t make it to the finish line, but there are so many candidates like that in places where they were able to really move the needle, when you saw this incredible uptick in the electorate of Black and Latino voters, a real shift. And even if they didn’t get to the finish line, I hope the overall story people see is that the South is increasingly competitive and that there’s a real opportunity for engaging more voters and really pushing the region in a more progressive direction.

AMY GOODMAN : Chris Kromm, we want to thank you for being with us, executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies, speaking to us from North Carolina, and Cliff Albright, co-founder and executive director of the Black Voters Matter Fund. He spent the week in Jackson, Mississippi, just back at his home in Atlanta, Georgia.

Coming up, we look at some of the historic elections for Latinos with our own Juan González, author of Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America . And then Hasan Piker will join us from Los Angeles to comment on the elections overall. He had one of the largest broadcasts in the United States on election night. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “When First Unto This Country,” rendition by Down Hill Strugglers, performing at the Brooklyn Folk Festival last year. This year’s festival is this weekend, and we’ll bring you more of those musicians.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.title: Is There a Left Candidate for President?
scraped.description: “All I know is that the populist lane is wide open for someone to seize it.”
scraped.author: Akela Lacy
scraped.h1: Is There a Left Candidate for President?
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

“All I know is that the populist lane is wide open for someone to seize it.”

The race for 2028 is already starting, and progressives are all asking one question: Who will take up the left’s mantle in the next presidential election?

An obvious first choice for many self-described leftists, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has said she is seriously considering a run. Ocasio-Cortez laid the groundwork for a potential presidential bid rooted in economic populism and “ fighting oligarchy ” while campaigning alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., for midterm candidates around the country this cycle.

Democratic strategists, however, have pointed out it would be far easier for Ocasio-Cortez to run for Democratic New York Sen. Chuck Schumer’s seat in 2028; and it’s even possible the 75-year-old presumptive majority leader will retire.

There isn’t a clear pick for another Democratic candidate with star power who could mount a truly progressive campaign — presenting the left with the threat of losing the momentum that fueled a democratic socialist wave during the primaries and animated campaigns across the ideological spectrum on Tuesday.

That, said her former spokesperson Lauren Hitt, is not Ocasio-Cortez’s problem.

“The wrong reason to run would be because nobody else is running in the progressive lane.”

“I think the wrong reason to run would be because nobody else is running in the progressive lane,” said Hitt, who now advises progressive and moderate candidates. “She has made a lot of good investments in the midterms and in helping build up the progressive bench, but it was not her job to make sure we had another person to run.”

(Representatives for Ocasio-Cortez did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

So if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t run from the left, who will?

Most Read Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point Nick Turse Abdul El-Sayed Wins Senate Seat With Pro-Palestine Campaign Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez

Candidates exploring potential presidential bids include a few newer faces alongside a very similar cast of moderates who campaigned for the Democratic nomination in the 2016 and 2020 primaries.

Names like New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker , former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and even the party’s former nominee Kamala Harris are making the rounds; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has also laid the groundwork for a run. The recently reelected Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has long been viewed as a potential contender, as has Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, though he said last month he’s not planning on a run.

None of them are people you would necessarily liken to someone like Ocasio-Cortez or the grandfather of the movement behind her, Sanders himself.

Rep. Ro Khanna of California is so far the most “progressive” person openly considering a run. Khanna served as national co-chair of Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign, and he’s long been a voice for an anti-interventionist foreign policy . He drew the ire of tech billionaires for supporting a wealth tax in California.

Yet there’s a palpable skepticism around Khanna among leftists, even if they can’t quite put their finger on why. Some weren’t impressed when he defended his support for funding Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system after publicizing an arrest in the West Bank earlier this year. (Khanna later came out against funding the Iron Dome). And as a multimillionaire, he’s also drawn criticism from the right and the left for his personal wealth.

There’s a palpable skepticism around Khanna among leftists, even if they can’t quite put their finger on why.

Like Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna has said he will back Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., for House Speaker despite pledges from other candidates to withhold their support for either Jeffries or Schumer, both moderates, for leadership positions next session.

It’s still incredibly early, but there’s one unifying theme emerging from Tuesday’s results for whichever candidate decides to try to court the progressive vote.

“All I know is that the populist lane is wide open for someone to seize it,” said Ravi Mangla, the spokesperson for the Working Families Party.

Victories over the past two years, from Zohran Mamdani’s election as mayor of New York City to the clutch of democratic socialists and progressives heading to Congress in January, show that Democrats can marshal discontent with Donald Trump and the far right to elect candidates running on progressive policies.

”Voters were very clear: People are very, very angry,” said Greg Krieg, a progressive Democratic strategist who works with Slingshot Strategies and is the spokesperson for the pro-Palestine super PAC American Priorities. “There is a focus on economic populism that transcends the ideological splits in the party.”

With the rising cost of living, and candidates tapping into that populism, the question for progressives is how to best wield the blue version of economic populism against the right-wing version that powered Trump’s rise.

“Right-wing populism didn’t really defeat left-wing populism, it just ran against a kind of corporate slop for many years,” Krieg said.

This era’s new “kitchen table” issues are a constellation of economic woes that voters are increasingly connecting to the forces concentrating wealth and political power in the hands of the few . Democrats should respond to that by fighting, visibly, against the things that take money out of people’s pockets, corruption and price-gouging among them, Krieg said.

“I think that the American people, if they are presented a choice of right-wing populism and left-wing populism, will opt for the left-wing populism,” Krieg said. “And I think that’s quadruply true now that we’ve done the right-wing populism experiment and it’s been such a fiasco — so let’s give them that option.”

The factors influencing how Democrats approach 2028 are taking shape now. They include the debate over who will lead the party in the House and Senate, though any effort to stop Schumer or Jeffries from leading roles would face long odds. And how Democrats fare in the next presidential race will depend in large part on what they do with their control of Congress during the last two years of Trump’s final term in office.

Then there is the group that helped power the rise of Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani, the next mayors of Washington and Los Angeles, and the largest incoming bloc of socialist members of Congress in history: the Democratic Socialists of America.

Any candidate that gets buy-in from DSA will have to support policies like Medicare for All, taxing the rich, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on U.S. arms to Israel. DSA, which endorsed both Sanders’s 2016 and 2020 primary bids, is running a presidential exploratory committee that will eventually vote to endorse a candidate after collecting input from its members.

DSA passed a resolution to explore a 2028 endorsement at its national convention last year. And there isn’t necessarily a consensus among its members — more than 125,000 people across 130 chapters in 43 states — on whether or not they want to see Ocasio-Cortez run, said Ella Teevan, who chairs the group’s presidential exploratory group and sits on its National Political Committee.

“The Bernie case feels just a little bit different because I think the membership was a little bit more united around Bernie, although by no means unanimously,” Teevan said. “If and when we do consider an AOC endorsement, hers will be a little bit more contentious. But like I said, that’s the beauty of DSA.”

Though Ocasio-Cortez is no shoo-in , DSA members haven’t coalesced around any other candidate — and it’s not clear they will.

“I know that there are other quote-unquote progressives who might be considering a presidential run in 2028, but I think it’s really clear for us that they need to support DSA’s core demands that most people in the United States support,” Teevan said.

“If a candidate were to come along who supported those policies, I think a considerable portion of membership would think about whether we should endorse them,” she said. “But yeah, I don’t think that there’s a natural other person with name recognition in the field that, at least, I can think of right now.”

And there may yet be candidates who enter the race who aren’t yet on the radar, said Hitt, Ocasio-Cortez’s former spokesperson: “It’s totally possible there’s a progressive champion who could fill that lane that we aren’t even thinking of yet.”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.description: Palestinian liberation is the key to fighting racism, imperialism, and genocide around the globe.
scraped.author: Noura Erakat, John Reynolds
scraped.h1: Defeating Zionism to Free Palestine
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Palestinian liberation is the key to fighting racism, imperialism, and genocide around the globe.

Earlier this week, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race in Michigan after months of Islamophobic abuse, most notably from President Donald Trump, who referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed.”

“Mohammed goes back to the days of the Jihad. He is a RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last month. “Mohammed’s Values are not exactly those of Michiganders, or those of our Great United States of America!” The people of Michigan thought otherwise.

El-Sayed will be the first-ever Muslim U.S. senator. “He rose to victory,” my Intercept colleagues Matt Sledge and Jonah Valdez wrote , “with a campaign animated by his opposition to U.S. support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, making him a key figure for a left critical of entrenched foreign policy interests and a target for a political establishment intent on preserving the U.S. relationship with the Israeli government.”

In an Election Day equivalent of a Hail Mary, as El-Sayed and Democrats from coast to coast were in the midst of a rout of the GOP, Trump went on Fox News to announce the U.S. would stop providing $4 billion in annual aid to Israel , specifically blaming El-Sayed for making it a hot-button issue. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” said Trump.

There is no reason to believe the aid will stop. Trump is an inveterate liar, and structural issues with U.S. assistance make it unlikely. And even if it did end, Israel’s genocide will continue . Almost 75,000 Gazans have been killed since October 2023, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza. A recent U.N. report said, “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Ending the genocide will mean decolonizing Gaza and offering Palestinians a path to justice. That, Noura Erakat and John Reynolds write in their new book, means “confronting the problem of Zionism” and everything fundamental to it: racism, conquest, settler colonialism, and apartheid laws. Today, Erakat and Reynolds offer an essay adapted from “ Confronting Zionism ,” exploring how the Zionist project can be dismantled and Israeli colonialism can be demolished, leading to Palestinian liberation and a future built on redistribution, reparations, and refugee return.

—Nick Turse, editor and TomDispatch

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

Three years on from the onset of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, we are at a crucial hinge point. The world today, when it comes to Palestine, stands at the crossroads: meaningful support for liberation and decolonization, or the normalization of colonial expansion and erasure.

Since the 2021 “ Manifesto of Dignity and Hope ” and the unified call of Palestinians to confront Zionism, the Israeli political sphere has only continued to sustain and entrench its fascist trajectory and its racist laws . After 2023, Israeli settler colonialism and domination escalated into all-out destruction and elimination. Palestinians who had been enduring suffocating apartheid and siege for far too long were now subjected to genocidal assault. Though the context on the ground shifted, the urgent need for a better understanding and challenge to Zionism on political, legal, structural, and ideological grounds remained.

It was a new generation of Palestinian activists who produced the Manifesto of Dignity and Hope, but their text was shaped by the legacy and spirit of Palestinian revolutionaries and anti-colonial thinkers from earlier periods. Common language echoes through the generations. A quarter-century ago, Palestinian intellectual Edward Said wrote the core of the issue of Palestine “is intellectual truth and the need to combat any sort of apartheid. We should concentrate our resistance on … fully confronting the apartheid provisions inherent in Zionism.” And as diplomat Fayez Sayegh captured it in 1965: Racism is not an acquired or incidental or passing feature of the Israeli state; it is “inherent in the very ideology of Zionism.” Today, we can draw inspiration from these intergenerational reverberations across Palestinian theory and activism, in their consonant commitments to confronting Zionism.

Part of our own task as anti-colonial legal scholars is to expand our analysis of the limitations of narrow liberal legal readings of apartheid and inequality, and to highlight how a radical critique of Israeli apartheid is essential to dismantling Israel’s apartheid regime. This requires scrutiny not only of Zionism and Israeli settler colonialism, but also of the concept of apartheid itself. Apartheid was previously understood in the context of the African anti-apartheid struggle, in a formulation originally coined by the South African Communist Party, as “colonialism of a special type.” By the late 1990s, however, apartheid had been stripped in mainstream understandings of its global character and colonial essence, and effectively reframed as “ racial discrimination of a special type .”

Most Read Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point Nick Turse Abdul El-Sayed Wins Senate Seat With Pro-Palestine Campaign Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez

One factor in this analytical shift was the domestication of racism in international law, which has obscured its relationship to global capitalism and transformed racism into a problem for individual countries to resolve through juridical reform or diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. Racism is not merely abhorrent because people’s feelings are hurt or one feels unseen, however, but because it is entangled with power and economic structures, and because materially, the continuum of racist violence culminates in genocide, which is squarely understood as a global phenomenon. Martin Luther King Jr. pointed to this in 1967 when he said: “In the final analysis, racism is evil because its ultimate logic is genocide. … If one says that I am not good enough to eat at a lunch counter, or to have a good, decent job, or to go to school with him merely because of my race, he is saying consciously or unconsciously that I do not deserve to exist.”

International law attempts to capture this continuum. Three of the specific acts conducted to maintain apartheid are identical to the acts conducted to commit genocide under their respective legal definitions. In the former, they are done with the intent to dominate; in the latter, with the intent to destroy. These are not mutually exclusive, but rather interact with each other: Colonialism, apartheid, and genocide combine under the Zionist project in Palestine to produce a system of oppression based on conquest, structural racism, dispossession, and elimination.

Palestinian opposition to Zionism and the imperatives of decolonization — for political emancipation, material survival, and cultural flourishing — are the central thrust of our work. The colonial origins and early legal mechanics of Zionist settler colonialism and Israel’s apartheid regime reveal how Zionism functioned both as a colonial initiative and a racializing project. This manifested in colonial institutions even before the state was established in 1948, after which they were enshrined in racist legal regimes. A broad structural analysis of the institutional and economic processes of land and capital accumulation that have occurred under settler colonialism in Palestine is necessary to understand the machinery of conquest and dispossession — and the role that racism has played in driving it forward. Drawing on the anti-colonial Palestinian intellectual tradition, we can see that an antiracist analysis has been organic to the Palestinian liberation struggle and is precisely what shaped U.N. initiatives in the 1960s and 1970s that condemned Zionism as a form of racism and racial discrimination alongside apartheid and colonialism.

Read our complete coverage

Despite all the analysis of Israeli state racism and colonial violence since 1948 and all of the mass popular mobilizations and legal advocacy against Israeli apartheid, nothing substantive was done at an international, political, or institutional level to address or redress it. This inaction and the impunity afforded to Israel inevitably culminated in the situation that the world found itself in after October 2023: unsanctioned apartheid accelerating into unadulterated genocide — and given the green light by those who had the power to stop it. There was a decade of increasingly flagged warning signs leading up to this. But Palestinian scholars and international lawyers who had warned of a “prelude to genocide” or “ slow-motion ” genocide over the years were largely ignored, and in some cases castigated. The consequences have been catastrophic. The United States actively funded , armed , and cheer-led the butchery in Gaza. European Union leaders chose to “stand with Israel” as it announced its starvation policy and war of annihilation.

We would not have ended up in this present moment if the critiques of Zionism as colonialism and racism and the reality of Israel as an apartheid regime had been taken seriously. In 1975, the U.N., led by a Third World majority, declared “international co-operation and peace require the achievement of national liberation and independence, the elimination of colonialism and neocolonialism, foreign occupation, zionism, apartheid and racial discrimination in all its forms, as well as the recognition of the dignity of peoples and their right to self-determination.” Against this, the Western world, led by the United States, has worked to normalize Israeli apartheid.

We see part of our task now as one of continuing to build on the recent “mainstreaming” of condemnations of Israeli apartheid and genocide, but in a way that decisively resists the drift toward narrower, liberal articulations and insists on the importance of radical, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial analysis and praxis. In our work as critical legal scholars, we situate apartheid and the shape it has taken as a category in international law, and we explore the limits and potential of legal tactics, arguments, and institutions to dismantle Israeli apartheid and end the genocide in Gaza. We argue that while legal actions should be pursued in the service of political and social movements, legal logic is insufficient in itself — and can risk narrowing or distorting the horizon of Palestinian liberation. In our view, the proliferating condemnations of Israel by major human rights organizations and mainstream figures in recent years have belatedly reflected the popular consensus and a political reality that Palestinian activism had made undeniable. They also fit, to varying degrees, within a wider pattern of containment.

As one example, take the case of European officials and states finally beginning to acknowledge the heinousness of Israel’s obliteration of Gaza in mid-2025, but doing so primarily in the form of calling for a Palestinian state . They did so only after almost two full years of enabling untold destruction, and refusing to impose any serious sanctions to stem the genocide. Their moves to recognize Palestinian statehood were not about any genuine support for Palestinian self-determination, but rather a way to stabilize the apartheid status quo and try to slow down the Israeli–U.S. drive to continue the erasure of Gaza and full annexation of the West Bank.

With all of that in mind, it is important to situate the political moment we are in — the increasing focus on Israeli apartheid in recent years and subsequently on the genocide in Gaza — alongside the urgency of thinking about Palestine’s future and our collective responsibilities. In doing so, we have several core aims: to offer a deeper understanding of the nature and extent of Israel’s colonial rule over Palestinian lands and lives; to think through the relationship between the practices of Israeli settler colonialism, apartheid, and genocide on the one hand, and the institutions and ideology of Zionism on the other; to situate Palestinian liberation and its global solidarity alliances as an antiracist struggle and an anti-colonial movement; and to insist on the need for systemic anti-imperial understandings and critiques of Zionism. To properly confront Zionism and avoid the pitfalls of neo-apartheid, we must be attentive to the necessities and practicalities of decolonization.

The decolonization of Palestine today continues a legacy of other liberation struggles — against European colonization globally, against domestic regimes of fascism, against apartheid in southern Africa, and against white supremacy in the United States and elsewhere. These are political orders that Third World, antiracist, partisan, and socialist movements have fought against throughout the past century and more. We must continue that tradition in the service of decolonization by fleshing out the political, legal, historical, and moral reasoning of anti-colonial and anti-Zionist thinking and movements. In our own writing, we feel we are merely providing footnotes to the political education and organizing that has fanned out from Palestine around the world, and that has shaped what millions of activists and people of conscience have viscerally felt: that Zionist colonial rule should and can be dismantled, and that Palestinians must be supported in their struggle to do so.

The stakes of confronting Zionist settler colonialism are high for the entire world: first and foremost for Palestinians’ own liberation, but also because their struggle is at the epicenter of wider global struggles against structures of domination and exploitation. Zionism is a colonial project in Palestine, but also a vehicle of imperialism in the region — agitating for U.S. war and intervention, acting as an antagonist of imperial aggression against Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Yemen and beyond, and actively collaborating with reactionary geopolitical forces globally. Zionism has been further mobilized by ethnonationalists and imperial projects as a proposition on how to organize a society on a basis of racial hierarchy that leaves its excluded groups to perish. Palestinian revolutionary intellectual Ghassan Kanafani always insisted on the importance of understanding the Palestinian struggle in the context of “the alliance between Zionism and imperialism.” And in positioning Kanafani’s analysis in the context of global movements against imperialism today, educator and organizer Layan Sima Fuleihan reiterates the Palestinian cause is “a banner for all of humanity.”

Naji al-Ali, the Palestinian political cartoonist famous for his iconic Hanzala (or “Handala”) character who symbolizes Palestinian resolve and future return, was himself displaced from northern Palestine as a boy during the Nakba and grew up in refugee camps in Lebanon. Kanafani came across Al-Ali and his artwork in Ein al-Hilweh camp and began to publish his drawings in the early 1960s. Al-Ali went on to produce tens of thousands of cartoons over the next 25 years, and through his art was renowned as a voice of Palestinian and Arab political consciousness. In 1984, just a couple of years before he would be assassinated , Al-Ali reflected on what Hanzala and Palestine represented:

I feel that I can recall and sense every bush, every stone, every house and every tree I passed when I was a child in Palestine. The character of Hanzala was a sort of icon that protected my soul from falling whenever I felt sluggish or I was ignoring my duty. That child was like a splash of fresh water on my forehead, bringing me to attention and keeping me from error and loss. He was the arrow of the compass, pointing steadily towards Palestine. Not just Palestine in geographical terms, but Palestine in its humanitarian sense — the symbol of a just cause, whether it is located in Egypt, Vietnam or South Africa.

In the decades since then, the idea of Palestine as the compass has resonated in struggles for justice around the world. Most recently, in 2025, the Palestinian Youth Movement and a coalition of solidarity groups brought thousands of activists together for the People’s Conference for Palestine, under the banner “Gaza is the compass.”

A wide array of voices, from community activists to trade union organizers to political representatives, emphasized how central Palestine is to all of the social struggles they are engaged in.

Palestinian doctor Mohammad Mustafa articulated the perspective of the many involved in movements for justice across the globe: “Gaza is the measure of our humanity. It is the litmus test that reveals who we are; as individuals, as a nation, as a world. … The compass points in one direction no matter who you are or where you are. In this way it provides a mandate and direction towards freedom for everyone.”

Lawyer and organizer Huwaida Arraf echoed these ideas: “Gaza is our compass because it points us to the truth. … When we’re fighting for Gaza, we’re fighting for a world where no people live in cages or under siege, under the boot of militarism or of fascism.”

Monadel Herzallah from Gaza, who lost five family members in the genocide, insisted the same: “To fight for a free Palestine is to fight for a free Haiti, a free Congo, a free Sudan — a free and just world which will be molded by all of us.”

Palestine is the compass because of what it represents as a banner for all humanity, and because of the horizons it opens up everywhere in imagining and building a new world.

Excerpt adapted from “Confronting Zionism: Decolonizing Palestine and Building the World Anew,” coming from Haymarket Books on November 10, 2026.

scraped.title: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
scraped.description: The new Michigan senator will face an uphill battle to transform the U.S. relationship with Israel. But he has options — and public pressure.
scraped.author: Jonah Valdez
scraped.h1: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

The new senator from Michigan will face an uphill battle if he wants to transform the U.S. relationship with Israel. But he has options — and public pressure.

One senator out of the 100 who will fill the upper chamber of the 120th Congress was elected to his seat on a loud campaign promise to end U.S. complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Abdul El-Sayed will walk into a newfound Democratic majority after animating his base with pro-Palestine pledges seldom heard from a U.S. Senate contender. As a first-term senator, he’ll lack seniority on the committees to which he’s assigned. And although his critiques of the U.S. relationship with Israel have proven overwhelmingly popular in public opinion surveys and among voters at the polls, the same can’t be said for most of his soon-to-be colleagues.

“It’s going to be a fight,” said Beth Miller, political advocacy director for Jewish Voice for Peace Action, which supported El-Sayed’s campaign. “The Democratic establishment, when it’s in control, has not taken measures in support of Palestine in the past. And so this is about making sure that now they finally start listening to what the overwhelming majority of their bases say.”

El-Sayed’s run marked the first time the Jewish-led, anti-Zionist group backed a Senate campaign . Pro-Palestine lobbying groups like JVP Action have been pushing for legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel for years , aligning themselves with a small but growing number of left-leaning House members. The group helped author the Block the Bombs Act, introduced by Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., which netted 82 co-sponsors and became a pro-Palestine litmus test in some Democratic primary campaigns.

Building consensus around a single bill in the Senate is harder, but the upper chamber offers stronger levers to pull. Senators can force votes called Joint Resolutions of Disapproval that would block foreign security assistance, such as weapons sales to Israel. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has exercised this option repeatedly throughout the genocide in Gaza to try and block the sale of certain bombs, firearms, and other military equipment to Israel. While his resolutions failed in the Republican-controlled Senate , the most recent ones drew support from wide majorities of Democrats — soon to be the party in power.

Yet with the looming threat that Democrats might actually be able to pass legislation, El-Sayed would find himself under pressure from the likely Senate majority leader, Chuck Schumer, who has long maintained the support of the pro-Israel lobby , to fall in line with party priorities.

“The question is, ‘Who does he want to be?’ Does he want to be someone like Bernie, who is willing to sometimes stand up to leadership?” said Hamid Bendaas, communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which also backed El-Sayed’s run. “It’s hard to do that as a freshman and someone who’s just getting in there.”

Bendaas expressed confidence that the Michigan senator would be a champion of pro-Palestine legislation, but he noted that El-Sayed would have to balance his priorities, especially after running a campaign focused on economic populism and providing universal healthcare through Medicare for All.

Most Read Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point Nick Turse Abdul El-Sayed Wins Senate Seat With Pro-Palestine Campaign Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez

There is a tension revealed by the dilemma facing Sen.-elect El-Sayed: While a growing share of Americans — and an overwhelming majority of Democrats — disapprove of the U.S. spending billions of dollars on aid to Israel, voters’ clear No. 1 concern in the 2026 election cycle was the cost of living and their own economic precarity.

Some pundits have encouraged pro-Palestine candidates like El-Sayed to put their anti-genocide principles aside, arguing that more moderate Democrats performed better on Tuesday night. They compare El-Sayed’s 7-percentage-point defeat of Mike Rogers to James Talarico’s 12-point win over Ken Paxton in Texas — and some have already asked Talarico to defy his new colleague.

But on the campaign trail, El-Sayed often connected the issues of a high cost of living and outsized U.S. spending on aid to Israel. “We ought to be spending our money here, to build schools and provide healthcare and child care here, rather than sending our money abroad to a foreign government that’s done terrible things with our money,” he said in a September interview with Bloomberg TV. El-Sayed’s approach made him the target of nearly $40 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee , which supported widespread anti-Arab and Islamophobic attacks and accusations of antisemitism in an attempt to keep a vocal critic of Israel out of the Senate.

“None of it mattered,” said Yousef Munayyer , a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. who likened the gravity of El-Sayed’s win to that of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “And this is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”

“This is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”

In addition to bringing joint resolutions to block future weapons transfers — like the Trump administration’s planned sale of $2.8 billion in 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — El-Sayed could introduce resolutions citing the Foreign Assistance Act; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., used one to demand a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank. He would also be able to introduce amendments to the Pentagon’s annual spending bill that carves out billions of dollars in joint U.S.–Israel weapons research. (The Senate is currently sitting on this year’s $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, which would even more deeply enmesh Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.)

Munayyer, the former head of the U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights, said that despite the uncertainty over whether moderate Democrats will be willing to link arms with progressives next session, El-Sayed’s win creates an environment ripe for accountability over Israel.

“You have a climate now where there’s going to be a lot less intimidation felt by people who had previously been hesitant to speak out on these issues because they thought it was political suicide,” he said.

Even Republicans are beginning to feel the shifting winds. On the morning of Election Day, President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Fox News that the U.S. would halt the annual $4 billion in military aid to Israel. The move would only cut off one path for Israel to get weapons from the U.S. — still allowing direct weapons sales to Israel from U.S. companies and weapons development and sharing with the Pentagon — and Trump said it was made in agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had been previewing it for months . Tactically, Trump said the goal was to take a “talking point” away from Democrats. He cited El-Sayed by name.

While ballots were still being counted on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance, an expected 2028 presidential contender, posted on X an early post-mortem of the massive GOP losses across the country. He wrote that the party could bring back “voters who had abandoned us” if they “End the war” in Iran and “Change our relationship to Israel.”

Such recognition from the Trump White House is new territory for U.S. politics, Munayyer said.

“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics,” Munayyer said. “A robust debate in the presidential primary campaigns in both parties, where the question of the U.S.-Israel relationship is going to come up time and again. That’s never happened before, and it’s gonna be seismic.”

“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics.”

The question is whether Democrats will stay on top of the wave. If Schumer, a staunch supporter of Israel, remains in charge of the Senate majority, he’ll have power over appointments to key committees — giving him the opportunity to curb the influence of a figure like El-Sayed.

“I don’t think that Democrats want to have a messy fight about this stuff when the base is largely in agreement on it,” Munayyer said. But while Senate Democrats have evolved on the issue of Israel and Palestine — even Sanders expressed far weaker critiques of the Israeli state a few years ago — it’s one thing to be the dissenting party when you’re in the minority. It’s another to wield serious power.

El-Sayed is perhaps the most vocal supporter of Palestinian rights of any U.S. senator elected since James Abourezk of South Dakota, who in the late 1970s became the first Arab American to serve in the Senate. Abourezk frequently advocated for a Palestinian state and was an early critic of the pro-Israel lobby . After his time in Congress, he founded the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee.

El-Sayed, now the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, frequently referred to Israel on the campaign trail as an “ethnostate” and said he opposes any nation that organizes its government by ethnicity and religion. In an appearance on ABC News, El-Sayed argued Israel was not a U.S. ally. Two days before the election, he spent a large portion of his sit-down with “ 60 Minutes ” calling for Palestinians’ right of self-determination and repudiated the question of whether Israel had a right to exist. In his victory speech, he criticized attempts by pro-Israel critics to conflate advocacy for Palestinians rights as “hate.”

Even so, in the lead-up to the general election, El-Sayed started being subjected to pressure from some on the pro-Palestine left . Critics chastised his decision to stump with former Vice President Kamala Harris over her complicity in the Biden administration’s support for the genocide in Gaza. Similar ire was directed at his partnership with former President Barack Obama, who has yet to name or condemn the genocide and governed over U.S. wars in the Middle East that saw the United States kill thousands of civilians.

Advocates for Palestinian rights, however, told The Intercept they recognized the utility in El-Sayed’s campaigning with the highest-profile members of the Democratic Party, and they counted it as a success that he earned their support. But they said they were not pinning all their hopes on a single individual.

On top of all the other calcified interests and long-standing political biases that shape the U.S. Senate, there’s the influence of the sprawling U.S. weapons industry, with manufacturing giants like Lockheed Martin and Boeing lobbying for their interests and showering politicians in campaign cash . That industry wants to keep profiting off the genocide in Gaza, said JVP Action’s Miller, and El-Sayed alone is not enough to stop that.

“This is not gonna be that one man comes into the Senate and changes everything,” she said. “This is that one person has been elected with a mandate that has demonstrated where the masses of people are at on this issue, and now we have to keep fighting harder than ever before.”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
