scraped.title: Israel’s Shaky Democracy Continues to Crumble
scraped.description: From military rule over Palestinians to apartheid in the occupied territories, Israel has never been a democracy for Palestinians. Efforts to restrict expat voting ahead of the elections showed how barriers to democracy can reach Jewish citizens, too.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

From military rule over Palestinians to apartheid in the occupied territories, Israel has never been a democracy for Palestinians. Efforts to restrict expat voting ahead of the elections showed how barriers to democracy can reach Jewish citizens, too.

Israel has never been a democracy for Palestinians, who have been excluded through military rule, occupation, and apartheid. But now efforts to restrict the vote are also reaching Jewish citizens. (Alexi J. Rosenfeld / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

I n July 1950, speaking at the annual Zionist Organization of America convention, US Vice President Alben W. Barkley asserted that Israel was “an oasis of liberty in the desert of despotism,” articulating a precursor to the oft-repeated adage “Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East.” While the expression cannot be traced to a singular person, the sentiment that Israel — a nation with free elections and civil liberties — stands alone amid a sea of authoritarian regimes has been cultivated by Western institutions and Israeli leaders since the state was founded.

From the outset, Israel’s earliest laws legalizing persecution against Palestinians showed the incompatibility between Jewish supremacy and democracy. But the subjugation of one group is rarely self-contained, and throughout history, illiberal nations have almost always turned against a portion of their citizens, often as violence against the outgroup reaches its peak.

In the midst of the bloodiest three years in the country’s history, and particularly during the election campaign, this tendency began to play out. Israel has disenfranchised voters , at times even contradicting its own discriminatory laws, in efforts to marginalize Jews perceived as a threat to Benjamin Netanyahu and his increasingly violent political agenda.

I n the past three years, emigration from Israel has reached record heights. According to a study published by Tel Aviv University, 270,000 citizens have left the country in the past three years. Between 2013 and 2015, the corresponding period in the previous decade, the number sat at 183,000. Like much of the American Jewish diaspora , those who have left in recent years have become deeply critical of Benjamin Netanyahu.

While Israel guarantees every citizen over the age of eighteen the right to vote, it has never permitted absentee ballots. With the exception of diplomats , emissaries, and Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers occupying territory in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, voters must be in the country on Election Day. With this election largely seen as one of the most consequential in the nation’s history, a survey taken before the election estimated that up to 67,000 expats could be returning home to vote.

On October 27, Likud won twenty-seven seats, and Gad Eisenkot’s Yashar party won twenty-one. Netanyahu’s bloc took fifty-three seats, against forty-eight for the Jewish opposition bloc and nineteen for the Arab-led parties. No bloc won the sixty-one seats needed for a majority. The results have left the country facing uncertain coalition negotiations.

Leading up to the vote, Likud tried to stop Israelis outside the country from coming back. In September, Likud petitioned the Central Election Committee, demanding it block Fly & Vote, an initiative by the nonpartisan American-Israel Democracy (AID) Coalition, which sought to help Israelis abroad return and cast a vote.

Offering logistical help, including eligibility checks and passport renewals, the organization also coordinated six group flights and helped search for commercial flights. While participants were still required to pay their airfare, Likud argued the initiative violated financing laws and constituted election bribery.

While the petition was ultimately dismissed, the AID Coalition agreed to not subsidize tickets, organize any additional group flights, or provide transportation and accommodation.

This summer, a second spat broke out when hundreds of Israelis living abroad discovered they had been stripped of their voting rights after being classified by the Interior Ministry as nonresidents. The designation, known as Code 51, excluded citizens from the voter registry altogether.

Petitioning the Supreme Court, the expats argued that they were not notified of their status change, with several only realizing when checking their electoral eligibility. The courts dismissed the case on procedural grounds, stating the claim was filed too late.

While there is no definitive proof linking Likud to the Code 51 scandal, it is clear that the party has repeatedly tried to curtail the expat vote. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that informal discussions were held between senior Transport Ministry officials about the possibility of restricting designated landing slots at airports, making it more difficult to fly into the country.

Similar to the proposed judicial reforms of 2023, where Netanyahu sought to weaken the power of the Supreme Court, this democratic backsliding has prompted furor among the Israeli left. But as is often the case with liberal Zionists, the far greater repression affecting Palestinians remains largely ignored.

T he AID Coalition describes itself as a group “strengthening, and preserving the democratic foundations of the State of Israel.” While a valiant objective, a more honest statement would be about preserving an ethnocracy. Israeli Professor Oren Yiftachel describes this form of governance as one that “promotes the expansion of the dominant group in contested territory and its domination of power structures while maintaining a democratic facade.” This dynamic has been present since the state’s founding.

While the 150,000 Palestinians who remained in their homeland after the Nakba were declared citizens and granted the right to vote from the beginning, the community also faced systematic discrimination from the outset. From 1948 until 1966, Palestinian citizens of Israel were placed under military rule , which included measures that restricted their movement, prohibited political organizing, and imposed arbitrary curfews. Simultaneously, the government confiscated hundreds of thousands of dunams of land, uprooting farmers from their livelihood and forcing many to turn to low-wage labor to survive.

In 1967, a year after lifting the military administration, Israel would turn their attention toward Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza after occupying both territories in the Six-Day War.

Assuming control of around one million Palestinians, residents of the newly occupied territory were placed under military rule. This time citizenship and the right to vote were withheld from them, since such incorporation would threaten the Jewish demographic majority.

As Jewish settlers moved into the occupied territories, aided by generous Israeli government subsidies, an apartheid regime took shape, as authorities applied separate laws, courts, and democratic rights to Palestinians and Israelis living in neighboring areas.

Although Israel disengaged from Gaza in 2005, it lay siege to the Strip two years later, imposing a crushing blockade. After the October 7 attacks, it returned yet again as the occupying power, this time unleashing a genocide that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. In the West Bank, the apartheid regime continues, as roughly 500,000 settlers, excluding those in East Jerusalem, live with full rights outside of Israel’s internationally recognized border, beside Palestinians who cannot vote, travel freely, or even build on their ancestral land.

Amid the dire situation in the West Bank and Gaza, the plight of Palestinians living inside Israel is largely forgotten. Yet these 2.1 million residents continue to live as second-class citizens.

In 2018, the Israeli Knesset passed the quasi-constitutional Nation-State Law , stipulating that self-determination is unique to the Jewish people, without guaranteeing equality for its other citizens. Furthermore, Palestinian citizens of Israel continue to face entrenched discrimination in urban planning, economic development, and educational opportunities.

I n 2024, the Varieties of Democracy Institute downgraded Israel from a liberal to an electoral democracy. The demotion followed Netanyahu and his coalition’s attempt to overhaul the judiciary, their accusations the Supreme Court was “left-leaning,” and deterioration in protections against torture. This classification did not take into account the active atrocities that Israel was perpetrating in Gaza and the West Bank at the time.

Yet since this reclassification, Netanyahu has shed more of the democratic facade he has long sought to uphold.

More than five hundred humanitarian workers have been killed since the war in Gaza began. In December 2025, Israel attempted to bar thirty-seven nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) from operating in the West Bank and Gaza. The Supreme Court froze the ban, allowing the organizations to continue operating pending a final ruling.

More recently, numerous foreign journalists have been turned away at the border during the election campaign, with others facing arduous interrogations and detention before being allowed entry.

Perhaps most revealing is the government’s willingness to break long-standing supremacist laws, which uphold Jews as a privileged class in Israel.

Starting in 2025, several Jewish activists were detained and deported for engaging in protective presence, a form of nonviolent solidarity work in which civilians deter violent settlers from harassing Palestinian communities. Earlier this year, a Jewish American academic on a three-year residency visa was denied entry after being accused of being a “left-wing anarchist.”

After the backlash prompted by the film NAZA , in which IDF soldiers admitted to knowingly killing innocent civilians in Gaza, Netanyahu announced plans to introduce a bill that would strip those who defame the IDF of their Israeli citizenship.

Last month, it was reported that two Jews were denied citizenship for having previously partaken in anti-occupation activism in the West Bank. This was the first known case of the state violating the Law of Return, which stipulates that every Jew is entitled to immigrate to Israel.

Many saw Gad Eisenkot as the last chance to halt the country’s authoritarian drift. The election has left open the possibility that he could still lead the government, but he has no clear path to power. While he might reverse the emerging trend of discriminating against Jews and Israelis deemed insufficiently patriotic, none of his proposed policies address the core issues that make Israel an ethnostate.

The election has not changed the reality for Palestinians, with or without Israeli citizenship, or the refusal of every major party to address these injustices. What Eisenkot may offer is merely a return to the illusion of democracy.

Jared Hillel is a journalist based in Jerusalem. He has previously reported from London, Toronto, and rural Cape Breton.

scraped.title: Austerity Is Now the Central Conflict in Brazilian Politics
scraped.description: Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro to win a fourth term as Brazil’s president. Political scientist André Singer says the hardest fight is still ahead: Brazil’s bourgeoisie wants harsh austerity, and Lula’s coalition is split over it.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro to win a fourth term as Brazil’s president. Political scientist André Singer says the hardest fight is still ahead: Brazil’s bourgeoisie wants harsh austerity, and Lula’s coalition is split over it.

Lula da Silva has won a fourth term, but Brazil’s democratic front is split by two incompatible economic programs. (Evaristo Sa / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

O n October 4, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election nearly two points ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Three weeks later, Lula turned the result around and won a fourth term in the October 25 runoff. In between, left-led demonstrations filled the streets of hundreds of Brazilian cities. The government also banned online betting, backed a forty-hour workweek, and raised the benefit of Bolsa Família, the cash-transfer program for poor families that Lula created in 2003.

Few analysts know Lula’s political project better than André Singer. A professor of political science at the University of São Paulo, Singer served as Lula’s spokesperson from 2003 to 2007 and press secretary from 2005 to 2007. He developed the concept of Lulism in Os sentidos do lulismo (2012) and O lulismo em crise (2018), and his new book, Impasse: O Brasil diante da onda reacionária , came out in August.

After the runoff, Singer spoke with Catarina Príncipe and Aldo Cordeiro Sauda for Jacobin about Bolsonarism as autocracy with a fascist bias, the Brazilian bourgeoisie’s silence during the campaign, and why the second-round mobilization was not populism. He also discussed the fight over austerity that awaits Lula’s fourth term.

Catarina Príncipe

You’ve written about the idea of an “autocracy with a fascist bias” to understand the phenomena of Donald Trump in the United States and Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil. Could you explain this idea further?

André Singer

Honestly, I can’t speak directly about Trumpism, because I don’t have enough expertise. So I’ll talk about Bolsonarism, the experience from which I formulated the idea of an autocratic tendency with a fascist bias. Studying the Bolsonaro presidency of 2019–2022, one can show empirically that he tried to reshape Brazil’s institutions in the direction of an autocratic regime.

One of the major conflicts during his term was over the independence of the Federal Police. For an American audience: The Federal Police is equivalent to the FBI. It is a national police force for the country’s major security problems, because everyday problems fall to the state governments.

But the big questions of corruption, organized crime, drug trafficking, and arms trafficking are all the Federal Police’s business. That is why a convention that successive presidents have observed since the return to democracy in the 1980s is so important: guaranteeing the Federal Police’s independence. The president of the republic appoints the director, but presidents have made a practice of appointing directors who have a certain independence from themselves.

Bolsonaro made a point of violating that convention and appointing a Federal Police leadership at the service of his own political interests. I’m describing this because it is the most evident case of all: he tried to manipulate the Federal Police to concentrate power.

Why do I say this autocratic tendency has a fascist bias? Because I find in it certain elements in common with historical fascism. Why don’t I say it’s fascist tout court? Because there are many elements that don’t correspond.

Let me give one element in common: the activation, through propaganda, of the unconscious of the masses. It is a kind of advertising that aims to hook the voter, the citizen, and the supporter through unconscious identification rather than rational argument. That doesn’t mean there aren’t also arguments of a material nature, material interests; I’m not saying it is merely a technique aimed at the unconscious. But I think this is very typical of fascism and not of the nonfascist right.

What isn’t in common with fascism? For example, there is no political party organized into militias, as in Italian fascism and then German Nazism. There is also no warlike rhetoric, in the sense of external war: Bolsonarism has a very strange nationalism of submission to the United States — something hard to understand. But it has no rhetoric of confrontation with other countries or of territorial expansion, an important element of historical fascism.

Since some elements are in common and many are not, I proposed a way of understanding the Bolsonaro phenomenon. We are facing an autocratic tendency — that is proven — with a fascist tendency that we still need to test. Meanwhile, there is a more general theoretical problem: the concept of fascism isn’t well defined.

Strange as it may seem, that is the problem we have to face: arriving at a concept of fascism that lets us understand the present situation. Obviously we are interested in understanding history, but with a view to the present and the future.

Catarina Príncipe

In an interview, I heard you distinguish between fascism from below and fascism from above. Which class does this autocracy with a fascist bias mobilize most?

André Singer

Marxist-inspired thought has already made clear the characteristics of historical fascism, and one stands out: fascism is a movement that comes from below, not from above. Leon Trotsky first made that contribution, in his writings on Germany, and it still holds; it is a fundamental distinction.

Bolsonarism has this characteristic: it comes from below; it is not a movement of the ruling class. It draws in the middle strata, but it quickly spreads to intermediate popular layers, which form its backbone. So in Brazil today, the far right penetrates from below.

Catarina Príncipe

How do you analyze the relationship between the ruling class and politics, given the existence of what you call two cross-class coalitions: the Bolsonarist “confederacy” and the Lulist “ concertación ”? What is the composition of these two coalitions?

André Singer

I call one the “confederacy,” by a certain analogy with the nineteenth-century American case, and the other the “concertación,” by analogy with Chile after Augusto Pinochet. I developed these two hypotheses to understand the 2022 election. So I’ll answer with 2022 in mind, then briefly go through the changes in 2026.

The idea of the confederacy was that a coalition of agribusiness entrepreneurs and service sector entrepreneurs in the cities formed. Certain evangelical denominations, which represent a kind of Brazilian Bible Belt, joined them. These denominations account for about 30 percent of the Brazilian electorate, and Bolsonarism has repeatedly won 70 percent of their vote.

In the 2022 election, the whole of the security forces joined these two components, the entrepreneurs and the evangelical Bible Belt, from the armed forces down to the regional (state) police forces. These forces represent a large contingent. Besides everyone formally engaged in security work, Brazil has an enormous army of private security guards, because public security can’t cope with the very serious crime problem.

These three tracks of the confederacy, so to speak, created an enormous corridor through the interior of the country. It runs from the north of Rio Grande do Sul to the south of the North Region, through the interior of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, the country’s most industrialized states. That corridor aligned with Bolsonarism, which largely explains its significant electoral power. In addition, the evangelical Bible Belt gives Bolsonarism a very strong bridgehead in Brazil’s large metropolitan regions.

In 2026, there was a change: because of the failed coup attempt, the armed forces pulled back. They had been very important because Bolsonaro, a former army captain, went through the military academy with the men who, by coincidence, made up the high command when he took office. He brought them into the government, and so the armed forces were deeply committed to the Bolsonaro government.

That is no longer the case. You can’t identify anyone of note from the armed forces in the campaign of his son Flávio Bolsonaro. But we know that the police forces backed that candidacy discreetly, rather than explicitly, as they had with Jair Bolsonaro’s government.

I call it a confederacy, although it has no connection with slavery. But it does have this connection: it divided Brazil. It united the interior, as if against the big cities, even though, I repeat, the evangelical denominations have influence in the big cities.

You also notice a certain prejudice against the Northeast and an underlying ideology that a more modern Brazil would be better off rid of a more backward Brazil. It is a kind of implicit ideology, which sometimes shows up more, sometimes less.

As for the concertación: the name came to me because, to build the coalition that sustained him, President Lula made an alliance with sectors of the old Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB). Until 2018, the PSDB had been the main rival of Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT). The current vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, headed the sectors willing to join. The PSDB as a whole has shrunk to a small party, and it stayed neutral: it backed Lula neither in 2022 nor now.

But the alliance with Alckmin represented a union with former PSDB sectors willing to form the democratic front. So, as in Chile, the two great adversaries came together: in Chile, the Socialist Party and the Christian Democratic Party; in Brazil, the PT and the PSDB.

Along with this party coalition, there was an important class coalition. Lulism represents the base of the Brazilian social pyramid, as everyone knows. But the alliance with this faction of the PSDB also brought in what I call the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie, the most modern sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which backed President Lula in the second round of 2022, not the first. That was very important both for his victory and for the future of the government.

In this 2026 election, that sector of the bourgeoisie did not speak out; it stayed neutral and backed neither Flávio Bolsonaro nor President Lula. João Moreira Salles — founder of Piauí magazine, an important filmmaker, and an heir to one of Brazil’s biggest banking families — wrote a very powerful article on the importance of that silence.

The consequence of that silence was the acceptance, practically until the last minute, of a Flávio Bolsonaro victory. An extraordinary movement reversed that in this year’s second round. To conclude for now: the cosmopolitan sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which stayed silent, is no longer explicitly present in the concertación.

Catarina Príncipe

You define Latin American populism as a mass phenomenon: in certain circumstances, classes take the form of multitudes with little or no class organization, connecting people and leader directly. Was this type of populism what secured Lula’s victory? And how can we reconnect this expression of the multitude with more sustained class organization?

André Singer

I think the concept of populism doesn’t apply to the second-round victory. It’s a very interesting question, and it’s going to give me some work, because I’ll have to develop something more sophisticated to account for the phenomenon.

But at first sight, I think we had a social explosion — let’s call it that — without the characteristics of populism. It was more organized and more conscious of its aims than the populist phenomenon implies.

To be clear, my theoretical framework is Ernesto Laclau’s old definition, from 1978, not that of the so-called second Laclau. It is a good one for thinking about populism in Latin America and, of course, in Brazil too.

Why do I say the explosion is more conscious and more organized? More conscious because it aimed, first, to stop the far right. Flávio Bolsonaro won [the first round] by 2 percentage points and immediately began putting together his government and saying he would change the Constitution. That was a tactical error, even from his own standpoint: it had such an impact that the democratic sectors of Brazilian society immediately began to speak out and organize.

That is one side of the phenomena. The other is a feeling that President Lula needed a fourth term, because the government itself began to change during the campaign. It isn’t obvious, but President Lula changed the campaign in mid-September without saying so: he began to take measures.

One event seems revealing to me. On September 11, at a rally in Porto Alegre, he said, “I know you are finding products expensive at the supermarket,” referring to coffee and beef. That is very significant, because until then the government had not addressed the population’s material needs directly.

From then on, the president not only spoke to those needs but began taking measures. For example, he raised the Bolsa Família benefit, which the government had not adjusted in four years, and he banned online betting, the “bets.” Remember that Brazil is living through a triple crisis: a cost-of-living crisis, a crisis of household indebtedness, and, on top of it, an epidemic of bets.

People began gambling wildly, partly to earn extra income to pay off debts. Since betting companies design bets so that the great majority lose, people ended up worse off. President Lula faced great resistance to the ban. First, many companies are involved, and long-term legal contracts were already in place; second, soccer clubs, which are very popular and important in Brazil, depended to some extent on sponsorship from those companies.

The other very important decision was the switch from six workdays and one day off (6x1) to five and two (5x2), cutting the workweek from forty-four to forty hours: probably the greatest labor victory since the 1988 Constitution. Congress passed it, but everyone knows it was the president’s initiative and that he committed himself to it. Structurally, of course, it is even more important than the betting ban. But the ban has symbolic meaning, because the president decided on it during the campaign: an act of boldness and courage in defense of the popular economy.

Alongside it, the government took two measures to restructure the debts of the popular classes, and others such as free public transit on weekends, which speaks directly to the young people who took to the streets. What I mean is that all this is not populist rhetoric; these are actions. It is what I call a change in the character of the government.

Finally, these sectors that took to the streets are not completely disorganized. The demonstrations took place in hundreds of cities, but the largest, and most unprecedented, were in São Paulo, the country’s biggest metropolis. I have been comparing the two October demonstrations in São Paulo, on October 11 and 24, with the great right-wing demonstration for the impeachment of President Dilma Rousseff in March 2016. There had been no demonstration of this kind for at least ten years.

The Left led these demonstrations, although they were not only of the Left. They formed a democratic front, with centrist sectors and possibly even a democratic right: individually, people may have gone out to defend democracy. But the leadership clearly belonged to the Left, and these are possibly the largest left-wing demonstrations in Brazil’s history.

The Brazilian left has organizations: the PT, the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), the Communist Party of Brazil (PCdoB), the student organizations, the cultural associations, the unions, the neighborhood associations, and the popular movements, especially the Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) and the Homeless Workers’ Movement (MTST). On the center left, you have the Socialist Party of Brazil (PSB) and the Labour Democratic Party (PDT). In short, Brazil has an organizational structure, and it mobilized. So, from these two angles, I wouldn’t describe this as a populist phenomenon; something different happened.

Aldo Cordeiro Sauda

This year, you observed a pendular movement by the cosmopolitan wing of the bourgeoisie toward the far-right candidacy, the opposite of its support for Lula’s election in 2022. Internationally, US foreign policy shows the same pendular movement: sympathy for Lula under Joe Biden in 2022, explicit support for Bolsonarism under Trump in 2026. To what extent does the Brazilian ruling class’s shift toward Bolsonarism express mere deference to Washington?

André Singer

As far as I understand, the sector I call cosmopolitan — in the American case, the big technology companies — backed Biden in 2020. In 2024, it wasn’t very clear to me what they were doing, but they didn’t seem to back Trump either, with the exception of Elon Musk.

Yet when Trump took office, all of them were there. In the Brazilian case, though, it seems plausible that a conversion of the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie to the far right influenced the Brazilian bourgeoisie. Until the last minute, there was a certain expectation that this sector might speak out in favor of President Lula.

That sector committed itself to democracy in 2022, in a movement broader than support for President Lula. In August 2022, at a demonstration in São Paulo, those business leaders issued a letter. They said they would not accept, under any circumstances, a refusal to recognize the election result — exactly what the White House said.

Those two positions were very important in keeping most of the armed forces from joining the coup, because the military knew it could not govern without that support. So you see: there is a Brazilian phenomenon. A link to a transformation in the United States is a possible hypothesis.

Catarina Príncipe

Our understanding of the question is that the Brazilian cosmopolitan bourgeoisie is staying neutral now because of the political change in the United States from Biden to Trump. At the time of the coup attempt, the Biden presidency was very important in stopping it from going forward. Now, with Trump, there might be some attempt at direct intervention in Brazilian politics.

So, part of the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie doesn’t want to take a position today, to avoid a falling-out with US policy and with a possible Bolsonaro victory. It’s less a direct mirror between fractions of the bourgeoisie.

André Singer

Then I’ll take advantage of your interpretation to add something that makes the problem more complex. The major point of division between that sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie and Lula’s third government is the fiscal deficit. That sector demands a big cut in public spending, which in its view would have to fall on pension benefits, and it wants to delink them from the minimum wage. The Brazilian Constitution links the two, so raising the minimum wage in real terms also raises all benefits.

The other target is the constitutional floor for health and education: the Brazilian Constitution requires that a certain share of annual tax revenue go to health and education, and this cannot go down. The bourgeoisie’s aim is to remove that floor from the Constitution, so that this spending falls.

So, we have a very serious issue: on one side the pension system, all the retirees; on the other, the two main social policies that form the social core of the 1988 Constitution, health and education. That is the main problem. We still don’t know whether there is also a certain caution or a desire to align with the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie.

Aldo Cordeiro Sauda

National sovereignty took center stage in the campaign, perhaps for the first time since the return to democracy. What role did this issue play in the second-round turnaround against Flávio Bolsonaro?

André Singer

The Trump administration’s offensive against Brazil — the tariffs and its direct or indirect intervention in the elections — has put national sovereignty on the agenda. Trump justified the first tariffs by saying that Brazil was persecuting his preferred candidate, Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazil today does not have a very strong nationalist current. A nationalism is now starting to grow, because the global situation has changed and the country faces political-economic aggression — let’s call it that. So nationalism has come onto the agenda, but in my opinion — and I may be wrong — it has still not become a central issue.

Catarina Príncipe

Lula wants to transform the Brazilian economy by investing in the green economy, infrastructure, and artificial intelligence (data centers) and by using Brazil’s resources in rare metals and minerals. How much room for maneuver does he have to do this, given the New Fiscal Framework, the Lula government’s 2023 fiscal rule capping annual spending growth at 70 percent of revenue growth? How should we think about his government’s relationship with the bourgeoisie in this fourth term and the new balance of forces?

Do you believe the bourgeoisie will tend to deepen its conflict with the PT, intensifying the pendular movement? And in this context, what happens to the mass mobilization from below that we saw in the second round?

André Singer

I think this is the central point regarding the fourth term: what the outcome of this conflict will be. The stock market fell nearly 14 percent the day after the election. As I have been saying, the market has no vote, but it has money, and its message is clear: if you don’t cut public spending, we’re leaving.

The question of fiscal adjustment is truly central, because the bourgeoisie is demanding harsh austerity. In my opinion, the demand for austerity is the fundamental issue in Brazilian politics today, but in general nobody puts it openly: it remains an implicit debate. That is partly because we are not managing to politicize the problem, to make the popular classes, the working class, aware that this is what is at stake. This is the main confrontation.

This organizes Brazilian politics. In my recent book, Impasse : O Brasil diante da onda reacionária , I tried to show that this issue splits the democratic front in two. It is, as Americans say, an elephant in the room: everyone treats it as if it didn’t exist. I felt that my role was to bring it to the surface; obviously I can’t do that alone, but I can contribute to some extent.

The conflict is immediate, because the transformation Brazil needs, which runs through reindustrialization, is a gigantic task. Brazil is an enormous country, and you don’t change a structure of this order without major investment.

This transformation can’t rely on public investment alone; there must also be private investment. But we have to think with the instruments we have. Perry Anderson says Keynesianism no longer works, so we need to create new mechanisms; but until we have them, I’ll use the old ones. The state will have to induce this development process, although it also has to bring in other investors.

There is, therefore, an incompatibility between the country’s needs and this radical cut in public spending, which goes in the opposite direction. This is the central point. Even if the terms of the debate were not clear, I think the large demonstrations in hundreds of Brazilian cities point toward the government having this commitment. We’ll have to follow events to see how it unfolds.

Catarina Príncipe

Your earlier book defined Lulism as “combating poverty without confronting capital.” Can Lulism go beyond itself, and does it want to? Is there room to do so today, given the current party arithmetic in Congress? And how can the Brazilian left organize to force it to take measures that go beyond welfarism?

André Singer

I’ll start with Congress, which I think is simpler. In the Congress that takes office in 2027, the far right has grown, not at the expense of the Left but of other forces on the Right. In the Chamber of Deputies, it went from 91 to 121 deputies, out of 513 seats.

That is significant: since the return to democracy, we would hardly find such a large single-party caucus. But it decides nothing on its own. What we will have is permanent negotiation, which is already happening: Lula’s third government already negotiated permanently with what we in Brazil call the Centrão .

To be clear, the Centrão is the established right, the traditional right, so to speak. It generally holds the majority in Brazil’s National Congress, because the Brazilian electoral system reproduces small local oligarchies that tend to dominate legislative elections.

This is structural in Brazil, and it will continue. President Lula has specialized in negotiating with those sectors. The third term was the most difficult in this respect, because Congress gained power from what we in Brazil call the “secret budget” ( orçamento secreto ) [budget amendments through which lawmakers steer federal funds without disclosing who requested them]. Even so, the president managed to pass his two boldest proposals.

The first was the income-tax exemption for those who earn up to R$5,000 (about US$940) a month, offset by a levy on those who earn more than R$50,000 (about US$9,400). The Chamber of Deputies approved it unanimously. The second was the change of the work schedule from 6x1 to 5x2, which we have already discussed. The Chamber had already approved it unanimously, and the Senate has just passed it by an overwhelming majority.

This shows that such negotiation is possible. The traditional right makes concessions on one side and concessions on the other. Its concession to the far right is an effort to reduce the sentences the courts imposed on Jair Bolsonaro and on everyone they convicted of taking part in the 2022 coup attempt, and that effort will expand.

It will probably have real consequences: the far right will try to make it possible for Bolsonaro to run in 2030. I think that is its outlook. I repeat, it won’t achieve this without the support of the Right, but depending on the back-and-forth negotiations, it could happen.

I now turn to the problem of the Left. The Left should not leave the democratic front. The central problem in Brazil, as in many countries around the world, is to isolate the far right and reverse its advance toward power everywhere.

Looking at the long term, we are witnessing a gradual, slow, but constant advance of the far right, sometimes faster, sometimes slower. If the far right comes to power and consolidates itself around the whole world, the working class will suffer a tremendous setback in every respect.

Our task, then, is to avoid this by isolating the far right and defeating it as an alternative for power in Brazil. For that, we have to stay in the democratic front. But two incompatible economic programs divide the democratic front.

We have to fight explicitly inside this democratic front for our position to win a majority. I’m convinced that democracy depends on the majority of the population recognizing in it an answer to their problems; if it doesn’t, it won’t last. That is the best contribution the Left can and must make to the defense of democracy.

Lulism, as I characterized it, is a movement that seeks to combat poverty, which is fundamental in Brazil, without confronting capital. I stand by that definition. But political reality is dynamic. We and all the other actors are facing new situations, so new things are bound to happen.

As you know, we can’t predict the future; we can only see tendencies. I would end by saying that a popular commitment is in Lulism’s nature: it depends on a popular base; it is a popular movement. Beyond that, only the political process will tell.

André Singer is a political theorist who served as press secretary for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration in Brazil.

Catarina Príncipe is a political activist from Portugal. She is a member of Bloco de Esquerda, a coeditor of Europe in Revolt , and a Jacobin contributing editor.

Aldo Cordeiro Sauda is a journalist, lawyer, and PSOL activist who covered the Arab Spring from Cairo and Beirut for O Estado de S. Paulo and Folha de S.Paulo . He is a PhD candidate in political science at the University of São Paulo and the founder of Contrabando Editorial .

scraped.title: Equality Is About Who Rules
scraped.description: What do we actually mean by “equality”? Few thinkers have answered that question better than Elizabeth Anderson: not identical outcomes but a society where no one gets to dominate anyone else, including at work.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

What do we actually mean by “equality”? Few thinkers have answered that question better than Elizabeth Anderson: not identical outcomes but a society where no one gets to dominate anyone else, including at work.

Your boss is an unelected ruler you can’t vote out. Elizabeth Anderson thinks egalitarians should treat that as the scandal it is. (Bettmann Archive via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T here is a complex debate about the extent to which socialists prioritize equality above the full flowering of each person’s individuality. But you’d have to be quite the contrarian to deny that socialists take equality very seriously; perhaps more seriously than any other major political ideology. Prominent socialist thinkers like G. A. Cohen and Thomas Piketty have dedicated much of their work to defending the philosophical and economic merits of egalitarianism. Socialist Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech put equality at the core of his vision: “that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: ‘We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.’”

That said, the commitment of socialists and other egalitarians to equality can often seem frustratingly vague. It invites accusations of ill-defined “social justice” advocacy or even pursuing the much dreaded “equality of outcomes” through a Harrison Bergeron–like willingness to cut everyone down to size. Of course, many of these charges are lobbed in bad faith, and even the more refined versions ignore how other core principles — like liberty or order — are equally contestable and vague until explicitly defined. But having a firmer grasp on what we mean by equality and what we want would help the Left understand itself better.

F ew living thinkers have done more to answer this question than University of Michigan philosopher Elizabeth Anderson. A former doctoral student of John Rawls, Anderson made her name in the 1990s criticizing contemporary egalitarian philosophy and developing her own version of relational equality. More recently, Anderson has become a vigorous proponent of workplace democracy, contending that there is something deeply tyrannical about the forms of work that exist today. Her most recent book , Hijacked: How Neoliberalism Turned the Work Ethic Against Workers and How Workers Can Take It Back , argues for rehabilitating the tradition of social democratic and socialist political thought as a counter to the Right’s moralizing about work.

From the beginning, Anderson was fiercely critical of many dimensions of contemporary capitalism and its inequalities. Her early book Value in Ethics and Economics (1993) is a careful critique of how market relations and their distinct ways of reasoning about ethical questions are increasingly colonizing many spheres of society. She insisted that realizing many forms of “freedom, autonomy and welfare demands that certain goods be produced, exchanged, and enjoyed outside of market relations or in accordance with non-market norms.” While in this book Anderson typically appeals to ideas of autonomy and welfare rather than strict equality, there is a clear egalitarian undercurrent. She criticizes libertarians’ “fetishism” of property and markets as the sole site of freedom, and how this leads them to be blind to the “social relations of domination that exist prior to market transactions and that condition the choices individuals make there.” For instance, a long history of patriarchal subordination means that women may feel compelled to enter into exploitative contracts, say, in the sex industry, to get by day to day.

In her important paper “What Is the Point of Equality?” Anderson clarifies the role equality plays in inhibiting domination. It opens with a sardonic question: “If much recent academic work defending equality had been secretly penned by conservatives, could the results be any more embarrassing for egalitarians?” She chastises both Marxists like G. A. Cohen for trivializing equality by reducing it to debates about whether we ought to compensate people for being temperamentally gloomy or easily bored, and liberal egalitarians like Ronald Dworkin for proposing an envy-free distribution of resources — implying conservatives are right that the push for equality is ultimately about nothing more than resentment.

Anderson wanted egalitarians to finally get serious and realize that we aren’t, in fact, all that interested in building a society where people get the same bundle of goodies. Inegalitarian societies have built hierarchies whose social relations enabled some people to dominate others, often by insisting that those atop the social hierarchy were intrinsically worth more than those at the bottom. Egalitarians, Anderson argued, are fundamentally committed to undoing those forms of social hierarchy that enabled domination and oppression:

Egalitarian political movements oppose such hierarchies. They assert the equal moral worth of persons. This assertion does not mean that all have equal virtue or talent. Negatively, the claim repudiates distinctions of moral worth based on birth or social identity — on family membership, inherited social status, race, ethnicity, gender, or genes. There are no natural slaves, plebeians, or aristocrats. Positively, the claim asserts that all competent adults are equally moral agents: everyone equally has the power to develop and exercise moral responsibility, to cooperate with others according to principles of justice, to shape and fulfill a conception of their good.

In The Imperative of Integration , Anderson further defined the parameters of what she called the “relational theory” of equality and inequality. It located the “causes of economic, political, and symbolic group inequalities in the relations (processes of interaction) between groups, rather than in the internal characteristics of their members or in cultural differences that exist independently of group interaction.” Anderson emphasizes that in our society what makes people unequal often isn’t intrinsic to them but the result of the social relations in which they are embedded. But to invoke Karl Marx’s language of fetishism, this is very often obscured by ruling ideologies, which redirect the source of inferiority from social relations onto the individuals and groups themselves. Someone sold into slavery is described, in Aristotle’s terms, as a “natural slave” rather than someone who has been trapped in an oppressively hierarchical social system. Moreover, to reinforce hierarchy we often impute still worse forms of inferiority upon those at the base of the pyramid. For instance, when Senator John C. Calhoun called slavery a “positive good” because slaves were racially inferior, and the best thing for everyone was their paternalistic subordination to the superior race.

There is a lot to commend in Anderson’s relational equality. It helped steer egalitarians away from arguing about whether people with highfalutin tastes should be supplied with plovers’ eggs and truffle oil and back toward the hierarchies of oppression that it is the Left’s job to confront. If there is a limitation to her approach, it’s an enduring ambiguity about what a flourishing life ought to look like. This is a necessary part of making the case for equality; namely, why and how would people live better lives if they were more equal through being free of domination. Here Marx provides us with a helpful clue in the third volume of Capital , where he posits that under socialism the cooperative development of human powers and capabilities will become an end in itself for the first time, rather than just a means of training more efficient workers. The development of human powers to foster a rich individuality in community with others ought to be on our horizon, and doing so will mean transcending capitalism.

I n her more recent work, Anderson has become one of the sharpest critics of both capitalist practices and ideology. In Private Government , she asks us to imagine “a government that assigns almost everyone a superior whom they must obey.” This government offers routines but no rule of law: orders can be arbitrary, can change without notice, and can’t be appealed. Worst of all, the bosses answer to no one below them. “They are neither elected nor removable by their inferiors.” Most of us, Anderson point out, don’t have to imagine this. It’s what most of us encounter every day when we go to work. And yet, despite the oppression it entails, we are often told that not only is there no alternative, but that such a system is nothing less than freedom itself.

Anderson’s point is well taken. If we were told that tomorrow the federal government was going to tell most Americans when to wake up, what they were going to wear, when they could go to the bathroom and eat lunch, how and when they were going to talk to others, there would be riots in the street. Everyone with a “Don’t Tread on Me!” flag would be making liberal use of their Second Amendment rights, Rand Paul would be weeping on live television, and the Daily Wire would proclaim this the Communist States of America. And yet Anderson observes this is the reality for millions of Americans subject to “private government” every day. She rejects the claim that that the modern commercial firm is a realm of individualism, as opposed to the collectivism of the state. Anderson notes that in the “great contest between individualism and collectivism regarding the mode of production, collectivism won, decisively. Nearly all production is undertaken by teams of workers using large, indivisible forms of capital equipment held in common.” Firms are collective enterprises, where the social relations grant capitalists and managers enormous domineering powers at the expense of their workers. She recommends that the way to respond to these forms of domination is to extend the liberal and democratic norms we already apply to statist collectives to private government: allow workers more democratic rights, greater protections, and the right to assemble and check unaccountable private power.

In Hjjacked , Anderson examines some of the ideological reasons many on the Right consider this unacceptable. She points out how from the beginning of the modern era there have been fierce debates over the work ethic and who deserved greater power and rewards: workers or capitalists. Anderson shows how socialists and a surprising number of liberals argued a “progressive work ethic” holding that, since workers did most of the work under capitalism, they were getting a raw deal. But they were always confronted by capitalists advocating a “conservative work ethic” that “stressed discipline, frugality, and asceticism for workers, while reaping the lion’s share of productivity gains for themselves in their capacity as capital owners.” The spirit of this conservative ethic was well captured in Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises’s letter to Ayn Rand, congratulating her on the publication of Atlas Shrugged :

You have the courage to tell the masses what no politician told them: you are inferior and all the improvements in your conditions which you simply take for granted you owe to the effort of men who are better than you. If this be arrogance, as some of your critics observed, it is still the truth that had to be said in the age of the Welfare State.

Anderson thinks that there are several ways we can confront this ideology. One is by reconstructing and re-canonizing the work of socialist and social democratic thinkers who tried to conceive of better ways to organize the economy. Anderson quips that it is “telling that in the history of political thought, no social democrat has been canonized, despite the huge influence of social democracy in many wealthy capitalist countries.” This is something of an exaggeration outside the United States, where left-wing economic thought has gained more traction, but her point still stands. A major goal of left-wing philosophers ought to be reintroducing large numbers of people to the rich and thoughtful tradition of socialist and social democratic thought, to help inspire thinking about where to go in the future.

Anderson is esteemed in academic circles but deserves a much wider popular audience. The times are certainly ripe for her message: in his second administration, Donald Trump has gone on a warpath against workers’ rights and needs, making it harder for public sector employees to engage in collective bargaining. Recently, he even went as far as to adopt an explicit “Let them eat cake” attitude toward rising costs to pay for his siege of Iran: “We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare.” Anderson offers us ways to both criticize these forms of domination and think through how to envision a better future where workers take back the world they built.

But above all else, Anderson reminds us that equality is about more than who gets what. Fundamentally, it’s a question of who rules and who is ruled. For most of us, for most of our waking hours, the answer is that the boss rules and we are ruled. Anderson’s work is an invitation to change that answer.

Matt McManus is an assistant professor at Spelman College. He is the author of The Political Right and Equality and The Political Theory of Liberal Socialism among other books.

scraped.title: Congress has a chance to fix the Endangered Species Act
scraped.description: Next week, Congress will vote on a bill to modernize the regulation that hurts property owners and conservation efforts.
scraped.author: Megan Jenkins, John Nagle
scraped.h1: Congress Has a Chance To Fix the Endangered Species Act
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Energy & Environment

Megan Jenkins and John Nagle | 11.6.2026 2:35 PM

Next week, the Senate will consider a new permitting deal that promises to make it easier to build in America. From mines and pipelines to transmission lines and renewable energy projects, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would prune our regulatory thicket that delays development and increases costs for commonsense projects.

While the bill's proposed reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act have attracted much of the attention, its changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) are especially promising in helping the law achieve its goals while reducing unnecessary obstacles to infrastructure, energy production, and economic growth.

More than five decades after its enactment, the ESA has struggled to achieve its ultimate objective: recovering endangered species so they no longer need federal protection. Meanwhile, its regulatory requirements can discourage conservation and create costly uncertainty for landowners and businesses.

According to a 2023 analysis by the Property and Environment Research Center , just 3 percent of species listed under the ESA were delisted due to recovery. That's 57 of 1,732 species over the law's first 50 years. Meanwhile, the ESA's costs are huge . Federal agencies spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually administering the law, but those expenditures capture only a fraction of its potential economic burden. The costs of delayed projects, restrictions on private property, and regulatory compliance remain largely unmeasured.

One major problem with the ESA is the uncertainty surrounding its application. The law requires federal agencies to rely on the "best scientific and commercial data available" when deciding on species protections. But Congress never clearly defined that standard, leaving agencies substantial discretion in determining what evidence is sufficient, and courts often defer to those judgments.

Consider the Delta Smelt, a fish, typically no longer than three inches, native to California's Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta. This small fish created big problems for California farmers. In a 2008 biological opinion , the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) concluded that two major water projects that deliver water from the Delta to California's agriculture-rich Central Valley needed to reduce operations substantially to protect the endangered fish.

In practical terms, federal protections for the Delta Smelt meant restricting water deliveries to farmers in one of the nation's most productive agricultural regions.

However, the scientific basis for that decision raised serious questions. The FWS' biological opinion imposed onerous water-pumping restrictions when smelt caught in the pumps reached a certain threshold, without accounting for the overall smelt population. This departed from standard industry practice, as raw numbers provide little context for assessing threats to a species without population data. When challenged in court, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals found that FWS had departed from standard scientific methodology. Nevertheless, it upheld the agency's approach, deferring to its determination of the "best scientific data available."

The Delta Smelt controversy illustrates a major flaw in the ESA: When Congress leaves a key scientific standard undefined, agencies can, and often will, exercise broad discretion over decisions that affect water supplies, private property, and economic livelihoods.

BAAJA would address this problem by establishing clearer scientific standards for such decisions. The bill defines best available science as "all relevant and objective scientific and commercial information available at the time of the agency action."

It would also establish criteria for evaluating scientific evidence, including whether models account for potential errors and use accepted professional methods. These requirements would make ESA-related decisions more transparent and easier to evaluate, and would prevent agencies from putting a thumb on the scale when evaluating scientific evidence.

The bill would also give states a stronger role. State wildlife agencies frequently possess extensive population data and local expertise, yet federal decision making does not always adequately incorporate their findings. BAAJA would require federal agencies to consider specified scientific information submitted by states and create pathways for qualified states to conduct certain ESA consultations.

Perhaps most importantly for project developers, BAAJA would shorten the standard timeline for formal ESA consultations from 90 days to 60 days.

These consultations are required when federal projects may adversely affect protected species or their critical habitat. They can affect everything from mining operations to roads and energy infrastructure.

A 2015 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that approximately 20 percent of formal ESA consultations exceeded the applicable 135-day regulatory timeline. Some dragged on for years.

Shorter deadlines won't eliminate every permitting delay. But they could help prevent prolonged reviews from creating unnecessary uncertainty and expense for businesses seeking to invest in American infrastructure.

Taken together, the proposed reforms would make ESA administration more transparent, predictable, and efficient while preserving its conservation responsibilities.

After more than 50 years, Congress has an opportunity to reform the ESA to ensure it is serving both wildlife and the people whose cooperation is essential to conservation. Protecting endangered species and allowing Americans to build, invest, and develop natural resources should not be mutually exclusive goals. BAAJA offers Congress an opportunity to move toward a system that better achieves both.

Eugene Volokh | 11.6.2026 2:27 PM

The old provision dated back to 1868, and read, "The citizens of this State shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for their common defense." The new , which passed 71%-29%, will read :

(a) The citizens of this State shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for: (1) Their common defense; (2) Lawful hunting and recreational use; and (3) Any other lawful purpose. (b) The right to keep and bear arms under subsection (a) of this section includes without limitation the possession and use of: (1) Ammunition; (2) Firearm accessories; and (3) Firearm components. (c) The right to keep and bear arms under subsection (a) of this section is a natural, fundamental, and individual right that shall not be infringed.

scraped.title: Houston voters approve restrictions on marijuana arrests and a ban on no-knock police raids
scraped.description: The first provision might curtail local pot busts, but the second one is unlikely to have a meaningful impact.
scraped.author: Jacob Sullum
scraped.h1: Houston Voters Approve Restrictions on Marijuana Arrests and a Ban on No-Knock Police Raids
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

War on Drugs

Jacob Sullum | 11.6.2026 2:20 PM

This week Houston voters overwhelmingly approved a ballot initiative that instructs local police to make marijuana misdemeanors their "lowest possible enforcement priority" and prohibits them from seeking or executing no-knock search warrants. The first provision might significantly reduce low-level marijuana arrests in Houston, which have risen dramatically in recent years. But the second one, although well-intentioned, is unlikely to make much difference in practice.

More than 70 percent of voters said yes to Proposition A , which requires the Houston Police Department (HPD) to deprioritize marijuana arrests involving possession of two ounces or less, a Class B misdemeanor punishable by a maximum $2,000 fine and up to six months in jail, or two to four ounces, a Class A misdemeanor punishable by a maximum $4,000 fine and up to a year in jail. The initiative, which amends the city charter, says "the City shall update its annual budget, police department manual, and relevant policies and procedures to ensure that public safety resources are not wasted on misdemeanor marijuana enforcement."

Although the HPD arrested just 10 people for marijuana misdemeanors in 2022, Houston Public Media reports , that number shot up in subsequent years, peaking at 538 in 2024 before falling to 426 in 2025. As of September, the number for this year was 232. From 2021 through 2025, 74 percent of marijuana arrests involved black people, who account for less than a quarter of Houston's population.

Proposition A requires the city to conduct an audit of arrests and citations during that period, including "demographic information for each person charged with an offense." The audit is also supposed to estimate the time and money spent on those cases.

Voters in Austin and Dallas have approved similar measures. But for a couple of reasons, they had little measurable impact.

By the time Austin voters passed their initiative in 2022, the city council had already restricted low-level marijuana arrests. In 2020, the Austin Police Department reported that possession arrests involving two ounces or less had fallen from 319 in 2017 to 54 in 2019 and dropped further in 2020, when police reported just three such arrests in the first quarter.

In Dallas, low-level marijuana arrests likewise declined before the ballot initiative passed in 2024. The Dallas Police Department implemented the measure in January 2025 by instructing officers to stop arresting people for simple possession of four ounces or less. But that July, the city agreed to stop enforcing the policy after a state appeals court ruled , in response to a lawsuit by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, that Austin's initiative was preempted by state law. Paxton had sued Dallas on the same grounds.

Assuming the Houston initiative does not suffer a similar fate, it should accelerate the downward trend in low-level marijuana arrests that began last year. But the ban on no-knock raids seems less promising.

The controversy over no-knock search warrants in Houston was driven largely by the January 2019 drug raid that killed a middle-aged couple, Dennis Tuttle and Rhogena Nicholas, whom veteran narcotics officer Gerald Goines had falsely implicated in drug dealing by describing a heroin purchase that never happened. That fiasco prompted a new HPD policy requiring officers to obtain high-level approval for no-knock warrant applications. And since then, the Houston Chronicle reports , no such warrants have been issued.

The details of the operation that killed Tuttle and Nicholas provide further reason to doubt that Proposition A's knock-and-announce rule will have a meaningful impact. After breaking through the front door around 5 p.m. without warning, police immediately shot the couple's dog. At that point, Nicholas was sitting on a couch in the living room, where she had been watching TV. Tuttle, who had been napping in a bedroom, responded to the tumult and gunfire by grabbing a revolver and firing at the intruders. By the time the shooting stopped, Tuttle and Nicholas were dead, and four officers, including Goines, were grievously wounded, mostly by friendly fire .

After Goines' lies were revealed, he was convicted of felony murder and sentenced to 60 years in state prison. During his trial, the prosecution argued that Tuttle did not realize the intruders were cops and reacted as "any normal person" would to a violent home invasion. But it is not clear that the outcome would have been any different if the cops had knocked, announced themselves, and waited "at least 15 seconds" before entering, as Proposition A requires.

Perhaps Nicholas would have heard the cops, digested what was happening, restrained the dog, and managed to open the door within 15 seconds. But if not, the cops still would have broken in and opened fire, and Tuttle still would have responded the same way.

Something similar happened when Louisville police officers killed Breonna Taylor during an early-morning drug raid in March 2020. In that case, which likewise involved dubious drug-trafficking allegations, the cops also had a no-knock warrant. They nevertheless banged on the door for at least 30 seconds, and they claimed that they also identified themselves as police officers.

All but one of Taylor's neighbors said they heard no such announcement. Taylor's boyfriend, who was in bed with her at the time, likewise said he did not know that the men who broke into the apartment were police officers. Like Tuttle, he grabbed a gun, which he fired once, prompting the hail of bullets that killed Taylor, who was unarmed and standing near him in a dark hallway.

The 15-second requirement imposed by Proposition A clearly would not have saved Taylor. Nor would it make a difference in other cases where police enter homes in the middle of the night, a practice that invites potentially deadly confusion . Since a knock-and-announce rule works only when people can reasonably be expected to hear, comprehend, and promptly respond, it is unlikely to have an impact without restrictions on the timing of police raids and a presumption against the "dynamic entry" tactics that cops tend to use when they execute drug warrants.

Whatever such reforms might accomplish, they do not address the fundamental problem , which stems from the decision to criminalize peaceful transactions between consenting adults. When politicians authorize police to invade people's homes in the hope of discovering arbitrarily prohibited intoxicants, they should not be surprised by the ensuing violence.

scraped.title: Trump Names Stephen Miller New Chief of Staff
scraped.description: State of the Union: Miller will replace Susie Wiles in the position.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump said Friday that Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to Chief of Staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Announcing the move on Truth Social, Trump wrote that Miller would start in the position on Monday, and that Wiles—who the president praised as having done “an outstanding job”—would move to another role in the “Trump Political Operation.”

Miller has played a major role in driving the White House’s domestic policy agenda, particularly when it comes to immigration. He has worked for the president since the 2016 campaign, and is widely viewed as a hard-liner within the administration. The shake-up comes just three days after Republicans suffered devastating losses in the midterm elections.

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
On Thursday, President Trump told reporters he was close to a decision on whether to restart strikes against Iran. “I would prefer not to destroy what is left of the country, if possible,” the president said, “but I may have to do so. You will know very soon.” This is the first time Trump has touted the possibility of new strikes since the GOP’s stunning midterm losses earlier this week, which many read as a referendum on the war and its economic consequences.

Three tankers attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz were reported hit Friday morning. Iran’s IRGC said two of the tankers had struck mines while attempting to use “unauthorized” routes to cross the Strait. Iran also claimed to have shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm Island on Friday.

Also on Friday, President Trump held a phone call with Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, during which the two leaders reportedly discussed the potential for a diplomatic resolution of the conflict.

Oil prices continued to ease Friday, with Brent crude opening just under $99 per barrel. AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline in the United States is $4.07 per gallon, and the average price of diesel is $6.23 per gallon.

scraped.title: DeSantis’s Unconvincing Iran Flip-Flop
scraped.description: The Florida governor’s criticism is undercut by a long paper trail of Iran hawkery.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
The Florida governor’s criticism is undercut by a long paper trail of Iran hawkery.

Republicans were eviscerated in an election President Donald Trump and his opponents saw as a referendum on his second term. The outcome bodes ill for the GOP, which now faces strong Democratic majorities in Congress and the prospect of endless investigations and legislative stonewalling.

One prominent Republican with an eye for 2028 decided to attack the president’s record just before the midterms. In an interview with Stephen A. Smith , Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis lambasted the Iran War and other failures of the administration. “We just got to be honest. Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just a fact,” DeSantis said.

He continued his criticism of the White House in a press conference after the Tuesday massacre, chastising the president and the GOP for poor messaging and not delivering on their promises.

It’s a clear sign DeSantis plans to run in 2028 and wants to pitch himself, once again, as a Trump critic from the right.

Central to that pitch will be the Iran War. Unlike anyone in the administration, DeSantis bears no responsibility for it. He can present himself as a critic, without the awkwardness of having been in the meetings at which Operation Epic Fury was planned. It’s a smart move—but it also contrasts with his past hawkery on the issue.

DeSantis knows he needs to change his tune to be a viable candidate for ’28. Republicans lost big because of the disastrous war, and many within the GOP base want someone who can deliver the truth. But the governor’s past stances may undermine this pitch. He’s not exactly a consistent non-interventionist.

In his previous presidential bid, DeSantis sought to distinguish himself as a stronger hawk than Trump on the Islamic Republic. This was a central theme of a speech he delivered to Christians United for Israel in 2023, for example, and it featured consistently in his foreign policy messaging. His campaign website promised to “turn the screws on Iran beginning on Day 1—abandoning the naïve, disastrous Obama-Biden foreign policies.”

The Florida governor even attacked Trump for offering mild criticism of Benjamin Netanyahu in the fall of 2023, saying it was “absurd that anyone, much less someone running for President, would choose now to attack our friend and ally, Israel.” DeSantis made this rift a major part of his campaign and kept hammering Trump about it. It didn’t work, with one Republican operative saying it made him “look like members of the Lincoln Project to the base right now.”

DeSantis’s ’24 bid earned the support of many influencers and commentators who still defend the Iran War. That included none other than THE Iran War supporter, Mark Levin . Levin’s stepson worked on pro-Israel outreach for DeSantis’s gubernatorial and presidential campaigns. Unsurprisingly, Levin hosted DeSantis on his show several times throughout the primary to discuss the governor’s strong support for Israel.

Much of DeSantis’s online network that was devoted to his presidential campaign is now devoted to supporting the Iran War.

DeSantis praised Operation Epic Fury when it first began, arguing that it was delivering justice for Americans killed during the Iraq War. “As somebody who was over in Iraq at that time, that saw the casualties, that saw that it was the Iranians behind it. They never really faced justice,” he said in March. “Now... all the ayatollahs are dropping like flies.”

He also backed bombing Iran last year, saying Trump showed “decisiveness.” He claimed military action against the Islamic Republic was necessary because of the state’s “apocalyptic, radical ideology.” The only way to deter the regime was through bombings.

DeSantis’s pitch as a Iran War critic will also be hampered by his rabid support for Israel. He famously signed bills to target “antisemitism,” in Jerusalem, twice . He sent weapons to Israel during its war in Gaza. He has even claimed America wouldn’t exist without Israel being the cradle of Western civilization. These opinions are supported by his pro-Israel donors , a number of whom want America to back the Jewish state’s annexation of Gaza and the West Bank.

It’s also worth recalling that the Florida governor initially sought to position himself as a staunch non-interventionist in the ’24 primary, at least when it came to regions outside the Middle East. He told Tucker Carlson in early 2023 that defending Ukraine was not a key security interest for America. But after receiving backlash from donors, he walked back those comments .

There’s a chance he could reverse himself again in the ’28 primary.

DeSantis is a smart politician. One doesn’t become the most successful Republican governor in the country without some brains. He knows which way the wind is blowing, and he understands that the Iran War offers an opportunity to align himself with the majority of Americans. It sets him apart from potential rivals currently serving in the admin, who can’t easily shed their association with the conflict. It also differentiates him from Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who is loud and proud about his support for the war. DeSantis has the freedom to openly criticize the war and other admin failures, creating the distance between himself and Trump that may be necessary for any Republican to win in 2028.

But he will still face the challenge of convincing the public that he’s a genuine critic of the war and foreign interventionism more broadly. It’s easy to say the war hurt Republicans. Even Vice President J.D. Vance and Trump say that. It’s hard to prove DeSantis will avoid similar catastrophes as president when he’s on record championing military action against Iran.

That DeSantis can recognize reality and understand the GOP’s predicament are positive signs. The base may be ready for a clean break from Trump in the primary, and someone who vows to keep the good things about the admin and ditch the bad would be a strong contender.

To do so, a candidate will have to convince the public that he will learn from Trump’s mistakes and avoid harebrained foreign interventions. After the midterms, it’s clear voters want a different direction. That’s something even an Iran hawk can recognize.

Scott Greer is an award-winning journalist, host of Highly Respected, and author of No Campus for White Men .
