scraped.author: PSL Webmaster
scraped.h1: Texas rejects the Republican establishment in historic midterm election: What comes next?
scraped.body_text:
Texas has long been upheld as a crown jewel of Republican, even far-right political dominance. For decades, the state has been treated as virtually unwinnable territory for Democrats, with Republicans controlling statewide offices and presenting their rule as an inevitable reflection of Texas politics. This midterm election season has flipped that claim on its head. Millions of Texans delivered a resounding rejection of the Republican establishment, producing a historic Democratic sweep that will reverberate far beyond the state’s borders.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Republican Greg Abbott by approximately seven percentage points, ending more than three decades of Republican control of the Texas governor’s office. Abbott, who had won his previous three elections by at least 10 percentage points, was seeking a fourth consecutive term – which would’ve made him the state’s longest-serving governor.

James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton by approximately 12 percentage points, making him the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since 1988. Democrats also won the other major statewide elections, including the lieutenant governor’s race against incumbent Dan Patrick.

These Democratic victories in Texas are historic – and reflect a growing rejection of the political establishment, the billionaire class and the increasingly repressive policies that have defined the Trump era and been willingly carried out within the Texas political realm. And further, they expose the fact that the Republican Party’s supposed stronghold in Texas is not fixed – in fact, even in seemingly the most conservative places, a light for a different future exists when the people will it into existence.

The question now is not simply whether Texas has “turned blue.” It is whether the millions of people who mobilized against the Republican agenda can build a movement powerful enough to demand something fundamentally different.

The midterm results in Texas cannot be divorced from the broader political climate across the country. Working people are confronting rising grocery prices, housing costs, stagnant wages and an increasingly precarious economic future. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has doubled down on policies that scapegoat immigrants, attack LGBTQ people, undermine public education, seek to strip us of our civil liberties and funnel enormous resources toward war, militarization and repression.

Republicans across the board have offered few solutions to these worsening crises, and instead have relied on culture-war politics, racist scapegoating and gerrymandering and increasingly authoritarian measures in desperate attempts to consolidate their own power.

Abbott and Paxton embodied this agenda. Abbott’s administration has spent years attacking reproductive rights, restricting public education and expanding the state’s repressive apparatus. Paxton has become synonymous with corruption allegations and the interests of the wealthy political establishment. Both figures have been central in an administration that has prioritized attacking working people rather than addressing the conditions making their lives increasingly difficult. And in Texas, that rejection also extends to the enormous influence of billionaires like Elon Musk, whose growing political and economic footprint in the state has become a dangerous symbol of the power wealthy individuals wield over public life and safety.

Texas is one of the wealthiest states in the country. It is also a place, like many across the country, where millions of people who produce that wealth struggle to afford housing, healthcare, groceries and other basic necessities – not to mention mounting Texas property taxes. The contradiction is impossible to ignore, and the election results are an expression of growing frustration with that reality.

The results have also been fueled by the escalating assault on immigrant communities. Texas sits at the center of the country’s deportation apparatus. It leads the nation in ICE arrests, with 1 in 4, or 25%, taking place in Texas (the next closest is Florida, at around 11%). Harris County and the greater Houston area, specifically, lead the nation in ICE arrests and active detainments. And despite the administration’s continued claims that ICE is targeting “criminals,” a rising share of those being detained and deported have no criminal record.

ICE raids in Texas have affected far more than only the families of those taken into custody – they create a culture of fear that extends into all of our communities. The March 2025 ICE killing of 23-year old Ruben Ray Martinez in South Padre Island, the July 2026 ICE murder of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and the October 2026 ICE shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin have mobilized immigrant and non-immigrant communities alike with anger.

The Trump administration has attempted to use immigration enforcement to divide working people, blaming immigrants for economic insecurity while corporations and billionaires actually profiting from exploitation and rising costs continue to accumulate wealth. But the growing opposition to ICE demonstrates the limits of that strategy. More and more people recognize the culprit as not immigrants, but the very political establishment seeking to blame immigrants while failing to provide us with basic human needs.

Perhaps one of the most extraordinary developments in this election was the level of voter participation. More than 7.7 million Texans voted early, surpassing the previous midterm record set in 2018. More than 40% of registered voters cast ballots before Election Day. Particularly significant was the increase in Black and Latino voter participation. Early voting surged in the heavily-Latino Hidalgo and Cameron counties, while Black turnout saw a substantial increase, especially in the Houston area.

This mobilization is especially important given the state’s long history of voter suppression and efforts to undermine the political power of communities of color. It also comes amid aggressive Republican redistricting efforts designed to consolidate political power and weaken the electoral influence of communities that have historically challenged the status quo.

Black people have played a central, detonator role in driving political change in this country. From Reconstruction to the Civil Rights Revolution, Black political mobilization has forced the political establishment to capitulate to demands it would’ve otherwise ignored. The increased participation we saw in Texas should be understood within this historical context – as it represents a refusal to accept that the political direction of the state is predetermined and that working class communities have no meaningful power to change it.

The significance of these results extends well beyond Texas. Democrats made major gains across the South and other traditionally-Republican strongholds, including historic victories in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and South Carolina.

Together, these results demonstrate that the political landscape in this country is not fixed. States that have been written off as permanently conservative can, in fact, become centers of political upheaval. The idea of an immutable “Trump country” obscures the millions of people living in these places who are struggling with the same economic and political conditions as working class people everywhere else.

Texas has always had a rich history of working class struggle, labor organizing, and anti-racist resistance. The notion that the state is inherently conservative has often served to discourage people from imagining a different political future. This election challenges that assumption. But we should be careful not to confuse a rejection of Republican rule with an automatic mandate for the Democratic Party’s entire agenda. That distinction is critical to understanding what comes next.

The Democratic Party will undoubtedly present the results as proof that its electoral strategy is working. But what happens now that voters have gone home?

History offers us plenty of reasons to be skeptical of the “blue wave.” Democrats have repeatedly campaigned on opposing deeply unpopular Republican policies, mobilized people around promises of change, then retreated to the same status quo politics once in office. They’ve absorbed the energy of mass movements, channeled it into electoral campaigns and ultimately failed to deliver the fundamental changes people were demanding.

Take immigration enforcement as an example – which is bipartisan in both its development and continued expansion. Talarico has compared ICE to a “secret police force,” reflecting the deep-seated anger that has developed around its increasingly violent operations. Yet, he’s stopped short of supporting the agency’s abolition – where the mood of the majority of people is really at. If ICE is functioning as a repressive force, why should the movement settle for reforms that leave the institution intact, and simply change the party that manages it?

The same issue applies to the broader political landscape in Texas. A Democratic victory in the governor’s office doesn’t automatically undo the laws and policies that have been implemented over years of Republican rule. Many of them are embedded in state legislation, and require a square confrontation with the Republican-controlled legislative infrastructure that has built and maintained them. Can we count on Hinojosa to do that on her own, without mass pressure from below?

Consider just a few examples:

If Democrats are serious about representing the people who mobilized to defeat the Republican establishment, they should be held accountable for repealing these measures, ending state-mandated collaboration with ICE, restoring local democratic authority, protecting workers’ rights, expanding reproductive rights, and directing public resources towards housing, healthcare, education and other essential services.

The Democratic victories in Texas are significant, but they should not be mistaken for a solution to the problems that brought millions of people to the polls. The Democratic Party has a long record of campaigning against Republican attacks, mobilizing working class communities and promising change, only to retreat once in power and preserve the same systems that produced the crisis in the first place.

The question is whether we allow our energy to dissipate after Election Day, or whether we use it as a foundation for building a sustained movement capable of winning real material change. None of this will happen simply because Democrats won an election – history shows quite the opposite. It will take organization and pressure from below: from workers, students, immigrants, Black communities, women, LGBTQ people and everyone else whose interests are so clearly at odds with the billionaire class and the political establishment that serves it.

The Texas election has demonstrated that millions of people are willing to mobilize against the status quo. The task now is to build something that can carry that struggle forward, well beyond the ballot box – an independent, multiracial, working class movement that does not limit its political horizon to the Democrats or Republicans.

The Republican political establishment has been dealt a historic blow in Texas. What comes next depends on whether people who made that defeat possible keep up the pressure.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

items.title: PSL Statement: The Democratic wave and the fight ahead
items.summary: Tens of millions voted to punish Trump over inequality, war and ICE terror. The new Congress will deliver nothing on those issues unless it is forced to.

scraped.title: PSL Statement: The Democratic wave and the fight ahead
scraped.description: Voters handed Donald Trump and the Republican Party a crushing defeat on Nov. 3. Democrats took both houses of Congress, flipping Senate seats in Kans
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: PSL Statement: The Democratic wave and the fight ahead
scraped.body_text:
Voters handed Donald Trump and the Republican Party a crushing defeat on Nov. 3. Democrats took both houses of Congress, flipping Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988. Alaska and Mississippi may be called for the Democrats too. It was the same story in the House, where Democrats won in districts Trump had carried by 15 points in 2024 (like Kentucky’s 6th) and even newly gerrymandered districts in North Carolina and Alabama. The national popular vote in the House is projected to show a Democratic margin of about 13 points, the largest margin for either party in 50 years.

The election was a referendum not just on Trump as an individual but on the reactionary MAGA agenda to shred democratic rights and put the whole country on the platter for the billionaires. The country voted against not just the price of groceries and fuel, but against an unprovoked war on Iran. In the NBC News exit poll, 62% of voters said Trump made the wrong decision in starting the war, and about three-quarters called it a crucial or major factor in their vote. Even the “cost of living” issue has to be placed in class terms to be properly understood. The issue is not just economic hardship in the abstract, but that this pain comes at a time when billionaires’ wealth has surged upwards by 32% in just the last year . The S&P 500 is up 28% since Trump’s election. While the recession is already here for huge sections of the working class, the country’s 977 billionaires are doing better than ever before. Everyone can see that the mass introduction of AI will only deepen these trends.

Trump and Fox News have tried to spin this loss, deflecting blame onto individual Republican candidates. But the electoral map provides an indisputable single picture. According to a Washington Post analysis, voters moved at least 15 points toward the Democrats in every kind of county: whether rural, suburban or urban, racially diverse or majority-white. MAGA’s supposed inroads among Black, Latino and Gen-Z voters — which many exaggerated to begin with — proved to be a short-lived and passing phenomenon. The shifts were stark in areas that have been wrongly called “Trump Country” for the last decade; now that term can be retired. Democrats won Senate seats in South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Texas, and may even win Mississippi; Trump carried every one of those states by 13 to 23 points in 2024. This means they swung between 17 and 26 points toward the Democrats in just two years time — a stunning reversal.

The vote in rural states and regions requires special attention. Farm bankruptcies have jumped 85 percent over the last two years, largely due to Trump’s tariffs, combined with the bungling and chaotic response to other nations’ retaliatory tariffs. Then the Iran war choked off shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, so diesel prices soared by nearly 70 percent and fertilizer and farm equipment, the other key input costs, followed. “Compared to last year, our fuel bill is $50,000 higher,” Kansas farmer Vance Ehmke told the Hastings Tribune. When grocery prices became a political problem for consumers, Trump quadrupled the quota for low-tariff Argentine beef, hitting cattle producers a second time.

The more detailed election results will allow for more in-depth local analysis but already these swings disprove the caricature of all Trump voters as some sort of solid fascist bloc. In 2020, millions of working people voted for Joe Biden in hopes he would make life more bearable. Instead, the COVID-era social support programs expired, consumer prices soared anyway, and in 2024 many of the same voters gave Trump a chance to deliver on his promises to improve their lives. Now he’s failed them too.

The limits of Congress and the Democratic Party

Anyone disgusted by Elon Musk’s attempt to buy the elections will delight in his failure. Anyone who has suffered under this administration, or has been outraged by MAGA’s extreme racism, will no doubt enjoy watching Gina Hinojosa unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, and watching South Carolina’s Black working class turn out in droves to remove Darline Graham, appointed to the seat after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham. That Mississippi may end up with its first Black Senator since 1881 is historic, and itself a searing indictment of white supremacy. It cannot be disconnected from the recent upsurges in response to the police killing of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley and the apparent cover-up in the Nolan Wells case.

But the feeling of satisfaction of seeing MAGA defeated must not turn into illusions about the role of Congress or the Democratic Party that now holds it. Put simply, there is no indication that the Democrats have either the will or the program to fight on the issues that drove mass turnout: ending the war, bringing down prices, ejecting the billionaire class from power, defending civil rights, or stopping ICE terror.

This isn’t just about Democratic politicians “selling out.” The obstacles are built into the capitalist political system. Only a third of the Senate faces voters in each election cycle exactly so that these defenders of the capitalist system can’t be dislodged by any voter “wave.” The filibuster survives as an internal procedural rule (not in the Constitution), and the lifetime-appointed Supreme Court sits above it all, for the same reason. In addition, nearly $12 billion was spent on these midterms — that’s not just to win the race, but to purchase influence with whoever comes into office. The 50 largest donors contributed almost $2.8 billion of it, and OpenSecrets found that 1 percent of donors supplied 98 percent of the money given to outside groups. Small donors contributed less than 10 percent of the overall midterm funds raised. Big Money sets the stage for Election Day, and then kicks right back into motion the very next day.

Three times in two decades a wave election has handed the Democrats control of Congress: after the 2006 midterms, then in 2008, giving them 59 Senate seats in Barack Obama’s first term, and then again the White House and both chambers in 2021. Each time they promised universal health care, immigration reform, climate action, a $15 minimum wage, a law protecting abortion rights, not to mention universal childcare, a permanent child tax credit, student debt relief, the protection of voting rights, and so on. Each time a section of the party exercised a veto on behalf of corporate America.

The political system is riddled with such “veto points” precisely to frustrate the popular sentiment for transformative change, and the Democratic Party, as a ruling-class party, always produces the figures ready to use these vetoes. This cycle of failure and frustration is what opened the road for Trump.

The longer historical record tells the same story. For the 48 years from 1933 until 1981, Democrats controlled both houses of Congress the entire time , except for brief windows from 1947 to 1949 and again from 1953 to 1955. Yes, those majorities passed the Wagner Act and Social Security in 1935, in the wake of the 1934 general strikes in Toledo, Minneapolis and San Francisco. But the same majorities let Southern Democrats filibuster an anti-lynching bill to death in 1938 and kept Jim Crow intact for another generation, until the civil rights movement forced the issue. What Congress delivered in terms of progressive reforms always depended on the forces built outside it, and it’s a body that has not delivered anything substantial in favor of the working class in half a century.

The midterm vote was a gauge of mass consciousness and it measured the anger of the masses. But it did not magically transform this undemocratic political system into something new. On all the issues, super-majorities want the Iran war to end, want to stop AI-induced job destruction, want to win Medicare for all, and oppose ICE’s campaign of terror. In a democratic system, the mass turnout yesterday would translate into immediate policy change. But that’s not going to happen. Not one ICE detainee will be released because of this result. Trump can still order strikes on Iran at any second. The billionaires still control all the board rooms that set prices, wages and the introduction of job-destroying technology. What appears as a “democracy” is in fact the dictatorship of capital, and that is as true today as it was before the midterms.

That makes it all the more necessary for people who voted for change to immediately start demanding it from the incoming Congress. The new Democratic majority has real powers if it chooses to use them. It could pass Medicare for All and legalization for the undocumented, and could make Trump veto them in public. Even if he does, this would create real legislative momentum that the next president couldn’t ignore. Congress controls the power of the purse, and could hold up budgets until it claws back the money Republicans pushed through by reconciliation in June, which funds ICE through the end of Trump’s term. It could use its investigative power, as the Church Committee did with COINTELPRO in 1975, to expose this administration’s surveillance of activists and deportation of people for their political views. This is just scratching the surface of what can be demanded. People voted for real change, not to have one thousand meaningless committee hearings full of theatrical speeches made for social media and fundraising videos.

On the appeal of socialism

Notably, Trump’s anti-communist ads did not stop candidates who call themselves socialists, nor did it scare away Democratic voters. This attack line has become less and less potent, and voters are tired of it. A 2025 Cato Institute/YouGov poll found 62 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 view socialism favorably, and when you look across all ages, the total number of people who hold such a view now numbers 100 million. The fog of anti-communism has lifted in a big way, even if the definition and understanding of socialism remains quite weak — in part because of the incorrect definitions given by many who proclaim themselves “socialist.”

Nor did the issue of Palestine scare away voters. Quite the contrary. What last year was waved away as “exceptional” New York City, when Mamdani was elected, was repeated elsewhere. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate, and he carried real movement energy against the Gaza genocide and ICE, while speaking to working-class concerns. On Election Day, Trump himself announced the end of U.S. military aid to Israel in the coming period. This is just an accounting trick, planned with Netanyahu himself, meant to hide full support for the apartheid state, but it does reflect the real change in consciousness that has taken place across the entire electorate, largely due to the work of the Palestine solidarity movement. That movement’s nonstop organizing and advocacy, its constant presence in the streets and on social media, has created such a powerful argument that it now impacts even the Republican base.

While the progressive and democratic socialist wing of the Democratic Party scored important victories, the strategy of changing the Democratic Party from within is nothing new. Throughout history the party has changed its insurgents far more easily than they have changed it. Elected without an independent base, they must observe a discipline set by party leaders and donors, starting with votes for Hakeem Jeffries as Democratic leader. On November 1, the New York Times reported that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is urging fellow democratic socialists toward a “culture of welcoming” over the “purity-minded litmus tests” of the Gaza movement. This is ridiculous. Every political trend, from right to left, must draw lines. The question is whether backing the party leaders who armed a genocide falls inside them.

Operating inside a party that by design does not hold members to its platform is what allowed Manchin, Sinema and now John Fetterman and Haley Stevens to do as they please. We must also recognize the Democratic Party, as an imperialist party, is wholly devoted to the idea of the encirclement of China and Russia, US domination over trade routes and energy supplies in the Middle East, the exploitation of Africa for its natural resources, and the management of Latin America as its “backyard.” It was the Democrats in power that led the country into the Korean War, the Vietnam War, and, more recently, the US/NATO-instigated war between Russia and Ukraine, and the genocide in Gaza. This isn’t an incidental aspect of the Democratic Party, and for progressives to advance anything domestically, they’ll be first asked to go along with the needs of the Empire. That’s where AOC’s “litmus test” comment is really headed.

Independent campaigns and the road ahead

PSL candidates ran against that machinery, and made significant inroads in the working-class with mass grassroots canvassing gaining new levels of visibility for the socialist program. Greg Levy, the PSL member who ran for Senate in Ohio, has about 94,500 votes, 2 percent of the total, despite exclusion from every debate and a smear campaign built on a Republican-funded PAC that promoted him without his consent. Joe Tache in Massachusetts faced the same debate exclusion, even while polling over 10 percent and meeting all the fundraising thresholds. He still built a campaign with the feel of a social movement, and brought around 55,000-60,000 votes after closing his campaign with a 700-person rally in Boston. Andre Easton, running for a House seat in the Bronx, is nearing a 9 percent total — which is the highest percentage of any House candidate representing a socialist or communist party since the early 1940s. Meanwhile, Frank Lara won his election for the school board of South San Francisco, campaigning on an anti-billionaires platform to put the needs of public school students and teachers first. The Peace and Freedom Party’s Alexander Kraft, who was endorsed by the PSL, brought in a strong 39% running for mayor of El Cajon, in San Diego County, against a Republican incumbent.

PSL candidates are distinguished from those running in the Democratic Party because they are beholden to the platform and perspective of the Party; it is not something they can cast to the side for short-term convenience.

Each of these campaigns was run vigorously, and will produce many lessons that now must be studied and expounded further, which we will do in the coming days.

Across the board, tens of millions went to the polls to politically punish Trump, and they succeeded. But they were also dreaming of peace, justice and good jobs — a dream that the capitalist system will not deliver.

Rebuilding a socialist movement in the historic heartland of anti-communism is no simple task. But the gap between what the majority wants and what this system will allow is exactly where the socialist movement can grow. That is what the PSL will keep doing, 365 days a year.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

Democrats took both houses of Congress, flipping Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988. Alaska and Mississippi may be called for the Democrats too. It was the same story in the House, where Democrats won in districts Trump had carried by 15 points in 2024 (like Kentucky’s 6th) and even newly gerrymandered districts in North Carolina and Alabama. The national popular vote in the House is projected to show a Democratic margin of about 13 points, the largest margin for either party in 50 years.

items.title: Only people power can transform society: Lessons from the Minnesota Socialism Summit
items.summary: ...we have to realize that we can have a socialist system in our lifetime, only if we are willing to fight for it!

scraped.title: Only people power can transform society: Lessons from the...
scraped.description: On Oct. 24, hundreds of people attended the Minnesota Socialism Summit to discuss the lessons from Minnesota’s role as the site for historic struggle
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: Only people power can transform society: Lessons from the Minnesota Socialism Summit
scraped.body_text:
On Oct. 24, hundreds of people attended the Minnesota Socialism Summit to discuss the lessons from Minnesota’s role as the site for historic struggle over the past decade. First in the summer of 2020, after the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis, 35 million people poured into the streets across the country against racism and police brutality. Then in January of 2026 after Operation Metro Surge, the tactic of a general strike was put on the table and Minnesotans flooded the streets to kick out ICE following the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Organizers and community members mobilized to the summit from 13 different states to discuss organizing for a better future and what it will take to get us there. More than 550 people registered for the event from across the country. More than 20% of the registrations were college and high school students — young people who have the most to gain in fighting for a future they deserve. The day was filled with programming about a variety of topics, including the fight to end ICE terror, the legacy of the Black freedom struggle, the need to end the US war machine, climate change and data centers, and more.

The PSL Twin Cities branch first began discussing this conference after the historic general strike and nationwide shutdowns of January 2026. The Trump administration launched Operation Metro Surge and carried out a campaign of racist terror against immigrants and their allies in the state of Minnesota. In the face of such intense state violence, Minnesota revived the tactic of the general strike for the first time in decades, which ultimately forced the drawdown of Operation Metro Surge. Both Jan. 23 and Jan. 30 demonstrated a fundamental truth — society does not run without workers and workers have the power to shape society if they get organized.

In the months following Jan. 30, there was a concerted effort to turn people’s attention towards the horizon of the midterms. Emphasis was placed on getting people to the polls and out of the streets. We knew that we could not let the lessons of January be forgotten, and we could not let our class limit their horizon to the same endless cycle of midterms.

We organized the Minnesota Socialism Summit because of two things:

Jan. 30 really made clear the need for working-class organization and the power of mass mobilization. When Black and immigrant students put out the call for a nationwide shutdown after the murder of Alex Pretti, the PSL was ready to answer the call immediately to make this the biggest possible show of working-class power. We answered the call because we knew from countless previous experiences of working-class struggle that there was a real crisis at hand. The hearts of thousands of people in the Twin Cities were on fire. We recognized that the people were willing to fight, so we threw ourselves into fighting alongside them. Sure enough, on Jan. 30, tens of thousands of people poured into the streets again in the middle of a work day, only one week after shutting down the city of Minneapolis. A few days later, the Trump administration was forced into a tactical retreat, declaring a drawdown of Operation Metro Surge.

Jan.23 and Jan. 30 proved that the power is in our hands. The question is, are we willing to be organized enough to take it?

Across the United States, we can see that socialism is on the rise. A poll by the Cato Institute found that 62% of young people aged 18 to -29 have a favorable view of socialism, while 34% of them have a favorable view of communism. In August, a Gallup poll reported that 43% of all Americans view socialism positively — 100 million people!

In a time where the billionaire class is causing crisis after crisis in their reckless pursuit of profit, people are hungry for a political alternative. We knew that it was essential to use this summit to provide a definition of socialism and a clear picture of how socialism will address the countless struggles we face as working people.

On the day of the summit, the space was filled with hundreds of people curious about socialism. They were fed up with the constant attacks the billionaire class levies on the working class and wanted to know what can actually create the change we need to see in society.

The existing major political parties are incapable of addressing the crises of capitalism. To place our hope in them is a dead end. They have no real solutions for the cost-of-living crisis caused by endless wars, mass job loss due to billionaire-controlled AI, or the intensifying climate catastrophes that set our Boundary Waters ablaze. None of these crises have to happen. The crises brought on by the capitalist system are political choices made by a tiny clique of billionaires that are willing to sacrifice us all for a little more profit. The system is not broken, it is working exactly as it was intended.

Therefore, nothing will change until we actually seize political power and reorganize society as a socialist society, where the needs of people and the planet are treated as real priorities. We already create all of the wealth in this society — we just need the power to actually decide how it is used.

The moments in history where sweeping change has occurred, were anchored by the Black freedom struggle during the reconstruction era and the Civil Rights movement. These ruptures have actually created historic transformations in society that were previously unimaginable, such as the abolition of slavery and the end of legal segregation. People did not believe their conditions could completely shift but they did through organized struggle from below. Similarly, we have to realize that we can have a socialist system in our lifetime, only if we are willing to fight for it!

While an incredible intervention, the Socialism Summit is just the beginning. We aim to use it as a launching pad for expanding socialist consciousness in the Twin Cities and throughout Minnesota, to magnetize people to socialist ideology, propel socialist consciousness forward and spur people to involve themselves in the movement in various ways. The Socialism Summit provided us the opportunity to give people hope beyond the midterm elections, to pull the lessons out from our collective struggle and to help people see themselves as part of this movement, and to see socialism as an achievable path forward.

The working class deserves much better than what we face today. If the people held political and economic power, we would put the health and wellbeing of us, our communities and our planet above profit. Toppling the capitalist order means treating land, water and energy as things a planned society manages for collective well-being. We could have a system of collective ownership and decision making. One where corporations don’t have the power and ability to exploit our environment because we have taken that power away from them. One where technology doesn’t destroy our drinking water and take our jobs but actually is used to help us meet our climate goals, improve our infrastructure and land management and allows us to have more time with our friends and family.

Fighting for our future is our right and we can win that future together. Don’t let your passion end with the Minnesota Socialism Summit — join us in the struggle to build our collective power to create a full socialist transformation of society!

items.title: Turkish parliament approves Mecca defense pact amid Middle East war
items.summary: Türkiye’s parliament has ratified the Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, a step tied to the Yemen war and the US-Israeli war on Iran.

scraped.title: Turkish parliament approves Mecca defense pact amid Middle East war
scraped.description: Türkiye’s parliament has ratified the Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, a step tied to the Yemen war and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The Turkish parliament on Thursday evening ratified the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on August 7.

Of the 279 votes in favour, 222 came from President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s Islamist Justice and Development Party (AKP), 24 from its fascist ally the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), and 25 from the Kemalist Republican People’s Party (CHP) led by Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu.

Of the 119 votes against, 60 came from the New Party, a split from the CHP, 22 from the Kurdish nationalist Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), 15 from Islamist New Path and 13 from the far-right Good Party. The Workers Party of Turkey (TİP) and the Labor Party (EMEP) each cast one vote against.

Two TİP deputies and one EMEP deputy did not take part. According to reports, 34 of the DEM Party’s 56 deputies, 30 of the New Party’s 90 and 19 of the CHP’s 44 were absent from the vote.

Speaking for the AKP, former Defense Minister Hulusi Akar said, “This agreement is in no way an alternative to NATO or anything of the sort.” According to the Associated Press (AP), Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Fuat Oktay said that Türkiye would “not be drawn into an uncontrolled process against its will.” Declaring his party’s support, the MHP’s Kamil Aydın said, “Türkiye’s place in world politics is the center.”

Speaking to the daily Milliyet , Kılıçdaroğlu said he had spoken with the foreign minister of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, adding, “I told them as well: We want to go there not to fight but, on the contrary, to bring peace and tranquillity to the region.” He went on: “We are not supporting the [Erdoğan] government. We are supporting the state of the Republic of Türkiye.”

Murat Emir, Deputy Parliamentary Group Chair of the New Party, a split from the CHP, told parliament, “They brought this agreement to send Turkish soldiers to the deserts of Yemen,” while his party colleague Yunus Emre said, with this agreement “We will shoulder America’s burden.” The DEM Party’s Gülcan Kaçmaz Sayyiğit said of the alliance, “It is not clear whether its target is Iran, Israel or Pakistan’s rival India.”

The New Party’s objection is directed not at the alliance itself but at its timing and procedure. New Party deputy Utku Çakırözer, who asked in the parliamentary committee, “What business do we have in the deserts of Yemen?” had, in September 2025, while then a member of the CHP, presented a report to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly. This advocated a “maximum pressure” strategy against Tehran, repeated imperialist propaganda by declaring Iran the source of regional instability and proposed that NATO consider expanding toward the Middle East.

A pamphlet by Keith Jones

The Sosyalist Eşitlik Partisi – Dördüncü Enternasyonal (Socialist Equality Party – Fourth International), the Turkish section of the International Committee of the Fourth International, declared its unconditional rejection of the agreement in a video statement before the vote.

The statement explained that what the agreement would “defend” is the Saudi regime, which has opened its bases to the US war on Iran and is slaughtering the people of Yemen through bombardment and starvation, along with the reactionary geopolitical interests that the Turkish bourgeoisie seeks to advance in collaboration with US imperialism. As military spending rises and the cost of war is imposed on workers through falling wages and social cuts, it is accompanied by growing political repression in Türkiye.

The Mecca Agreement is a product of the global imperialist war bound up with the genocide in Gaza, the US-Israeli war against Iran, the Saudi monarchy’s war against the Houthi Ansar Allah movement in Yemen, NATO’s war against Russia over Ukraine and US preparations for war against China. The pact ties workers to a chain of conflicts stretching from the Eastern Mediterranean to South Asia. Under the agreement, which is modelled on NATO’s Article 5, an armed attack against one party is considered an attack on all three, and the parties may withdraw only after 10 years. Although the text contains no provision on nuclear weapons, Pakistan’s nuclear umbrella is effectively being extended over its allies.

The parties’ own statements refute claims that the pact represents an alternative to alliance with the US and NATO or a step toward independence from them. US President Donald Trump hailed the agreement as a “big, bold, and important first step,” and Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gümrükçü described it as “complementary” to NATO. The real issue driving Washington’s three allies into such an alliance is the regional powers’ pursuit of their own reactionary interests amid the violent US-led restructuring of the oil-rich and strategically vital Middle East.

Reuters reported that the ratification in the Turkish parliament was “clearing the way for Ankara to send military support to Riyadh.” Al-Monitor , for its part, described it as a “boost to Saudi Arabia” and claimed that “any Turkish deployment is likely to be limited to training, advisory services and supplying military equipment.”

According to an AKP deputy who spoke to Reuters in October, “the mandate would be sent to parliament once a bill ratifying the accord has been approved.” Although Defense Minister Yaşar Güler said, “We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis,” the mandate will now be voted based on a collective defense commitment.

The agreement’s target is not only the Houthis but also their principal ally, Iran, against which the US and Israel launched war on February 28. In March, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Riyadh declaration, which did not condemn the US war of aggression but rather Iran’s retaliation.

On October 17, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera regarding the alliance, “This is a step forward. Muslims should unite. We are ready to participate in this process.” This move by Tehran represents an attempt to ward off, from within, an alliance directed against it.

On October 26, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani Army Chief Asim Munir and National Intelligence Organization (MİT) head İbrahim Kalın travelled to Tehran. According to AP, the aim was “to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war”—that is, to prevent an escalation of the war and protect themselves by persuading Iran to submit to the demands of the US and Israel.

The bases in Saudi Arabia used in the US war on Iran became targets of Iranian retaliation in legitimate self-defence. The other Gulf regimes, too, do not want the conflict to escalate again, both because they have been targeted for collaborating with the US and Israel and because the war’s devastating economic consequences are further intensifying social anger.

The expansion of the Mecca alliance is also on the agenda. Asaad al-Shaibani, foreign minister of Syria’s new Al Qaeda-rooted regime, said in Manama on October 31, “Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” adding, “Gulf security is an ‘integral part of Syrian regional security.’”

According to Al Jazeera , Shaibani said they support Yemen’s Saudi-backed government. Reuters reported that Damascus was considering assisting in the war against the Houthis. According to the Jerusalem Post , the Saudi and Syrian defense ministries signed a military cooperation agreement, the contents of which have not been disclosed, during a visit to Riyadh by Syria’s new “president,” Ahmed al-Sharaa, the day before the vote in Türkiye.

The agreement is sharpening the rivalry between two US allies, Türkiye and Israel. Three days after the signing in August, a senior Israeli official told Ynet , “This alliance is aimed against Israel,” adding: “The Shiite axis has weakened, and for a long time we have seen the Sunni axis getting stronger. … Israel needs to build alternative alliances, especially with the Hellenic axis, Greece and Cyprus, together with India and the United Arab Emirates.”

On August 18, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase, 70 kilometers from the Turkish border; Netanyahu’s office claimed that by permitting a Turkish military deployment at the base, Damascus was threatening Israel’s security. If Syria joins the Mecca alliance, every Israeli attack on the country could be considered an attack on all parties, bringing NATO member Türkiye and nuclear-armed Pakistan into direct confrontation with Israel. This underscores that the Mecca Agreement, for all its “defensive” claims, is a preparation for broader wars.

The war policy confronts overwhelming popular opposition in Türkiye: In an Areda Survey poll in March, 93.2 percent of respondents said they opposed the US and Israeli attack on Iran. The political establishment and the trade union confederations, however, are doing nothing to mobilize this opposition. Their real role is to keep this social opposition, which is merging with anger over the cost of living and growing political repression, under control.

The vote in parliament has confirmed that the struggle against war cannot be waged through the political establishment. The SEP advances a socialist programme based on mobilizing the working class in Türkiye and internationally as an independent social force against imperialist war and for a Socialist Federation of the Middle East.

We call on workers and young people to build independent rank-and-file committees in workplaces and schools and to demand the cancellation of the Mecca Agreement, Türkiye’s withdrawal from NATO, the closure of US-NATO bases and a halt to oil shipments to Israel through Türkiye.

Fill out this form and we’ll contact you soon.

items.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Five
items.summary: Part five of a 10-part series on British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa examines how it erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.

scraped.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Five
scraped.description: Part five of a 10-part series on British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa examines how it erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ] [ Part Four ] [ Part Five ]

This is the fifth part of a 10-part series responding to British-based historian Hakim Adi’s recently republished book, Pan-Africanism and Communism: The Communist International, Africa, and the Diaspora, 1919–1939.

Between its Fourth Congress in 1922 and its Sixth Congress in 1928, the Communist International, founded by Lenin and Trotsky, underwent a profound political transformation. The internationalist programme on which it was founded was repudiated in favour of the nationalist doctrine of “socialism in one country”, while the emerging Soviet bureaucracy consolidated its control over the Communist parties. Adi passes over the immense political struggles through which this transformation occurred.

Indeed, Stalin enters Adi’s narrative as Lenin’s “successor” to present the Stalinised Comintern’s policies as a further development of those formulated by Lenin. [ 1 ] The description is deeply misleading. Lenin appointed no political heir, and when illness removed him from active political life, Trotsky, not Stalin, was widely regarded in the Soviet Union and internationally as the figure most likely to inherit Lenin’s leading role. Lenin’s final Letter to the Congress described Trotsky as the “most capable” member of the Central Committee, while warning that Stalin had concentrated “unlimited authority” in his hands, and proposed removing him as General Secretary. [ 2 ]

What took place was not a smooth transition between Lenin and Stalin, but a bitter struggle between the Soviet bureaucracy led by Stalin against the revolutionary internationalism defended by Trotsky and the Left Opposition from 1923 onwards, on which the Comintern had been founded.

The material foundations of the Stalinist bureaucracy lay in the isolation of the first workers’ state. The Bolsheviks took power in an economically backward country devastated by the First World War. They understood that the ultimate fate of the revolution depended upon its extension internationally, above all into the advanced capitalist centres of Europe. Instead, Soviet Russia suffered imperialist intervention, civil war, famine and enormous economic destruction. Large sections of the revolutionary working class that had made October were killed, dispersed from the great industrial centres or absorbed into the expanding state and party apparatus. The defeats of the revolutionary upsurge that swept Europe between 1918 and 1923, culminating in the German catastrophe, left the Soviet Union isolated and the working class exhausted. A growing administrative bureaucracy acquired increasing weight within the state and party. Its outlook was conservative and nationalist, reflecting its role as administrator of an impoverished state and its material interest in preserving its stability and privileges.

The theory of “socialism in one country,” advanced by Stalin and Nikolai Bukharin, gave this emerging bureaucratic layer its political programme. The enforced isolation of the Soviet Union, which the Bolshevik leadership had regarded as a grave danger to be overcome through the victory of the international socialist revolution, the Stalinists transformed into a program for constructing socialism within the borders of the USSR. This nationalist conception fundamentally repudiated the internationalist foundations of October. The struggle for world socialist revolution ceased to provide the strategic orientation for Soviet policy, and the international communist movement was increasingly subordinated to the national requirements of the Soviet bureaucracy.

Trotsky and the Left Opposition fought against this nationalist turn, insisting on the inseparable connection between the fate of the Soviet Union and the victory of the international socialist revolution. The Stalinist apparatus responded with systematic repression: supporters of the Left Opposition were removed from leading positions, denied access to the party press, subjected to administrative reprisals, and eventually expelled. Trotsky was expelled from the Communist Party in November 1927 and deported to Alma-Ata in January 1928.

The suppression of the Left Opposition was the necessary condition for the bureaucratic transformation of the Comintern. The emerging Soviet bureaucracy could not establish “socialism in one country” as the governing doctrine of the Soviet party and the International while permitting an organised Marxist opposition which fought for the programme of world socialist revolution.

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

For the colonial and semi-colonial countries, the nationalist transformation in the Comintern had fatal consequences. Trotsky’s theory of Permanent Revolution rejected the conception that the democratic and national tasks of the revolution required the proletariat to submit to bourgeois leadership: in countries of belated capitalist development, the struggle against imperialism, landlordism and national oppression could be carried through only under the independent leadership of the working class, drawing the peasantry behind it and extending the revolution internationally. The Stalinist doctrine assigned to the national bourgeoisie in oppressed countries a potentially revolutionary role, in a separate democratic stage, opening the way for the political subordination of Communist parties to bourgeois nationalist organisations.

In China, this programme was put to a decisive test, an experience that Adi’s book excludes.

The Chinese Revolution of 1925–27 developed amid an immense mobilisation of workers and peasants against imperialist domination, warlordism and capitalist exploitation. In May 1925, after British-commanded police opened fire on workers and students in Shanghai, killing demonstrators and wounding dozens, a strike wave swept the country. Approximately 400,000 workers participated in some 125 strikes, accompanied by mass protests and the Canton–Hong Kong general strike, in which around 100,000 workers left Hong Kong and organised a boycott of British goods.

By 1927, the revolutionary movement had reached enormous proportions. In Shanghai, hundreds of thousands of workers joined a general strike and armed insurrection, defeated the warlord forces and seized control of much of the city. Across Hunan, Hubei and other provinces, millions of peasants entered associations, challenged landlord power and began establishing organs of local authority.

The democratic tasks of national unification, liberation from imperialist domination and agrarian transformation were becoming bound up directly with questions of class power. The central issue was whether the working class would establish its own leadership over the revolutionary movement or remain politically subordinated to the bourgeois Kuomintang.

The Comintern leadership under Stalin and Bukharin insisted that the Chinese Communist Party be subordinated to the Kuomintang. The latter was presented as the political expression of a revolutionary “bloc of four classes”—workers, peasants, the petty bourgeoisie and the national bourgeoisie—united in a common anti-imperialist struggle.

Trotsky and the Left Opposition opposed this policy. They warned that the Chinese bourgeoisie feared the revolutionary movement of the workers and peasants more than it opposed imperialism, and that the independence of the Communist Party was indispensable to the victory of the revolution.

These warnings were confirmed catastrophically in April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek turned against the Shanghai working class and carried out the mass repression of Communists and militant workers. The Stalinist leadership then transferred its political orientation to the supposedly left-wing Kuomintang government in Wuhan, which likewise turned against the Communist Party and the revolutionary workers’ and peasants’ movement.

The Chinese Revolution was the most important practical test of Comintern policy towards bourgeois nationalism in a colonial and semi-colonial country. Its defeat occurred barely a year before the Sixth Congress of 1928. But Adi excludes this experience from his discussion of the Congress and its colonial programme.

The omission becomes more glaring because the Kuomintang does appear in Adi’s account. In his discussion of the International Congress against Colonial Oppression, held in Brussels in February 1927—barely two months before Chiang Kai-shek’s massacre of the Shanghai working class—Adi presents it as an important achievement because it brought together an extraordinarily heterogeneous collection of political forces. These included communists, the Indian National Congress, representatives of the British Labour and Independent Labour parties, nationalist movements from Africa and Asia, and the Kuomintang. Among them were Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress, later the first prime minister of independent India; Messali Hadj, who would become a central founder of modern Algerian nationalism; and J. T. Gumede of the African National Congress, the party that has ruled South Africa since 1994.

Adi writes:

The great significance of the Brussels Congress was that it brought together those who were struggling for national independence in Asia and Africa, those in Latin America and elsewhere who were determined to safeguard their sovereignty, as well as representatives of organisations in the imperialist countries that had a critical attitude towards colonialism or were opposed to it. Both the Indian National Congress and the Guomintang [Kuomintang] government in China were represented, as were the British Labour Party and Independent Labour Party. Representatives from China, India and Britain, including British Communists, even signed a joint resolution against “suppression and intervention in the colonial countries.” [ 3 ]

Thus, in February 1927, Kuomintang representatives joined Communists in declarations against imperialism. Barely two months later, in April, Chiang Kai-shek’s forces massacred the revolutionary workers of Shanghai. This was a brutal demonstration of the Stalinised Comintern’s role in providing revolutionary credentials to bourgeois nationalist tendencies that would turn savagely on the working class.

The principal outcome of the Brussels Congress was the establishment of the League Against Imperialism (LAI) which Trotsky would later denounce as a “second-line Kuomintang on the international scale”. [ 4 ] Yet Adi moves from the broad anti-imperialist alliances of Brussels and the LAI to the Sixth Congress without confronting any of the practical consequences of this disastrous political line.

It was Trotsky, and the Trotskyist movement that would extract the central lesson from the Chinese catastrophe: the national bourgeoisie could come into conflict with imperialism while remaining violently hostile to the independent mobilisation of the working class. As Trotsky explained:

The question of the nature and the policy of the bourgeoisie is settled by the entire internal class structure of a nation waging the revolutionary struggle; by the historical epoch in which that struggle develops; by the degree of economic, political, and military dependence of the national bourgeoisie upon world imperialism as a whole or a particular section of it; finally, and this is most important, by the degree of class activity of the native proletariat, and by the state of its connections with the international revolutionary movement.” [ 5 ]

Trotsky’s conclusion from the Chinese experience was categorical: “For fear of the masses the bourgeoisie subsequently deserts the revolution.” [ 6 ]

To be continued

Op. cit., p. 7.

V. I. Lenin, “Letter to the Congress,” 23–26 December 1922, with addition of 4 January 1923, Marxists Internet Archive, https://www.marxists.org/archive/lenin/works/1922/dec/testamnt/congress.htm

Op cit., p 29.

Leon Trotsky, “The Krestintern and the Anti-Imperialist League” (1930). Available at: https://wikirouge.net/texts/en/The_Krestintern_and_the_Anti-Imperialist_League

Ibid., p. 208.

Ibid., p. 213.

David North visited Trotsky’s final residence during his exile (1929-33) on the island of Prinkipo, and paid tribute to the life of the great theorist of world socialist revolution.

scraped.description: The book contains just one mention of the strike’s most significant and farsighted contemporary observer, Leon Trotsky. Joseph Stalin, whose policy destroyed any potential for a revolutionary road forward for the working class, does not appear once.

scraped.body_text:
This is the first part of a three-part article.

Callum Cant and Matthew Lee’s The Future in Our Past uses the experience of the 1926 British General Strike, with some references to contemporary events, to advance a struggle based solely on trade union militancy. It makes clear the dangers posed to the working class by such a syndicalist outlook: distorting and denigrating the questions of political programme and history which are essential to understanding the defeat of the General Strike and which are of fundamental relevance today.

This is epitomised by the book containing just one mention of the strike’s most significant and farsighted contemporary observer, Leon Trotsky—in a footnote which writes off his analysis for placing “far too much emphasis on the Anglo-Russian Freedom [sic] Committee and Soviet foreign policy.” [ 1 ] The name of Joseph Stalin, whose policy destroyed any potential for a revolutionary road forward for the British working class, does not appear once.

Cant and Lee oppose the claim of many bourgeois authors that the strike was doomed from the start, “that further development of the General Strike was objectively impossible”. [ 2 ] They argue that “When the General Council [of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which betrayed the strike] threw in the towel, only one organisation could have facilitated the successful continuation of the General Strike: the Communist Party.” [ 3 ] But their diagnosis of the failure of the strike and the errors of the Communist Party is false.

According to The Future in Our Past , “a lack of emphasis on the independent development of rank-and-file structures meant that it [the strike] was organisationally hamstrung at the vital moment.” [ 4 ] Therefore, “The CP’s fundamental mistake was failing to build or coordinate rank-and-file structures before or during the strike.” [ 5 ] The Communist Party, write Cant and Lee:

took for granted that the TUC bureaucracy would betray the strike, and treated that betrayal as an educative process: workers would endure defeat, realise the bankruptcy of their leaders, and then turn to the Communists to construct an alternative leadership. Two problems followed. First, by setting preparation aside until after the bureaucracy collapsed, the CP in effect accepted defeat in advance. Unless new leadership emerged almost instantly, the strike was doomed. Second, waiting until after defeat meant trying to build in the worst possible conditions, when militants were demoralised and Communists were under attack. [ 6 ]

This is a gloss on the opportunist and disastrous policy of the Communist Party of Great Britain (CPGB), pursued under the direction of the dominant Grigory Zinoviev-Joseph Stalin bloc in the Communist International (CI). It turns 1926, a critical moment in the degeneration of the Communist Parties worldwide under the growing influence of Stalinism, into an episode of tactical misjudgment.

In fact, the Stalinist leadership betrayed the revolutionary potential of the General Strike by subordinating the CPGB to the opposed class forces represented by the trade union and Labour Party leaders. As Zinoviev declared at the Fifth Congress of the Communist International in 1924:

In Britain we are now going through the beginning of a new chapter in the Labour movement. We do not know exactly whence the communist mass party of Britain will come, whether only through the Stewart-MacManus door [Bob Stewart and Arthur MacManus were CPGB leaders] or through some other door. [ 7 ]

This line culminated in the CPGB’s slogan during the General Strike, “All power to the General Council!”—the leadership body of the Trades Union Congress, an avowedly counter-revolutionary organisation working to sabotage the strike from the off. The policy in 1926 was part of a longer process of surrendering the leadership of the working class to the TUC.

The Anglo-Russian Committee (ARC) was central to this. As Trotsky explained in 1928 in The Third International after Lenin :

Zinoviev gave us to understand that he counted upon the revolution finding an entrance, not through the narrow gateway of the British Communist Party, but through the broad portals of the trade unions. The struggle to win the masses organized in the trade unions through the Communist Party was replaced by the hope for the swiftest possible utilization of the ready-made apparatus of the trade unions for the purposes of the revolution. Out of this false position sprang the later policy of the Anglo-Russian Committee… [ 8 ]

Formed in April 1925, the Anglo-Russian Committee was a joint body of British and Soviet-Russian trade unions. The left-wing pressure of the masses at the time forced certain British trade union leaders to make friendly overtures to the Soviet Union to preserve their reputations. This opportunity was seized by the Soviet leaders to formally commit them and their organisations to the defence of the Soviet Union and collaboration in the international class struggle.

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

Such a commitment was a potentially powerful tool for the young Communist Party: a promise which could be used to mobilise workers and hold their leaders to account, and then as a weapon against those leaders when they betrayed it. This approach would demonstrate the commitment of the CPGB to defending the essential interests of the working class, combating accusations by the trade union bureaucracy of sectarianism, while enabling workers to judge in practice the actual merits of the reformist bureaucracy on the one hand and the communist revolutionaries on the other.

The problem was not that this delayed the struggle for communist leadership of the working class, but that the CPGB under the leadership of Stalin and his allies never fought for that leadership. Instead, in Trotsky’s words, the Anglo-Russian Committee was transformed from an “episodic bloc of the tops which would have to be broken and which would inevitably and demonstratively be broken at the very first serious test” into “a long lasting ‘co-partnership’... and if not the gate, at least an approach to the gate through which would stride the revolution of the British proletariat… an inviolable principle standing above the real class struggle.” [ 9 ]

In January 1925, Stalin was pointing to a supposed “incipient split between the General Council of the TUC [on which sat members of the Anglo-Russian Committee] and the Labour Party” as a sign of “something revolutionary… developing in Britain.” [ 10 ] In Trotsky’s later description, Stalin and the other leaders of the Communist International at the time “considered that by means of personal influence upon [British trade union leaders] Purcell, Hicks, Cook and the others (conversations behind the scenes, correspondence, banquets, friendly back-slapping, gentle exhortations), they would gradually and imperceptibly draw the ‘left’ opposition (‘the broad current’) into the stream of the Communist International.” [ 11 ]

In July 1926, long after these individuals had betrayed the British working class, Stalin was cheering the fact that “we have severed these vacillating reformist leaders… from the General Council and linked them with our trade unions”. The “success of our policy”, he said, had been indicated by the fact that Walter Citrine, the right-wing, anti-communist leader of the TUC, “now writes that the General Council and he are agreed to the Anglo-Russian Committee being convened”. [ 12 ]

These “dear friends”, as Trotsky cuttingly characterised them, were in fact making use of their association with the Anglo-Russian Committee as a shield against the workers for their treachery. Once they felt sufficiently clear of the crisis, they dispensed with the charade and broke relations. In Trotsky’s words, “The British trades-unionists waited until their acute inner crisis was at an end, and then uncivilly kicked their generous but muddle-headed ally away.” [ 13 ]

Stalin’s policy in Britain was inseparable from the broader disorientation and degeneration of the Communist International. Its roots, as Trotsky and his Left Opposition faction identified, were in the response of an increasingly bureaucratised and demoralised layer of the Russian Communist Party (the leading force within the Communist International) to the stalled progress of revolutionary developments after 1917—a pessimism in the international working class which crystalised into the concept of “socialism in one country”.

The aborted German Revolution of 1923, for which the hesitancy of the Communist International under Zinoviev was substantially responsible, was a serious defeat for the world revolution, ushering in a period of relative retreat of working-class struggle. The leaders of the CI refused to acknowledge this or to seriously examine their role in the experience; instead, they insisted that the revolutionary wave continued unabated.

Defeats and disappointments suffered along this line, coupled with a belated recognition of a temporary “stabilisation” of world capitalism—and the necessary reintroduction of elements of the capitalist market in the Soviet Union after the destruction of the Civil War—encouraged a highly conservative shift to the right in the CI. Stalin declared in Pravda that capitalism had “extricated itself from the quagmire of the post-war crisis”, with “favourable” winds “gaining the upper hand” and leading to “a sort of lull”. [ 14 ]

Trotsky expertly drew out the relation between the CI’s disorientation and its opportunism, describing how, initially, “In order to conceal the significance of the mistakes and defeats of 1923 from others as well as from oneself, the process of the swing to the Right that was taking place in the proletariat had to be denied and revolutionary processes within the other classes optimistically exaggerated.”

This, Trotsky explained, saw the beginning of a shift in the class orientation of the CI, which later “was to liberate itself from its ultra-Left shell and reveal itself as a crude collaborationist line,” including in Britain. [ 15 ] Moreover, it did so at precisely the point in Britain’s history when a turn towards a revolutionary crisis and radicalisation was beginning. Trotsky wrote:

Towards the middle of 1925, it finally became necessary to admit officially the existence of the stabilization (a year and a half after it visibly began); that was done at a time when profound fissures were already being produced in it (in England, in China)…

The ultra-Leftism of 1924-1925, incapable of understanding the situation, was all the more brutally supplanted by a shift to the Right, which under the star of the theory of “not leaping over stages,” brought the policy of adaptation to the colonial bourgeoisie, to the petty bourgeois democracy and the trade union bureaucracy… [ 16 ]

Trotsky explained how this shift was bound up with an abandonment of the perspective of world socialist revolution for that of “socialism in one country”. It had always been understood by the leaders of the Russian Revolution, above all Vladimir Lenin and Trotsky, that the defence of the workers’ state established in the Soviet Union demanded the extension of the world socialist revolution, of which it was the first outpost. The Communist International under Stalin reversed this perspective.

Rather than follow a policy of aiding the international working class in revolutionary struggles, which would inevitably mean a battle against the labour bureaucracy and other bourgeois and petty-bourgeois tendencies, the Communist International increasingly subordinated workers to these forces. Discounting the revolutionary capacity of the working class, the CI advanced alliances like that struck with sections of the British trade union bureaucracy through the ARC as the necessary means of “neutralising” the world bourgeoisie and defending the Soviet Union against military attack. This theory sunk its roots in the material interests of a bureaucratic stratum in the Soviet Union: increasingly hostile to the working class at home, over whom it enjoyed a privileged position.

The counterrevolutionary logic and rank opportunism of “socialism in one country” was made clear in the case of Britain by Stalin’s worry that the “demonstrative rupture” with the Anglo-Russian Committee called for by Trotsky and the Left Opposition would result “only” in “our own discomfiture”. Stalin claimed:

What they want is that our Soviet trade unions should either break with the Anglo-Russian Committee, or that they, acting from here, from Moscow, should overthrow the General Council. But that is stupid, comrades. To demand that we, acting from Moscow, and by-passing the British workers’ trade unions, by-passing the British trade-union masses, by-passing the British trade-union officials, skipping over them, that we, acting from here, from Moscow, should overthrow the General Council—is not that stupid, comrades? [ 17 ]

Besides the bundling together of the “masses” and “trade-union officials”, and the servile fear of “skipping over” those bureaucrats, what is striking is the pigheaded nationalism: “acting from here, from Moscow… acting from Moscow… acting from here, from Moscow”. Hiding behind implicit allegations of Russian high-handedness was a policy of allowing the British nationalist policy of the “trade-union officials” to proceed unchallenged by a revolutionary internationalist perspective. There is more than an echo of this in Cant and Lee’s criticism of Trotsky’s too-heavy emphasis on “foreign policy”.

Trotsky recognised Stalin’s perspective for the mortal threat to the international socialist movement it was. He wrote in The Third International after Lenin that with the theory of “socialism in one country” the “backbone of internationalism has been broken.” The “very heart of revolutionary internationalism” was the “invincible conviction that the fundamental class aim, even more so than the partial objectives, cannot be realized by national means or within national boundaries”. [ 18 ]

Contrary to Cant and Lee’s suggestion that international developments are external to questions of revolutionary strategy within a given country, Trotsky defended the Marxist conception that “The revolutionary party of the proletariat can base itself only upon an international program corresponding to the character of the present epoch.” [ 19 ]

The most essential characteristic of that epoch, as Trotsky later summarised it in his book The Permanent Revolution , was that the process of world socialist revolution begun with October 1917 “begins on the national arena, it unfolds on the international arena, and is completed on the world arena.” [ 20 ] Therefore, “The fate of the Soviet republic cannot be separated from that of the world revolution… The construction of socialism is a contest between the Soviet state and not only the internal bourgeoisie, but also the world bourgeoisie, a contest waged on the basis of world-wide class struggle.” [ 21 ]

This was an essential, historic corrective. Trotsky’s revolutionary perspective foreclosed any subordination of working-class struggle anywhere in the world to tactical alliances convenient to the Soviet bureaucracy, or to the fantasy of diplomatically securing a Soviet state in which to build socialism. Against the “obstinacy evinced” in Stalin’s policy of “retaining the bloc with the General Council… explained away by the ever recurring reference to the very same ‘stabilisation’”, Trotsky declared:

The whole so-called stabilization of British capitalism is maintained only upon the conservative forces of the old labour organizations with all their currents and shadings in the face of the weakness arid irresoluteness of the British Communist Party. From this we see what depths of theoretical absurdity and blind opportunism are expressed in the reference to the existence of “stabilization” in order to justify the political bloc with Purcell. Yet, precisely in order to shatter the “stabilization”, Purcellism had first to be destroyed.

It was at the level of global perspectives that strategic questions in Britain, and every other country, were ultimately decided; from which flowed the decisions to wage or not wage struggles for political clarification and leadership, against tendencies reflecting the pressure of hostile class forces; and from which flowed the tactical initiatives taken or not taken.

To be continued
