scraped.author: Juan Chingo
scraped.body_text:
October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo

“Why did no one see it coming?” various analysts ask, following the mass demonstrations that rocked France on October 17. The bewilderment reflects the distance between the predictions of those in power and the depth of pent-up rage. Those who expected a limited protest found themselves facing a mass mobilization whose determination, in several places, broke through the security arrangements put in place to contain it.

The surprise has political roots. Successive governments have repeatedly mistaken the defeat of mobilizations for the disappearance of the capacity to rebel. They have interpreted weariness as resignation, and the difficulty of imposing an alternative as acceptance of the existing order.

This powerful upsurge reveals, once again, just how much had accumulated beneath that apparent normality. Since 2016, France has become a laboratory of class struggle. Different sectors have experimented with methods of struggle, confronted repression, and come up against the limits of their leaderships’ strategies. The events of October 17 draws on part of that experience and raises a decisive question: How can the willingness to confront those in power be transformed into a force capable of winning?

October 17 introduced an element that qualitatively transforms the advanced erosion of Macronism: sectors of the youth and popular classes went into action on a scale and with a determination that challenged the state’s ability to impose order.

We are witnessing one of the symptoms that Lenin identifies in The Collapse of the Second International when he defines a revolutionary situation: an extraordinary intensification of mass activity, with the masses drawn by the crisis and by the rulers themselves into independent historical action. Lenin links this phenomenon to a crisis of the ruling classes and an exceptional worsening of the suffering of the oppressed.

In the French case, the combination of a prolonged political crisis at the top and this independent irruption from below allows us to speak of the opening of a pre-revolutionary period. Its distinctive feature is that the erosion of power is beginning to collide with a social force capable of materially hindering the exercise of its authority. The still-uneven intervention of the workers’ movement and the weakness of the organs of self-organization leave open how far this dynamic can develop.

The significance of Lenin’s formulation lies in the fact that it places the initiative of the masses at the center of the analysis. The political crisis shifts when sectors that are usually subject to decisions made by others begin to intervene directly in those very decisions. This independent action does not yet presuppose a common program or its own leadership: it expresses the seizing of an initiative capable of altering the course of events.

Samuel Hayat sees the police being overwhelmed as part of a deeper erosion of state authority. The state requires its decisions and hierarchies to be recognized as legitimate. Among sectors of the youth, this acceptance is weakening.

Those entering the struggle today have known governments that turn a deaf ear to mass mobilizations, degrade public services, and protect the interests of the wealthiest. Even electoral rebukes seem unable to change the course of policy. The promise of upward mobility through effort in school loses credibility when educational credentials lead to uncertain prospects.

This experience calls into question the legitimacy of those in power to demand obedience. Mockery and images shared on social media help erode the distance that shields authority: a feared power now appears as something that can be challenged. Drawing on the work of historian Roger Chartier on the French Revolution, Samuel Hayat notes that “the end of the Old Regime had been made possible by a long process of desacralization of traditional authorities, notably through practices of sociability that escaped their control.” He suggests an analogy to the present day: “Everything seems to indicate that a similar process is at work today.”

The experience of resisting together also changes how those mobilized perceive themselves. Seeing for themselves that they can regroup, hold the streets and break through police lines fuels confidence in their collective capacity to act. The loss of authority of those in power thus finds its counterpart in protesters discovering and expanding a force of their own.

Data from the French research institute L’ObSoCo allow us to place this readiness within a broader social climate. Before October 17, 57% of those who expressed an opinion on the question believed that violent activist actions would be necessary to compel political leaders to take public opinion into account. This figure does not measure an individual willingness to take part in such actions, but it does show how widespread the perception is that the usual channels are insufficient to be heard.

The Gramscian notion of a “crisis of authority” helps us to understand how the erosion of political leadership can compromise broader relations between rulers and ruled. However, this concept loses its analytical power if it is reduced merely to the discrediting of political parties or a decline in consent.

The problem in France becomes more acute when this estrangement fuels action that materially hinders the exercise of power. Bans meet resistance; containment measures are overwhelmed; regaining control of public space requires greater effort than anticipated.

This does not mean that the repressive apparatus is fractured, nor that the state has lost control overall. There is a difference between an overwhelmed police operation, a prolonged crisis in maintaining order, and a rupture of state cohesion. Conflating these levels would lead to overstating the adversary’s weakness.

Nevertheless, reducing what occurred to technical failures would be equally mistaken. When the scale and determination of a mobilization render the usual means insufficient, the operational problem expresses a political relation: those in power meet a resistance that their ordinary mechanisms can no longer absorb.

Reconstructions of the day’s events show how the proliferation of protest flashpoints and the mobility of the protesters forced the police to pull back in several cities. An underestimation of turnout combined with the attrition accumulated over weeks of high school revolt. Planning errors mattered, but their significance can only be understood in relation to the force they came up against. The decline of Macronism is thus beginning to turn into a broader crisis of authority. Initiative from below deepens the crisis at the top and changes its very nature.

The government seeks to restore an obedience that has, in practice, been broken. The central role of the law-and-order response stems from this need: to regain control of public space, divide the mobilized sectors, and demonstrate that challenging its decisions carries an unbearable cost.

The repressive offensive also aims to impose its own standard for which forms of political action are legitimate. By recognizing certain interlocutors and criminalizing initiatives that outflank them, those in power try to steer mobilization back into channels that they can manage and negotiate within.

Repression can yield results. It can intimidate and wear people down, especially if labor organizations leave the youth isolated. But escalation carries growing risks. If the security deployment is overwhelmed, those in power display their powerlessness, which may encourage new challenges. If it multiplies its victims, it may spread outrage and draw in sectors that had so far remained on the sidelines. The images of dozens of young people crammed in appalling conditions at the Bobigny courthouse detention center; the attack on the right to protest that Emmanuel Macron openly embraced this week, or the deployment of the army and the elite tactical units RAID, GIGN, and BRI to control the marches –all of these could backfire on a delegitimized government. The outcome will depend on the social and political response it meets.

Act II on October 24 showed that intimidation had failed to stamp out the mobilization. From Paris to Marseille, crowds marched through the streets. Bans on demonstrations were defied, at least in part, in Nantes, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Metz, Tours, Montpellier, Sens, Besançon, Caen, Annonay, Lorient, and Le Havre. Repression also fuels determination, as summed up by a slogan seen on several signs in Paris: “I was afraid to come; that’s why I’m here.”

In Paris, the massive turnout coexisted with a sense of bitterness over having been relegated to the area around the Périphérique , the ring road encircling the city. This dissatisfaction may also express a desire to go further: having marched is not enough when those in power manage to keep the protest at a distance. The government was able to channel the march geographically, but that containment does not mean the participants’ determination has been defused.

Furthermore, coercion requires resources, coordination, and cohesion. Sustaining an extraordinary effort over a prolonged period places a strain on the apparatus itself. Its capacity must be assessed concretely, without imagining it as an unlimited reserve of force.

The government may regain ground through repression. It is more difficult, however, to turn these gains into lasting authority while the causes of the revolt remain unresolved. The headlong rush into security measures displaces and concentrates the very contradictions it seeks to resolve.

One such contradiction lies in the economic foundations of the government’s policy. It aims to regain consent while maintaining an orientation that degrades living conditions and fuels the revolt. Financial pressure and commitments to deficit reduction narrow the scope for addressing social demands, while preserving the interests of big property owners. The demand for austerity thus clashes with a population that rejects further sacrifices. While those in power retain the option of making cosmetic concessions, a substantive response on education, wages, and public services would require confronting the interests of big capital that their policy protects.

This contradiction allows us to understand why the exhaustion of Macronism could jeopardize something broader than the fate of its president. Its potential successors would inherit the conflict between the demands of the ruling classes and the popular aspirations that the mobilization has brought to the fore. Their responses would differ, but they would all have to solve the same problem: which social forces to rely on and whom to make pay for the crisis. Hence a change of government does not, by itself, guarantee a lasting reconstitution of state authority.

The erosion of Macronism may offer the far right an opportunity to present itself as the force capable of reconstituting state authority. Its argument is to blame the crisis on the government’s weakness and to promise a capacity to command that, it claims, the government has lost.

A way out of the crisis led by Le Pen would seek to rely on the presidential, administrative, and police instruments of the Fifth Republic, deepening its authoritarian character and articulating it with a policy of national and racial exclusion. The promise of order would make it possible to bring together diverse aspirations and interests: propertied sectors concerned about instability, frightened fractions of the middle classes, and popular layers that would be offered a racist explanation for their social decline.

Le Pen’s project can be framed in terms of a Bonapartist reconstitution: an attempt to strengthen the executive power and its autonomy from society, presenting it as arbiter and savior of a threatened nation, while preserving the fundamental relations of domination.

Carrying it out would require rallying support among the ruling classes, building a social base for reaction and containing or defeating mobilized sectors. Winning executive power at the ballot box would not, by itself, accomplish those tasks.

The very depth of the crisis that creates an opening for the far right could also become an obstacle to stabilizing its government. The demand for authority does not guarantee the existence of a force capable of satisfying it lastingly, even less so when the current revolt reveals the strength of “anti-far right” sentiment, which is one of the main concerns at high school students’ marches or blockades.

For the time being, the far right appears to be channeling the expectations of the “party of order.” However, new leaps in the class struggle and, above all, the decisive entry of the workers’ movement into the struggle could strengthen another attempt to resolve the crisis: a left-wing governmental alternative that would channel popular aspirations toward an institutional way out.

Mélenchon could play a central role in such an attempt. It would take on the character of a popular front if it were to articulate workers’ and popular organizations with bourgeois political forces under a common governing strategy, subordinating independent mobilization to the preservation of that alliance and the continuity of the capitalist state.

Its strength would come from an understandable expectation: to translate the energy of the struggle into immediate gains, to halt the repression and to oust those who govern. But that expectation would come into contradiction with a strategy that, to preserve its alliances and institutional viability, would need to contain the initiative of the very people who had propelled it.

The promise to give political expression to the movement could thus turn into a mechanism for handing the initiative back to the institutions: moderating demands to retain support, calling off strikes to facilitate a transition, or subordinating the organs of struggle to the electoral calendar.

This outcome is not inexorable. A deeper mobilization could strengthen Mélenchon and, at the same time, generate experiences and aspirations that outgrow his strategy. The decisive question is whether workers and youth build and defend their own means of deliberation, organization, and action, maintaining their independence, including from those who present themselves as their representatives.

Mobilization can provoke movements of reaction in other social sectors. The reports of store owners preparing to defend their businesses, some by acquiring weapons or means of self-defense, deserve attention. For now, the available information does not allow us to establish the overall extent of these initiatives.

The racist attack in Trappes and La Verrière introduces a particularly grave dimension. According to Le Monde , the alleged perpetrator told police that he wanted to avenge the store owners whose shops had been looted on October 17, and that he selected his victims based on their skin color. The attack left one person dead and five others injured.

These statements show how the appeal to order can turn into a justification for racist terror: people selected for their appearance are held collectively responsible for social disorder. The purported defense of the store owners thus serves to legitimize reprisals against racialized populations, regardless of whether they actually participated in the events.

Private defense of property and racist violence are different phenomena, and their articulation should not be taken for granted. However, the motive attributed to the attacker reveals a concrete mechanism through which they can be connected: the racist identification of those deemed responsible for disorder transforms the demand to protect property into a will to punish entire sectors of the population.

This turn to violence does not, by itself, prove the existence of an organized reaction. But it gives concrete form to one of the dangers of the current situation: that the criminalization of the revolt and its identification with the enemy within could fuel violent initiatives against popular and racialized sectors. The demand for order can offer a meeting ground for social fears, defense of property, and reactionary projects.

Fighting this threat requires linking the defense of the movement against repression with the struggle against racism. Solidarity organized in workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods must prevent reaction from isolating the most exposed sectors and fracturing those who share conditions of exploitation and precarity.

The situation poses a twofold difficulty. Those in power face growing obstacles in enforcing obedience, while those who challenge them have not yet built an equivalent capacity to set the political course.

The irruption of the youth is also beginning to shift the position of union leaderships. On October 21, as she left Matignon, the prime minister’s office, CGT general secretary Sophie Binet called for moving to a new stage through strike action and for organizing workplace assemblies to generalize the strike on November 5 and beyond. The CGT, one of France’s two largest union confederations, formalized this call in its statement the following day.

This shift allows us to gauge the pressure that the mobilization is exerting on the traditional organizations of the workers’ movement. But it raises a decisive question: how to turn those statements into effective preparation for the strike without leaving the youth isolated until November 5. Cross-sector assemblies, known in France as interpros, can serve right now to decide on actions, organize solidarity, and establish direct links with mobilized youth.

The generalization of the strike needs to be built during this interval. One challenge is to set back in motion sectors that were in the vanguard of the struggles against Macron —oil refinery workers, rail and Paris public transit (RATP) workers, electricity workers, and sanitation workers— by drawing on their experience and discussing how to overcome the weariness and skepticism left by the 2023 defeat.

Another challenge is to bring in precarious workers, whose participation on the streets is suggested by the occupations of some of those arrested on October 17: delivery workers, cooks, temp workers, and others. The task is to build a link between that willingness to mobilize and collective organization in their workplaces.

Preparing November 5 as a genuine active strike requires discussing its organization now: assemblies, picket lines that sustain and extend the strike, outreach tours, and efforts to win over workers at the strategic centers of production, transport, distribution, and finance.

More strategically, the entry of the workers’ movement with its own methods of struggle can change the terrain of confrontation: extending it from the streets to the places where wealth is produced and circulates, bringing in sectors that still remain on the sidelines, and offering a common reference point for scattered demands.

The general strike would turn the difficulty of those in power in controlling the streets into a confrontation over the functioning of the country. As Trotsky writes in Once Again, Whither France? :

Whatever may be the slogans and the motive for which the general strike is initiated, if it includes the genuine masses, and if these masses are quite resolved to struggle, the general strike inevitably poses before all the classes in the nation the question: Who will be the master of the house?

This dynamic does not automatically follow from a one-day national strike. It entails a process of extension of the strike and the entry of new sectors into action, as shown, under its own specific historical conditions, by the chain of events linking the youth revolt and the workers’ strike in May 1968. Preparing for this perspective requires that workers discuss and decide in their workplaces, articulate their demands with those of the youth and build organs capable of sustaining the struggle and contesting its direction.

Workplace and school assemblies, mandated delegates, and interpro meetings serve a concrete function in this process. They make it possible to discuss objectives, decide on actions and build an authority born of the mobilization itself. They can also articulate the defense of democratic liberties and the struggle against racism with social demands, preventing reaction from fracturing those who share conditions of exploitation and precarity.

The fight for the release of those arrested and for amnesty for those persecuted for taking part in the movement can become a common rallying point for this organizing effort. In the face of the attempt to isolate and punish the most exposed sectors, solidarity must be rooted in workplaces and schools, making the defense of those targeted by repression the responsibility of the movement as a whole.

October 17 revealed a force whose political expression remains open. Its future will depend on whether the determination it displayed finds lasting forms of organization, extends workers’ intervention, and wins political independence. The crisis of authority opens up a possibility: to transform the capacity to challenge power into a force of the exploited capable of contesting the course of society.

scraped.author: Left Voice
scraped.body_text:
In this episode, Tatiana Cozzarelli speaks to Andrew Feffer, author of Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism. They discuss the Rapp-Coudert investigation and the anti-communist witch-hunt of the early 1940s — and the parallels to today’s repression against the movement for Palestine.

Left Voice

*

In 1940, the New York State legislature established the Rapp-Coudert Committee to investigate communist activities among public education workers. For two years, there were hearings focused mainly on the City University of New York (CUNY), especially at City College, but also at Brooklyn College, Hunter College, and Queens College.

Over 500 people were interrogated during the Rapp-Coudert hearings, and more than 50 workers were fire for so-called “conduct unbecoming.” Some were fired because they were outed as communists by colleagues who sold them out, others because they refused to testify at all.

The Rapp-Coudert hearings set the stage for the McCarthy era of intense repression against the U.S. left, particularly those affiliated with the Communist Party. In this sense, McCarthyism was a continuation of previous moments of repression, like the Rapp-Coudert hearings.

This history matters because there are clear parallels between the anti-communism of the 1940s and 50s and today’s attacks on free speech, immigrant students, and, in particular, the movement for Palestinian rights.

In fact, Rapp-Coudert hits particularly close to home when it comes to repression of the Palestine movement, which has been growing since 2023.

Four CUNY faculty members were fired for their pro-Palestine activism in the summer of June 2025 for “conduct unbecoming” — the same charge levied against those targeted by the Rapp-Coudert investigation. Three have been reinstated, but one member is still fighting to regain their job.

The fight for the fired fourth is crucial for students and workers across universities, especially CUNY, to take up. The outcome has stakes for the fight against repression across the country. If teachers can be fired for their political expression on Palestine, it creates a more repressive environment for all political speech on campus.

On today’s episode, Tatiana Cozzrelli interviews Andrew Feffer, author of the book Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism, which is about this two-year witch hunt and the consequences that rippled for decades after. Andrew talks about the context that led up to the Rapp Coudert hearings, including teacher organizing, the rise of fascism, and the New York City political party machine, Tammany Hall. He also explains how the Communist Party defended itself at the time– including the limits and problems in their defense campaign–and the role that liberals played in this witch hunt.

Importantly, Tatiana and Andrew discuss the lessons that this period holds for leftists today.

Andrew Feffer, Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism (New York: Fordham University Press, 2019), 320 pages, $43.

scraped.title: DSA Won Big in New York, but So Did the Democratic Establishment - Left Voice
scraped.description: All of Mayor Mamdani’s endorsed candidates won landslide victories on Tuesday night, including Governor Hochul.
scraped.author: James Dennis Hoff
scraped.body_text:
All of Mayor Mamdani’s endorsed candidates won landslide victories on Tuesday night, including Governor Hochul.

James Dennis Hoff

Tuesday’s elections in New York were no doubt a welcome reprieve for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has recently faced criticisms from the Left for a growing list of betrayals and failures, including his refusal to fire police commissioner Jessica Tisch. That criticism had spilled over into open protest against the mayor in October, particularly after the shooting of Bronx resident Oscar Belgal by ICE ignited outrage over his handling of the NYPD. But last night, rather than face crowds of jeering protesters, the Mayor was instead basking in the glow of the victories of all four of his endorsed candidates alongside hundreds of their enthusiastic supporters. These included DSA members Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, former Comptroller Brad Lander, and, curiously, Governor Kathy Hochul.

The most resounding and impressive victory of the evening by far went to Chevalier, who won her district in Northern Manhattan and the Bronx with 87.5 percent of the vote. Her challenger, Republican Jomo Williams, earned less than 12 percent. This incredible landslide shows clearly that Chevalier’s platform, which includes calls for taxing the rich, universal healthcare, housing for all, and the abolition of ICE, among other progressive demands, resonates with large sections of her new constituents. Her victory also shows that candidates can run as open socialists, and even face off against the police on the streets, without fear of “alienating their base.” In fact, Darializa’s combative tone and her now famous confrontation with police the day of the Bronx ICE shooting no doubt won her several votes.

Although Chevalier, along with the DSA, has strongly criticized the mayor for his failure to fire Tisch or to disband the NYPD’s hated Strategic Response Group, Mamdani nonetheless — though perhaps a bit awkwardly — stood by her during her acceptance speech . Chevalier blasted ICE and talked about the importance of affordable housing, while wearing a Keffiyeh, symbolizing her support for Palestine. Surprisingly, her speech said little about international politics, and the only time Palestine was mentioned was when the audience spontaneously began chanting “Free Palestine.”

In addition to Chevalier, the DSA won a second congressional seat in District 7, where Valdez, also endorsed by Mayor Mamdani, sailed to an easy victory with more than 83 percent of the vote against her Republican challenger. Valdez, who is a member of the DSA, will replace establishment Democratic congressperson Nydia Velázquez, who is set to retire in January. Like Chevalier, Valdez ran on a platform of universal healthcare, housing for all, and the abolition of ICE. Importantly, unlike Mamdani, neither Valdez nor Chevalier endorsed or said they would vote for Governor Hochul.

As a result, the DSA will now have three members of congress from New York: Alexandria Ocasio Cortes, Claire Valdez, and Darializa Avila Chevalier. If you throw in the newly elected congressperson and former DSA member Brad Lander, whom Mamdani also endorsed, the mayor will now have a sizable coalition representing his interests and many of his ideas in Congress. What the Mayor and his allies choose to do with this newfound power and platform remains to be seen, but it is clear already that there are some meaningful differences between the mayor and the DSA’s new electeds.

But Chevalier’s was not the only election night celebration that Mamdani attended. Before heading up to the Bronx, the mayor spent the early evening after the polls closed with Governor Kathy Hochul and her supporters. In the speech he delivered there , Mamdani described the votes that day as a “turning point” for the Democratic Party, saying that “we have begun the work of transforming our party and making it belong to working people once again.”

Although Mamdani’s plan to transform the Democratic Party is highly unlikely to succeed, his endorsement was absolutely essential to transforming Hochul’s campaign, and not for the better. Less than two years ago, Hochul looked like a lame duck. Still recovering from a tight 2022 election race , where New York Democrats had lost five congressional seats in part because of her failure to turn out Democratic voters, her prospects for winning the nomination, much less re-election, were looking thin. Her approval ratings were consistently in the low forties (near or below President Trump’s), and polls showed that a 2026 match up against a strong Republican candidate could be close.

But then along came Mayor Zohran Mamdani. His phenomenal rise to power was a wave that, like yesterday’s “blue wave,” lifted every boat with a capital “D” on its prow, and his early and very public endorsement of Hochul breathed new life into her campaign. Tuesday’s results showed exactly the power of that endorsement. Not only did Hochul win re-election, she absolutely crushed her Republican opponent Bruce Blakeman by more than 20 points. Much of this victory can be attributed to the same set of forces that led to similar Democratic victories across the country : hatred of Trump and the Republican Party; anger about ICE terror and the war on Iran; and frustration about rising prices and the cost of living. Indeed, much of the success of Democrats across the country was more about hatred of Trump than anything the candidates themselves had to offer. But Hochul’s victory was not only thanks to the failures of Trump. Mamdani’s endorsement played a key role in rehabilitating the centrist Democrat’s image ahead of the elections, transforming her from a frumpy, unappealing centrist into an ally of the most popular and one of the most progressive-leaning politicians in America. Likewise, the Mayor’s repeated arguments that the Democratic party can be made to represent the interests of working people and the oppressed, only helps the party to more easily conceal its ongoing attacks on those very same people. Even worse, this is happening at a time when the party itself is being rejected by huge swaths of the working class and is most in need of such help.

And this is a contradiction that the DSA and the Left more broadly has to wrestle with: it is impossible to build working class power in coalition with or by supporting the very same people who are attacking the working class daily. By endorsing Hochul, Mamdani not only guaranteed her victory against her equally unsavory Republican opponent, he helped paper over the tainted image that she and her party represent. It is precisely this kind of narrow and pragmatic popular front mentality that has led time and again to the eventual destruction of the left wing of any partnership with the Democrats.

Both DSA candidates and establishment candidates won big riding the blue wave and Mamdani’s popularity and anger against Trump. But it remains to be seen how much these new DSA candidates will distinguish themselves from and against the rest of the Democratic Party, or allow themselves to be subsumed by it. But regardless of what path Chevalier and Valdez choose to follow, the DSA are already providing cover for and assistance to the establishment wing of the party, and this contradiction cannot hold for long. Either the DSA becomes more entrenched in the Democratic Party, or it will have to break from it. By not endorsing Hochul Darializa and Valdez showed signs that they may govern differently than Mamdani, but their indebtedness to him and the DSA ballot line strategy will make that difficult.

Democratic Party

Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)

New York

scraped.h1: Mary Peltola’s on Track for the Win
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

I am headed back West this morning (I am at a remarkable conference on community and data centers. More about that next week.)

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com .

A bit of news: Mary Peltola, Yup’ik, is on track to win the Alaska Senate seat. She has a small lead now and the uncounted ballots that remain favor her (significantly). The count still may go to Ranked Choice Voting but she should win on a second tally.

From Alaska Survey Research:

“AK SENATE UPDATE: There are still 70,000 votes yet to be counted. The vast majority are absentees and early votes. Peltola will win these VERY easily. The biggest vote count will happen 11/10. The outcome will become clear then.

“Peltola will likely win in Round 2, when Daniel J Sullivan is eliminated.”

Peltola will give the Democrats at least 55 seats and Mississippi remains contested so the number could climb again to 56 seats. And that’s before jockeying. (For example: What if Lisa Murkowski left the Republican Party, and shifted at least to an independent? That would give her — and Alaska — more of a say in the next Congress.)

Your contribution is appreciated.

We should expect legal challenges from Republicans in both Alaska and Mississippi. (Mississippi has no provisions for a recount, so that could be interesting.) But the whole narrative about “will Peltola be seated?” was buried election night.

Another election watch: Former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in one of the last undecided races in the House. He and Rep. Eli Crane, the Republican incumbent, continue to go back and forth as votes come in from different regions in the district.

From the Navajo Times:

“Republican incumbent Eli Crane led former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez by 966 votes Wednesday afternoon in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District race, a margin narrow enough to trigger an automatic recount if it holds through the official canvass.

“Unofficial results posted by the Arizona Secretary of State’s Office at 3:15 p.m. showed Crane with 138,582 votes, or 49.28%, and Nez, a Democrat, with 137,616, or 48.94%. Libertarian Curtis Goodwin had 4,848 votes, or 1.72%.

“The lead changed during election night and early Wednesday. An earlier state update showed Nez ahead by 86 votes, 136,344 to 136,258.

“Between the two updates, Crane gained 2,324 votes and Nez gained 1,272. Most of those gains came from Yavapai County, where Crane’s total rose from 63,132 in its 4:31 a.m. report to 65,453 at 3:15 p.m. Nez’s total increased from 38,582 to 39,826.

“State law requires an automatic recount when the margin between the top two candidates is one-half of 1% or less of the votes cast for both. Based on Wednesday afternoon’s totals, that threshold was about 1,381 votes. Crane’s lead was about 0.35%.”

Native Vote 2026 Three Blaine County voters have filed a federal lawsuit challenging the county’s commissioner district […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Native Voters Challenge Unequal Voting Districts in Blaine County, Montana
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Three Blaine County voters have filed a federal lawsuit challenging the county’s commissioner district map, alleging that population disparities violate the constitutional principle of one person, one vote and dilute the voting power of Native American residents.

Three Blaine County voters have filed a federal lawsuit challenging the county’s commissioner district map, alleging that unequal population distribution across the three districts violates the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause and diminishes the voting power of Native American residents.

Represented by the UCLA Voting Rights Project (VRP) and Helena-based Upper Seven Law, the plaintiffs are seeking a new district map that ensures equal representation among Blaine County voters.

The lawsuit centers on the constitutional principle of “one person, one vote,” which requires electoral districts to have roughly equal populations so that each resident’s vote carries comparable weight. According to the complaint, Blaine County’s current map creates significant population disparities, leaving its most populous district with substantially less voting power per resident than its least populous district.

Your contribution is appreciated.

District 1, which is 94.9% American Indian, is reportedly overpopulated by 16% and contains nearly 700 more residents than District 2, the county’s smallest and predominantly white district. District 2 is underpopulated by 12%, according to county figures cited in the complaint.

As a result, the plaintiffs allege that approximately 1.32 votes in District 1 carry the same electoral weight as one vote in District 2, creating an unequal distribution of political representation.

“The weight of a person’s vote should not depend on which side of a district line they live on,” said Sonni Waknin, senior voting rights counsel at the VRP. “Blaine County’s map goes against the principles of our representative government. We are asking the Court to enforce the Constitution and require districts that give voters an equal voice in their county government.”

Longtime Blackfeet voting rights activist Tom Rodgers (One Who Rides His Horse East) draws parallels between the loss of Native American voting rights and the historical injustices inflicted on Indigenous peoples.

“Their ancestors took our land, they took our children, they destroyed our spiritual sustenance, the bison. They have always stolen our vote and thus now is the time for a moral and legal reckoning,” Rodgers told Native News Online.

Blaine County adopted its district-based commissioner system in 2002 after a federal court determined that the county’s previous at-large election system diluted American Indian voting strength. However, county officials have since interpreted that earlier ruling as requiring the preservation of the districts’ racial composition.

The plaintiffs argue that this interpretation is incorrect and that the county’s 2024 redistricting plan retained boundaries established in 2013 despite population changes. According to the complaint, those decisions have perpetuated and worsened population disparities between districts.

Molly Danahy, litigation director at Upper Seven Law, emphasized the importance of equal representation in local government.

“The right to vote is the starting premise of our free society–it ensures that we, the people, can hold our government accountable to the rule of law,” Danahy said. “Districts that violate the basic principle that every vote should count the same are unconstitutional. Blaine County’s Commissioner map must distribute power equally among its voters.”

The plaintiffs are asking the federal court to declare the current district map unconstitutional, prohibit its use in the 2028 elections and any subsequent elections, and require the county to adopt a new plan that equalizes district populations.

The defendants include Blaine County, its county commissioners and county election officials.

Read the filing here.

scraped.author: Neely Bardwell
scraped.h1: Native Youth Among Arizona’s First Gen-Z Legislators
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Diné leader Ian Teller makes history as the only Native Gen Z candidate elected to Arizona’s State House, bringing Indigenous representation and youth leadership to Legislative District 6.

The 2026 Midterm General Elections, held Tuesday, November 3, were full of historic firsts for diverse representation among today’s political leaders. Arizona’s state races were no different, with three Gen Z candidates elected.

Ian Teller, a Diné leader from Tsaile, Arizona, was one of three Gen Z legislators elected to Arizona’s State House and the only Native youth elected. Teller ran for one of two seats available in Arizona Legislative District 6 and won alongside Mae Peshlakai, also Diné. Both are Democrats.

Peshlakai won 47 percent of the vote, while Teller received 43.4 percent, with an estimated 80 percent of the votes counted at the time.

Your contribution is appreciated.

“I am so grateful and honored by this privilege of service and servitude to the great people of Legislative District 6, which encompasses many tribal nations and many rural citizens of Arizona,” Teller said in a video posted to his social media. “Thank you for putting your faith in me.”

Teller has a strong background in civics. He is the founder of When Natives Vote, a 2024 youth-led initiative focused on increasing civic engagement in Native communities. Teller also serves as the Southwestern Representative for the Young Democrats of America Indigenous Caucus.

Teller earned a B.A. in Business Administration from Fort Lewis College and an M.S. in Music Industry from the University of Southern California. He is also a UNITY National 25 Under 25 Honoree and a 2024 Center for Native American Youth Champion for Change.

His main platform issues included affordable housing, building a more affordable economy, climate and water rights, and quality education for Arizona youth. Teller says he is ready to take on the challenge.

“We are going to make some historic change. We are bringing the fire. We are bringing the fight. We are fighting for everyday hard-working Arizonans who just want a fighting chance—who just want the opportunity to build a life for themselves,” Teller said in his video.

Teller, whose campaign and platform were driven by his Diné values, says he plans to carry those values with him into his work in the Arizona State House and is thankful for the opportunity.

“Thank you for believing in me and my vision, and this philosophy—the Diné traditional philosophy and culture that guides me and that roots me to my ancestry and my heritage.”

At the time of reporting, Democrats had won three of the four currently called State House races, with five races still to be called. This puts Arizona Democrats in a position to end 60 years of Republican control of the state legislature.

scraped.title: Manitoba Métis Federation 'appalled' they were left out of budget
scraped.description: The president of the Manitoba Métis Federation says he's 'appalled' that Métis were not included in the federal budget.
scraped.author: Mark Blackburn
scraped.h1: Manitoba Métis Federation ‘appalled’ by being left out of budget
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

MMF President David Chartrand, seen here at a news conference in Ottawa in 2025, says it's not acceptable for the government to leave Métis out of the budget. Photo: APTN.

The Manitoba Métis Federation (MMF) says it’s “appalled” that it was left out of the federal budget.

“In recent years, Canada has finally started to address the long-overlooked needs of the Red River Métis in areas such as housing, early learning and childcare, and post-secondary education,” said David Chartrand, president of the MMF, in a statement released Friday.

“However, a significant gap still exists between our Nation and the general population. There’s no doubt our people will be angered that their needs have been dismissed by this Budget.”

On Thursday, the federal government tabled a budget with $50 billion worth of promises, mainly for First Nations housing and infrastructure. For Inuit, the budget renewed the Inuit Child First Initiative / Piratsiagutiit at $575 million over five years, and the government is also putting $610 million over four years for the Nutrition North subsidy.

Métis are only found once in the 532 page budget document, “as part of the title for a piece of legislation, An Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families – a piece of legislation that Canada has claimed they do not have a mechanism to fund us for.”

“The hugely successful distinctions-based approach has vanished, and government is reverting to phrases like ‘Indigenous’ when, in reality, they mean First Nations and Inuit,” said Chartrand. “The Red River Métis pay billions in taxes in this country, yet we have been forgotten by this government.”

Read More:

Budget 2026 commits $32B to First Nations housing, infrastructure while leaving most Métis, Inuit budget asks unaddressed

In its pre-budget submissions, a document that lists its needs for the government to consider, the MMF said it met with “numerous Ministers as well as the Prime Minister” to talk about its financial needs including infrastructure, housing, health, child and family services.

“We are disheartened that none of these priorities found their way into this Budget,” Chartrand said.

“We are never looking for a hand-out – rather, we are looking for our tax dollars to be reinvested in the Red River Métis so we can put a shovel in our hands and continue addressing the critical needs of our Nation, and strengthen Canada.

“We hope that the commitments made in these meetings become a reality so we can continue the historic progress we’ve made in recent years.”

APTN News reached out to the MMF to see if there were any meetings planned with Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in Winnipeg Friday to discuss his homelessness plan, but did not hear back before this story was published.

Before moving to become the APTN News social media producer, Mark was the executive producer for the news in eastern Canada. Before starting with APTN in 2009, Mark worked at CBC Radio and Television in Newfoundland and Labrador and Ottawa.

scraped.title: Indian Act debate lingers as First Nations discuss the future
scraped.description: Everyone has been hashing out just what it could mean to abolish the Indian Act after it was raised by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew in Ottawa.
scraped.author: Leanne Sanders
scraped.h1: Indian Act controversy lingers more than a week after abolishment was raised in Ottawa
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Everyone, from pundits, constitutional lawyers and scholars to people in coffee shops and online, has been hashing out just what it could mean to abolish the Indian Act after it was raised by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew on Oct. 26 in Ottawa.

However, Kinew hasn’t provided context for his comment, which came out at what was the first First Nations First Ministers meeting in decades and touched off a firestorm of debate over what doing away with the controversial Act would actually do.

APTN News has reached out to Kinew’s office and requested an interview on several occasions, but those requests have been denied.

“We just had one of the most impactful meetings of the decade in Ottawa and everyone on social media is talking about the Indian Act and the complexities of whether or not it can be abolished and the problems if it is and all these different things, said Jennifer Laewetz, the CEO of Paskwâw Strategies, an Indigenous advisory firm in Saskatchewan. “It’s a little bit frustrating because we need to be united on a lot of other bigger issues right now.”

“I just really wish that our leaders would recognize sometimes that they have so much impact in these spaces that if you are going to say something as big as ‘you need to abolish the Indian Act’ you need to be prepared to follow up with people in Canada about what that looks like… and communicate how you see that happening exactly,” Laewetz said, appearing on APTN News Truth and Politics on Friday.

Abolish the Indian Act. We have nothing to lose but our chains.

We will, of course, need new legislation that is an interface between the Federal government and First Nations. And this MUST be created alongside Chiefs and First Nation governments every step of the way. But it is time to move past the era of this outdated, racist, and patriarchal legislation.

I support Prime Minister Carney’s work to position Canada as a global leader in human rights and democracy. The Indian Act is inconsistent with achieving that vision.

Our laws at home should reflect the values we champion around the world.

It’s time for a relationship with First Nations people that reflects who we are as Canadians today, recognizes nationhood, and lives up to the true nature of reconciliation.

— Wab Kinew (@WabKinew) October 26, 2026

In a video shared hundreds of thousands of times online, Kinew said, holding up his status card, that he thinks it’s time to abolish the Indian Act, calling it “long overdue.”

Kinew appeared in a weekly scheduled interview on CTV Winnipeg after making the comment, but has refused to respond to requests to elaborate on his pronouncement from APTN News.

Winnipeg Free Press columnist Niigaan Sinclair said on the same Truth and Politics episode that abolishment of the Indian Act would create a “vacuum.”

“The Indian Act is so deep,” Sinclair said, “it doesn’t just impact Indigenous People. The Indian Act impacts the Department of Agriculture, the RCMP…it impacts all the different ways we see property ownership in this country.

“This is something that is going to not just be a conversation about Indigenous Peoples, because we have to realize our rights don’t come from the Indian Act, even though Canada thinks…they come from the recognition within the Indian Act.”

Sinclair said most significantly, it would lead to a debate of Section 91(24) of the Constitution Act, 1867 , which says that the federal government takes control of Indians and land reserved for Indians.

“We’ve been down that road and we know that constitutional debates end up in everybody under the sun talking about every single thing and everybody freaking out about referendums and separatism and Meech Lake and Charlottetown…,” Sincliar said.

“And if people aren’t radically running for the hills at this point, I would say its going to involve decades and definitely not something four-year governments can deal with directly.”

Honour of the Crown precludes talks of abolishment

The honour of the Crown, a foundational, unwritten constitutional principle in Canadian Law could halt any talks of abolishment before they start.

According to the Centre for Constitutional Studies , Supreme Court of Canada landmark rulings like Haida Nation and Sparrow established that “the honour of the Crown is not a mere moral suggestion; it is a binding legal duty meant to protect Indigenous peoples from state exploitation and to facilitate long-term reconciliation. It directly gives rise to the Crown’s fiduciary duties and the mandatory “duty to consult and accommodate”.

The Centre said “if the Government of Canada ever attempts to move forward with plans to abolish or radically overhaul the 1876 Indian Act , the honour of the Crown serves as a massive constitutional roadblock against unilateral government action… because a “Stroke of the Pen” repeal would be a direct breach, and would instantly be struck down by the courts as unconstitutional.”

It also triggers a “deep, mandatory Duty to Consult”, according to the Centre, the scale of which would be huge. As Sinclair referenced on Truth and Politics, since the Indian Act governs everything from band governance and reserve land management to estate laws and the legal definition of “Status,” dismantling it impacts virtually every aspect of First Nations life, and would require “consent, not just discussion.”

Honour of the Crown also separates the Indian Act from inherent rights. The Centre said “A crucial misunderstanding in Canadian politics is the idea that Indigenous rights are derived from the Indian Act . The honour of the Crown reminds lawmakers of the exact opposite: Aboriginal rights, treaty rights, and title are inherent, existing pre-contact, and are protected under Section 35 of the Constitution.”

Common concerns being raised by First Nations peoples is that abolishment would somehow do away with their rights. But the Centre said “because the honour of the Crown attaches itself directly to Section 35, the government cannot extinguish inherent rights or title by dissolving the Indian Act,” and even if the Act vanished, “the Crown’s foundational fiduciary obligations to Indigenous peoples remain completely intact and permanently binding.”

While First Nations chiefs generally agree the law that has governed First Nations peoples and lands is outdated and restrictive, there is little consensus on whether it should be repealed and what might take its place.

Assembly of First Nations Regional Chief Terry Teegee from B.C. said the backlash over the idea of getting rid of the Indian Act comes out of not having a framework for developing what would replace it. He also said in an interview with APTN that some of the more problematic sections of the Indian Act have already been amended.

“The pass system is gone and we’re allowed to have our potlatch gatherings. It does have provisions for tax exemptions and the issue of enfranchisement could be dealt with under Bill S-2,” Teegee said. “What the Indian Act does do, is it recognizes each individual First Nation in this country has special rights and provisions and it does recognize First Nations communities are nations and being a sovereign nation in and of itself coupled with the Section 35 rights we have the ability to protect our rights as a collective.”

Teegee also said nations which have turned to the courts to resolve Aboriginal rights and title have been able to do so by asserting their rights.

“Since the earliest court cases of Calder, right up to Sparrow, Delgamuukw v. British Columbia , Haida, Taku Tlingit and also the Chilcotin Decision, which proves title and Cowichan-they’re all embedded and were utilized under Section 35 rights from the Indian Act. Without a framework to replace the Indian Act? It’s not being replaced,” Teegee said.

“This concern across the country we’ve heard for and against (the Indian Act) speaks to what a massive issue this is and to have a very cavalier comment about it really distracted from the main issues of Crown-Indigenous relations, which was what the meeting was about.”

Teegee said what chiefs at the meeting would rather have heard from Kinew is how the government of Manitoba is implementing the treaties in Manitoba.

While First Nations leaders broadly support changing the rules on how the Indian Act determines who qualifies for status, the federal government has not committed to changing those rules.

Bill S-2 , which would amend the portion of the Indian Act that deals with new registration entitlements, is currently stalled in the House of Commons. The federal Liberal government is facing mounting pressure from First Nations advocates, opposition parties, and independent legal experts to pass Senate amendments that would eliminate the Indian Act’s second-generation cut-off rule.

“You know, it’s so interesting,” said 21 Things You May Not Know About the Indian Act author, Bob Joseph, in an interview with APTN. “This thing that controls your life from birth to death, that exists exclusively as an instrument to get your name off a list and make you a non-status Indian, designed for the sole purpose of assimilation, that people are not wanting to move away from it.”

Joseph has inherited a chief’s seat in the Gayaxala (Thunderbird) clan, the first clan of the Gwawa’enuxw, one of the 18 tribes that make up the Kwakwaka’wakw in B.C.

Joseph said he got insight for his more recent work, 21 Things You Need to Know About Indigenous Self-Government, from his dad.

“And he said, ‘Are we ready?’ And that was my first sort of soul-searching question, right? Are we ready? That’s such a great question, and I tried myself to come up with ideas about how do you answer the readiness question because that’s where the fear is coming from,” Joseph said.

“So why would I stick up for this thing? Why would I defend it and fight over the minutia? What instead? We can do what they always talk about, I can use my inherent right to self-government, and I can decide along with my nation who my people are… where if you can just make that mental leap to ‘I have the right from the creator to determine who our people are. That’s who I should be fighting for.’ I think the first easy thing that we can do is decide on citizenship.

“Years could be spent arguing about the minutiae of what is and what will be,” Joseph added. “Let’s decide for ourselves as a member of our nation- let’s come up with those rules together and I think that is more in line with the cultural value of all First Nations. We’re supposed to look after all of our people, not just the ones whose name appear on a government of Canada list that was designed to track who you were so that they can find ways to take it off that list.”

Is self-government the answer?

One chief who is working to ready his Nation for whatever comes next is Samuel Crowfoot of Siksika in southwest Alberta. Siksika is a large First Nation with 7,800 members and is part of the Siksikaitsitapi or Blackfoot Confederacy.

Crowfoot said he addressed Carney at the Ottawa meeting.

“In my comments, I said Siksika Nation just fought a battle on behalf of Canada by trying to keep us united. It was our treaties that helped form and shape Canada a 150 years ago. And now today (it was) the power of our treaties that helped take the teeth out of the separatist bite,” Crowfoot said of the recent Alberta referendum vote where 75 per cent voted against starting the process to separate.

“It was our duty to consult argument that we brought forward that Alberta lost on. That is actually what helped save and protect Canada. So now, when you ram Bill C-39 through and add Bill C-5 to that and adopt looser and weaker standards of consultation, you’re diluting the very thing that protected you.”

Crowfoot said he felt blindsided when Kinew brought up the Indian Act.

“We’ve been talking about wanting to amend or tweak or even abolish the Indian Act for decades. And a lot of things that they’re saying were right, but I’m concerned about the timing and I’m concerned about what the actual net effect is going to be,” he said.

“I don’t know if there was any discussion beforehand. I don’t know if it was spontaneous. But I do know that as soon as that comment was made about abolishing the Indian Act and Premier Carney ran with it, he gave it life; it negated our main messaging while we were there.”

Crowfoot said that while there are obvious problems with the Indian Act, it wasn’t raised in an appropriate fashion.

“Very early on in this country’s history, the Indian Act and the government of Canada adopted a blood quantum standard. That blood quantum standard is fine print for an extermination of treaty rights. Because there’s going to come a point where there’ll be nobody born that meets this blood quantum requirement, where treaty rights can actually be passed on and processed,” Crowfoot said.

“There are membership provisions in the Indian Act that are racist, that are meant to dilute us. But if we’re going to talk about abolishing these things that have the ability to affect us like the Indian Act, then there needs to be an adequate solution brought forward, or you’re going to have exactly what you’re having here-a lot of fear, a lot of confusion, and a lot of distraction away from the real pressing issues of the day.”

Nations already opting out of Indian Act

Some Nations have taken back control of some of their own affairs to get out from under the government. According to federal government figures, Canada is currently implementing 27 modern treaties. Six of those are Comprehensive Land Claim Settlement Agreements-Tsawwassen, Maa-nulth, Yale and Tla’amin Nations in B.C., the Nunavik Inuit and the Eeyou Marine Region of the Cree in Quebec.

One of the modern treaties is a self-government agreement only and is unrelated to a land claim. The Whitecap Dakota Nation treaty was signed in 2023. It officially recognizes members of the nation located 30 km south of Saskatoon as “Aboriginal Peoples of Canada” under Section 35 of the Constitution. It moved the nation out from under most provisions of the federal Indian Act, although status cards and tax exemptions remain.

The treaty gave Whitecap Dakota Nation direct jurisdiction and law-making authority over governance, reserve lands and natural resources, membership, culture, education, health and social services as well as financial management, taxation and business development.

But First Nations policy analyst Russ Diabo argues that “self-government and modern treaties are used to download responsibilities and cap Crown obligations” and may not be the answer.

“Canada’s self-government policy treats self-government as delegated authority, not Inherent jurisdiction. It also links funding to a First Nation’s own-source revenue and “capacity,” not Treaty obligations,” Diabo said.

In a presentation Diabo prepared for consultations with First Nations ahead of the Alberta referendum, he pointed out that modern treaties and Self-Government Agreements often require release of Crown liability and certainty clauses and convert Aboriginal Title into defined parcels and cash, limiting future claims.

Still, many First Nations have taken steps to self-government by drafting community land codes under the First Nations Land Management Act framework . Policy research by the Yellowhead Institute and legal reviews outline some core problems with the framework, including that its scope is limited to reserves and doesn’t include broader traditional territories, unceded lands, and modern treaty or title agreements.

The high cost of drafting, implementing, and managing an independent land code, setting up registries, and running local environmental and zoning systems also imposes heavy administrative and financial burdens on communities. That leaves smaller or underfunded First Nations to struggle to absorb the operational costs required to manage lands previously administered by the federal government, according to the Yellowhead Institute.

According to Hayden King at the Yellowhead, there have been six attempts going back to 1951 to abolish the Indian Act.

The latest was in 2018 when former prime minister Justin Trudeau attempted to move First Nations “toward self-government by encouraging a piece-meal devolution of administrative powers from the Federal (and in some cases provincial) governments to First Nations,” according to King. It was rejected.

Opting in to the First Nations Elections Act

Another option for nations is to decide how their elections are held. First Nations have been critical of the election process under the Indian Act, which they believe is antiquated and paternalistic.

According to the federal government, some of the key concerns in the Indian Act election process identified by First Nations are that two-year terms of office are too short for First Nation governments to accomplish important priorities. Federal, provincial and most municipal governments generally have terms of four years. Opting in to the First Nations Election Act means nations can decide those things for themselves.

Other major concerns First Nations identified are a loose process for the nomination of candidates and a mail-in ballot system that is open to abuse, according to the government.

A small Ojibway community in northwestern Ontario opted to transition from the election provisions under the Indian Act to the First Nations Elections Act. Musk-kosiminiziibing’s (formerly Big Grassy River First Nation) 277 residents will vote in their new chief and council in the next band election set for Jan. 22, 2027. Musk-kosiminiziibing is currently in the process of hiring an electoral officer.

“We did community engagement sessions in 2024 and it came out from our comprehensive community plan,” said Chief Lynn Indian in an interview with APTN. “We wanted to be able to try and have more of the community voting in elections. Under the Indian Act, you’re pretty much limited to the mail in ballot process or the polling station the day of the voting.”

According to Carolane Gratton, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada and Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, 97 First Nations who have opted-in to the First Nations Elections Act, which was passed in 2014 under former prime minister Stephen Harper.

Chief Indian called the Indian Act restrictive and said it limits what they can do with their lands. But Kinew and Carney’s brief comments left a lot of questions unanswered. Indian said Kinew should clarify why he said what he said about getting rid of the Indian Act.

“I think we have a lot of work to do in terms of understanding what the implications of it would mean. I think there are different ways you can withdraw yourself as a band from the Indian Act,” Indian said.

“We’ve done some work in and around First Nations land management, we’ve entered into referendum, we’ve developed and passed a whole land code, technically taking us out of the Indian Act as it applies to the land and now we have control over it. But in saying that, I know that there are still limitations.”

Read more:

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew calls on prime minister to abolish the Indian Act at meeting with chiefs

Carney open to conversations around ‘moving beyond’ the Indian Act

Liberals running out of time on proposed law to remove one kind of discrimination from Indian Act .

The next opportunity where chiefs from across the country will have the chance to meet and discuss the Indian Act will be at the Assembly of First Nations Special Chiefs Assembly in early December; however, the agenda has not been released yet.

Leanne has a certificate in broadcasting and has more than 12 years of radio news experience, both as an anchor and reporter in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Métis journalist is a passionate writer and born storyteller and loves to connect with people and learn about their life experiences.

APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

An Algonquin environmental activist says the Carney government’s priorities are misplaced when it comes to climate change initiatives.

“Essentially in 2025, the budget committed $81.8 billion in increased military spending over five years and so that’s telling us that while they may be making these commitments for environmental protection for workers and jobs – at the end of the day they’re still heavily interested in the global military complex which is one of the main drivers of climate change,” Dara Wawatie-Chabot said on the latest episode of Nation to Nation.

“Their commitments are just not meeting the demands that they are actually committing to in these budgets.”

Earlier in the week, a group called the Youth Climate Corps held a news conference in Ottawa calling on the Liberal government to do more when it comes to climate change.

The organization says the 2025 budget put $40 million toward a Youth Climate Corps pilot program but a year later it has yet to be launched.

They are also calling for a further $1 billion to be invested in green jobs for young people.

The federal government’s 2026 budget pledges more than $32 billion over 10 years for First Nations housing and infrastructure but largely leaves Métis and Inuit requests unaddressed | Story by Keelan Jacobs. https://t.co/tF4zLWI3IR

— APTN News (@APTNNews) November 5, 2026

Airports in northern Ontario

The Chiefs of Ontario says airports serving First Nations in the northern part of the province are in a serious state of disrepair and require $1.2 to $1.5 billion to bring them up to standard.

“The runways are gravel, they’re not long enough, many of them are short for standards by 1,500 feet at a minimum,” Ontario Regional Chief Abram Benedict said. “The infrastructure that supports them – the hangars – are old and outdated. The electrical systems, lighting, is very old – not adequate in many cases.

“So, all of the infrastructure surrounding these airports needs to be severely replaced immediately and upgraded.”

The COO, Nishnawbe Aski Nation and northern First Nations recently held a press conference in Toronto calling on both the Ontario and federal governments to provide necessary funding.

They say the 29 airports provide services to more than 20,000 people living in remote First Nations including Medevac flights, emergency evacuations, food and supply deliveries and healthcare access.

Value for money

A Conservative MP says Indigenous people are not getting value for money spent when it comes to the federal government departments that serve them.

“From 2015 to 2025, a span of ten years, Indigenous spending has grown by about $30 billion dollars,” Jamie Schmale, who is the Conservative critic for Crown-Indigenous Relations, said. “It’s almost seven times faster than federal spending. So, we’re seeing the money there but the results aren’t equal to that and that’s the issue right now.”

For example, Schmale said the size of Indigenous Services Canada has doubled the number of employees working there to more than 8,000 people in recent years but education, health and income levels continue to be much lower for Indigenous people when compared to other Canadians.

Fraser spent the last 20 years working in both print and radio in Saskatchewan – mostly in the northern part of the province. Before joining APTN’s Ottawa bureau, he was news director for the Missinipi Broadcasting Corporation working out of their Prince Albert office. He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.
