scraped.h1: Inside the Big House connecting generations to Haíɫzaqv knowledge
scraped.body_text:
Twenty years ago, Haíɫzaqv community members raised λáλix̌sístala to help Youth reconnect with their language, songs, dances, culture and ceremony. Today, the first generation to grow up here is carrying that vision forward

Matt Simmons

●

●

This story was produced in collaboration with The Narwhal .

As smoke rises from the fire at the centre of a Haíɫzaqv Big House raised two decades ago on a beach crowded with cedar, the song begins.

The dancers emerge and circle the floor, their feet tracing stories in the sand. Drummers seated at the log drum hold the beat and their voices carry the song. Around the room, from among all the people here to witness the ceremony, women stand. Swaying like kelp in tidal currents, their movements and hand gestures mirror those of the dancers, protecting them.

Leading this ceremony, dancing life into the walls and the world around, are children. This is Kvai , a place where Haíɫzaqv kids come to connect with song and story, language and ceremony. Received by the lands and waters, this is their lineage, their inheritance.

Standing next to the log drum, leaning on the talking stick, Thomas Dixon extends a welcome.

“The name of this Big House is λáλix̌sístala,” he says. “λáλix̌sístala in our language translates to ‘complete the circle’ — and the circle we’re referring to is the circle of knowledge, because of the amount of knowledge that gets passed on here, from generation to generation.”

Like many of his peers, Dixon came here as a Youth and learned from the land and from the stories. Now, as a cultural leader, he’s passing on the teachings he received, completing the circle.

“These songs and dances are very sacred,” he says, asking guests not to share photos or videos on social media. “When we were given permission to teach these songs and dances, we promised the chiefs and Elders we wouldn’t put it out publicly like that.”

He pauses. In the space between his words, the snapping of the fire.

“ W̓álas ǧiáxsix̌a ,” he says, sitting down at the log. The drumming begins.

In 2008, Opaskwayak Cree scholar Shawn Wilson, said: “When listeners know where the storyteller is coming from and how the story fits into the storyteller’s life, it makes the absorption of the knowledge that much easier.”

These are not my stories — but I am part of it because I was there. ​’Cúagilákv Jess Housty invited me, extending the welcome to my seven-year-old daughter. I was invited to witness, given permission to share a story of this place and what it means to many Haíɫzaqv. This place also holds deep meaning for Wuìk̓inux̌v people and the watershed is an area of shared importance. Gently warned about past harms done by well-meaning journalists, I am walking lightly, honouring the trust.

I listen to my recordings while I write: the sound of the waves, ravens squawking, an eagle chittering. A light wind.

Inside, a couple of teenagers add logs to the flames, sending a burst of sparks through the hole in the roof. Outside, a grizzly bear walks the beach with her cubs under sheets of rain while salmon jump from the bay, their silver backs glistening against a grey ocean.

Dixon stands, again holding the talking stick, and speaks in Haíɫzaqvḷa: “Yáu sásṃ, sas húmíɫṇƛa?”

As one, the kids respond with an affirming ‘mm-hmm.’

“I want to explain what I just asked the kids,” he says. “I asked the kids: ‘Sas húmíɫṇƛa?’ — ‘Did you hear me?’ [Are you listening?] I asked them that because I want to make sure that they’re listening before we tell the story. At every practice, after every dance, I would ask them that before I tell them the story. I would tell the story behind each dance so the stories get told over and over and over again and hopefully it gets embedded in their heads.”

“This was an old teaching we got from Thistalalh Ed Martin , when he was our camp Elder out here,” he continues. “When I was a camper, that’s what he used to say to us. So when I say, ‘Sas húmíɫṇƛa?’ you guys can say ‘mm-hmm,’ to make sure you are all paying attention.”

The sounds of the rain and the fire are one and the song begins again.

Haíɫzaqv have always been here, caring for w̓áxv:w̓uísax̌v. W̓áxv:w̓uísax̌v is the land, ocean, submerged land, surface water, groundwater, subsurface and air space as defined by the boundaries of the five tribes which make up the Haíɫzaqv Nation: Wúyalitx̌v, ’Qvúqvay̓áitx̌v, w̓u̓íƛ̓itx̌v, ’Yísdáitx̌v and X̌íx̌ís. On colonial maps, Haíɫzaqv w̓áxv:w̓uísax̌v is on “B.C.’s” central coast.

As affirmed by the nation’s constitution, ratified in 2025, the “relationship of the Haíɫzaqv people to the w̓áxv:w̓uí sax̌v is ancient, sacred and complex,” and the nation’s “ancient rights, inherent jurisdiction and responsibility for the w̓áxv:w̓uí sax̌v, which have never been surrendered, flow from our relationship to it.”

The sun rises every morning, even when it can’t be seen in all the clouds. The moon completes its cycles, waning and waxing, inexorably tugging our bodies and the waters we come from. The seasons shift like slow stretching tides, bringing herring and salmon and berries.

These are the places where the stories are from, the stories that get told over and over and over again. Story, song, ceremony, place: same thing, different forms. Sas húmíɫṇƛa?

Ten years after λáλix̌sístala was raised, a tugboat called the Nathan E. Stewart ran aground near the village of Q’vúqvai in Gale Passage. Eight hours later, it sank, spilling more than 100,000 litres of diesel and other pollutants into Haíɫzaqv waters.

Everything is connected, of course, and all the threads matter — but this is not a story about the legacy of pollution and trauma, of diesel spills and shipping lanes. This is a story of knowledge, ceremony and the future of stewardship. This is a story about λáλix̌sístala.

Kvai, sometimes spelled Koeye, is pronounced kway.

Depending on the boat and weather, it takes around an hour-and-a-half to two hours to get here from Wágḷísḷa (Bella Bella, B.C.)

On the way down, you might see whales — humpbacks or orcas, probably — and in the summer you’ll likely see fishing boats, a smattering of pleasure craft of various types and sizes, maybe a coast guard vessel and perhaps a BC Ferries vessel on its regular run between “ Port Hardy “ and “ Prince Rupert. “

When you get here, you’ll see a flash of white sand against the dark green of the coastal rainforest. λáλix̌sístala will greet you as you enter the bay. Atop a bluff, you’ll see the lodge and other buildings, tucked into the trees. It’s welcoming, protective.

Before all this, the Kvai watershed was home to several Haíɫzaqv villages and fishing sites. For thousands of years, this place was a vital part of culture, ceremony, harvesting and stewardship. Then came the colonizers.

In 1884, the federal government amended the Indian Act to prohibit Potlatches: “Every Indian or other person who engages in or assists in celebrating the Indian festival known as the ‘Potlatch’ or in the Indian dance ‘tamananawas’ is guilty of a misdemeanor, and shall be liable to imprisonment,” the amendment stated.

Gilbert M. Sproat, a Scottish-born businessman and government agent at the time, described the Potlatch ceremony to then-prime minister John A. MacDonald as “the parent of numerous vices which eat out the heart of the [native] people.”

Israel Wood Powell, the provincial government’s first superintendent of Indian Affairs, went further, advocating for the federal government to “adopt every practicable means to put a stop to the custom.” Powell went on to champion and oversee the residential “school” system in the province, forcibly removing Indigenous children from their homes, cultures and languages. (Powell’s name continues to be used in geographic place names, including the community of Powell River. Tla’amin Nation leadership has been petitioning to have the name changed for several years.)

MacDonald agreed with Sproat and Powell and their contemporaries.

“The great aim of our legislation has been to do away with the tribal system and assimilate the Indian people in all respects … as speedily as they are fit to change,” he said in 1887.

In the years that followed, widespread persecution of any expression of Indigeneity or ceremony was severe, sanctioned and often enforced by government agents, including the newly formed federal police force that is now the RCMP. Around this time, with the nation’s communities already devastated by the spread of smallpox, including attempts to exterminate entire communities with disease-ridden blankets, the only remaining Haíɫzaqv λiác̓ilacx̌i (Big House) was destroyed, likely by missionaries.

More than a century would pass before the next was built.

λáλix̌sístala was the first, raised on the beach at Kvai in 2006. Next came Gvakva’aus Haíɫzaqv, the larger λiác̓ilacx̌i raised in Wágḷísḷa in 2019. Last year, Haíɫzaqv ratified its new constitution and celebrated with a Potlatch in that space.

The importance of the Potlatch cannot be overstated. In Potlatch, songs and dances breathe life into the world. Within them are stories that span generations, past, present and future, and speak of place, lineage, spirit and so much more. These stories, as they are shared in all their shapes and forms, preserve the circle of knowledge.

In Indigenous Storywork , Sto:lo scholar Q’um Q’um Xiiem Jo-ann Archibald said that “storytellers not only learned stories from master storytellers but also by being connected to land” and explained how “stories can become a teacher, and … we can live life through stories.” She also said the oral tradition challenges the listener to “make meaning and gain understanding from the storyteller/teacher’s words and stories, which is an empowering process.”

Remember: “The stories get told over and over and over again and hopefully it gets embedded in their heads.”

In coming together, at places like Kvai, or in the Big House in Wágḷísḷa, or anywhere else where knowledge is passed on through story, time takes on a new shape, layers and threads where there is no beginning and no end, just a continuous unfolding. As Haida and Tlingit artist Robert Davidson said in Potlatch as Pedagogy , we are “all connected to the past by a thin thread. And when we come together as a group, then these threads form quite a thick rope.”

In Haíɫzaqvḷa: m̓ṇukvs w̓úwax̌di; one mind, one heart.

The river feels eternal, its banks renewed time and time and time again. The beach is washed by the tides and the rain. From ‘Cúagilákv’s newest collection of poems:

Cup sea water in your hands.

Bring it gently above the highest tide line.

Wait for the precious sun;

wait in your posture of petition

for the gift of salt.

When you have enough

to make a little mountain on your palm,

pinch it between your fingers

and use it to spell the words

closest to your heart.

Lick your fingers clean

and know that the ocean

is the holder, now,

of your prayers.

The old spruce tree absorbs a cloud of swallows; their symphony of chirps dying abruptly, swallowed by the endless riffling river.

Sas húmíɫṇƛa? (Are you listening?)

After ceremony, and after all the guests have been gifted the salmon and seaweed the kids harvested and processed, most community members head back to Bella Bella on a handful of boats and the kids move their things into λáλix̌sístala to sleep. For some, it’s their final night here before returning home. Others will be back next week, and maybe again the week after that.

Singing and drumming and practicing dances, cooking hot dogs on the fire, the big kids guide the little ones and there’s a comfortable, controlled chaos to it all. A few of the boys swim in the ocean, laughing and splashing as the rain continues falling and the sun slowly dips down to the western horizon behind the clouds.

Before λáλix̌sístala and before all the infrastructure that exists today, kids camped on the beach in a handful of tents from Canadian Tire. ​’Cúagilákv was one of those kids, and today they’re a camp leader.

“I had some moments this summer around the celebration where I would be talking to campers about what my experience was like as a camper in the first years of camp, when it was tents on the beach and on feast day we literally used to rake a flat spot on the beach to light a fire and dance around the fire, and they were just like, ‘What dark times are you from?’ ”

​’Cúagilákv laughs, their eyes twinkling.

During the more recent chapters of colonization, the site where the current lodge, cabins, garden and other infrastructure sits was once logged and later sold to settlers who built a sport fishing lodge there. Haíɫzaqv leaders stood firm in upholding their sovereign rights and established the youth science and culture camp, first on the beach and later buying back the land in 2001.

Those original buildings were burned in an arson fire in 2011. With the insurance money, the organization bought a sawmill, rebuilding everything from the ground up. Working with timbers harvested on the land, milled by Haíɫzaqv workers, they created a beautiful new lodge and cabins.

“It’s really cool that kids who attend camp today don’t ever remember not having a Big House down there,” ​’Cúagilákv says. “They don’t remember a time when there wasn’t a lodge providing safety and support and hosting their families. They don’t remember a time when there weren’t comfortable cabins to sleep in. They just totally take for granted that that’s always been there and it will always be there — and I love it.”

Central to all this safety and support is Qqs.

Qqs (pronounced kucks) is the non-profit organization that oversees programs including the Youth science and culture camps at Kvai, as well as a variety of programming in Haíɫzaqv communities in support of health, culture, food security and more. ​’Cúagilákv is the executive director, a position they took on after their dad, Larry Jorgensen, stepped back from his leadership role. Qqs means ‘eyes’ in Haíɫzaqvḷa.

Keeping the camp running isn’t always easy, nor is it cheap. Transport alone is a huge expense: running boats back and forth accounts for about a third of the entire annual budget. For eight weeks every summer, Kvai is home to kids, Youth and staff, with groups of anywhere from15 to 30 people rotating in and out weekly. Some kids come for multiple weeks, others just for one. A lot of the staff are youth themselves, former campers who are stepping into leadership roles or getting experience and earning a wage in their first jobs, cooking and cleaning or otherwise supporting the programs. At the end of each week is feast day, when the kids are responsible for leading the ceremonies in front of community members who come down for the day.

“Programs like this are beautiful, but the reality of running them in a remote location is that certain aspects are astronomically more expensive and complicated,” ​’Cúagilákv says.

Yet, somehow, for the past 28 years, Haíɫzaqv Youth have gathered here every summer to learn from the land. When I ask some of the staff how long they’ve been coming out to Kvai, most say their connections thread through their whole lives. It’s as if they’ve always been here.

Allie, a staff member, puts it simply: “Since I was a baby. I grew up out here.”

“I think back to that really early wisdom that guided the creation of Qqs and it was this idea that people protect what they love,” ​’Cúagilákv says. “So you want to teach them to love themselves, so they’re protecting themselves. You want to teach them to love each other and their community, so there’s a strong, cohesive community mind. You want to teach them to love the land and the waters so that they are standing up as stewards. And you want to teach them to love language and culture, so they are stewarding that as well.”

“I mean, it’s stupidly simple, but I really believe it is the most important thing we do.”

Both ‘Cúagilákv and their brother Dúqva̓ísḷa William Housty now have their own kids among the campers. Faye, William’s wife, is one of the camp leaders, and his teenager is also on staff. Across the fire one night, Faye tells me their youngest, George, listened to the songs while in the womb. William is there singing and drumming with the kids in the Big House on feast day.

“I think one of the really beautiful things about having done this work for as long as we have, is that we can see what Kvai kids do when they grow up,” ​’Cúagilákv says. “Stewardship is a really obvious one.”

William was one of the earliest camp leaders and is now director of the nation’s stewardship department , which manages policy and planning in support of ecosystem health, jurisdiction and protection of Haíɫzaqv lands, waters and resources. Gíƛa Elroy White was similarly an early leader out at Kvai and is now the department’s in-house archaeologist.

“Many of the Guardian Watchmen and people who work at all levels in that office were Kvai campers or Kvai staff at one point over the years,” ​’Cúagilákv says. “By no means would we ever take all the credit for that — they are extraordinary in their own right and we’re really lucky that we got to support them for portions of that formative time in their lives.”

For Louisa Housty-Jones, Kvai not only shaped her — it saved her life.

“I was the victim of domestic violence,” she tells me. When she was around nineteen, drinking heavily and spiraling from the trauma of an abusive relationship, Larry took her down to Kvai and left her there, alone. “Larry had this vision of helping our young people in their healing journeys through the land, guiding them to finding their identity.”

At first, she was angry with him. Slowly, yielding to the lands and waters, her anger subsided. This was before λáλix̌sístala and the current trail which links the lodge to the beach. Somewhere near where the Big House now stands she found a rock to sit at.

“Every day, rain or shine, I would make it a daily thing to go and sit on that rock,” she says. “I wailed, I cried, I screamed — I did a lot of healing at that rock. And then I would go in the ocean and I did that pretty much every day.”

Among the many roles she now holds, Louisa works with the W̓úm̓aqs du M̓ṇúyaqs, the council of high-ranking Matriarchs and Knowledge Keepers, supporting “their responsibility to pass on knowledge, teachings and wisdom from one generation to the next.”

“We are Haíɫzaqv women. We are as strong as cedar trees,” the M̓ṇúyaqs affirm in the Heiltsuk Women’s Declaration. “We are the mothers who give birth to nations. We are the mothers who bring future generations into being. We are the lifeblood of our people.”

When she was alone at Kvai, Louisa once heard women singing the Haíɫzaqv songs. And near her rock, she kept hearing a lady crying. It scared her: it was fall, cold, and there was no one else out there. A couple of months later, back in Bella Bella, she told her grandmother the story.

“She grabbed my hand and she said: ‘That lady crying was you. That was you, your spirit.’ Everything just totally came together. It’s what our Elders talk about. It was the way she explained it to me, that it was a part of me that was leaving, that was fighting not to leave.”

She started taking the canoe out in the bay, to harvest crabs, and up the river. It was there she found the most peace, she says.

“There’s so much healing in our land.”

After the kids leave and staff head back to Wágḷísḷa for the weekend, it’s quiet and the bears come back. The sand is white and golden and the story of their morning walk along the beach is fresh and new, even as it reflects one that has been told here for thousands of years. Little birds dart around the shallow waves that lap at the shore. A few gulls congregate by the kelp and barnacle encrusted rocks.

The river is tea-coloured, rich with tannins. A flotilla of canoes leans against an old cedar tree. In the deep stillness away from the beach, the land opens to receive you. The light plays on the waters, creeks tumble from the forest. Later, the tide is so high it stretches into the tangle of trees that line the long beaches. In the mornings, the clouds sit so low it’s hard to tell where the fog ends and the ocean begins.

​’Cúagilákv skims the little boat expertly along the water. In the hum of the engine, the slap of the waves and the cool salt spray, their words are offerings:

When I was small,

I loved the stories of people who—

with unhurried gestures—

lifted the edges of the sea

and walked into other worlds.

Of course water is a portal,

the pathway between us

and some magnificent other space

beyond our imagining.

What else could we expect

of a substance that,

even in this heavy world,

lets us float?

In his living room overlooking the bay at Wágḷísḷa, Ian Reid, a Haíɫzaqv artist and carver, puts a book of oral histories on the table.

Gusgai’in William Beynon, a hereditary chief whose mixed lineage includes Nisga’a, Ts’msyen and the Allied Tribes of Lax Kw’alaams, spent decades listening to and carefully recording oral histories, starting in 1914 and continuing until the 1950s. His great-granddaughter, Samantha Beynon, recently wrote a children’s book about Potlatches based on his work.

These stories, Ian says, and all the stories we haven’t lost are part of the fabric of everything that matters.

‘Nusi shares old stories about the animals and people and new stories about the times we’re living in. He talks about Pops, Ed Martin, about mosquitoes and grizzlies. He talks about being on the water, being away from community and coming home, carving poles, receiving his chief name. He explains how the songs and dances the kids learn at Kvai are connected to stewardship because they come from specific places and lineage. Those places and lineages belong to the children and the kids belong to the stories. They are held through time, shared on a continuum.

More than a hundred years ago, as the federal government prohibited Potlatches and set about taking up the lands, Haíɫzaqv Chief Bob Anderson spoke of that continuum:

“The government have not bought any land from us so far as we know and we are simply lending this land to the government. We own it all. We will never change our minds in that respect, and after we are dead our children will still hold on to the same ideas.” Anderson’s words, spoken to representatives of the colonial government in 1913, form part of the preamble of Q̓áikasas Ǧvi̓ḷás: The great laws of the Haíɫzaqv .

“It does not matter how long the government take to determine this question, we will remain the same in our ideas about this matter … We consider that the government is stealing that land from us, and we also understand that it is unlawful for the government to take this land.”

A moment stretches and becomes endless, unfurling like a spring fiddlehead. The stories are a presence. Through time, an echo: “… Our children will still hold on to the same ideas.”

And through time, I’m in λáλix̌sístala, listening. Above the crackling of the fire and the murmur of twin babies, ƛ̓istalaɫ Maria Martin’s voice rings out:

“Kvai has become the place where our children, youth and community come for wellness, healing, guidance and, most importantly, learning our Haíɫzaqv culture,” she says. ƛ̓istalaɫ is one of Ed Martin’s daughters. “This Great House has been here for 20 years and that’s what we are here to acknowledge and celebrate today. It strengthens our identity and gives us much hope for our future generations. Our children that have been here are the strongest and the greatest little leaders on the ground. This is exactly what my late dad envisioned. … This place was our dad’s home.”

“I am proud to have watched our children and youth grow confidence, respect and pride,” ƛ̓istalaɫ continues. “They have learned not only our songs, dances and our protocols, but also kindness and what it means to listen and be accountable — and they will become strong leaders for our nation.”

“We continue to find healing here. We remember who we are here.”

The twins are brought onto the floor and danced around the fire in the arms of their relatives.

Sas húmíɫṇƛa?

In reporting this story, Matt leaned into participatory, community-driven storytelling as part of a decolonized approach to journalism. He wrote about why this is important in a companion piece you can read here .

Matt Simmons is a writer and editor based in Smithers, B.C., unceded Gidimt’en Clan territory, home of the Wet’suwet’en/Witsuwit’en Nation.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

scraped.description: Seeking truth when reporting in Indigenous communities sometimes meansabandoning the idea of journalism as ‘observation at a distance’ — and embracing reciprocity
scraped.author: Matt Simmons
scraped.h1: ‘Not at a distance’: listening and participating as decolonized journalism practice
scraped.body_text:
Seeking truth when reporting in Indigenous communities sometimes means abandoning the idea of journalism as ‘observation at a distance’ — and embracing reciprocity

Matt Simmons

●

●

This story was produced in collaboration with The Narwhal .

I reach out to ​’Cúagilákv Jess Housty around the time of the Haíɫzaqv new year, when the wán̓ái (herring) return and harvesting season begins again after the long, dark winter.

We first connected six years ago, when Xenaksiala Elder Wa’xaid Cecil Paul left this world for the next and I was tasked with writing a tribute to his life and legacy. I called ‘Cúagilákv and they told me stories about their interactions with him. Our paths have intersected a few times since — and before, unknowingly, in the neighbourhood I grew up in where they also spent time during their Youth. ‘Cúagilákv’s poems are part of my love story, too, a thread of words and wild mint, mail and ferries.

This time, I’ve reached out because I’m thinking about a tugboat called the Nathan E. Stewart, which ran aground near the village of Q’vúqvai in Gale Passage 10 years ago. Eight hours after it hit the rocks, it sank, spilling more than 100,000 litres of diesel and other pollutants. Grief and anger and trauma remain.

Much has been done since to protect Haíɫzaqv lands and waters from another tragedy. ‘Cúagilákv tells me how many others, including their brother, Dúqva̓ísḷa William Housty, are working on the technical and policy side of marine protections and stewardship. But ​’Cúagilákv is following a different path to care for Haíɫzaqv territory.

“I’m going to deepen my commitment to land-based Youth programming so every kid in the community loves the territory and wants to protect it — and eventually they’ll be the system,” they explain.

And they invite me and my daughter to attend the anniversary of the opening of λáλix̌sístala, a Haíɫzaqv Big House which was raised two decades ago on a beach in the Kvai watershed, around two hours by boat from the Haíɫzaqv capital of Wágḷísḷa (Bella Bella, B.C.) . I accept with gratitude, and following the words of Wa’xaid, I listen. I follow the Wedzin Kwa to where it meets K’sien, and from there follow the river to the ocean.

In his house overlooking the bay at Wágḷísḷa, Ian Reid, a Haíɫzaqv artist and carver, tells me old stories of the animals and people, and some new ones too. We’re sitting together in his living room while our daughters play in the kitchen. Veda, my kiddo, and Hazel, theirs, met at Kvai and became fast friends. Eli, Hazel’s big brother, is in and out of the house, trying out some newfound freedom on his bike. Ian’s partner, Cayce, offers me a coffee. Cayce and I grew up a few blocks from each other and spent a year at the same elementary school — but we’re only meeting now. Ian’s brother, Garney, is outside the house fixing a water line in the street. I sat with Garney and his wife on the boat down to Kvai. We talked about movies.

I brought a blanket for Ian from the Unist’ot’en feast hall, delivering it for a friend. Ian, whose Haíɫzaqv name is ‘Nusi, meaning “Full Moon,” made a frog crest that was used by Dinï ze (Hereditary Chief) Nedïbïs of the C’ihlts’ehkhyu (Big Frog) Clan of the Wet’suwet’en Nation. Ian puts the blanket on “the way they would put it on me in the feast hall” and poses for a photo.

Why am I telling you all this?

Because, as Opaskwayak Cree scholar Shawn Wilson says in Research is Ceremony, “… it is important for storytellers to impart their own life and experience into the telling. When listeners know where the storyteller is coming from and how the story fits into the storyteller’s life, it makes the absorption of the knowledge that much easier.”

In a word: trust.

I’ve been leaning into participatory journalism as a means of getting closer to stories that centre and prioritize the Indigenous communities where I’ve been welcomed and trusted, letting respect and reciprocity be my guides. In this practice, I’m not only finding deeper truths and more connection — I’m discovering richer, more nuanced stories.

Kim TallBear, in Standing With and Speaking as Faith , wrote: “Inquiring not at a distance, but based on the lives and knowledge priorities of subjects — helps open up one’s mind to working in non-standard ways. It may take you to new and surprising places.”

Or, as Anishinaabe journalist and professor Duncan McCue put it in Decolonizing Journalism : “if our goal is to seek truth, how would it change our journalistic process to centre the needs and priorities of the Indigenous people we report on? … This dovetails with Indigenous understandings of reciprocity.”

This summer, I trusted in the process, and my daughter and I joined around 300 community members and guests at λáλix̌sístala. I had no plans for what the story might be. Instead, I asked: what story is needed? When I returned home, my heart was full but my pages were empty. I listened to my tapes over and over, especially one eight-minute recording of ravens, the waves on the beach, an eagle. I walked down to the river by my house and sat on its banks, reading and writing short sections of prose in my notebook:

The river feels eternal and the sand I sit on is renewed time and time and time again, sediment carried each year from deep within the glacier-scoured mountains. Last summer, the kids dug its banks out and we wondered if it would reclaim its shape. It did.

Wa’xaid said to wash our eyes in the river, and our ears. I think maybe he also meant our hearts. He was talking about the Kitlope, his homelands, but I do it here, now, in Wedzin Kwa, while I’m remembering. It feels right and I listen to the river and watch the birds dance across the sky.

A question keeps floating up: Sas húmíɫṇƛa? Are you listening? And then the story tells itself .

At Kvai, Veda and Hazel shaped the clay and mud with flower petals and cedar branches, little gifts left lovingly in the absence of human voices and the return of the bears. We took a canoe up the river and laughed when the clouds followed and watered us, helping us to see and hear. The tide came up into the forest and I waded through the brackish water up to my waist, walking the trail with bare feet as sheets of rain washed the grizzly tracks from the dirt.

Heeding Wilson’s words, I write myself into the story, showing the reader who I am and why I was there. Because I was there — and I felt the presence of the songs and dances that aren’t mine to share, and I opened myself to the stories they contain. I am changed by them.

Súq̓vsnúgva. I am grateful. W̓álas ǧiáxsix̌a. Thank you.

Matt Simmons

Matt Simmons is a writer and editor based in Smithers, B.C., unceded Gidimt’en Clan territory, home of the Wet’suwet’en/Witsuwit’en Nation.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

— Eden Fineday, Publisher, IndigiNews

scraped.h1: After decades of suppression, poll suggests ‘Canadians’ are embracing Indigenous cultural burns
scraped.body_text:
With some practices formerly illegal, new data from the Indigenous Leadership Initiative suggests a shift in perspective

Santana Dreaver

●

●

This article has been co-published with The Narwhal as part of their 2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship .

Generations of Indigenous fire stewards have long advocated for their knowledge to be respected as science, in “B.C.” and across “Canada.” And now, a national poll suggests “Canadians” agree Indigenous-led fire management is critical for the future.

The poll, conducted by Pollara Strategic, says “Canadians” are starting to learn more about what Indigenous fire stewardship means, shifting public opinion in support of it.

According to the Indigenous Leadership Initiative data released in September, 49 per cent of those surveyed had never heard of Indigenous fire stewardship before, but once it was described, 84 per cent said it is important for “Canada.”

The poll, which surveyed 2,250 “Canadians” in August, found that 76 per cent support First Nations cultural burning. For Sheri Lysons, that finding is long overdue.

“It’s about time,” she said.

Lysons is Secwépemc from the Adams Lake Indian Band, located in “B.C.’s” Southern Interior, and has decades of experience fighting and stewarding fire.

Lysons says that non-Indigenous people are changing their minds about practices such as cultural burns, “because they’ve seen the benefits of it.”

Reflecting on “B.C.” provincial legislation amendments made two years ago to support cultural burning, she says Indigenous firekeepers are doing “the work that needs to be done.”

“There’s so much misinformation out there,” she says.

Lysons says education about cultural burns helps remove stigma, and with wildfires becoming more rampant, people are becoming more open to different preparedness methods.

As for the 82 per cent of “Canadians” in support of federal Indigenous fire stewardship funding, Lysons wants to see that number reach 100 per cent.

Fire has been used by Indigenous people for countless generations as an ancestral land management and ceremonial practice.

But today, a campfire is as close as some Indigenous people get to it, which is by government design. For more than a century, colonial policies disrupted and outlawed the practice of cultural burning, viewing fire as a threat and something to immediately suppress.

For those who come from families who managed to keep the tradition of cultural burns going, many wait year-round for the opportunity to hit the land with their torches.

While it is serious business, burning days are days when families and the community come together and spend time on the land.

The jokes about which uncle or auntie are going to let the fire get away from them, the stories shared between generations and the smells and crackling sounds of the burn create memories which last a lifetime.

Tiffany Traverse is Secwépemc and has more than a decade of experience working in the fire industry.

She’s held various positions with the BC Wildfire Service and currently has a board position with the Salish Firekeepers Society, a non-profit organization committed to promoting and revitalizing cultural burns in Interior “B.C.”

“When I was drilling down into the particulars about that poll, it was really nice to see that people are changing their opinions … on what cultural fire means and how important it is,” she says.

“I was really pleasantly surprised to see that.”

She says education is key to those statistics, having started her career at a time when Indigenous fire stewardship practices were less supported.

“A percentage of people didn’t know about cultural fire and once they were educated on that, their opinion on it changed,” she says.

“I thought it was really refreshing to see, especially with all of the anti-Indigenous racism that we’ve been seeing.”

It’s a sentiment shared by Nlaka’pamux firefighter George Campbell, who was also surprised by some of the statistics.

With 25 years of experience in the fire industry, Campbell remembers when Indigenous people had less engagement with the province.

He attributes a shift in “British Columbian” attitudes about Indigenous fire practices back to a 2018 report on the record-breaking floods and fires of the previous year.

“Ever since then, things have kind of shifted to more engagement in terms of cultural and prescribed fire,” he says.

Back in the day, firefighting was a low stress summer job for Campbell. But today, fires are more extreme and aggressive due to global warming.

“It was identified in the early 2000s that our forest health was declining. We were getting good at suppressing fires and because of that, everything started to become overgrown and disease started to set in,” he says.

“We got away from our cultural and prescribed fire practices, which in my opinion resulted in an unhealthy forest.”

Reflecting on “Canadians’” newly identified support for Indigenous fire stewardship practices outlined in the poll, Campbell says “it’s been a long time coming, to be honest.”

Amy Cardinal Christianson is the Indigenous Leadership Initiative’s director of fire stewardship. She grew up in northern “Alberta” and has Métis ancestry.

“We’ve had a bunch of severe fire years where there’s been a lot of people impacted. I think when that happens people usually start trying to look for solutions,” she says.

The same national poll found 93 per cent of respondents identified wildfires as a national concern.

Christianson says wildfire smoke is a large factor in those statistics.

“Other hazards, for example earthquakes and flooding, stay very localized. Fire does not. Even if there’s a fire in one area, smoke can travel hundreds of kilometres away. It impacts a lot of people.”

“We found there’s been many Canadians impacted by smoke in the last five years,” she added. “I do think that’s really been the game changer. No one wants to spend their summers in smoke.”

The impacts of wildfires fall disproportionately on Indigenous communities; in 2023, still the most severe wildfire season on record in Canada, 42 per cent of all communities evacuated were Indigenous . This past summer, First Nations communities in “B.C.” and “Ontario” were ravaged by wildfires.

The Canadian Senate released a report earlier this year titled: Canada on fire: The catastrophic and escalating effects of wildfires on lives and communities .

It says wildfires are a national crisis, attributing the past three years as record-breaking wildfire seasons. According to the report, millions of “Canadians” are being exposed to wildfire smoke, for days, weeks and sometimes months at a time.

“Indigenous communities — who have lived with fire for millennia — remain under-resourced and sidelined,” the report states. Many have endured repeat evacuations, loss of homes and long-term economic losses,” it says, in part.

“Despite their deep expertise in fire stewardship, Indigenous firefighters often encounter barriers to participating fully in wildfire management and urgent response. Strengthening Indigenous-led governance, training, equipment access and long-term funding is imperative.”

In the Indigenous Leadership Initiative poll, Christianson was surprised more than twice as many “Canadians” say they would rather the federal government fund year-round Fire Guardians, compared to spending the same money on water bombers. In 2025, Kainai Nation partnered with Natural Resources Canada to launch the first federally funded Fire Guardians program in the country .

Christianson says Fire Guardian programs are a natural way forward, as they proactively mitigate risks such as built-up fuels and balance the ecological needs of wildfire-prone landscapes.

Fire Guardian programs employ people in their nations year round to work on fire. Responding to fire, doing cultural burns, fire-smarting the community, emergency management and evacuation planning are some of the responsibilities of Fire Guardians. And after a fire has passed, they work with the land to recover.

“If you get to the point where an air tanker is the only saviour of your community, you’ve really lost the plot on living in a good relationship with fire,” she says.

Another Indigenous Leadership Initiative study found the return on investment of Indigenous Guardian programs is even greater than previously found, with every dollar spent putting between nine and 12 dollars back into the economy. But Christianson said these programs need government support, not just public support — and not only in the summer, when wildfires are on everyone’s mind.

“As Indigenous people, we’ve always treated fire as a year-round thing. It’s not something you just fight against in the summer,” she says.

She’s calling for long-term sustainable funding to implement these programs. So far, Kainai’s Fire Guardians program is still the only one of its kind in “Canada,” and the federal government’s future investments in Guardians programs remains uncertain .

“It’s fine for the Canadian public to support these things, but what we really need to see is actual action in these areas.”

Santana Dreaver

Santana Dreaver is a Saulteaux and Plains Cree journalist based in Nlaka’pamux territory. She has worked in daily news, social and for The Early Edition radio show with CBC Vancouver, as part of the Indigenous Pathways to Journalism Program, before finding her way to The Narwhal’s Indigenous Journalism Fellowship. She is from Mistawasis Nêhiyawak and has called B.C. home for the past 5 years. Her spirit name is Red Thunderbird, known to live in the West Coast mountains and create thunderstorms throughout the prairies.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

scraped.description: Artists contributing to the “Temporal” exhibition describe how their contemporary work explores Indigenous present and future.
scraped.author: Nika Bartoo-Smith
scraped.h1: Olympia museum takeover explores Indigenous futures
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Nika Bartoo-Smith Underscore Native News + ICT

OLYMPIA, WA — Since Oct. 2, the Coast Salish Museum of Fine Arts has “taken over” the Thurston County Museum of Fine Arts for a two month exhibition.

Through Dec. 11, “Temporal: Stories of Indigenous Present, Re-imagining Indigenous Futures” features work by 14 Indigenous artists interpreting their own ideas of Indigenous futures through mediums including performance art, digital art, paintings, sculpture and traditional Indigenous art forms such as beading and weaving.

Now in its fourth year, the Coast Salish Museum of Fine Arts is an annual takeover in which the Thurston County Museum of Fine Arts hands the keys over to Indigenous Creatives Collective for a two month show.

Exhibition curator, Mikaela Shafer , Hopi, was inspired by thinking about how Indigenous people are often perceived as “relics” or “artifacts” of a past rather than looking at the present and future in today’s gallery and museum spaces.

“We wanted to create a space that showed that Indigenous people are here in the present, and we have ideas for the future, and we create all kinds of art beyond just traditional art,” said Shafer.

An artist herself , Shafer wanted to curate an exhibit that encouraged Indigenous artists to take up space and have full creative control.

The theme, “Temporal,” came to her after seeing a beadwork sculpture by Tammie Dupuis.

“I saw a picture of the “Long Walk” on our Indigenous Creatives roster, and it made me so excited thinking about a future where all of the public art and all of the decor was all Indigenous, and people’s furniture was Indigenous-made, and this idea of a future where we are fully represented in the lands that we are from,” Shafer said. Indigenous Creatives is a woman-led nonprofit based in the Pacific Northwest focused on land stewardship and amplifying Indigenous artists’ voices.

With the exhibit, Shafer sought to hold space for each artist to express their ideas of the Indigenous future they envision.

Underscore Native News + ICT interviewed seven of the 14 featured artists.

Tammie Dupuis: ‘No longer a craft’

Tammie Dupuis , Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the Flathead Reservation, makes her own beads, the size of a fist, out of resin, cast foam and paper clay in order to turn beadwork into sculpture.

“It dominates the space,” Dupuis said, speaking about her piece “Long Walk” that commemorates the forced removal of the Bitterroot Salish people to the Flathead reservation. “I think the statement behind that is that this is no longer a craft. I mean, it’s beadwork, but it’s no longer a craft. It’s actually a sculpture. Because my personal feeling is that craft is a word used by fine art to keep women and minorities out.”

Each year, Dupuis adds another row of beads to her living art piece, commemorating the 1891 removal and marking its passage of time.

In her other piece on display at the exhibit, Dupuis created a war shirt out of resin beads, each face sculpted in the beads representing an ancestor giving her strength.

The colors in the beads, ranging from deep red to yellow, also represent the passage of time and a reflection of herself — the yellow at the bottom representing herself as a white-presenting Indigenous person.

“Time is a huge thing for me because I look a lot at the assimilationist systems that produced me,” Dupuis said. “I am, for all intents and purposes, exactly what the reservation system was designed to produce — an Indian so white as to be unrecognizable. And it took me a while to really make peace with the fact that whatever this voice is inside of me, it is Indigenous, and if I silenced it, I would be doing the work of the colonizer.”

Ash Frantz: ‘Imagining this other space’

Weaving cedar in new ways, Ash Frantz, Makah Tribe, brought the idea of Indigenous futures to life by playing with what’s possible.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

One of their pieces features a mold of their own hands with intricately woven red cedar nails “for an Indigiqueer baddie.” In this piece, Frantz thought about bodies as an extension of the land and wanted to find a way to decorate queer bodies with the land as well.

“All three of my works that are in this show, but also throughout my whole practice, kind of speak to me imagining this other space or like what the world would look like or could look like,” Frantz said.

In another room, Frantz has installed an obsolete desktop computer from the early 2000s displaying a loading screen with the words “Indigenous Futures Loading,” inviting viewers to contemplate what that means to them.

Next to this piece, a stack of old TVs are placed, as if woven together. They each loop a digital weaving made up of videos of Frantz processing cedar and a video tutorial they watched in the learning process.

“It’s really speaking to the fact that I’ve had to rely on what’s available in the digital realm in our current society to reconnect to my own community cultural practice of working with cedar,” Frantz said.

“This is one of my favorite pieces I’ve made because I’m taking these feelings of not belonging and feeling disconnected and unsure, and I’m turning them into something that feels really comforting and beautiful for me,” they continued.

Cynthia Masterson: ‘The game of Telephone’

Cynthia Masterson , Comanche, has spent nearly the last two decades studying the delicate intricacies of different forms of beadwork — namely, the different styles that often all get called ”peyote stitch” or “gourd stitch”. Her work centers the three-drop stitch, which is unique to Southern Plains tribes.

As a teacher, much of her artwork is interactive. At the exhibit in Olympia, one piece invites viewers to dial an antique candlestick phone to hear a recording about the beadwork that adorns the phone itself.

“I wanted to do the telephone because it feels like the game of Telephone, like these stitches started and it’s been passed down, and the message has gotten muddled through time,” Masterson said.

Another of her pieces, a vintage gumball machine, encourages viewers to pop in a coin and get back a tray full of beads. She wanted to encourage people to touch the beadwork and have a chance to be creative on their own.

“Growing up, you’re always touching beadwork. It was never in a museum,” Masterson said, thinking about regalia and other forms of beadwork she grew up with. “It’s kind of meant to be interacted with, played with.”

Inanna kʷaɁowišč tyee McCarty: An inside joke turned political commentary

Ever heard of a whale slider? What about an Ozette potato fry? The pop art inspired paintings by Inanna kʷaɁowišč tyee McCarty , a citizen of the Makah Tribe and a descendant of the Tsawout First Nation, depict playful images of each.

McCarty comes from a long line of whalers on her father’s side. The Makah Tribe is the only Native nation in the Lower 48 that has an exclusive treaty right to whaling , but has been blocked from exercising those rights for close to three decades.

Though McCarty’s idea of a whale slider started off as a family joke, it soon became an artistic political statement.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“It was a response to the anti-whaling comics that were in a lot of the local papers in Port Angeles and around the area that were pretty degrading, too, and derogatory,” McCarty said.

Living in Neah Bay, it’s an hour and a half to the nearest grocery store, according to McCarty. This series for her is a part of the conversation about food sovereignty — from whale meat to Ozette potatoes, some of the only foods that can be harvested in the area she said.

“I hope that this makes people think a little bit more about, for one, the land that they’re on, and for two, just the foods that they eat,” McCarty said. “And maybe hopefully taking a little bit better care of each other, the water, seeing people who are different from them as human rather than this monstrous other thing.”

Liz Chikayaasix̂ Morrow: ‘What an Indigenous story can be’

Liz Chikayaasix̂ Morrow is an Unangax̂ storyteller. A citizen of the Naknek Native Village, much of her work is inspired by stories from ancestors and family members of hers that have been passed down.

Reflecting on Indigenous futurisms, Morrow also created a story of her own for the exhibit at the Thurston County Museum of Fine Arts. “Raven Daughter” explores themes of parenthood and choosing to have children.

“The artwork that I make is Native. It is Unangax̂ because I am Unangax̂. So anything that I create is a part of that heritage and is a part of that ancestry,” Morrow said. “I think that’s the story of this exhibit is that idea of ‘this is Native art,’ whether or not you recognize that as an outsider, as a non-Indigenous person.”

She hopes people walk away from her work with an expanded idea of what an Indigenous story and Indigenous artwork can be.

Justin Olmstead: ‘She’s waiting for us to remember’

Justin Olmstead , Santa Ynez and Barbareño Band of Chumash Indians, started painting after he had a dream in which an elder came to him and said he needed to paint sun wheels. Now, sun wheels are a part of every piece he makes.

He said the sun wheels represent confusion, different realities and memories for Chumash people.

Olmstead’s acrylic painting, “Hutash: She’s Waiting for Us to Remember,” depicts Mother Earth gazing into the horizon surrounded by pictographs and sun wheels. It represents a critique of a world that “weaponizes time” with little room to sit, reflect and remember.

“She’s just waiting,” Olmstead said. “She’s sitting here gazing at us, looking at us playing, making these make-believe civilizations and illusions of reality and just waiting for us to come back to her.”

He describes that his work is also a form of storytelling and teaching to pass on to his daughter.

“I started creating all these pieces that’s connected to generational wisdom to give her, almost like generational clarity through the traumas and triumphs,” Olmstead said.

Taylor White: ‘Everything I do is Indigenous futurism’

Taylor White , Skokomish Indian Tribe and Squaxin Island Tribe, lives her life with a love for all things monochromatic. From her own outfits to her home with an olive green living room and baby blue bedroom.

Her latest collection features a skateboard deck, an adorned “Final Fantasy” gunblade, a chair, a breastplate, a bra, deer hoof nunchucks and a medieval mace all covered in purple leather with sparkles of dentalium, pearls and glass beads.

White’s collection feels both fantastical and fierce — created “for the NDN princess.”

“I’ve always been in the belief that modesty was something that was brought over to us [through colonization],” White said. “I’ve never been afraid of my body or shameful of it. I feel like in my family, I don’t think we’ve ever felt shame or felt like modesty was something we lived by, and so when I make things, I just make them for how I was born.”

For White, creating is a form of healing.

“I think inherently everything I do is Indigenous futurism,” White said. “From making new things and decking them out in dentalium and shells or using old things.”

The exhibition runs through Dec. 11 with an artist talk on Nov. 27. For information on the exhibit and open hours visit the Thurston County Museum of Fine Arts website .

scraped.description: A biweekly column from ICT with the latest news from the arts and entertainment world
scraped.author: Sandra Hale Schulman
scraped.h1: INDIGENOUS A&E: LA Film Fests, an ‘Old School Indian’ story, Winter Market
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Sandra Hale Schulman ICT

The latest: Film premieres and awards, ‘avatar’ fiction, Santa Fe art market

FILM FESTIVALS: Los Angeles hosts two Indigenous film fests

Two big Indigenous film festivals are taking over Los Angeles for Native American Heritage Month, featuring screenings with the directors and actors in attendance, some major premieres, and awards shows.

Red Nation Celebration Institute (RNCI) is running the 31st Red Nation International Film Festival Nov. 8-15 with screenings at the Grove AMC theater. There are 96 official selections, including six features, 28 documentaries, one animated feature, 38 documentary shorts, 14 narrative shorts, and nine animation shorts.

The competition offers audiences a first look at new voices from Native and Indigenous perspectives in independent film.

The opening night feature is “Timber Lands,” from Director Baylee Toney, starring Wes Studi, Irene Bedard, Robert Clohessy, Tanaya Beatty, Owen Crowshoe, and Myles Clohessy. In the remote Oregon timber country, the sudden death of a celebrated bronc rider exposes a violent rift between two powerful families who will stop at nothing to protect their sovereign land.

Another screening is “Nine Little Indians,” Shannon Kring’s wrenching documentary about nine Charbonneau sisters, members of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, and their decades-long fight for acknowledgement, justice, and healing after the abuses they suffered in the American Indian boarding school system. Executive producers are Leonardo DiCaprio and Tony Robbins.

Acclaimed actor Lou Diamond Phillips, Filipino/Cherokee, will receive the RNCI Lifetime Achievement Award on Nov. 14 after a screening of “Gangland .’ The RNCI Red Nation Award show with several Native actor presenters takes place at the Beverly Hilton on Nov. 15.

The LA Skins Fest runs Nov. 18-22 at TCL Chinese Theater in Hollywood, California, launching the 20th year with a special screening of the acclaimed series, “North of North.” presented by Netflix. The series shows winter is settling over Ice Cove, and young Inuk mother Siaja, played by Anna Lambe, is still determined to make life better — for herself and everyone around her.

Feature films include, “ What The Crows Saw ,” on Nov. 20. The film features a determined Pueblo woman who must confront the mysterious inhabitants of a strange tavern as she searches for her missing sister.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Excellence in Indigenous storytelling will be celebrated at the 15th Annual Native American Media Awards, hosted by Kiowa Gordon, of “Dark Winds,” at the Hard Rock Hollywood on Sunday, Nov. 22 starting at 7 p.m. The awards recognize the talent, creativity, and contributions of Native American artists and filmmakers.

In addition to the film festivals, “People of the West” will be streaming on FNX.org all of November with a marathon of all 10 episodes on Thanksgiving Day of the hard-hitting series that frames California’s complicated history through Native voices.

Creator/executive producer Brad Munoa, Payómkawichum, uses oral storytelling, cinematic dramatization, archival material, and expert testimony to trace five centuries of how California tribes were affected by colonizers who came by sea and by land. Its wealth of natural resources — gold, fish, crops, minerals, and water — made it a last frontier in the push for western expansion.

BOOKS: ‘Old School Indian’ gets schooled

A new book, “ Old School Indian ,” by Aaron John Curtis, Ahkwesáhsne, tells an irreverent coming-of-middle-age story about an Indigenous man’s search for intimacy, healing, and a second chance.

The book’s main character, Abe Jacobs is Ahkwesáhsne, from the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe. At 18, Abe left the reservation where he was raised. He met the love of his life, started writing poetry, and chose to open his marriage — building a life far from the Rez.

Now he’s 43, facing a relationship collapse and a rare yet fatal diagnosis. When he returns to the Rez to undergo a healing from his Great Uncle Budge — a wry, recovered alcoholic — Abe is forced to reckon with who he’s been, and who he might still be.

Curtis jumps the barrier and addresses the reader directly in this unusual format, to explain Indigenous words and customs.

“I did a lot of direct address,” Curtis, who worked as a buyer at Miami’s top tome seller Books & Books for 20 years, told ICT. “A lot of that came from my writers group. Although at some points I was assuming some negative thoughts that the readers weren’t having. So I did have to play around that a little bit.”

Abe is Curtis’s avatar; Curtis did have serious health issues and went home to heal them.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“I had an autoimmune disorder as described in the book,” he said. “I’ve been in remission since about 2021. It started off as a short story and I was venting all this frustration of everything I was going through and fear, and my writers group was really excited by it. So I fleshed it out, and it’s me, but it’s fiction, not a memoir.”

The tone is humorous and serious, sarcastic and direct. It took him 10 years from start to publication.

“The original manuscript was twice as long as it is now,” Curtis said. “I cut out a lot of Miami backstory and may publish that down the road.”

The artsy cover art of a Native in shades and open crown hat,is by artist Alex Jacobs, a former writer for Indian Country Today, and Curtis’s real life uncle.

“That’s my Uncle Alex Jacobs,” Curtis said. “I had that image of his art on my computer for 20 years. Alex had sold the original, so they got Emily Mahome, a digital illustrator, to recreate it digitally for the cover.”

Reviews have been stellar and Curtis embarks on a book tour through the fall.

ART: SWAIA Winter Market

The Southwestern Association for Indian Arts (SWAIA) hosts its 21st Annual Winter Indian Market on Saturday and Sunday, Nov. 28-29, at the Santa Fe Community Convention Center.

The indoor holiday market gathers 160 juried Indigenous artists displaying jewelry, pottery, paintings, textiles, and holiday ornaments.

Smaller and more intimate than the summer Indian Market, Winter Indian Market offers a chance to slow down, linger at the booths, and have genuine conversations with the artists themselves. One can hear firsthand about the techniques, traditions, and inspirations behind each piece, from finely crafted jewelry and hand-coiled pottery to paintings, sculpture and more.

A silent auction adds another way to take home a remarkable work. Winter Indian Market is a meaningful way to celebrate the season and support Native artists directly.

“Winter Indian Market is built for connection,” said Jamie R. Schulze, Northern Cheyenne/Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate, SWAIA executive director. “In a more intimate setting, visitors can spend real time with an artist: hearing the story behind a piece, learning the process and traditions that shaped it, and getting to know the person making contemporary Native art today. That conversation changes what a purchase means. You’re not just taking home something beautiful. You’re investing directly in an artist and carrying their story with you.”

Sales go directly to the artists and their home studios, generating economic support for Native entrepreneurs across New Mexico and North America.

Sandra Hale Schulman, of Cherokee Nation descent, has been writing about Native issues since 1994 and writes a biweekly Indigenous A&E column for ICT. The recipient of a Woody Guthrie Fellowship, she... More by Sandra Hale Schulman

scraped.title: Potawatomi man is Michigan's first Native congressman-elect
scraped.description: Sean McCann made history, defeating an eight-term incumbent and flipping a Republican stronghold blue for the first time in nearly a century.
scraped.author: Amelia Schafer
scraped.h1: Potawatomi man to be the first Native to represent Michigan in Congress
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Amelia Schafer ICT

A Potawatomi man has made history in Michigan’s Fourth Congressional District.

In addition to being the first Native American to represent Michigan in Congress, Sean McCann, Citizen Potawatomi Nation and a Democrat, flipped a seat held by republicans for nearly a century.

“I think people were looking for a change, looking for a new direction from the policies they’ve gotten out of Washington in the last two years,” McCann said during a press conference on Nov. 4 in Kalamazoo, Michigan.

McCann, 55, defeated eight-term incumbent U.S. Rep. BIll Huizenga by just 1.78 percentage points – 6,492 votes. McCann’s win marks the first time a Democrat will represent Michigan’s Fourth Congressional District since 1933.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Michigan’s Fourth Congressional District includes the lands of the Nottawaseppi Huron Band of the Potawatomi, one of nine federally recognized Potawatomi Nations.

McCann said he was excited to be able to represent Michigan’s Fourth Congressional district.

“It’s one day post election, but we’re going to be making plans to be everywhere in the district and meet all the folks we can,” McCann said.

McCann is one of two Anishinaabe people (Ojibwe, Potawatomi and Odawa) who won their races to join the United States Congress this week, alongside Peggy Flanagan, White Earth Ojibwe and the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

McCann, a former Michigan state house representative and senator, is also one of five Native American people elected to the U.S. House on Tuesday. He joins the newly elected Rep. Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., Ysleda del sur Pueblo, and re-elected incumbents Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kansas, Ho-Chunk, Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., Chickasaw Nation and Rep. Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, R-Okla.

McCann campaigned on addressing the affordability crisis across America. He promised to fight to lower everyday costs while creating new good-paying jobs in southwestern Michigan.

“I think young people turned out because they’ve been concerned about their futures and they felt that folks like me were showing that we were concerned about their futures,” McCann said. “In terms of affordable housing, in terms of national debt, social security and medicare being available for young people that are just starting out their careers.”

Amelia Schafer is ICT's North Central Correspondent based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Schafer covers MMIP, Indian Gaming and business for ICT. She is of Wampanoag and Montauk-Brothertown Indian Nation descent.... More by Amelia Schafer

scraped.title: B2K returns with new album ‘Eclipse,’ marking a new chapter for the R&B group
scraped.description: B2K reunites for ‘Eclipse,’ its first full-length album since 2003, showcasing the R&B group's musical evolution and new era.
scraped.author: Jahaura Michelle
scraped.h1: B2K returns with new album ‘Eclipse,’ marking a new chapter for the R&B group
scraped.body_text:
The new album introduces longtime fans to a new side of B2K while inviting a new generation of R&B listeners.

Boy band B2K released their highly anticipated album , “Eclipse,” on Friday, marking the first time the millennial heartthrobs have released a new project in more than 20 years.

The group, made up of Omarion, J-Boog, Raz-B, and Lil’ Fizz, rose to fame in the early 2000s, capturing the hearts of young girls nationwide. Known for top-charting hits like “Girlfriend,” “Uh Huh” and “Bump, Bump, Bump,” B2K returns more than two decades later as evolved artists with a more mature sound, according to a news release.

“Eclipse,” B2K’s first full-length album since “Pandemonium!” in 2003, features 12 tracks, including singles “Mileage” and “Lil Freak,” which showcase a more mature side of the group. The project also features fellow Millennium tourmate Bow Wow on “Boyfriend,” a track that builds on the nostalgia of “Girlfriend,” the 2007 single from Omarion and Bow’s joint album “Face Off.”

B2K’s reunion means more than releasing new music. As teenagers, they navigated the pressures of fame in the entertainment industry while working through personal challenges in the spotlight. Now adults, the bandmates bring their individual experiences and personal growth to their new music, inviting their longtime fans along for the ride.

The group has made several public appearances since their reunion. In June, B2K participated in a musical showdown during BET Weekend with R.S.V.P., featuring Ray J, Sammie, Bobbie V and Pleasure P. That same month, they also had the highly anticipated Verzuz with fellow tourmates Pretty Ricky.

Earlier this year, they wrapped up “The Millennium Tour Presents: The Boys 4 Life Tour” for the group’s 25th anniversary with Bow Wow as co-headliner. Other performers included Jeremih, Waka Flocka Flame, Amerie, Yung Joc, Crime Mob, Dem Franchize Boyz (DFB), Pretty Ricky, and B5.

With “Eclipse,” B2K gives longtime fans a new collection of music while introducing a different side of the group to a new generation of R&B listeners. The album is available on all major streaming platforms.

scraped.description: Crump says the family deserves answers and accountability after Javits Frimpong was killed just one year after moving from Ghana to New York.
scraped.author: TheGrio Staff
scraped.h1: Ben Crump to represent family of Javits Frimpong, 15-year-old killed on his way to school
scraped.body_text:
The civil rights attorney says the family deserves answers and accountability after Javits Frimpong was killed just one year after moving from Ghana to New York.

The family of Javits Frimpong, the 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager fatally shot while walking to school in the Bronx, has retained prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump as they seek answers and accountability for his killing.

According to a Nov. 6 press release from Crump’s law firm sent to theGrio, Crump will represent the family of Frimpong, who was shot on the morning of Oct. 29 in the Claremont section of the Bronx, just blocks from his school. He was taken to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he later died.

Frimpong had moved from Ghana to New York in 2025 to live with his father. The teenager reportedly dreamed of becoming a doctor.

In a statement announcing his involvement, Crump emphasized that Frimpong was simply doing something millions of children do every morning: walking to school.

“Javits was a 15-year-old boy walking to school, something children across this country do every morning,” Crump said. “He came here from Ghana a year ago dreaming of becoming a doctor, and he deserved to make that walk safely, like every child does, no matter where they come from.”

Crump added that his firm would stand with the family until those responsible are held accountable and Frimpong’s loved ones receive the answers they deserve.

The attorney’s involvement comes as investigators continue examining the circumstances surrounding the teenager’s death. As TheGrio previously reported , Frimpong’s father, Thomas Frimpong, said school officials had informed him that two students accused of bullying his son had been suspended shortly before the shooting. Police have been pursuing school records as part of their investigation, but have not established whether the alleged bullying was connected to the killing.

Frimpong’s death has sparked grief and calls for justice throughout the Bronx and Ghanaian communities. His classmates and neighbors have also gathered to remember the teenager and demand an end to violence against young people.

Police are investigating several possible motives and have not publicly identified anyone in connection with the shooting.

scraped.title: Harmeet Dhillon resigns as Trump's civil rights chief after Democrats sweep Congress
scraped.description: Harmeet Dhillon resigns as DOJ Civil Rights Division chief after Democrats' midterm victories, following a controversial tenure.
scraped.author: Peter Kerich
scraped.h1: Harmeet Dhillon resigns as Trump’s civil rights chief after Democrats sweep Congress
scraped.body_text:
The DOJ official stepped down just two days after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate, setting the stage for increased scrutiny of Trump's administration.

Harmeet Dhillon , the head of the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation Thursday, November 5, following the Republican Party’s losses in the 2026 midterm elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that he had accepted her resignation in a statement on X, praising Dhillon for what he described as her commitment to defending civil liberties and enforcing the law. Dhillon also reflected on her tenure, calling the position the “honor of a lifetime.” In her farewell statement, she highlighted efforts to challenge diversity, equity and inclusion programs and oppose transgender participation in women’s and girls’ sports.

Her departure comes just two days after Democrats secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for increased congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration. During her leadership, the Civil Rights Division underwent a significant restructuring, with its enforcement priorities shifting toward issues central to the Trump administration’s agenda.

The division pursued legal action against universities over alleged discrimination, filed lawsuits seeking access to voter registration records in 30 states and Washington, D.C. It also brought a criminal case against former CNN journalist Don Lemon and protesters following a demonstration at a Minnesota church. Federal judges dismissed 27 of the lawsuits seeking state voter registration records, according to NBC News.

Dhillon’s departure prompted criticism from civil rights advocates and former Justice Department officials. Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel and former head of the Civil Rights Division under President Joe Biden, accused Dhillon of abandoning federal civil rights enforcement responsibilities. Clarke said Dhillon had “abandoned cases, purged the work force and weaponized the Division to target institutions to achieve illegitimate, partisan goals.” Stacey Young, executive director of Justice Connection, also criticized Dhillon’s leadership

The resignation comes at a significant political moment as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress. Dhillon, a longtime Republican election lawyer, had also maintained a visible presence in conservative media while promoting the administration’s civil rights agenda.
