scraped.title: Meghan Markle's Dad Arrested, Feds Raid Storage Units
scraped.h1: Meghan Markle’s Dad Arrested in Child Sex Abuse Material Case. Here’s What the Feds Have to Say
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Things have officially gone from bad to worse for Meghan Markle’s dad in connection with his child sex abuse material investigation. Here’s the latest updates.

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Photo by MEGA/GC Images; Aaron Chown/PA Images via Getty Images

Things are continuing to go downhill for Meghan Markle’s father, Thomas Markle Sr. , in the aftermath of his child sex abuse material investigation. Now, more details about his new arrest and what the FBI has found have been released.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told the AP that federal agents searched two Los Angeles-area storage units that Markle had been renting since 2008. Once inside, they “seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books” that had child sexual abuse images.

Per an official FBI affidavit, the feds were tipped off about the U.S. storage units after learning about other images and videos depicting child sexual abuse on Markle Sr.’s electronic devices that were reportedly found at his former home in the Philippines and the national police investigation that followed.

Related: New Developments in Child Sex Abuse Material Allegations Against Meghan Markle’s Father

As a result of those findings and this new search, Markle Sr. was arrested outside of Tampa, Florida, and charged with “one count of possession of child pornography,” per NBC 6 Miami. He’s expected to appear in court at some point on Friday. If convicted, he faces 20 years in federal prison.

In response to the arrest, Essayli said in a statement: “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

FBI Director Kash Patel also commented on the arrest: “Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. The agency will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids— any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country, or anywhere they try to hide.”

As we previously told you, the Duchess spoke out about the allegations against her father when her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., contacted authorities in the Philippines after allegedly discovering images and videos depicting child sexual abuse on their father’s electronic devices at his former home. In her statement, she said she was “deeply distressed” by the news and expressed hope that justice would be served. Markle Sr. has denied the allegations, calling them lies and “bullsh*t.”

items.title: 15 Essential Books to Read for Hip-Hop History Month
items.summary: Hip Hop has come a long way, from its birth in the Bronx to one of the most influential cultures worldwide. For this Hip Hop History Month, we have recommendations for the best books to learn about the origins of this cultural force.Read more...

scraped.title: Essential Books to Read for Hip Hop History Month
scraped.h1: 15 Essential Books to Read for Hip-Hop History Month
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Hip Hop has come a long way, from its birth in the Bronx to one of the most influential cultures worldwide. For this Hip Hop History Month, we have recommendations for the best books to learn about the origins of this cultural force.

By

Mahalia Otshudy

Published

American rapper, songwriter, record producer, and actor LL Cool J, performs on stage in Boston, Massachusetts in December 1985. (Photo by John Nordell/Getty Images)

November is Hip-Hop History Month, and we are celebrating the culture born in the Bronx that has become one of the world’s most recognized musical and artistic movements. From masters of lyricism to breakdancing and street style, hip-hop remains one of the most influential forces across the globe. What better way to explore its legacy than by diving into books filled with vivid memories and facts about how the genre grew to become such a powerful cultural force?

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

We’ve rounded up some essential reads to add to your collection this Hip-Hop History Month.

J Dilla was one of the most iconic hip-hop producers, and “Dilla Time” by Dan Charnas is a biography that delves into his rise from an underground mastermind to a revered name in the culture with his innovative beats that helped define a new, unique sound.

Many of our favorite head-banging hip-hop tracks incorporate samples drawn from songs ranging from legendary hits to rare finds. In “Bring That Beat Back,” Nate Patrin traces the origins of sampling and explores how it became a defining art form within rap music.

Related: Why The No Limit Records Reunion Means Everything to Hip Hop Culture

Let Grandmaster Flash take you on a musical journey in “Birth of a Culture,” where he narrates the beginnings of hip-hop—a movement he helped pioneer through his DJing innovations and creative vision—culminating in the genre’s landmark anthem, “The Message.”

When discussing hip-hop history, conversations often default to legendary male artists. But we can’t forget the trailblazing women who worked just as hard to move the culture. In “The Motherlode,” Clover Hope highlights these revolutionary women and illustrates why they deserve equal acclaim.

The backstory behind every iconic moment, song, and album in the genre—from its genesis to the present day—is explored in Chuck D’s deep dive into hip-hop history. If you are looking for a comprehensive schooling on how rap became so revolutionary, sit down with this book and prepare to learn.

Queen Latifah paved the way for women rappers to dominate the mainstream, evolving into a powerhouse mogul—a monumental feat for a young woman from Newark, New Jersey. In her autobiography, Queen Latifah shares the unfiltered story of her rise from neighborhood royalty to a true monarch of hip-hop.

Hip-hop and fashion have always gone hand in hand. “Fresh Fly Fabulous” chronicles the vibrant, head-turning style pioneered by rap icons such as Slick Rick, LL Cool J, and many more across multiple decades.

“Sweat the Technique” is the definitive guide every burgeoning lyricist needs to elevate their pen game. Rakim breaks down the creative framework he uses to craft sharp rhymes that stick with folks long after the beat fades. From his five pillars of creativity to behind-the-scenes stories, this book offers actionable insights to hone your songwriting.

In “Hip Hop is History,” six-time Grammy Award-winning artist Questlove delivers a sweeping breakdown of the musical phenomenon. He examines the legendary and overlooked moments that shaped the culture into a global force.

Tricia Rose provides an academic analysis of the politics, origins, and themes driving rap music in “Black Noise.” She illustrates how the genre empowered Black folks to voice critiques of contemporary society set to a compelling rhythm that people could not ignore.

In “The Tao of Wu,” Wu-Tang Clan co-founder RZA shares the philosophical wisdom gained from an extraordinary life—from forming one of the world’s most famous hip-hop groups to becoming one of the industry’s most influential leaders.

For a firsthand account of how breakdancing became a core pillar of hip-hop, look no further than Richard “Crazy Legs” Colón. As a pioneer of the dance form, Crazy Legs shares fascinating stories and rare archival imagery that place readers directly into hip-hop’s earliest days.

As a writer on Netflix’s hit series “The Get Down,” Nelson George brings incredible historical insight to his work. In “Hip Hop America,” George chronicles how hip-hop evolved from a vibrant underground culture into a globally celebrated art form.

If you watched and loved the 2016 biopic “Straight Outta Compton,” add “Parental Discretion Is Advised” to your reading list. Functioning as a literary time machine, Gerrick D. Kennedy digs into the deepest archives to deliver the definitive story of how N.W.A came to be and birthed gangsta rap.

Rounding out the list is “The Come Up” by Jonathan Abrams. The New York Times bestselling author compiled hundreds of interviews conducted over three years with hip-hop’s key figures. To understand how the culture was built from the ground up, there is no better way to learn than directly from the pioneers themselves.

items.summary: Wiz Khalifa finally gets his happy ending in his legal case in Romania. But the good news may not last for too long thanks to a new twist.Read more...

scraped.title: Wiz Khalifa Avoids Prison Time in Romania Case...For Now
scraped.h1: Wiz Khalifa Avoids Prison Time in Romania, Here’s Why He’s Still Not In the Clear
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Wiz Khalifa finally gets his happy ending in his legal case in Romania. But the good news may not last for too long thanks to a new twist.

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

US rapper and singer Wiz Khalifa attends the premiere of Amazon MGM Studios’ “Madden” at the Culver Theatre in Culver City, California, on November 4, 2026. (Photo by Lisa O’CONNOR / AFP via Getty Images)

There’s finally some good news related to Wiz Khalifa ‘s legal drama in Romania. Unfortunately for him, though, his good deal may not last as long as he’d like. Let’s break it down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

On Thursday, it was announced that the “See You Again” rapper would not have to serve his nine-month prison sentence related to his December 2025 conviction on charges of illegal possession of a risk drug after he brought weed into the country and was subsequently investigated for allegedly smoking it while onstage during a performance at the Beach Please festival in July 2024, per Vice News. In May 2026, Khalifa was added to Romania’s most wanted list, making international travel and touring complicated.

Related: You Won’t Believe The Ironic Reason Wiz Khalifa Was Arrested in Romania…Or Maybe You Will

However, nearly a year later, a judge in the case decided to annul the decision, overturn the conviction, and strike the occurrence from the record. But in a twist the rapper didn’t see coming, Romania’s DIICOT (Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism) has decided to appeal the ruling and has opted to go through the process of trying Khalifa again in court, according to VICE.

This means that while the “Black and Yellow” rapper may be a free man now, he may end up behind bars once DIICOT returns to court in early November 2026. The investigation is still open, and it doesn’t mean that Khalifa’s been acquitted. But it does mean that he has a little room to breathe easy before things heat back up again.

As we previously told you, video footage of Khalifa smoking a joint onstage and getting arrested at the festival went viral at the time, with fans voicing their concerns about how things were going to play out. In the immediate aftermath, he did sound remorseful about the incident, writing in a post on social media then : “Last night’s show was amazing. I didn’t mean any disrespect to the country of Romania by lighting up on stage. They were very respectful and let me go. I’ll be back soon. But without a big ass joint next time.”

Here’s hoping that statement will help him avoid prison for a second time.

scraped.title: Trump Goes on the Attack Against a Decorated War Hero He Can’t Even Identify, and One Word Gives It All Away
scraped.description: President Donald Trump issued a ‘big warning’ to a top military planner fired by Defense Chief Pete Hegseth, except there’s one big problem. Trump seems
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: Trump Goes on the Attack Against a Decorated War Hero He Can’t Even Identify, and One Word Gives It All Away
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump issued a ‘big warning’ to a top military planner fired by Defense Chief Pete Hegseth, except there’s one big problem.

Trump seems to have no idea who Army Lt. General Brett Sylvia is.

Hegseth fired the director for strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff on Oct. 29, without giving a reason, according to USA Today .

Hegseth accused Sylvia of misconduct related to allegations that he leaked classified information on the Iran war and Russia’s war in Ukraine, CBS News reported .

The former lieutenant general failed three polygraph tests over whether he shared classified intel with the press, CBS reported, citing anonymous sources. Those sources also confirmed the firing was related to the polygraph tests but maintained the allegations against Sylvia are false.

‘You’re Going to Jail!’: Mother Gets Swarmed by Cops at California Pumpkin Patch After Sitting at Table Woman Was Saving for Relatives

More of Sade Robinson’s Remains Wash Ashore Two Years After the Black Teen Was Killed and Dismembered After First Date

The Pentagon also confirmed it has turned the Sylvia case over to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation.

A day later, a reporter asked Trump about the situation with “Gen. Sylvia,” as the reporter put it.

Trump’s response shows how little he seems to know about what’s happening under Hegseth.

“She’s got problems. She’s going to have big problems. She did,” Trump barked.

“We’re very much looking for leakers, and uh, she’s going to have big problems, long-term problems,” he threatened.

Social media exploded in glee over Trump’s ignorance about his own military as some commenters pointed out the seriousness of being so clueless.

“It’s a good thing that question wasn’t on the cognitive test,” an X user joked.

“The commander in chief threatening a three-star general while not knowing who he is sums up the whole operation. maximum menace, minimum command,” another chimed in.

This observer is tired of it all. “Just 25th amendment him already.”

This X user pointed out the obvious: “He is seriously clueless.”

Hegseth has presided over turmoil at the Pentagon since taking control in early 2025. He’s fired or pushed aside more than two dozen military leaders .

The departures include former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. CQ Brown Jr.; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, the Navy’s former top officer; and former Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George.

Gen. David Allvin, the former Air Force chief of staff, left before completing his term. Gen. James Mingus, the former Army vice chief of staff, retired early.

Another General, Gen. Christopher Donahue, also retired after Hegseth reportedly blocked efforts to extend his career leading Army forces in Europe and Africa.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned over the summer following months of reported clashes with Hegseth.

Driscoll repeatedly clashed with Hegseth over removing longtime, qualified leaders, including George’s abrupt removal in April.

The Army has operated without a permanent chief of staff since George’s ouster. Gen. Christopher LaNeve currently holds the position in an acting capacity, but his path to Senate confirmation remains uncertain.

Against that backdrop, his purge of veteran military officials continues amid his crackdown on leaks.

Sylvia has a long, distinguished 32-year service record, including serving as commander of the 101st Airborne Division and deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan, CBS reported. He also earned a Bronze Star and a Purple Heart after sustaining wounds while fighting the Taliban.

"She's got problems" — Trump gets asked about Lt. Gen. Sylvia (Brett Sylvia, a guy!) leaking classified information, and he's so clueless that he thinks the reporter is talking about a woman with the first name Sylvia pic.twitter.com/3iAxkauzTG

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

We know a request for support isn't why you came here. But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's. If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.

If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice. It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account. Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.

Atlanta Black Star is a narrative company. We publish narratives intentionally and specifically to enlighten and transform the world.

Contact us: [email protected]

Sign up to receive The Atlanta Black Star Newsletter in your inbox.

Contribute to Atlanta Black Star today and help us share our narratives.

scraped.h1: New Report Reveals the Moment Trump Realized Stephen Miller’s Immigration Agenda Went Too Far — and It Wasn’t After Two Americans Were Killed By Feds
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump has picked Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, elevating the architect of his immigration crackdown just days after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller takes over Monday, while Wiles moves to Trump’s political operation.

The promotion comes despite Trump reportedly telling aides that Miller had pushed his immigration agenda too far.

Trump entered his second term believing voters had given him a mandate to crack down on illegal immigration. But the aggressive enforcement campaign sparked private complaints from Republican officials in Texas and Florida, according to The Wall Street Journal’s examination of the party’s midterm losses .

Still, according to the report, it wasn’t the fatal shootings of two Americans by federal agents in Minnesota that prompted Trump to reconsider the approach. The concerns that got through to him came from inside his own home.

First Lady Melania Trump complained that people she knew were being deported. Only then, the Journal reported, did Trump begin privately questioning the direction of the crackdown.

Family Tried Everything to Get 10-Year-Old Out of Foster Care, Now Foster Mom Faces Murder Charges for Her Death

‘You’re Going to Jail!’: Mother Gets Swarmed by Cops at California Pumpkin Patch After Sitting at Table Woman Was Saving for Relatives

The political consequences became increasingly difficult to ignore after federal agents fatally shot two Minnesota residents during separate confrontations in January.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents killed Renee Good, 37, on Jan. 7 while she sat in her car during an encounter in Minneapolis. Weeks later, on Jan. 24, Border Patrol agents fatally shot Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, while he recorded officers attempting to arrest someone.

Videos of Pretti’s death circulated widely, drawing further scrutiny of the administration’s immigration operations. According to the report, Trump grew concerned about footage showing the shooting and instructed Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt to distance him from statements made by members of his administration. He also directed immigration czar Tom Homan to travel to Minneapolis and “fix it.”

The administration’s initial response had been markedly different. Miller and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem defended the officers involved in Pretti’s shooting and described the nurse as a “domestic terrorist.”

WSJ said Trump’s advisers recognized the political damage surrounding the shootings, with the president eventually replacing Noem and directing her successor to keep immigration enforcement out of the headlines.

The administration’s enforcement strategy had initially delivered a result Trump could point to as evidence that he was fulfilling a campaign promise to decrease illegal border crossings.

But the crackdown increasingly reached beyond the southern border. Federal operations targeted Home Depot parking lots, construction sites and other workplaces, rounding up people described as nonviolent offenders in reports.

Those operations brought immigration enforcement into communities where the administration had expected its policies to remain popular. The backlash also showed up at the ballot box. In Tuesday’s elections, counties where Hispanic residents made up at least 80 percent of the population favored Democrats by 40 percentage points.

The immigration controversy was not the only issue weighing on Republicans. Trump’s decision to launch the war against Iran also contributed to the party’s losses, with the conflict costing taxpayers more than $47 billion, claiming the lives of more than 20 U.S. service members and driving up expenses across several industries, including freight and fertilizer.

Advisers had warned Trump during the spring that the war could hurt Republicans in the midterms, but he reportedly told them there was still plenty of time to address the political fallout.

Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the conflict “the greatest political blunder in the last two decades,” arguing that Trump had abandoned the America First movement.

“We’re going to have to find a new leader because Trump abandoned it,” Walsh said in an interview.

The findings suggest that immigration enforcement, once a central part of Trump’s political appeal, had become another source of frustration for voters already concerned about the economy and the administration’s decision to enter a prolonged foreign conflict.

The Minneapolis shootings was an early turning point for the administration, with the first signs of internal strain emerging months before the Iran war began. By the time voters headed to the polls, the immigration crackdown had become a political burden rather than the advantage Trump expected it to be.

The report has also sparked criticism across social media, with commenters questioning whether Trump is now trying to distance himself from an immigration crackdown he once championed. One user dismissed the reported shift as too little, too late, writing , “Sounds like backpedal to me. Too late.”

Another argued that Trump should not be allowed to shift responsibility onto Miller, pointing out that the president had the authority to rein in his adviser or remove him from the administration at any time.

“Sorry, but Trump can’t place all the blame at Stephen Miller’s feet. Miller serves at the pleasure of the president, and Trump could have reined him in at any time or even fired him. Don’t let Trump pass the buck on this,” the commenter wrote .

Others took aim at Miller personally, with one user asking , “What did he expect a racist, Nazi wannabe, sociopath was going to do?”

Another commenter responded with little sympathy, writing , “Good that her friends were deported I’m shocked though. Imagine how others feel.”

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

scraped.description: Grammy-winning singer Kandi Burruss has spent much of the past year watching her personal life become public entertainment. Between her bitter divorce
scraped.author: Nicole Duncan-Smith
scraped.h1: ‘You Deserve It!’: Kandi Burruss Cries Tears of Joy for Long-Overdue Career Win After a Year of Ups and Downs
scraped.body_text:
Grammy-winning singer Kandi Burruss has spent much of the past year watching her personal life become public entertainment.

Between her bitter divorce from Todd Tucker, courtroom battles over money and accusations, she’s had plenty of reasons to cry.

But her latest tears are of joy and have absolutely nothing to do with her ex-husband.

After months of headlines about her marriage and her kids, the former “Real Housewives of Atlanta” star finally has something worth celebrating.

And this time, the spotlight is on the talent that made her famous long before reality television came calling in 2009.

‘Mama Joyce?’: Kandi Burruss’ New Look After Filing for Divorce Has Fans Saying She Resembles the Woman Who Warned Her Against Marriage

Kandi Burruss Slams Ex-Husband Todd Tucker for Exposing Intimate Details of Their Marriage to ‘Stretch His Five Minutes of Fame’

The Xscape singer recently broke down after learning she was being considered for induction into the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame.

On Nov. 5, Burruss, 50, shared an emotional Instagram video after receiving a phone call informing her about the nomination.

“I cannot stop crying because Big John just called me to tell me that I am nominated,” she said through tears. She described the recognition as “the most amazing news that I’ve heard in so long.”

The Big John, she mentioned, is formally known as music executive Jon Platt.

“It’s been so much crazy stuff being said about me over this past year,” Burruss continued. “Sometimes it’s real heavy.”

Still, Burruuss insisted she refused to let the negativity derail her.

“What God got for you is still gonna happen,” she declared, explaining that the nomination reminded her that other people’s opinions cannot erase her accomplishments.

Burruss’ emotional reaction comes after a particularly messy chapter involving Tucker, whom she married in 2014. They met on the set of “RHOA.”

Burruss filed for divorce in November 2025 after 11 years of marriage . What initially appeared to be an amicable split has since turned into a public dispute over their children, finances and their reported $30 million business empire.

According to court documents reported by TMZ, Burruss accused Tucker of occupying the guest house on her Atlanta property without contributing to household expenses. She also alleged he failed to help cover certain costs associated with their children.

Tucker pushed back, claiming he had been removed from the main residence. He insisted he remains nearby to provide stability for their family.

Their prenuptial agreement, which nearly derailed their wedding, has also attracted renewed attention.

Adding to the tension was Tucker’s September trailer for “Til Divorce Do Us Part.” In it, he discussed intimate details of his marriage with fellow reality TV ex-husband Peter Thomas.

Burruss was furious.

“A man who has already hurt me to my core is furthering the damage by choosing to sensationalize our sex life to stretch his five minutes of fame,” she told People.

Even her post-divorce appearance became a talking point. When Burruss debuted a black bob with bangs during an Amazon Live appearance, fans compared her to the one person who famously questioned Tucker’s intentions before the couple married, Mama Joyce

But while her marriage continues to make headlines, Burruss’ songwriting résumé tells a different story.

She co-wrote TLC’s Grammy-winning anthem “No Scrubs” and Destiny’s Child’s chart-topping hit “Bills, Bills, Bills.” Her credits also include Pink’s “There You Go,” *NSYNC’s “It Makes Me Ill” and her own hit “Don’t Think I’m Not.”

Her Instagram announcement drew an outpouring of congratulations from fellow entertainers.

“Omgggggg GURL congrats Kandi you had me wanting to hop on a plane at first to see who we needed fight!!!! This is awesome news!!!” actress Tisha Campbell wrote. Naturi Naughton cheered, “You deserve it all girl!!!”

Producer Dallas Austin added, “You got my vote !! let’s get it congratulations !!!”

Tina Knowles praised Burruss, writing, “Well deserved!!! You are an incredible writer!!!! So happy that you can put the bull aside! God bless you.”

Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms also offered words of encouragement, writing, “God ALWAYS sees you. Congratulations my sister, well deserved.”

Another supporter declared, “Stay strong!!!!! Congratulations!!!! God is the ULTIMATE!!!!!”

Burruss is among the nominees for the Hall’s 2027 class, along with Grandmaster Melle Mel, Ne-Yo and will.i.am. Voting members have until Dec. 14 to submit their ballots, with the inductees expected to be announced next year.

For now, the woman who helped write “Bills, Bills, Bills” has a reason to celebrate that has nothing to do with who is paying them.

“It’s not sad at all,” Burruss assured her followers. “I am like so happy.”

scraped.title: Across the South, Voters Turned Anger Into a ‘Blacklash’
scraped.description: Black voters approached the elections with an urgency fueled by concerns ranging from threats to voting rights to the rising cost of living.
scraped.author: Brandon Tensley, Raisa Habersham
scraped.h1: Across the South, Voters Turned Anger Into a ‘Blacklash’
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

MIAMI — As the raindrops eased on the evening of Election Day, a fellow voter helped to lift Niecy Rahming out of her daughter’s car and into her wheelchair.

Rahming, 95, made it to the polling station with 10 minutes to spare, casting her vote for what she hoped would be Florida’s first Black senator, state Rep. Angie Nixon. A native Floridian and longtime Miami Gardens resident, Rahming has lived long enough to experience Jim Crow and the passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But that evening, her focus was on the economy.

“Prices are going higher and higher, and it appears there’s no concern for poor people,” she told Capital B.

To Rahming, Nixon’s authenticity was appealing, and she believed that the community organizer would alleviate the financial stress in her community: “She would help the people who are less fortunate,” Rahming said. “She wouldn’t compromise.”

That enthusiasm wasn’t limited to Florida.” Though final tallies aren’t yet in for Election Day, early voting increased across the South — what some are calling a “ Blacklash . From Louisiana and Mississippi to Georgia and Texas, Black voters say that they approached the midterms with a sense of urgency fueled by concerns ranging from the rising cost of living to threats to voting rights and Black political representation.

Data paints a picture of this enthusiasm nationwide. In U.S. House races, about 91% of Black voters backed Democrats, compared with just 8% who supported Republicans, according to The New York Times . This was a 10-point shift toward Democrats from 2024.

Whether you call it a “Blacklash” or something else, the message from Black voters, especially those in the South, was clear: At a moment when representation secured through generations of struggle was once again under threat, they weren’t about to surrender it without a fight.

Eleven miles south, in Miami’s Liberty City neighborhood, Roots Bookstore co-owners Phil Agnew and Isaiah Thomas hosted an election night watch party with Berkeley, California-based pastor Michael “Pastor Mike” McBride, holding a live podcast as election results trickled in throughout the evening.

The inside of Roots Bookstore was packed with Black and brown residents watching the Florida election play out. As results for the hotly contested race between Nixon and her Republican rival, U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, came in, so did the groans from about two dozen attendees. Nixon lost to Moody narrowly, by 2.9 percentage points, according to the AP.

Thomas, 37, cast his vote for Nixon, who’d been a fervent supporter of the Black-focused bookstore when it was still just a concept. He credited her presence and energy with Miami-Dade County going “blue.”

“Angie is the people,” he said. “She is the community.”

Despite her loss, residents are excited about the new energy Nixon brought to the city, with some saying that she sparked a fire they hadn’t seen in years. This week, they say, was a reminder of what Black voters could accomplish when they’re loud enough.

More than 900 miles away in Baton Rouge, Sonya Knox admitted that she hadn’t followed every development in Louisiana’s midterm elections. But she felt that she couldn’t stay home.

“I hadn’t paid much attention to [what’s going on], but I know that I needed to get my Black ass out and vote,” the 65-year-old told Capital B.

For Knox, it was impossible to separate this determination from fears she has about the future of Black political representation. She believes that, for months now, the political gains that Black Americans before her fought for have been the deliberate targets of political attacks.

“They trying to take all our voting rights from us,” she said. “So that’s why I get out. I walk out and make sure I vote.”

Her concerns reflected the stakes of an election in which Louisiana’s Black political representation was under significant pressure. Following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling , Republicans eliminated one of the state’s two majority-Black congressional districts, prompting Democratic U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields to give up reelection. Meanwhile, Black voters accounted for more than 34% of early ballots, a record for a congressional midterm in Louisiana, as Democrat Jamie Davis mounted a surprisingly strong Senate campaign against Republican Julia Letlow, despite ultimately losing.

Regrettably, Knox said, this enthusiasm wasn’t matched by financial support from national Democrats. State party chairman Randal Gaines and Democratic strategist James Carville both expressed frustration over their unsuccessful efforts to attract national campaign money. Davis said that the national party had provided no financial support.

Still, the priority for Knox and others was making sure that as many Black Americans as possible participated in the election. After voting, she planned to go home and bring her grandson to the polls.

“He’s a young Black man, and he needs to be out here,” Knox said.

At the same polling site in Baton Rouge, Mark Harris was equally determined. He, too, pointed to the fact that Black Americans have been battling for the right to the franchise for generations, and he rejected the notion that casting a ballot is inconsequential.

“The best thing we could do to show them that we not scared is to show up,” the 29-year-old told Capital B. “If it didn’t count, why all the people in power stop us from voting?”

With all the talk about the generational divide and younger people not voting, Harris offered a reminder that not everyone his age was blind to the importance of the franchise.

As a little girl, 34-year-old Holmes County resident Aisha Scaffold accompanied her parents to the polls every election. This nurtured a habit: She hasn’t missed an election since she became old enough to vote.

“We’ve been voting before we could even vote,” she told Capital B.

But this year’s midterm elections felt especially consequential. Scaffold had watched loved ones struggle with high grocery and gas prices, including her father, a cattle farmer. Their experiences bolster her belief that elections directly impact the financial pressures many Mississippi families grapple with.

“It just makes you want to go ahead and make sure you’re doing your civic duty,” she said.

Such fears were front and center in one of Mississippi’s most closely watched races in years. Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, challenged Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, potentially becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. The contest, which may not be called for days, has attracted national attention. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Colom, while President Donald Trump threw his support behind Hyde-Smith. Black voters who are frustrated by rising prices and Mississippi’s political future see the competitive race as an opportunity to challenge Mississippi’s deeply entrenched Republican establishment.

Colom said that the enthusiasm for his campaign springs from the people. He noted contributions from all 82 counties as well as town halls that brought in crowds of hundreds of people, arguing that it was grassroots support that eventually convinced national Democrats that the race was worth paying attention to.

“The best thing we could do to show them that we not scared is to show up.”

Mark Harris , voter

“What people are telling me is they want a fighter for Mississippi, a fighter that understands the issues that matter, and somebody that’s going to work to make their life better,” Colom told Mississippi Public Broadcasting.

Scaffold cast her ballot for Colom. She believes that Hyde-Smith’s time in office has brought little improvement to the lives of ordinary Mississippians, and she was impressed by Colom’s familiarity with the concerns of communities such as hers.

“He’s a politician, but it just makes you feel like, OK, this is the person I want to speak for me, to represent me in Washington,” Scaffold said.

While Scaffold has been voting since she was 18, it took others a few years to understand why they needed to vote.

Aliyah Jackson was frustrated with the economy and with people in power making decisions about her future. At 22, she had never voted in an election, but this year, she concluded that sitting out wasn’t on the table.

“This was my first time voting, and so I’m really proud to have had the opportunity to come out here and make sure that my vote matters,” the Atlanta resident told Capital B.

Not wanting to cast a ballot without knowing the candidates, she researched their positions and considered who might take her priorities seriously.

“If I really feel passionate about that, then I’ll make sure that my say counts,” she said.

Georgia’s elections offered a significant display of Black voting power, led partly by concerns about the economy and an insistence on making every vote count. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, faced Republican Rick Jackson for governor. She ultimately won, a triumph that will make her the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history. This stunning breakthrough came in a state where Black voters have long played a vital role in politics. About 9 in 10 Black women supported Bottoms, the same share that backed Kamala Harris’ 2024 run for president, according to the AP. The figure was the same for Black men, though just three-quarters supported Harris.

For Schuyler Bond, 36 and a native Atlantan, the election brought to mind another concern — whether younger Black Americans fully appreciated the sacrifices from their elders that made their participation possible.

He said that he too often encounters people, including millennials like himself as well as members of Generation Z, who write voting off. He urges voters with these impulses to research candidates and recognize the power of their ballots.

“It’s something you shouldn’t leave to the wayside, or you’d be spitting in your ancestors’ faces,” he said.

Election Day in Houston was dreary and rainy, with storms rolling through the eastern part of the state. Despite the weather, though, the mood around the midterm races was the furthest thing from subdued, according to Algenita Davis, a 76-year-old resident of the city’s Third Ward.

“There has been more conversation about this election than any other election in my entire life,” she told Capital B.

Across Houston, Davis said, volunteers had been stepping in to help voters, and particularly seniors, get to the polls. Some were even offering rides in their personal vehicles. Davis feared that the weather and Texas’ lengthy ballots might discourage participation, but she was “prayerful” that voters would push through and make their voices heard.

Her prayers came true. Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race, delivering the party its first statewide victory in more than three decades . The win highlighted the significance of Black voter participation in a state where voting restrictions still are cause for concern. But the outcome wasn’t a foregone conclusion. After Talarico beat U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary, many wondered if he’d be able to mobilize Black voters, who had largely backed Crockett. Talarico pledged to spend millions on Black voter outreach, hoping to energize a constituency he couldn’t win without.

Even before Election Day, those efforts bore fruit. According to the NAACP, Black early and absentee voting in Texas was up 53% compared with the same point in the 2022 midterms, with the increase driven by early in-person voting. This figure provides a snapshot of the enthusiasm that helped Talarico to achieve a breakthrough in the state.

“The story of this election is not just about who won,” said Dominik Whitehead, the NAACP’s chief of field, membership growth, and unit sustainability. “It’s about the Black wave of voters who understood what was at stake and made their voices heard.”

Capital B staff writers Aallyah Wright, Alyssa Johnson, and Ann Hill Bond contributed to this report.

Brandon Tensley is Capital B's national politics reporter. More by Brandon Tensley

Raisa Habersham is a freelance reporter based in South Florida. She was most recently the race and culture reporter at the Miami Herald, where her most recent work focused on South Florida politics. A Georgia native, Raisa previously worked for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and the Savannah Morning... More by Raisa Habersham

scraped.title: From FAMU to Spelman, HBCU Alumni Make History in the Midterms
scraped.description: Keisha Lance Bottoms, Donna Miller, and Justin Jones are among Tuesday’s winners with Black college ties.
scraped.author: Alecia Taylor
scraped.h1: From FAMU to Spelman, HBCU Alumni Make History in the Midterms
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

For decades, Black leaders have been preaching that HBCUs consistently punch above their weight, producing some of the nation’s best and brightest doctors, educators, and lawmakers.

If it wasn’t understood before, this year’s midterms proved their point … again.

From Howard University’s hilltop to the highest of seven hills at Florida A&M University, HBCU graduates won state and local offices nationwide. Notable alumni include Georgia Gov.-elect and FAMU Rattler Keisha Lance Bottoms and Spelmanite Adrienne Adams, who will be New York’s first Black woman lieutenant governor.

Keisha Lance Bottoms: Florida A&M University . Atlanta’s former mayor made history as the first Black woman governor in the U.S. The Democrat’s campaign emphasized expanding Medicaid, building more workforce and affordable housing, and protecting Black voting rights. Bottoms received her bachelor of arts in broadcast journalism from FAMU in Tallahassee, Florida.

Byron Donalds: Florida A&M University. The Brooklyn, New York, native will be Florida’s first Black governor. Running on affordability, inflation, and housing concerns, the Republican also focused on immigration crackdowns in the workplace and tax cuts for Florida residents. He attended Florida A&M University before transferring to Florida State University, where he earned a bachelor of arts degree in finance. During his campaign, he emphasized an initiative he led to secure $25 million for FAMU .

Milton Potter: Florida A&M University. Before his win as the lieutenant governor of the U.S. Virgin Islands, he was a senator in the U.S. territory. He also served as the Senate president during his tenure. Potter and his running mate, Gov.-elect Stacey Plaskett, highlighted issues such as healthcare, tourism and education. One of their standout promises is to restructure the islands’ Office of Disaster Recovery and create a high-accountability task force, pointing out that many residents are still waiting for aid post-hurricans Maria and Irma. He received his bachelor’s degree and master’s degrees from FAMU.

Adrienne Adams: Spelman College. Adams’ election night victory is not the first time she made history. In 2022, the Democrat was elected as the first Black speaker of the New York City Council. On the campaign trail, Adams and Gov. Kathy Hochul focused on childcare, the cost of living, and public safety. Adams graduated with a bachelor of arts in psychology with a minor in early childhood development from Spelman.

Oliver Gilbert III: Florida A&M University. This Rattler was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives for Florida’s 24th District. The predominantly Black and Latino area in Miami-Dade County includes Little Haiti and Miami Gardens. During the Democrat’s campaign, he centralized affordability, including rising gas prices. He proposed expanding access to healthcare by lowering the eligibility age for Medicare and raising Medicaid income limits. The former mayor of Miami Gardens has also served on the Miami-Dade County Commission since 2020.

Donna Miller: Howard University. This alumna was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives for Illinois’ 2nd Congressional District, which is 50% Black. Miller has a track record serving the community through her seats as a Cook County commissioner and previous board chair for Planned Parenthood of Illinois. In a voting questionnaire , Miller criticized President Donald Trump and the Republican Party tax cuts. The Democrat vowed to support legislation such as expanding Earned Income Tax Credit and to boost take-home pay for low- and moderate-income workers if elected to Congress. She also criticized artificial intelligence and the government’s usage, given research as shown its racial bias in facial recognition . The Bison received a bachelor of business administration from the university.

Nikema Williams: Talladega College . The Democrat represents Georgia’s 5th Congressional District. She campaigned on affordability, homeownership, and closing the wealth gap. She also emphasized the importance of affordable higher education and programs aimed to support first-generation college students. In 2024, Williams faced backlash from Black Democrats in Georgia following Kamala Harris’ presidential loss, with some Georgians claiming she and the Democratic Party didn’t spend enough resources encouraging local voters. Williams led the party at the state level.

Justin Jones: Fisk University. The outspoken Democrat will continue to serve as the House representative for Tennessee’s District 52, which covers Davidson County in the Nashville-Davidson metropolitan area. The Fisk graduate has spoken out against data centers, including a campus masterplan from his alma mater that proposed a data center on campus grounds. Jones was first elected in 2023. As of now, the data center proposal is on pause. With his reelection, Jones’ current term is extended until 2028.

Letitia James : Howard University School of Law. The well-known Bison was reelected as New York state attorney general. She is the first Black person and first woman elected to the position. First elected in 2019, James brought a fraud case against the Trump Organization. During her reelection campaign, James stood on “holding bad actors accountable” and protecting New Yorkers’ safety. In 2025, the Trump administration indicted James on a charge of bank fraud, but a federal judge dismissed the case, with a grand jury following suit and refusing to reindict her.

Letitia Plummer: Spelman College. Plummer became the first Black woman elected as a judge for Harris County in Texas. The Spelman alumna previously served as a member of the Houston City Council, representing the at-large Position 4 from 2020 to 2025.

Plummer’s agenda heavily relies on disaster relief. On her campaign site, she highlights that previously she secured $900,000 in funding for a new permanent generator that was installed at the Kashmere Gardens Multi-Service Center.

Also a trained dentist, she continued to operate two locally owned practices in the area. In a debate with her opponent Orlando Sanchez, he brought up Plummer’s three-time sanctioned record with the Texas Board of Dentistry. Plummer still defeated her opponent, receiving nearly 61% of the vote, according to Houston Public Media.

scraped.title: Black Democrats Made History, So Did a Black Farmer
scraped.description: In a major upset, Katherine Juhan-Arnold defeated a Republican incumbent to lead Georgia’s agriculture department, the oldest in the nation.
scraped.author: Aallyah Wright
scraped.h1: Black Democrats Made History, So Did a Black Farmer
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

On Election Day, Black women in Georgia broke barriers in more ways than one.

Voters there not only elected the first Black woman governor in U.S. history, but also chose Katherine Juhan-Arnold as the state’s first woman and Black commissioner of agriculture.

“Georgia, we did it! I am overwhelmed with gratitude,” Juhan-Arnold wrote in a Facebook statement. “The campaign may be over, but our work is just beginning.”

In her first run for office, the farmer defeated incumbent and seventh-generation farmer Tyler J. Harper. Harper, 40, has been the state’s agriculture commissioner since 2023, and previously served as a state senator from 2013 to 2022. Juhan-Arnold, 37, founded Baby Katie’s Pharm & Kitchen, a nonprofit focused on bringing fresh foods and gardening to low-income communities.

She’ll represent 67,000 farmers, nearly 3,000 of whom are Black. Capital B reached out to Juhan-Arnold but did not hear back.

The win is no small feat for this often overlooked, but powerful role. Every state has a commissioner or secretary of agriculture who shapes farming and environmental policy.

The official oversees and enforces policies and regulations for agriculture, livestock, food safety, forestry, and pest control. The department can conduct gas and oil inspections, administer the National School Lunch Program, inspect grocery stores, or oversee benefits for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and the federal supplemental nutrition program for women, infants, and children known as WIC.

However, only 12 states — mostly in the Southeast — allow voters to elect their commissioners. The rest of the states give that power to the governor, board or commission that appoints their agriculture leader. Historically, white Republican men have held these offices more than other statewide officials combined, according to an analysis by InvestigateMidwest.

This isn’t surprising to John Boyd Jr., president and founder of the National Black Farmers Association. For decades, Black farms have declined, and producers have been pushed out of the industry. They continue to remain underrepresented in positions of power — from the federal Department of Agriculture to state directors and even local-level county committees.

With voters electing Juhan-Arnold, it is vindication for Black farmers, especially women who have been degraded by President Donald Trump and his administration, Boyd added.

“It’s a real leg up for us,” Boyd said. “Having a person who looks like you and can relate to the struggles a Black family farm goes through is a real breakthrough.”

This year, only seven states held elections. Juhan-Arnold wasn’t the only Black person hoping to make history as a state’s top agricultural official. Yet, the three Black men who ran in other states lost those races.

In South Carolina, fourth-generation farmer and Democrat DeShawn Blanding saw an opening to fill the seat, which hadn’t had someone new in office for the past 20 years. With only 45% of the vote, he lost to Republican Cody Simpson, a seventh-generation white farmer. United Citizens Party candidate Chris Nelums, a Black pastor in South Carolina, also faced defeat in the race, receiving less than 1% of the votes.

In Florida, Kyle “KC” Gibson, an AME pastor, ran for agriculture commissioner this year, after unsuccessful bids for governor in 2022, 2018, and 2014, and lieutenant governor in 2022. While he hopes to fulfill his childhood dream of becoming governor one day, the 56-year-old also loves agriculture.

Unlike other agencies, the Florida Department of Agriculture & Consumer Services does more than food, water, and agriculture. It issues licenses for private investigators, concealed weapons permits, and conducts inspections for rides at the county fair. As a firearm instructor, former firefighter, and beekeeper hobbyist, Gibson felt this role would be a good fit. His love for agriculture grew through his grandfather, who was a farmer.

He had only three months to campaign, and as a result secured less than 1% of the vote. He lost to incumbent Republican Wilton Simpson. On the campaign trail, he said, many Black voters were not aware of the race, didn’t understand the role of commissioner, or were dismissive of farming.

“Most people are saying, ‘Well, Black people don’t do that.’ I say, ‘Well, how many Black people do you know that are farmers? If you go back two generations, you had some agriculture, and that’s how you survived,” Gibson recalled, as he approached voters.

He added: “It’s very vital, but it’s an under-watched and an underrepresented position. There are still a lot of African Americans that live in rural areas that depend on that department.”

However, he isn’t deterred. He’s already filed paperwork to run again in 2030.

Capital B reached out to Blanding and Nelums, but they didn’t respond by the time of publication.

ALABAMA: Commissioner of Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries

Candidates: Democrat Ron Sparks ran against Republican Corey Hill.

Sparks, 74, previously served two terms as the state’s agriculture commissioner from 2003 to 2011. He was one of the youngest elected officials in Alabama when he became a county commissioner for DeKalb County. Hill, 56, is a cattle and poultry farmer who owns a local grocery store. He is currently the mayor of Douglas.

Salary: $100,833

Results : Hill won with 54% of the vote. Sparks garnered 45%.

GEORGIA: Commissioner of Agriculture

Candidates: Democrat Katherine Juhan-Arnold ran against incumbent Republican Tyler J. Harper.

Salary: $125,987

Results: Newcomer Juhan-Arnold defeated Harper 53% to 46%, respectively.

FLORIDA: Commissioner of Agriculture and Consumer Services

Candidates: Incumbent Republican Wilton Simpson ran against Democrat Joey Mendoza Atkins and Kyle “KC” Gibson, who has no party affiliation

Simpson, 60, is a lifelong egg farmer who was backed by Trump and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. He was a state senator for a decade. Mendoza, 41, is a trial attorney who has provided legal aid to farm workers. Gibson, 56, is a pastor and ran for governor several times.

Salary: $139,987

Results: Simpson won his reelection bid, garnering 51% of the vote to Atkins’ 48%. Gibson had less than 1%.

IOWA: Secretary of Agriculture

Candidates: Incumbent Republican Mike Naig ran against Democrat Chris Jones.

Naig, 48, grew up on a family farm and has been the state’s secretary of agriculture for two terms. Jones, 65, is an environmental scientist and researcher. His expertise is in water quality and sustainable agriculture practices.

Salary: $103,212

Results: Naig defeated Jones 52% to 47%.

NORTH DAKOTA: Agriculture Commissioner

Candidates: Incumbent Republican Doug Goehring ran against Democrat Vern Thompson.

Goehring, 61, is a farmer and rancher and seeking re-election. He’s been agriculture commissioner since 2009. Thompson is a former farmer and now trucker. He is the mayor of Minnewaukan and previously served in both the state legislature and other local councils.

Salary: $145,003

Results: Goehring will keep his seat. He secured 62.7% of the vote whereas Thompson pulled only 37%.

SOUTH CAROLINA: Commissioner of Agriculture

Candidates: Republican Cody Simpson ran against Democrat DeShawn Blanding, Libertarian Michael Sullens and United Citizens Party nominee Chis Nelums.

Simpson, 35, is a fifth-generation farmer and state executive director for the USDA’s Farm Service Agency. Blanding, 29, is a fourth-generation farmer and agriculture researcher and policy advocate. He’s worked as a policy analyst for the U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture and aide for USDA’s National Resources Conservation Services. Sullens is a restaurant operator, and Nelums is an entrepreneur.

Salary: $162,000

Results: Simpson beat his challengers with 51% of the vote; Blanding received 45%, Nelums 0.79%, and Sullens 1.9%.

TEXAS: Commissioner of Agriculture

Candidates: Republican Nate Sheets ran against Democrat Clayton Tucker and Libertarian Austin Kelly.

Sheets, 55, is a rancher and served in the U.S. Navy Reserves. He received an endorsement from Gov. Greg Abott. Tucker, 35, is a rancher, former kindergarten teacher, and agriculture researcher for the National Science Foundation. He was backed by several congressional leaders, including Reps. Jamie Raskin and Lloyd Doggett. Kelly is an agriculture scientist and a student pursuing his doctorate at Texas A&M University.

Salary: $140,937

Results: Tucker won with 51% of the votes, becoming the state’s first Democratic agriculture commissioner in four decades.

scraped.title: Guatemala faces a human rights court over violent evictions of Indigenous communities
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Guatemala faces a human rights court over violent evictions of Indigenous communities
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Years after Indigenous communities in Guatemala were forcibly evicted from their ancestral land, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) is asking a court to hold the government responsible and provide reparations.

On Oct. 28, the IACHR announced it had referred a case to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, which rules on human rights violations in the Americas. The case involves 14 Maya Q’eqchi’ communities in Alta Verapaz that were removed from their land to make way for sugarcane plantations.

“Sugarcane cultivation caused displacement and the loss of rice, maize and bean crops that supported the health and food security of the Indigenous Maya Q’eqchi’ population, and substantially affected the environment,” the IACHR said in its referral , submitted to the court Sept. 17.

Disputes in the territory date back to at least 2005, when private companies started buying Indigenous land that the Maya Q’eqchi’ had occupied for centuries, according to the IACHR referral. The government hadn’t granted the communities proper land titles, creating confusion about who could occupy the area.

In 2011, following years of protests, a court authorized the eviction of the 14 Indigenous communities, whose residents had refused to leave the land.

“The government of the republic has a legal and moral obligation to stop the growing number of illegal actions that pose a serious risk to the country’s governability,” the government said in a statement at the time.

The evictions were carried out “violently and with a disproportionate use of force,” the IACHR’s referral said. The Commission also found that officials failed to research the communities’ historical occupation of the land, and the social and cultural impacts that displacement would have.

In May 2013, during the eviction of 95 families on the Río Polochic farm in Panzós, five Indigenous people suffered gunshot wounds and had to be taken to a hospital.

Around the same time, the government approved mass sugarcane plantings without consulting the communities or conducting environmental impact studies, resulting in the destruction of traditional crops, according to the IACHR referral.

“The state didn’t guarantee the communities’ right to food, understood as the right to adequate nutrition that preserves their health,” the referral said.

The IACHR asked the court to order the Guatemalan government to repair damages inflicted upon community members. It said the state should guarantee the displaced communities “safe return” to their land and access to food, drinking water and housing.

The state should also demarcate their land and grant collective land ownership to the 14 communities, and develop a legal framework to guarantee them ancestral rights, the Commission concluded.

The Inter-American Court’s judgments are binding on states that have accepted its jurisdiction, including Guatemala. The IACHR submitted the case on Sept. 17 but has not announced a date for future proceedings.

Banner image: Sugar cane workers in a field near Retalhuleu, Guatemala. Image by Rodrigo Abd via Associated Press.

scraped.title: Peru’s drive for critical minerals threatens a disappearing glacier
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Alexandra Popescu
scraped.h1: Peru’s drive for critical minerals threatens a disappearing glacier
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Like many in the community of Phinaya, in southeastern Peru, Donato Bermúdez makes his living from alpacas. His flock of 500 roams the slopes beneath the vast Quelccaya glacier, the site of the second-largest tropical ice cap in the world . Reaching 5,600 meters (18,400 feet), its white peak is home to centuries of tradition.

“We believe the glacier is essentially alive,” Bermúdez, a lifelong resident and former community president of Phinaya, told Mongabay by phone. “We say it gives us the water, the lifeblood that flows to the community.”

But he and other Phinaya locals now fear that a threat may be looming from the other side of the mountain.

In the shadow of Quelccaya, long-delayed lithium and uranium mining projects are gaining fresh momentum under President Keiko Fujimori, who is determined to put transition minerals firmly on Peru’s economic agenda.

“Lithium and uranium mining would be catastrophic for the Quelccaya glacier,” said Yolanda Quispe, 44, a community leader and park ranger from Phinaya, who has spent a lifetime beneath the glacier. “The fauna and flora that exist around it, the people — all of this would be destroyed,” she told Mongabay over the phone.

Through Peruvian subsidiary Macusani Yellowcake, Canadian firm American Lithium controls major deposits of lithium and uranium — two minerals the Peruvian government describes as critical to the clean energy transition — across at least 174 concessions covering more than 1,090 square kilometers (421 square miles) in the department of Puno, beneath the Quelccaya glacier.

The Falchani Lithium project, an open-pit mine that includes four of those concessions and expands more than 2,800 hectares (6,900 acres) a few kilometers east of the Quelccaya glacier, is set to begin construction in 2028. The project is expected to produce 25,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate per year and generate more than $6 billion over its lifetime. But scientists and activists fear Peru’s push for transition minerals could threaten the glacier and communities that depend on it.

“What’s at stake here is the very existence of this glacier,” said Bladimir Martínez, an environmental engineer working with Red Muqui, a Peruvian network of organizations monitoring the impact of mining, in a video call with Mongabay.

But while some communities fear the consequences of mining development, others are hopeful that it may alleviate the poverty that blights Peru’s third-poorest region . In Carabaya, the province where the concessions are located, hopes are that mining could provide as many as 5,000 jobs.

With communities divided, and the new federal administration aiming to fast-track mining projects, Puno’s mineral-rich earth is fast becoming a battleground for the future of Peru’s energy transition — and for its disappearing glaciers.

Covering the eastern flank of the Quelccaya glacier, American Lithium’s Peruvian concessions are split between three projects: Macusani, one of the world’s largest uranium deposits; Falchani, the world’s sixth-largest hard rock lithium deposit; and Quelcaya, a third lithium exploration project.

American Lithium’s published economic assessments have described the Falchani project as being “highly amenable” to open-pit mining, which activists fear will result in large quantities of metal-rich dust being discharged onto the Quelccaya glacier.

“We’re convinced that the dust generated here is going to fall on the glacier,” Martínez said. “That means a rise in temperature and accelerated deglaciation.”

Martínez also believes that the presence of uranium in this dust could pose a risk to the surrounding area. “Our biggest fear is that the population, the animals, and the tourists who visit the glacier will be exposed to uranium radioactivity,” he said.

The glacier supports 56 plant species and 76 bird species — including the glacier finch, ( Idiopsar speculifer ) one of only two bird species known to nest directly on ice — as well as endangered species like the Andean mountain cat ( Leopardus jacobita ).

Quelccaya’s meltwater is a vital source of fresh water for the Amazon basin and the departments of Cusco and Puno. According to Peru’s National Research Institute for Glaciers and Mountain Ecosystems, the ice cap holds 2.43 billion cubic meters of water — enough to supply Cusco for a century.

But over the last 40 years, Quelccaya has lost 58% of its ice.

“ There is a lot of fear,” said Vito Calderón, head of communications at environmental and human rights NGO DHUMA, speaking over the phone to Mongabay. “If the glacier disappears, it’ll be even worse. There will be a water crisis across this whole area.”

According to American Lithium ’s website, the company adheres to the “highest standards” of environmental stewardship, while baseline studies show that no endangered species or habitats are present within the areas of the Macusani and Falchani projects.

American Lithium did not respond to Mongabay’s request for comment.

Originally explored as a uranium-only deposit, the area was found to be rich in lithium in 2017 . When American Lithium acquired the concessions in 2021, the projects were already mired in controversy. A year prior, Macusani Yellowcake had been sanctioned for unapproved exploration; while in 2019, 32 of the 149 concessions were declared invalid by the Peruvian government due to missed payments .

The ensuing legal dispute was finalized in August 2025, when Peru’s Supreme Court dismissed the case and confirmed American Lithium’s ownership of the disputed concessions. The decision would usher in a wider governmental effort to promote transition mineral mining.

In June 2026, Peru formally declared lithium and uranium minerals of national importance. A month later, more than 1,100 people attended the First International Forum on Lithium and Uranium.

“The time has come to start talking about a fourth country that leads energy development with lithium and uranium,” said Luis Arroyo, Peru’s prime-minister at the time, at the event.

Hailed by American Lithium as a positive step for critical minerals development, the subsequent inauguration of conservative President Keiko Fujimori further cemented the advance of mining interests in Peru. “It must be understood that Peru is a mining country,” she told Peruvian outlet El Peruano , “so we have to promote it.”

On Aug. 28, she would follow up on this promise, signing an agreement with Argentina, Chile and Bolivia to deepen cooperation and investment in strategic minerals.

But as Peru joins the regional push for mining development, some experts are concerned that accelerated development could come at the cost of adequate regulation.

“The approach is clearly one of lowering social and environmental standards,” said Roger Merino, an expert in environmental governance and professor at the Universidad del Pacifico, speaking on a video call. “I’m worried that this kind of push will happen and projects will get approved without necessarily having clear standards.”

Compounding experts’ concerns is the lack of clear regulation around the mining of uranium.

“The studies say that since uranium is especially radioactive, it needs special handling protocols,” Merino said, “but everything is very vague and general, precisely because there’s no approved law or technical regulation.”

Some critics believe that ongoing regulatory uncertainty is responsible for the historically slow progress of the Macusani uranium project. “The uranium project is completely stalled,” Martínez said.

Those complications explain why the company has sought to separate the uranium and lithium projects, according to Martinez, despite evidence that Falchani also contains uranium.

In 2023, Macusani Yellowcake CEO Ulises Solís denied that Falchani contains uranium, but a 2024 study from the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found uranium among several trace minerals in the site’s lithium-rich rock.

“They wanted to separate lithium on one side and uranium on the other because uranium was more complicated,” Martínez said. “If they want to extract lithium in Puno, they are going to extract uranium too. It is inevitable.”

Despite the concerns of civil society, communities close to the projects are reportedly in favor of mining.

“Most of the local communities were in favour of the activity,” Merino said, referring to his 2024 fieldwork in Corani, where Falchani is located. He said some communities, lacking state support, feel they have nowhere else to turn.

“Their only chance of having a better standard of living than what they have now is the mine — they don’t have another option,” Merino said.

But other communities dependent on Quelccaya fear they will bear the consequences without sharing the benefits. “I’ve already talked with people from Puno,” said Quispe, whose community of Phinaya sits on the opposite side of the glacier. “I told them: You can’t just sell yourselves so easily, right?”

As a park ranger, Quispe has already witnessed Quelccaya’s deterioration due to climate change. Now, she feels that mining could accelerate its decline. “Each time I arrive on my patrols, I see it further and further retreated,” she said. “With climate change alone it’s already advancing a lot. Mining on top of that would be catastrophic.”

Lonnie Thompson, a paleoclimatologist and research scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center in the U.S. state of Ohio, has been working on the Quelccaya ice cap since 1974. Using a solar-powered drill of his own design, Thompson himself drilled the first ice cores to be taken from glacier.

“If [mining concessions] were to develop fully, the whole ice cap is at risk,” he told Mongabay over video call.

Thompson believes mining development could combine with the predicted super El Niño to rapidly accelerate melting on Quelccaya — and he is advocating for legislation to prevent this. “There’s really no other option. If you want to protect it from future mining, you’ve got to turn it into a national park,” he said.

According to Thompson, stringent protections will buy communities more time to adapt to the loss of Quelccaya’s water resources — but it won’t save the glacier he has spent his life studying.

“When I look at Quelccaya, it’s like going to see a terminal cancer patient. I document the change taking place, but I can’t stop the change,” he said. “We need to preserve it as long as possible.”

Banner image : The Corani territory, with the Quelccaya Glacier in the background. Image courtesy of Red Muqui, photo by Rony Ramos – IDECA Perú.
