ASCEA and CASTEL VOLTURNO, Italy, and BARCELONA, Spain — In the early hours of a warm July day, regular rows of still-folded sun umbrellas stand along the shores of Castel Volturno, a coastal town in the Italian region of Campania, located about 35 kilometers (22 miles) northwest of Naples. A small group gathers around a control screen while a drone flies along the coast, searching for tractor-like tracks emerging from the waves. At the slightest sign, group members will quickly reach the location and fence off the area.

Summer is the nesting season for the loggerhead sea turtle ( Caretta caretta ). Loggerheads inhabit warm portions of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, as well as the Mediterranean Sea. However, despite its broad range, the species is listed as vulnerable to extinction by the IUCN. These large marine reptiles spend roughly two decades maturing at sea before the females return to land — usually to the same beaches where they hatched — to lay their own eggs.

Historically, loggerhead nesting in the Mediterranean has been concentrated in the warm sands of the sea’s eastern and central basins — primarily in Greece, Türkiye, and Cyprus — while the western basin has served mainly as a foraging ground by juvenile turtles. But over the past five decades, increasing numbers of nests have begun to appear in the western basin, including on the shores of Italy, France, and Spain.

In Calabria, Italy, signs of loggerhead nesting activity were first found in the early 2000s , gradually expanding northward all the way to the French coast and westward to Spain, according to researchers. In Spain, where the first confirmed nest was documented in 2001, regular annual nesting began in 2014.

“In the Western Mediterranean, we are observing an expansion of the population in real time,” Sandra Hochscheid, a researcher at the Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn in Naples, tells Mongabay. “For the first time in history, we are witnessing the new colonization [by this species] along this coast.”

What began as an occasional anomaly has evolved into a permanent geographical shift, Hochscheid says.

As loggerhead turtles’ range expands, their search for suitable nesting habitat collides with some of the most heavily developed coastlines in Europe. To protect and conserve loggerhead sea turtle populations in the Western Mediterranean, an international conservation initiative co-financed by the EU LIFE program — the European Union’s main funding instrument dedicated to environmental, nature conservation, and climate action policies — and coordinated by the Italian environmental NGO Legambiente , launched in 2023 the Life Turtlenest project , which includes partner organizations across Italy, Spain, and France.

Over the past few years, Hochscheid has been investigating why the turtles are expanding their nesting range. She does this by deploying satellite-linked transmitters on wild adult females immediately after they lay their eggs, to track their movements out at sea. She and her team have also attached trackers to captive-reared juveniles before releasing them to determine where this new population ends up during its early life stages, and the role ocean currents play in its dispersal.

Previous studies by her team suggest that loggerhead sea turtles moving in western Italy’s Tyrrhenian Sea remain close to marine areas where food is abundant, and the new data from the transmitters support this hypothesis.

“Competition with other turtles might be a factor [for migrating] if the historical feeding grounds become overcrowded,” says Hochscheid, who has studied sea turtle behavior for more than three decades. “But in reality, we still don’t know exactly why this has happened in the first place.”

At the University of Barcelona, marine researcher Carlos Carrera’s team is also investigating why the turtles are expanding their nesting range, using genomic data to trace the origins of turtles that have established new nests in the Western Mediterranean. By analyzing DNA from tissue samples collected from adults and hatchlings during post-hatching nest excavations in Spain and Italy, his team has found that they likely dispersed from established populations elsewhere in the Mediterranean and even farther afield. “These turtles are related to those in Greece, Turkey, and the Caribbean,” Carreras, also part of the Life Turtlenest project, tells Mongabay.

He says many nests along Spain’s Mediterranean coastline are laid dangerously close to the water, suggesting these turtles are younger and less experienced than those nesting in Italy. While the Italian population has had a few more years to establish itself — and now has more experienced mothers digging nests higher up on the beach — those in Spain are still in the earliest stage of colonization.

Carreras hypothesizes that rising sea temperatures due to global warming are accelerating juvenile growth in the foraging grounds of the Western Mediterranean, causing turtles to reach sexual maturity earlier when they’re thousands of kilometers away from their ancestral nesting grounds.

Irene Alvarez de Quevedo, a researcher at the BETA Tech Center in Barcelona, agrees with Carreras. “[Early maturation] turned out not to be a problem because now our beaches are warm enough for nesting,” Alvarez de Quevedo tells Mongabay.

Also, both genetic sequencing and GPS-tracking data suggest that pioneer mothers like their new homes and return to the same beaches time after time. Researchers say that as new turtles hatch and they too return to their natal beaches to lay the next generation, new nesting colonies will become permanently established.

However, not everyone has celebrated the loggerhead expansion. In Italy, nearly 27,000 private beach clubs, or lidi (plural of lido ), blanket roughly 43% of the peninsula’s beaches . In summer, when loggerhead turtles come ashore to nest, the Italian coast is a bustling playground of human activity. Beach clubs monopolize the sand with dense grids of sunbeds and umbrellas, with lights bright and music blaring into the early hours. Before dawn, in many places, tractors rake the sand beaches to clear debris, compacting the sediment and potentially even crushing shallow egg chambers.

When loggerhead sea turtles first began nesting in this region, commercial beach clubs often viewed conservation efforts with outright hostility, according to conservationists.

“At first, [lidi] gates were locked against us, and turtles’ tracks were erased, fearing that the presence of a nest could have negative impacts on their business,” Leda Tonizello, president of the Campania-based ELSA ETS environmental association, tells Mongabay.

Similar experiences have been reported in Calabria, where most of the conservation on the Tyrrhenian coastline is carried out under the direction of WWF Italy, as well as in Tuscany. “Lido operators would deliberately smooth over turtle tracks before morning patrols arrived,” says Francesca Capanni, an environmental scientist at the University of Siena.

However, due to the efforts of conservationists and civil society over the last few decades, there’s been a radical shift in how beach operators view the presence of nests, locals say.

“It’s the success of a coordinated work of many groups that, while generally having different overall goals, have all united for the sake of this charismatic animal,” Tonizello says.

Local business owners say these conservation efforts have even yielded commercial benefits. Pino Cappuccio, a lido owner in Ascea, a seaside resort town in Campania’s Cilento National Park, tells Mongabay that watching a turtle nesting or eggs hatching during dinner is an experience his guests won’t forget.

But hurdles to turtle survival remain. A study published July 2026 in the journal Mediterranean Marine Science by Hochscheid’s team found that 87% of nests in Campania were exposed to direct or indirect beachfront lighting in 2022 and 2023. Bright lights are problematic for sea turtles; they deter females from nesting and can confuse hatchlings, misdirecting them toward land instead of into the sea. The study’s authors write that because of these lights, 82% of the nests they surveyed needed active human intervention to prevent hatchling disorientation.

In response, some areas are instituting lighting regulations along beaches. The local municipality of Ascea, one of the nesting hotspots in Campania, collaborated with the Anton Dohrn institute to install turtle-friendly, low-intensity lighting along its seafront promenade. And starting in 2027, compliance with low-impact lighting standards will become mandatory for any business applying for a beach facility concession.

“In our changing world, environmental protection is also an economic strategy,” says Stefano Sansone, mayor of Ascea.

In late August in Castel Volturno, volunteers and researchers sit quietly, waiting with bated breath for the next generation of loggerheads to hatch. At last, after a few sleepless, disappointing nights, dozens of newborns begin to emerge from the sand. Then the work begins as the group takes measurements and collects other data for each tiny turtle, before releasing them into the sea.

As the Mediterranean continues to warm, scientists are rushing to identify which beaches pioneer turtles will choose next, and to establish protective measures before the animals arrive on crowded shores.

In Spain, Alvarez de Quevedo is also studying the thermal profile of the coastline, linking air and sea surface temperatures to ground conditions to assess which beaches are warming enough to support the development of loggerhead eggs. In doing so, she says she hopes to build predictive models to evaluate future beach suitability to inform management decisions.

In Italy, Capanni is analyzing the physical and chemical properties of sand collected during post-hatching nest excavations. She evaluates sand grain size distribution across all Tuscan beaches where nesting has occurred, as granulometry directly dictates gas exchange, moisture retention, and how easily female turtles can dig their egg chambers. She also tests sand and tissue samples for persistent organic pollutants to verify that prospective nesting sites are free of toxins.

“This is finalistic in trying to prioritize which beaches or environments are most important for the conservation of this species,” Capanni says. “If temperatures continue to rise, and previously suitable environments become less so, potential habitats narrow. It is critical to understand where they are and conserve them starting right now.”

items.summary: Latino voters are concerned about climate change – and among the most confident in their ability to create political change.

scraped.title: The midterms show that Latinos could be a powerhouse force on climate » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Latino voters are concerned about climate change – and among the most confident in their ability to create political change.
scraped.author: Pearl Marvell
scraped.h1: The midterms show that Latinos could be a powerhouse force on climate
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

As the dust settles after the midterm elections, one thing is glaringly obvious: Latinos are furious with Trump.

The New York Times estimates that Democrats won 69% of the Hispanic vote – a 29-point shift from 2024. That’s likely in response to the ICE raids that have deported and even killed loved ones and the rising costs of everyday living. But many Latinos also live in areas disproportionately affected by climate impacts like extreme heat and flooding – places known as frontline communities.

We can’t do this work without you! About 83% of every dollar you donate goes directly to paying our team of reporters, editors, meteorologists, and radio producers. The other 17% pays for this website, laptops, a payroll system, and similar expenses necessary for our work.

For insight on the midterms, Yale Climate Connections sat down with Jennifer Carman, director of survey strategy at the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication and lead author of a recent peer-reviewed study of climate attitudes in frontline communities . (YPCCC is the publisher of Yale Climate Connections.)

This interview has been edited and condensed.

Yale Climate Connections: How are you feeling about what we just witnessed?

Jennifer Carman: A lot of the places in America that have the frontline communities are also the most worried about climate change: Latinos and people in the Southwest and people in border areas. When you dig more deeply into those communities, you find that they experience a lot of swings in how they vote.

I consider them to be a group that’s very electorally up for grabs. But what we’re seeing is just how incredibly powerful and effective they can be as a voting bloc. We saw that in 2024 as well because they experienced some of the largest swings toward Trump in 2024, and that was the big story then.

What we see this year is that they’ve really snapped back. And in some places, especially if you look at the Texas border counties, some of those swings toward Democrats are even larger than the swings that happened in 2024.

My warning to the Democrats is that they shouldn’t consider this to be a permanent realignment, either. I think that depending on what Democrats do with the power that they have, that will be what makes or breaks whether they continue to have support from Latinos in the border areas in the next election cycle.

YCC: What do we know about what Latinos think about climate change?

Carman: Latinos care about climate change more than other racial and ethnic groups in the United States.

They are also affected by climate change in unique ways. Latino communities face a lot of climate impacts based on where they live; many Latinos work outdoors and work in hotter parts of the country. That’s why so many of our frontline communities are disproportionately Latino.

The important thing to keep in mind from my perspective is engaging frontline communities and engaging Latino communities, not just this election cycle but every election cycle. But I think that this cycle is a proof of concept that if this engagement happens, it is possible to win and to win in surprisingly large numbers – to swing even in states that Democrats didn’t think that they could win.

YCC: Do communicators of climate change need to do more to highlight that intersection between these topics and climate change?

Carman: I think that we need to have more conversations about climate change as a really practical issue, as something that affects people in their lives and affects the kinds of issues that we are already talking about: the fact that people are experiencing more harm from heat and higher bills. We know that if you’re experiencing higher temperatures, you have to run the air conditioner more often, and that’s expensive, or if you don’t have air conditioning, then you suffer. There are parts of the country that get extremely hot where people cannot afford air conditioning or cannot afford to run air conditioning.

YCC: Or don’t have the right to install one if they’re renting.

Carman: Yeah, exactly. There are studies that have found that apartments [without air conditioning] can get to be more than 100 degrees in the summer, and that has economic effects and health effects. A lot of these cost-of-living problems are exacerbated by climate change.

When it comes to talking about climate change, it is really important to talk about it not just as this sort of broad, esoteric issue that affects us all, but also as something that affects us personally. It also affects us all individually. For example, in my office today, it is 80 degrees in November.

There can be an aspect of talking about climate change that can be really intimidating. I think that’s part of why there’s this climate hushing that happens. It sounds so big, and you don’t want to have a conversation about giant systems and ocean currents and all of these various interconnected things. Climate change does have those effects, but it also has very personal and direct effects. And there are things that people can do about that. For example, voting.

Putting a name to what people are experiencing is really powerful. It’s getting hotter, and the fact that it’s getting so much hotter is dangerous. And the fact that there’s more flooding, that we’re getting these freak rainstorms in the Southwest and in Florida and wildfires in Hawaii and heat waves in Alaska – it’s really important to put a name to that, and we have a name for that. That name is climate change.

YCC: Where does climate hushing come from?

Carman: I think it comes from a bunch of things. One of them is which voices get amplified. The Dismissive [about climate change] demographic is about 11% [of the U.S. public] and Alarmed are about 25% of the population. So there are two and a half times as many Alarmed as there are Dismissive, but it always surprises people when you tell them that because the Dismissives are so loud and so highly platformed. There are whole news channels that primarily use the time and platform that they have for amplifying the voices of the Dismissive, like our president.

Read: Global warming’s six Americas

When those are the voices you hear, that’s what you think everybody thinks. It can also be intimidating to push back against.

Politicians have a lot more permission to talk about climate change than they think. Going into this next Congress, what I’m really hoping will happen is that members of Congress will be able to see that. A lot of policies to reduce the impacts of climate change and to protect people from climate impacts are really popular.

Ninety-two percent of registered voters support protecting workers from dangerous levels of heat, and it’s one of those policies that feels like a no-brainer. And yet Florida and Texas have banned heat protection laws.

Frontline communities are really central to coalition-building because they play an important role in not just connecting climate but all of these other issues. All these affordability things – frontline communities have been experiencing this for decades.

YCC: And Latinos are the demographic with the highest belief in their ability to collectively effect change at a government level.

Carman: I think that it’s important to recognize that frontline communities are not helpless. Because of the historical neglect, people have had to take a lot on themselves, but the potential for political action is really high.

There’s a lot that they’re already doing to protect themselves. There’s a lot of capacity-building and community power in frontline communities, and I think people within those communities know it. They can serve as powerful examples and powerful leadership and potential for political power. I think that is important for the climate movement and for politicians in general to keep in mind, especially as the new Congress goes forward.

items.summary: Ten years after the protest, Cody Two Bears reflects on how it led him to create energy alternatives for tribal communities.

scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: The Standing Rock protests launched one man’s renewable energy transformation
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

This year is the 10th anniversary of historic protests in North Dakota, when members of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe and thousands of supporters stood together to oppose the construction of an oil pipeline near tribal land.

Protesters argued that the Dakota Access pipeline would endanger water supplies, desecrate sacred sites, and increase reliance on fossil fuels.

The pipeline was built anyway. But for Cody Two Bears, who served on the Standing Rock Tribal Council at the time, the protests were still transformative.

Two Bears: “I’ve always seen on the news about how extraction affects communities around the world and … never really thought that would come to my backyard.”

The experience motivated him to learn more about the impacts of fossil fuels and to help tribes develop alternatives.

Two Bears: “I decided to get out of the leadership role from my tribe and start a nonprofit called Indigenized Energy.”

Indigenized Energy helped develop North Dakota’s largest solar farm right on the Standing Rock Reservation.

And it leads the Tribal Renewable Energy Coalition, a network of tribes working to install solar on tribal land.

So for Two Bears, the Standing Rock protests ignited a passion for clean energy that continues to drive him today.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

scraped.title: Oigan, políticos: está bien hablar sobre el cambio climático » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Los votantes latinos están preocupados por el cambio climático y se encuentran entre los más confiados en su capacidad para generar cambios políticos.
scraped.author: Pearl Marvell
scraped.h1: Oigan, políticos: está bien hablar sobre el cambio climático
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Mientras se asienta el polvo tras las elecciones de mitad de mandato, una cosa resulta evidente: los latinos están furiosos con Trump.

The New York Times estima que los demócratas obtuvieron el 69% del voto hispano, un cambio de 29 puntos respecto de 2024. Probablemente sea una respuesta a las redadas del ICE, que han deportado e incluso matado a seres queridos, y al aumento del costo de la vida cotidiana. Pero muchos latinos también viven en zonas afectadas de manera desproporcionada por impactos climáticos como el calor extremo y las inundaciones, lugares conocidos como comunidades de primera línea.

Para conocer mejor lo ocurrido en las elecciones de mitad de mandato, Yale Climate Connections conversó con Jennifer Carman, directora de estrategia de encuestas del Programa de Yale sobre Comunicación del Cambio Climático y autora principal de un reciente estudio revisado por pares sobre las actitudes frente al clima en comunidades de primera línea. (El YPCCC es la organización editora de Yale Climate Connections).

Esta entrevista ha sido editada y condensada.

Yale Climate Connections: ¿Cómo se siente ante lo que acabamos de presenciar?

Jennifer Carman: Muchos de los lugares de Estados Unidos donde están las comunidades de primera línea son también los más preocupados por el cambio climático : los latinos, las personas del suroeste y quienes viven en las zonas fronterizas. Cuando se profundiza en esas comunidades, se observa que experimentan muchos cambios en su forma de votar.

Valoramos mucho tus perspectivas, por lo tanto, queremos que nos mandes tus preguntas sobre el cambio climático y sus efectos.

Las considero un grupo electoralmente muy disputado. Pero lo que estamos viendo es cuán increíblemente poderosas y eficaces pueden ser como bloque electoral. También lo vimos en 2024, porque experimentaron algunos de los mayores giros hacia Trump en 2024, y esa fue entonces la gran historia.

Lo que vemos este año es que realmente han dado marcha atrás. Y en algunos lugares, especialmente si se observan los condados fronterizos de Texas, algunos de esos giros hacia los demócratas son incluso mayores que los que ocurrieron en 2024.

Mi advertencia para los demócratas es que tampoco deberían considerar esto como un realineamiento permanente. Creo que, según lo que hagan los demócratas con el poder que tienen, se definirá si continúan contando con el apoyo de los latinos en las zonas fronterizas durante el próximo ciclo electoral.

YCC: ¿Qué sabemos sobre lo que piensan los latinos acerca del cambio climático?

Carman: A los latinos les preocupa más el cambio climático que a otros grupos raciales y étnicos de Estados Unidos.

También el cambio climático les afecta de maneras particulares. Las comunidades latinas enfrentan muchos impactos climáticos según el lugar donde viven; muchos latinos trabajan al aire libre y en las regiones más calurosas del país. Por eso tantas de nuestras comunidades de primera línea son desproporcionadamente latinas.

¡No podemos hacer este trabajo sin ti! Aproximadamente el 83 % de cada dólar que donas se destina directamente a pagar a nuestro equipo de reporteros, editores, meteorólogos y productores de radio. El otro 17 % cubre este sitio web, computadoras portátiles, un sistema de nómina y otros gastos similares necesarios para nuestro trabajo.

Desde mi perspectiva, lo importante que hay que tener presente es involucrar a las comunidades de primera línea y a las comunidades latinas, no solo en este ciclo electoral, sino en todos los ciclos electorales. Pero creo que este ciclo demuestra que, si se produce esa participación, es posible ganar, y ganar por márgenes sorprendentemente grandes; incluso lograr cambios en estados que los demócratas no creían que podían ganar.

YCC: ¿Necesitan los comunicadores sobre cambio climático hacer más para destacar la intersección entre estos temas y el cambio climático?

Carman: Creo que necesitamos tener más conversaciones sobre el cambio climático como un tema muy práctico, como algo que afecta la vida de las personas y que incide en los asuntos de los que ya estamos hablando: el hecho de que la gente está sufriendo más daños por el calor y facturas más altas. Sabemos que, si se experimentan temperaturas más altas, hay que usar el aire acondicionado con más frecuencia, y eso es costoso; o, si no se tiene aire acondicionado, se sufre. Hay partes del país donde hace un calor extremo y las personas no pueden permitirse tener aire acondicionado o no pueden permitirse usarlo.

YCC: O no tienen derecho a instalarlo si alquilan la vivienda.

El clima está cambiando y nuestros periodistas están aquí para ayudarte a comprender lo que está pasando. ¡Suscríbete a nuestro boletín informativo y nunca te pierdas una historia!

Carman: Sí, exactamente. Hay estudios que han concluido que los apartamentos [sin aire acondicionado] pueden superar los 100 grados Fahrenheit en verano, y eso tiene efectos económicos y sobre la salud. Muchos de estos problemas relacionados con el costo de la vida se ven agravados por el cambio climático.

Cuando se trata de hablar sobre el cambio climático, es realmente importante hacerlo no solo como un problema amplio y abstracto que nos afecta a todos, sino también como algo que nos afecta personalmente. También nos afecta individualmente a todos. Por ejemplo, hoy en mi oficina hacen 80 grados Fahrenheit en noviembre.

Hablar sobre el cambio climático puede ser realmente intimidante. Creo que esa es parte de la razón por la que ocurre este silenciamiento climático. Suena como algo enorme, y uno no quiere tener una conversación sobre sistemas gigantescos, corrientes oceánicas y todas estas diversas cosas interconectadas. El cambio climático sí tiene esos efectos, pero también tiene consecuencias muy personales y directas. Y hay cosas que la gente puede hacer al respecto. Por ejemplo, votar.

Ponerle un nombre a lo que las personas están experimentando es muy poderoso. Está haciendo más calor, y el hecho de que haga mucho más calor es peligroso. Y el hecho de que haya más inundaciones, de que estemos teniendo estas lluvias torrenciales inusuales en el suroeste y en Florida, incendios forestales en Hawái y olas de calor en Alaska: es realmente importante ponerle un nombre a eso, y tenemos un nombre para ello. Ese nombre es cambio climático.

YCC: ¿De dónde proviene el silenciamiento climático?

Carman: Creo que proviene de varias cosas. Una de ellas es qué voces se amplifican. El grupo de los Desestimadores [del cambio climático] representa alrededor del 11% [del público estadounidense], mientras que los Alarmados constituyen aproximadamente el 25% de la población. Es decir, hay dos veces y media más Alarmados que Desestimadores, pero siempre sorprende a la gente cuando se le dice eso, porque los Desestimadores son muy ruidosos y reciben mucha exposición en las plataformas. Hay canales de noticias enteros que usan principalmente el tiempo y el espacio de que disponen para amplificar las voces de los Desestimadores, como nuestro presidente.

Leer: Las Seis Américas del calentamiento global

Cuando esas son las voces que se escuchan, eso es lo que uno cree que piensa todo el mundo. También puede resultar intimidante cuestionarlas.

Sigue nuestro canal de WhatsApp y suscríbete a nuestro canal de Youtube .

Los políticos tienen mucho más permiso para hablar del cambio climático de lo que creen. Al entrar en este próximo Congreso, lo que realmente espero que ocurra es que los miembros del Congreso puedan verlo. Muchas políticas destinadas a reducir los impactos del cambio climático y a proteger a las personas de sus efectos son muy populares.

El noventa y dos por ciento de los votantes registrados apoya proteger a los trabajadores de niveles peligrosos de calor, y es una de esas políticas que parecen de sentido común. Sin embargo, Florida y Texas han prohibido las leyes de protección contra el calor.

Las comunidades de primera línea son fundamentales para construir coaliciones porque desempeñan un papel importante no solo al conectar el clima con estos otros temas, sino también con todos ellos. Todas estas cuestiones de asequibilidad: las comunidades de primera línea las han estado experimentando durante décadas.

YCC: Y los latinos son el grupo demográfico que más cree en su capacidad de generar cambios colectivos a nivel gubernamental.

Carman: Creo que es importante reconocer que las comunidades de primera línea no están indefensas. Debido al abandono histórico, las personas han tenido que asumir muchas responsabilidades por sí mismas, pero el potencial de acción política es realmente alto.

Ya están haciendo mucho para protegerse. Hay mucho desarrollo de capacidades y poder comunitario en las comunidades de primera línea, y creo que las personas dentro de esas comunidades lo saben. Pueden servir como ejemplos poderosos, ejercer un liderazgo sólido y representar un gran potencial de poder político. Creo que es importante que el movimiento climático y los políticos en general tengan esto presente, especialmente a medida que avance el nuevo Congreso.

scraped.title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
scraped.author: Cecilia Keating
scraped.h1: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
scraped.body_text:
The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.

That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “ state of the climate ” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets. Dr Zeke Hausfather , Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ ask me anything ” session.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.

The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

Writing on CB Connect on 5 November, Hausfather wrote:

“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”

This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.

On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.

Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.

Membership

Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.

Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.

While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events .

The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.

Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.

This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.

scraped.title: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
scraped.author: Lauri Myllyvirta
scraped.h1: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid
scraped.body_text:
China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.

Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.

The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.

The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.

The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “ flat or falling ” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.

The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown .

Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “ wasted ” wind and solar fell.

Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.

The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates . This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.

Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.

The amount of electricity used by EVs grew by 53%, much faster than the number of EVs on the road, showing increased usage of the existing fleet in preference to fuelled vehicles.

Elsewhere, growth in the coal-to-chemical industry continued to slow down in the third quarter of 2026. The sector has been a key source of emissions growth, but high coal prices have weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand .

Finally, CO2 emissions from cement and steel production continued to fall in the third quarter, as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated .

Energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has been robust .

This makes it likely that the growth in clean-power generation will exceed total energy demand growth this year, maintaining the structural fall in fossil-fuel use.

Looking ahead, this balance also relies on progress in removing barriers to new solar and wind power being added to the grid, which result in some clean electricity being “ wasted ”.

The recent slowdown in energy demand growth is partly – but not fully – explained by exceptionally mild weather in the third quarter.

Another key factor is weaker GDP growth . Since reported GDP growth remains within target , however, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus policies.

The focus of the economic stimulus announced to date is “six networks”, which includes the power grid and the transportation network.

These networks are highly relevant for energy and emissions – and they are already covered by policies that emphasise “ green ” and zero-carbon solutions.

scraped.title: Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.
scraped.author: Carbon Brief Staff
scraped.h1: Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit
scraped.body_text:
The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.

These texts are hashed out behind closed doors in the “ blue zone ” at the COP, where diplomats from nearly 200 nations – not including the US – will be haggling over each individual verb .

Over the course of the two-week summit, negotiators will be trying to reach consensus on more than 100 separate agreements – but, first, they must agree which issues are on the agenda.

The complexity of this process can make it challenging to keep track of what countries are fighting about and how negotiations are progressing.

Carbon Brief’s real-time text tracker, below, offers a helping hand by decoding the agenda and keeping a searchable record of every document for each part of the negotiations.

The first column of the interactive tracker lists the topic of each agenda item, with further columns including dates, page counts and links to the original PDFs.

The table is searchable via the interactive text box and can be sorted using the arrow icons.

This year’s talks come with a twist: Turkey holds the presidency and is hosting COP31, but Australia is jointly running the show as “ president of negotiations ”.

The pair have already announced their intention to produce a “cover text” – an overarching political document summarising key negotiated outcomes, along with issues not on the official agenda.

This could include a recognition that warming is set to “ overshoot ” the 1.5C limit and the impacts this is already causing . It may also include potential solutions, such as the Turkish presidency’s “ electrification ” target, for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035.

While the summit is not seen as a banner year for the negotiations, falling half-way between two “ global stocktakes ” of progress, there are still plenty of major topics up for discussion.

These include efforts to finalise the “ global goal on adaptation ” and whether to continue a contested process on how to cut emissions, known as the “ mitigation work programme ”.

Negotiators will also be trying to agree on the details of a new “ just transition mechanism ”, also referred to as the “Belém-Antalya mechanism for global just transitions” (BAM).

While most of the items on the agenda are agreed in advance, parties can suggest late additions. These must be signed off before negotiations can begin, often resulting in an “ agenda fight ”.

COP30 agreed to put two new items on the agenda for future summits.

These are the provision of climate finance by developed countries, under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement , and making global “ finance flows ” consistent with the treaty, under Article 2.1c .

Ahead of COP31, the African group of nations filed a request to add climate-related trade tariffs to the agenda. COP30 had agreed to annual “ dialogues ” on this matter at the Bonn climate talks .

The African group also wants further items added, on tripling adaptation finance and on funding for the Green Climate Fund , a flagship UN body designed to support climate action.

Ahead of the opening of the summit, Carbon Brief’s text tracker counts 104 substantive items on the agenda, not including procedural matters, such as the election of COP officials.

The figure below illustrates the status of the COP31 negotiations overall, in a traffic-light format. Each agenda item is colour-coded according to its current status.

For topics shown in red, negotiators have not yet managed to put anything down on paper, perhaps because parties have fundamentally different views on how they should proceed.

For items in orange, negotiators are working on an “informal text”, which is an early draft setting out the views of different parties, but not yet expressed in formal legal language.

Once a draft legal agreement becomes available, topics will be colour-coded yellow. At this point, areas of remaining disagreement will be denoted in the text with [square brackets] and “options”.

As such, texts with many square brackets or options tend to be an indicator of a high level of disagreement between parties. For this reason, the tracker table above counts and displays the number of outstanding brackets and options in each document.

During the course of the summit, negotiators may work through many iterations of texts on each agenda item. These documents may include “bridging text”, designed to resolve differences of opinion and to find a “landing zone” that all groups can agree on.

Agreement is reached on a given topic once all brackets and options have been resolved, at which point the item will be coloured green in Carbon Brief’s traffic-light chart.

Where agreement cannot be reached, discussions may be subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning negotiations are postponed until the next session. These topics are colour-coded grey.

The figure below gives an at-a-glance overview of the status of the main topics up for negotiation.

As parties narrow down the options and brackets towards the end of each summit, they start to generate “clean” texts, which contain no areas of disagreement and can be converted into “draft decisions” that are ready for formal adoption at the closing plenary of the meeting.

Finally, at the closing plenary, each draft decision must be gavelled through by the COP president, signifying its formal adoption as a legal agreement and outcome of the summit.

This last step is usually a formality, but dramatic exceptions are possible.

During the closing plenary at COP29 , the president of the meeting failed to adopt a deal relating to the “ global stocktake ” from 2023, which had called for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.

Carbon Brief also ran text trackers for COP28 , COP29 and COP30 .

Words by Simon Evans. Tracker maintained by Ho Woo Nam.

scraped.description: Democrats who campaigned on reining in data center development swept congressional and governor’s races, and voters OK’d dozens of anti–data center ballot…
scraped.h1: Voters gave a big middle finger to data centers
scraped.body_text:

Next Upcoming

By Canary Media

Canary Media

6 November 2026

This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

Americans aren’t happy about the data center boom, and they made their displeasure pretty clear this Election Day. Voters not only selected a slate of Democratic candidates who campaigned against data centers; they also approved more than 30 ballot measures aimed at reining in the power-hungry facilities.

You could argue that the ​ “ data center elections” really started a year ago, when Virginians selected Democrat Abigail Spanberger as their next governor. Virginia has more than earned its status as the data center capital of the world, with the latest estimates counting more than 700 facilities around the state, and Spanberger ran on a promise to keep their intense power demand in check.

In the months that followed, it became clear that data center developers were circling in on Great Lakes states and their abundant water resources — and that fighting the facilities was a winning campaign strategy. Take Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who made data center regulation a prominent piece of his candidacy, and William Lawrence , a Democrat who won his U.S. House race after showing up at a local council meeting to fight a proposed data center.

Meanwhile in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, a three-term Democratic senator who was ousted in 2024 , will return to the chamber. Brown’s campaign painted his Republican opponent as ​ “ the face of data centers,” even though it cost Brown the support of some union labor allies who’ve backed him for decades but see data centers as creators of construction jobs.

Data centers’ threat is even more palpable in Georgia and Texas, which have more projects in the pipeline than any other state except Virginia. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was easily reelected after criticizing data centers as part of his campaign and investigating their impact on power bills in the Senate. Georgia’s Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has meanwhile pledged a ​ “ pause” on new data center construction once she takes office in January. And Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored historic wins in Texas for U.S. Senate and governor, respectively, after promising to pursue a slate of data center regulations.

Anti–data center sentiment this election cycle was so strong that even some Republicans promised restrictions — Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers called for a one-year moratorium in the state, for example. But some still sided with data centers, like Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who benefited from an industry-funded ad campaign before losing a seat she had been expected to retain.

And when the data center debate showed up in ballot measures across dozens of counties and municipalities, voters gave a resounding response : Rein them in.

How energy prices showed up on the ballot

Data centers weren’t the only energy issue motivating voters this week. With gasoline prices at their highest level of any Election Day in U.S. history, and falling temperatures getting Americans thinking about heating bills, it’s no wonder that voters were looking for a change.

While President Donald Trump has been promising to curb energy costs since his 2024 campaign, his decisions have driven prices in the opposite direction. Experts say that perhaps his most drastic mistake was starting a war with Iran, spiking oil prices that have yet to return to anything resembling the pre-conflict normal. That impact has been especially obvious in Maine, where half the residents rely on heating oil — and where voters ousted longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins on Tuesday.

Utility bills were literally on the ballot in nine states this week, as voters selected new members to regulatory boards that oversee utility rate hikes and other energy-related decisions. While most of the states preserved the status quo and elected Republicans, Georgia voters gave Democrats the majority on their Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years.

What do Democrats’ wins mean for permitting?

As the U.S. Senate prepares for its drastically new makeup come January, it’s also got a major vote to tackle in the next few days. The chamber is planning to vote Nov. 9 on long-awaited energy permitting reform legislation — that is, if newly emboldened Democrats don’t try to reshape the bill.

While the package was crafted by two Democrats and two Republicans, some Congress members on the left have demanded edits to minimize its benefits for fossil fuels and prioritize clean energy development. They’ve renewed that call in the blue wave’s wake, with Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to chair the House Natural Resources Committee in a Democrat-led Congress, saying that voters showed ​ “ they don’t want this dirty, fossil-fuel-expanding bill.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D) also called for revisions to the bill to protect tribal sovereignty and blunt impacts to the National Environmental Policy Act.

Bill co-sponsor Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) contended that the election results revealed the opposite: Americans are focused on ​ “ affordability,” he wrote on X, and achieving that requires building more clean energy projects by passing the permitting bill.

More election results: Democrats are poised to take full control of six more state governments, giving them leverage to enact more ambitious clean-energy policies. Voters also approved a handful of clean energy–boosting ballot measures, and rejected some that would prop up fossil fuels and weaken environmental regulations. ( Canary Media , Canary Media )

Thankful for solar: Two cranberry bogs in Massachusetts are marking their second harvest of fruit grown in the shadow of solar panels — and just may be the only cranberry bogs in the world paired with solar. ( Canary Media )

A real Revolution: Danish developer Ørsted says its Revolution Wind farm off the Connecticut and Rhode Island coasts is fully operating, a major win as the Trump administration tries yet another tactic to shut down the project. ( Canary Media )

Data center solutions? Two new reports make the case for how batteries and virtual power plants can address some of data centers’ biggest challenges to the grid and customers’ utility bills. ( Canary Media , Canary Media )

Sunny side up: The U.S. has built a strong solar panel and cell supply chain, but is still lacking in polysilicon and wafer manufacturing capacity. ( Canary Media )

Next Upcoming

By Canary Media

Canary Media

6 November 2026

See more from Canary Media’s ​ “ Chart of the Week” column .

Now that solar has become America’s go-to choice for new power plants , the pressure is on to assemble a fully domestic supply chain for the technology. Data from the latest Clean Investment Monitor shows that this onshoring process is well underway.

Factories in the U.S. can produce more than enough finished solar panels — also known as modules — to supply the nation’s annual installations, which last year hit 47 . 9 gigawatts (measured in direct current capacity). Module production could grow by about 83 % if all the projects that have been announced or are going through construction and commissioning come to fruition. The expansion represents a major change of fortune for domestic solar manufacturing, which had nearly disappeared, but has blossomed in recent years thanks to federal incentives and stiffer tariffs against foreign products.

Still, the panel is just the final step in the solar supply chain. To truly onshore this critical industry, the U.S. also needs to make the components that go into the module: photovoltaic cells, which are etched onto silicon wafers, which are made from processed polysilicon.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

This signup form requires necessary cookies.

Allow marketing cookies to load the newsletter signup form.

So far, cells have shown the most success among those precursors. Domestic factories can make up to 19 . 5 GW annually, after several factory openings this year. If projects currently wrapping up construction all come online, the country will be able to make enough solar cells to match 2025 deployments.

The more capital-intensive polysilicon and wafer production, however, is not on track to match the levels for cells or modules.

Crucially, it’s not guaranteed that solar developers will maintain 2025 levels of installations in the years to come, once lucrative federal tax credits run out. The Rhodium Group modeled a range of scenarios for the post- 2030 era, and found that the U.S. could install an annual average of anywhere between 8 and 52 GW of direct current solar capacity. That’s an enormous range: If the solar market tanks, the manufacturing sector could be self-sufficient, but if installations rebound, the country will need more polysilicon and wafer production to keep pace.

Ultimately, building out these factories is just the first step toward full self-sufficiency. Next, solar manufacturers need to prove that they can operate sustainably in the U.S. over the long haul.

scraped.title: Democrats' state wins open the door for major clean energy progress
scraped.description: Victories in governor races and statehouses mean Democrats in many states could now push utilities and data centers to adopt cleaner energy and curb costs.
scraped.h1: Democrats’ state wins open the door for major clean energy progress
scraped.body_text:
This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

Allow marketing cookies to load the newsletter signup form.

Next Upcoming

By Canary Media

Canary Media

5 November 2026

Democrats’ historic wins in Tuesday’s midterm elections will give them control of Congress and a chance to combat the Trump administration’s anti-climate agenda, but the president’s veto power will limit their options.

At the state level, however, Democrats’ victories offer immediate opportunities to advance clean energy as well as energy affordability.

Democrats flipped governor’s seats in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas — and likely Alaska. They won control of both houses of state legislatures in five states where they did not previously have it — Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin — and their chances are looking good in Arizona as well. Come January, Democrats will have trifectas — hold the governor’s office and both houses of the legislature — in 21 or more states, up from 16 , adding at least Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

States hold significant power over key facets of energy policy, including what kinds of power plants utilities can build or must shut down, how energy-efficient buildings must be, and how much pollution industries can emit.

“ Almost every policy you can think of to decarbonize our economy, except maybe border adjustment taxes, can be done at a state level,” Jay Inslee, former governor of Washington state, said at a Wednesday press conference. His state has instituted some of the country’s most aggressive climate policies , including a carbon cap-and-invest regime, a 100 % clean electricity standard, incentives for electric vehicles and EV chargers, and ​ “ the nation’s leading building code standards,” he said — all of which ​ “ could not be stopped by Donald Trump.”

Washington is one of about two dozen states with some form of policy calling for electricity to be 100 % renewable, carbon-free, or carbon-neutral in the coming years. Almost all these policies were enacted because Democrats held sufficient political power to overcome Republican opposition.

When Democrats are in power at the state level, ​ “ we don’t even have to wait for Congress,” Inslee said.

BloombergNEF highlighted this dynamic in a postelection memo, noting that newly empowered Democratic trifectas ​ “ should lead to policies boosting clean-tech sectors like renewables, energy storage, heat pumps and EVs.” Democratic state governments could also push through policies requiring data centers to use clean energy and curb costs for residents in Michigan , Minnesota , Pennsylvania , and Wisconsin , and measures that would boost solar and battery development in Arizona and Nevada .

Some states that have already passed clean energy mandates are eyeing opportunities to go further. In Michigan, Democratic leaders are considering new climate and energy measures after fighting back efforts from House Republicans earlier this year to repeal the state’s 2040 target for 100 % clean energy .

In Minnesota, two years of partisan deadlock in the state House held back efforts to expand virtual power plants and legalize plug-in solar , according to advocates promoting those policies. Now, bills will have a better chance to move forward.

Trish Demeter, managing director at clean energy trade group Advanced Energy United, highlighted other opportunities in a Thursday press conference, including in states where anger over data centers and rising utility bills has galvanized voters.

She pointed to Pennsylvania, where clean energy boosters are pushing a reform package meant to streamline the state’s ​ “ complicated and burdensome siting and permitting regime for building new large-scale wind, solar, and batteries.” Similar reforms have been gaining traction in other states that are struggling to build clean energy to meet growing demand for power, although those efforts face pushback from local communities.

Pennsylvania environmental groups are also tracking a dozen environmental or clean energy bills that have been blocked by Republicans in the state Senate. Among them are a legislative package backed by Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro that aims to impose pollution, clean-energy, and affordability requirements on data centers, and another that would expand access to distributed solar and other energy resources.

This signup form requires necessary cookies.

Allow marketing cookies to load the newsletter signup form.

In Wisconsin, where Democrats have regained their first trifecta in 16 years , climate advocates are pushing for policies that will constrain utility spending on fossil-fueled power plants to serve data centers and promote solar, wind, and batteries instead. To this end, Advanced Energy United is lobbying Wisconsin Democrats to impose more-stringent utility planning regimes .

The breaking of Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas could also ​ “ constrain those states’ support for fossil fuels and restrictions on clean power,” BloombergNEF wrote. Republicans in the Texas legislature have pushed a variety of pro–fossil fuel and anti–clean energy policies in recent years, though sometimes unsuccessfully .

And in Georgia, Democratic candidates for the state’s Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, won a 3 – 2 majority after two decades of Republican control. That could position the PSC to work with Democratic Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms to push utility Georgia Power to expand consumer access to rooftop solar and energy efficiency and to prioritize clean energy and batteries instead of fossil gas–fired power plants to serve uncertain data center demand.

Governors and state lawmakers are most directly responsible for dealing with public outrage over high and rising electricity costs.

Last year, Democrats won governorships in New Jersey and Virginia in large part by committing to lowering utility bills, which they’ve sought to carry out in conjunction with aggressive climate programs. This year’s Democratic gubernatorial victors — including Bottoms of Georgia , Amy Acton of Ohio , and Gina Hinojosa of Texas — ran on promises to promote clean energy, bring down utility bills, and curb unchecked growth of power-hungry data centers.

These issues have risen to the top of voters’ concerns, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet , a group that supports state and local pro-climate candidates. Of the 120 candidates her group backed this year, 86 had won election, nine had lost, and 24 were too close to call as of Wednesday morning.

“ This was the affordability election,” she said during a press briefing her organization held. ​ “ Talking to voters across the country, utility bills, electricity prices, gas prices, affordability came up over and over and over.”

She added, ​ “ The good news is that climate solutions and clean energy solutions and affordability are the same.” Solar, wind, and batteries are cheaper and can be built faster than gas-fired power plants, and have made up more than 90 % of new additions to the grid in the past several years.

The Trump administration has put its thumb on the scale for fossil fuels, weakening pollution restrictions on coal plants , forcing aging power plants to stay running , and directing massive investments to support new gas power plants, pipelines, and export terminals . But states regulate utilities that deliver electricity and gas to customers, and hold varying degrees of power to direct the mix of fossil-fueled and carbon-free resources those utilities rely on.

State regulators ​ “ have a lot more control over the incentives to bring cheaper, cleaner sources on the grid than we do at the federal level,” U.S. Rep. Sean Casten, an Illinois Democrat and outspoken climate champion, said at a press conference on Wednesday. ​ “ They’re the ones who set the interconnection rules. They’re in many cases the ones who are directly facilitating with the ISOs and RTOs,” the entities that oversee wholesale energy markets and regional grid operations for about two-thirds of the country. ​ “ They’re the ones who are making sure that you can actually monetize the value you create.”

Most of the country’s utilities have been backsliding on their carbon-cutting commitments over the past two years, primarily by delaying the closure of coal plants and dramatically expanding plans to build new gas-fired power plants. That shift in utility priorities has been largely driven by the seemingly insatiable demand for electricity from AI data centers.

But opposition to data centers was a decisive factor in races up and down the ballot.

“ Basically every sitting Dem governor or governor-elect embraced clean energy as a key guardrail against data center pollution,” Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power , a clean energy and climate advocacy group, said at a press event. She cited examples from the platforms of Nevada Governor-elect Aaron Ford and Wisconsin Governor-elect David Crowley, as well as Acton, Bottoms, and Hinojosa.

“ This is an issue that really defined affordability for folks, and governors, senators, House elect members, all saw it as a huge opportunity,” she said.

scraped.title: Voters Have Spoken: No Dirty Data Centers
scraped.description: Politicians will be ignoring this key midterm message if they vote for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
scraped.author: Abigail Dillen
scraped.h1: Voters Have Spoken: No Dirty Data Centers
scraped.body_text:
Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Our Stories

Politicians will be ignoring this key midterm message if they vote for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

By Abigail Dillen

No issue has activated more Americans in this historic election than opposition to the current data center build-out. And the current Congress faces an immediate test next week on whether they got the message.

Voters in at least 38 jurisdictions and counting passed data center bans or restrictions , and exit polling shows that a majority of midterm voters considered artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers to be a major factor in their vote . Data centers were at the center of countless races, including high-profile races like the Texas governorship and the Ohio Senate seat .

This historic election showed that voters are deeply skeptical about the way that data centers are getting built now and how the process is representative of what is not working for people in our country. Secret deals and corporate tricks. Sky-rocketing electricity bills. Air pollution and failures to protect water. Intolerable noise. The sheer scale of industrialization and loss of place. Not least of all: the raw power of the wealthiest companies in the world to speed past anything and anyone in their way.

Going into the election, voters overwhelming wanted more guardrails on data center development . A plurality wanted stronger regulations (39%), and another 25% wanted a moratorium on new data centers in their community; 22% even wanted a permanent ban. Large support for regulations and moratorium was consistent across those who self-identify as Democrats, Independents, and non-MAGA Republicans.

The data center backlash fueled the midterm election results. But before all the new members are sworn in, the old Congress is set to finish up some last-minute business.

A few days from now, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). Without major amendments that appear to be out of reach, a vote for this bill would ignore the message that voters around the county have just sent to Washington, D.C.

BAAJA is being promoted by its most vocal proponents as a bill to build new transmission lines to unleash clean energy, and that is critically important. We need to expand the grid and put it to much more effective use by addressing real transmission and interconnection bottlenecks.

But BAAJA is not only or even mostly a transmission bill. It is a sweeping overhaul of federal law . One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out. The speed-to-power rush for AI has become a rush to gas, and the industry is desperate to meet rising demand and lock in more gas consumption.

With its extremely targeted provisions for gas pipelines, BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers. Here’s the package: gutting federal environmental review , including an outright exclusion for pipeline expansions, rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act, blocking interference from States and Tribes , and prohibiting courts from issuing injunctions and other meaningful remedies. What this combination gives to the gas industry is an ultra fast-track for new and expanded gas pipelines that is insulated from court challenges and the kind of public opposition to data centers that is now expanding to associated pipeline projects.

Why does the fast-track matter so much? Some of the industry’s biggest players are poised to bring gas from hubs like the Marcellus Shale and the Permian Basin to fuel bigger and bigger data center complexes with gas. In a recent report with the Better Data Center Project , we identified 177 GW of planned gas capacity to power data centers on site or “behind the meter.” The scale of total and individual proposals is massive. As of August 2026, we identified nine proposed gas projects that are 4.5 GW or larger. If all are built, nine of the top 10 largest power plants in the U.S. would be data center gas projects.

From the perspective of AI hyperscalers, piping in gas for on-site power is the fastest, cheapest path to lock in power on a timeline and on terms that are most in their control. The only risk they have now is reliable gas capacity. BAAJA’s pipeline package would solve that problem for them immediately, sealing many deals that would enable the dirtiest version of the data center build-out to move even faster, while the transmission provisions that could enable more clean energy will take years.

With Tuesday’s election results, voters are clearly asking elected leaders to stop the build-out of dirty data centers. And, maybe more than anything else, people are demanding that government work for them. Instead, this bill gives more certainty to the most powerful AI and oil and gas companies, while dramatically weakening environmental protections and giving President Trump even greater license to drive his dangerous agenda and do damage that a future president will be unable to repair .

Data centers were on the ballot on Tuesday, and they lost. Across the country, voters came out to stop a “speed at all costs” build-out that is hurting communities and increasing costs and pollution. Voters overwhelmingly approved data center restrictions, and elected leaders who ran on ensuring safeguards and accountability for data center development. Super-charging gas-fired mega-data center projects is the opposite of that. Now is the time to make AI developers do better.

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“Earthjustice stands ready to defend the Antiquities Act and the national monuments protected under the law.”

Stay informed on how we hold accountable those who break our environmental laws.
